11800-u-s-copyright-renewals-1950-1977:
Compiled by the Library of Congress Copyright Office, this massive volume gathers all fifty-six half-yearly renewal catalogs from 1950 through 1977 into a single alphabetical sequence. Each of the original issues keeps its own heading, with page-markup retained, so the compilation reads as a continuous record across nearly three decades.

Entries cover literature, art, and film, excluding musical compositions. They give original and renewal registrations for each work. At over three million words it functions less as reading matter than as a reference tool. It lets researchers trace the copyright history of twentieth-century books, plays, and periodical contributions in one place.
14496-charles-the-bold-last-duke-of-burg:
Ruth Putnam's 1908 biography follows Charles the Bold, the last Valois duke of Burgundy, from childhood at the Burgundian court to his death in battle in 1477. Putnam had already written on William the Silent.

Chapters trace the Feast of the Pheasant, wars with France and Liège, his marriage, the meeting at Péronne, and the Swiss campaigns that broke his power. Putnam judges Charles harshly for trusting deputies, neglecting finance, and indulging his pleasures, while admiring his daring. The book is a solid early twentieth-century life, rich in chronicle detail.
15373-st-nicholas-vol-5-no-2-december-18:
This December 1877 number of St. Nicholas, a magazine for children, opens with Longfellow's Three Kings, riding from far away with a beautiful star as guide. Melchior, Gaspar, and Baltazar travel by night and sleep by day, bearing three golden caskets with golden keys. The poem sets a Christmas tone.

Other stories, verses, and pictures fill the issue in Scribner's handsome style for young readers. The magazine aimed to mix wonder, learning, and good fun without talking down. Families and historians of children's print will find the number a charming Christmas sample.
24416-life-and-work-in-benares-and-kumao:
James Kennedy, London Missionary Society missionary and author of Christianity and the Religions of India, wrote this life and work in Benares and Kumaon, 1839 to 1877. Sir William Muir, lieutenant-governor of the North Western Provinces of India, wrote an introductory note. Cassell and Company of New York published it in 1885, with pictures of the Union Church at Ranee Khet. Kennedy tells how a relative advised him to write his Indian reminiscences.

His health restored, after a life of more work than he could accomplish, he thought he had not enough to do. The counsel struck him as good. His theme lacks novelty, since he cannot tell of a new country explored or a new people brought to knowledge, but it has greatness. No book on Indian missions, he thinks, was written in vain, and here and there a reader gains a clearer view. Readers get a missionary's India, 1839 to 1877.
24741-the-campaign-of-trenton-1776-77:
Samuel Adams Drake wrote this history of the campaign of Trenton, 1776-77, published at Boston in 1895 as part of his Decisive Events in American History. Its contents open with a prelude, then New York as the seat of war, plans for attack, and the march to Trenton.

Drake follows Washington's crossing of the Delaware, the surprise at Trenton, and the Princeton campaign that followed, with maps and detail. His history is clear, spirited, and aimed at general readers. Students of the Revolution will find it a compact, reliable account of the campaign that saved the American cause.
25302-jack-1877:
Alphonse Daudet's Jack, translated by Mary Neal Sherwood and published in 1877, follows a boy whose godfather was an English major-general. Lord Pembroke was killed in a tiger chase at Singapore. Jack's story moves from Vaugirard and a school on the Avenue Montaigne through a troubled youth in Paris.

Figures around him include Ida and the poet d'Argenton, whose ham, wine, and mustard are sacred. Cécile's unhappy resolve shadows the later chapters. Jack works in an engine room at Indret and ends in a hospital, in a novel that made Daudet famous for tender, unsparing pictures of young lives gone wrong.
25725-that-lass-o-lowrie-s-1877:
Frances Hodgson Burnett writes That Lass o' Lowrie's, published by Scribner's Sons in 1877. It opens at a coal pit mouth with a dozen pit girls. Strangers might mistake them for men. Their dress was more than half masculine. They talked loudly and laughed discordantly. Some had faces as hard as their collier brothers, husbands, and sweethearts.

Pit girls worked early and late at the mouth since old enough for heavy labour, losing bloom of womanly modesty and gentleness, as mothers and grandmothers had before them. Burnett follows one lass through pit life, love, and hardship, finding spirit and tenderness beneath a rough surface in a Lancashire mining tale.
25766-the-immortal-or-one-of-the-forty-l:
Alphonse Daudet writes The Immortal, or One of the Forty, translated from French by A. W. Verrall and Margaret D. G. Verrall, published by Rand, McNally in 1889. The forty are the members of the Academie Francaise, and Daudet's satire turns on election, ambition, and literary vanity in Paris.

A notice from Men of the Day for 1880 introduces Astier-Rehu, born in 1816 at Sauvagnat to small farmers, schooled at Riom and Louis-le-Grand, then professor and chair of history at Mende. From such a career, Daudet builds a comic, biting portrait of an academician chasing immortality through a seat among the forty.
31085-the-galaxy-volume-23-no-2-february:
Held here is the February 1877 number of The Galaxy, volume 23, number 2, entered for copyright in 1877 by Sheldon and Company. Its opening article, on the administration of Abraham Lincoln, says the second session tested the strength of the very government. It ran from its commencement to its close.

Disappointment at no decisive military success in the first few months of the war caused a depressed feeling, which begot discontent and distrust expressed in Congress. Democrats complained, more than others, of the incapacity of the executive, while Republicans were dissatisfied because so little was accomplished. Only redeeming timely naval successes at Hatteras and Port Royal saved the whole belligerent operations from being pronounced weak failures. It is a serious Civil War magazine number.
4826-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
The twenty-fourth volume of Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1576 to 1577. Its file header numbers it as the twenty-sixth Gutenberg volume. Part five, Don John of Austria, chapter one, opens with birth and parentage of Don John, Barbara Blomberg, and his early education and recognition by Philip. A brilliant military career follows, with campaign against the Moors and the battle of Lepanto.

Extravagant ambition and a secret, rapid journey bring the new governor to the Netherlands. Contrast between Don John and William of Orange frames the chapter, with secret instructions of Philip and private purposes of the governor himself. Don John arrives as a celebrated soldier, son of an emperor, facing a prince who has survived a decade of war by patience and politics. Readers get Motley's account of a glamorous new governor meeting an opponent he cannot dazzle.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
By 1877 Allen's Encyclopaedia had reached its sixth volume, still adding remedies and symptoms at full length. The editorial rule never bends: report everything the provers reported, and trim nothing for neatness. Allen trusts the reader to weigh strong signs against weak ones, as a prescriber must.

That trust made the set a foundation stone for the school's later classics. Hering's guiding marks and Kent's repertory grades both rest on records like these. Volume VI also shows the wide spread of homeopathy itself, with proving reports drawn from two continents. The archive, not the argument, is the point.

Volume VII of Allen's Encyclopaedia, from 1877, adds another thick slice of the proving archive. Remedy by remedy, symptoms accumulate in their fixed bodily order, entry after long entry. Timothy Field Allen gathered them from the whole printed record of his school, plus reports sent to him directly by doctors.

A modern reader may find the lists overwhelming, and that flood is itself the lesson here. Nineteenth-century homeopaths built drug knowledge by mass watching, and this set is their storehouse. Volume VII keeps faith with the plan announced in the first volume: pure materia medica, whole and unsifted.
american-notes-pg977:
Rudyard Kipling's American letters report a young writer's trip across the United States, beginning at the Golden Gate in San Francisco. An introduction in this edition recalls that Kipling arrived in England from India at age twenty-four, already famous there. The letters that follow are sharp, funny, and often rude about the new country.

Sections cover American politics, salmon fishing, the Yellowstone, Chicago, the American army, and the unguarded coasts. Kipling admires American energy while mocking manners, newspapers, and public talk. The book reads as lively travel reporting and as a record of how a rising empire looked to a visitor from another one.
articles-of-confederation-1777:
The Continental Congress adopted the Articles of Confederation in 1777, giving the young United States its first frame of government. Thirteen jealous states, fighting a war together, wanted a league strong enough to win and too weak to rule them. Ratification took until 1781, as Maryland held out over western lands.

The Articles call the union a firm league of friendship among sovereign states. Congress could wage war and borrow money, but it could not tax, pay its debts reliably, or stop states from fighting over trade. Disorder after the war, capped by Shays' Rebellion, convinced many leaders that the league was unworkable. It gave way to the Constitution of 1787. Liberty's first American charter was noble in aim and flawed in form, a lesson its framers learned by governing under it.
arxiv-2509-00077:
Tai Vu, working alone, returns to speech emotion recognition in 2025 with a focus on doing more with less data. The task, telling feeling from voice, is key to human-computer interaction, yet high scores on small sets stay hard to reach. Vu builds and tests support vector machines, long short-term memory networks, and convolutional networks on the problem.

Transfer learning and fresh data augmentation tricks lift scores despite a small training set. The best model, a ResNet34 design, sets a new mark on the joint RAVDESS and SAVEE sets. Its accuracy sits near sixty-seven percent, with a strong F1 score to match. Careful reuse and varied training sound can offset scarce labeled speech.
arxiv-2509-00177:
Faizan Farooq Khan, Vladan Stojnić, Zakaria Laskar, Mohamed Elhoseiny, and Giorgos Tolias improve category-level text-to-image retrieval in 2025. A user types a category or description, and the system must fetch matching images. Models like CLIP map text and images to distant regions of one shared space, which caps retrieval quality.

Their two-step method first turns the text query into a visual query with a diffusion model that generates images. A vision model then scores image-to-image similarity. An aggregation network merges the generated images into one vector and fuses scores from both query forms. Extensive tests beat text-only retrieval across the board. Bridging the modality gap sharpens search by meaning.
arxiv-2509-00377:
Cong Yi, Shuo Fang, Dong-Lin Wang, and Shi Pu compute the local spin polarization of Lambda hyperons in nuclear collisions in 2025, with interaction corrections. Lambda hyperons are short-lived particles whose spin can align with the swirling flow of a collision fireball. The team studies a specific harmonic of the longitudinal polarization as a function of collision centrality.

Calculations use the CLVisc hydrodynamic framework for gold-on-gold collisions at two hundred GeV and proton-on-lead collisions at a far higher energy. Results match the gold data well. The proton-lead data remain a puzzle under the same account. Recent developments in quantum kinetic theory and spin hydrodynamics are also reported.
arxiv-2509-00477:
Vladimir Sokolov, writing alone, returns to black points in Born-Infeld electrodynamics, a nonlinear theory of electric fields that caps field strength. A black point is a charged black hole whose horizon, its boundary surface, becomes doubly degenerate, meaning two horizon surfaces coincide.

Sokolov describes the space-time shape of such an object. Its singularity, the point where usual physics breaks down, is timelike, while the effective space-time seen by photons, light particles, stays regular everywhere, with no break. That mix places extreme black points between ordinary black holes and fully regular ones, a useful case for testing how charge and nonlinear fields change black hole structure.
arxiv-2509-00977:
Fabio Ancona, with three co-authors, proves Holder regularity for solutions of scalar conservation laws. The laws are multidimensional and carry a bounded source term. Such laws describe quantities that are transported and preserved. Continuous isentropic solutions are the focus here. Isentropic means entropy stays constant along the flow.

The source term is assumed bounded throughout. The flux satisfies general assumptions of nonlinearity. The proof exploits the kinetic formulation of the balance law. That formulation lifts the problem into an extra variable. Linear tools become available in that lifted setting. Holder regularity means solutions cannot oscillate too wildly. That stability property matters for both theory and computation. It is a basic requirement for reliable numerical schemes.
arxiv-2509-01877:
Ricardo Paupitz leads eight co-authors in a review of newly made two dimensional carbon forms. Since graphene was first made, many flat carbon structures have been proposed and some have been built. The review covers graphynes, biphenylene networks, fullerene networks, and single layer amorphous carbon. Each class gets its structure, predicted traits, and synthesis route laid out.

Theory and experiment are weighed side by side for every class. The authors flag cases where lab work missed key prior theory that could have guided it. They also list predicted structures that no lab has tried to make yet. Those gaps mark clear chances for synthesis led studies in materials science.
arxiv-2509-02077:
Refat Othman, Diaeddin Rimawi, Bruno Rossi, and Barbara Russo link attack descriptions to known vulnerabilities with sentence transformer models. Vulnerabilities are public flaws cataloged in CVE reports, and tying an attack to its flaw speeds incident response. Manual mapping cannot keep pace with disclosure volume. The team evaluates fourteen leading sentence embedding models on this matching task.

One model leads on technique descriptions, with strong precision and recall scores. About half of its flagged flaws also appear linked to attacks in the official repositories. Manual checks uncover hundreds of predicted links missing from those repositories entirely. Automating the link thus sharpens detection and shrinks the window where flaws stay exploitable. The study covers both validation and discovery value.
arxiv-2509-02477:
Sagar Kumar, Unni V S, and Kunal Narayan Chaudhury present a 2025 image processing paper on fusing hyperspectral and multispectral satellite images. The first type records many colour bands but coarse detail; the second gives fine detail in fewer bands.

Their HyDeFuse method treats fusion as an inverse problem guided by a ready-made denoiser, which cleans images and acts as an implicit prior. Strong denoisers can destabilise iterations, so the design uses pseudo-linear denoisers with controlled behaviour. Applying the contraction mapping theorem, a classic fixed-point result, proves global linear convergence. Tests on public datasets confirm the theory and show competitive fusion quality. The work gives denoiser-based fusion a firmer mathematical footing for remote sensing use.
arxiv-2509-02877:
Kevin Derby and 12 co-authors reported in 2025 on a camera upgrade for a space telescope test bench in Arizona. The bench, called SCoOB, mimics space conditions so engineers can test ways to block starlight. Blocking that glare should let future observatories photograph planets much like Earth.

A small off-axis hole lets a trickle of starlight reach the detector. That light mixes with leftover speckles, which are stray bright spots, and reveals errors in the incoming wave pattern. Crew members explain how they designed and built the special masks for this camera. They also weigh its strengths and limits against an earlier control method. Such work sharpens tools meant to image distant worlds directly.
arxiv-2509-03677:
Vincent-Daniel Yun's 2025 research paper asks how gradients evolve during deep network training, and on a normalisation method drawn from that behaviour. Gradients are the signals that tell each network weight which way to move. Their spread across layers shapes both training stability and how well a model generalises to new data.

Yun first measures how gradient variance and standard deviation change over training, in convolutional networks layer by layer and overall. The patterns prove consistent enough to design around. The proposed method, Gradient Autoscaled Normalization, scales gradients to match their natural evolution, with no hyperparameters to tune. That prevents accidental amplification, stabilises optimisation, and keeps convergence guarantees intact. On the CIFAR-100 image benchmark, ResNet and VGG models maintain or improve test accuracy, even under strong generalisation pressure. The study argues for tracking gradient dynamics directly in optimisation research.
arxiv-2509-03777:
Reconstructing quadrature domains from a single function that encodes them is the focus of a 2025 mathematics paper by Andrew J. Graven and one co-author. A quadrature domain is a region in the complex plane where integrals of well-behaved functions reduce to a few point values. Their framework starts from the domain's quadrature function and rebuilds the region itself.

Using the Faber transform, a tool from complex analysis, they derive formulas linking that function directly to the Riemann map of the domain. The Riemann map is the standard conformal map from the unit disk onto the region. One-point domains carrying complex charge are classified completely. The theory then widens to weighted domains, where integrals carry power-shaped or logarithmic weights. Matching Faber formulas reconstruct those weighted domains from their quadrature functions too. Examples throughout illustrate the method, including cases with rotational symmetry.
arxiv-2509-04077:
Rishit Tyagi and two co-authors work on spotting hidden storylines in news articles in a 2025 computer science paper. News pieces can push slanted narratives, meaning preferred story frames, through subtle wording rather than plain claims. Older automated methods often miss that quiet messaging. The team tackles two jobs: labeling each article's narratives, and explaining the main one with evidence from the text.

One tuned BERT model, a language program, flags narratives with an emphasis on catching as many as possible. A GPT-4o step then checks those labels for consistency. A second setup reasons step by step and pulls matching examples before explaining. Adding a structured chart of narrative types improved both accuracy and trust in the explanations.
arxiv-2509-04177:
Davide Banzi and two co-authors test a star-based navigation trick for a Moon mission in a 2025 research paper. LUMIO is a small spacecraft meant to watch meteoroids strike the Moon from a halo orbit near the Earth-Moon L2 point. Radio tracking runs thin during science work, and faint lighting limits camera navigation. The team instead times occultations: moments when stars vanish or reappear behind the Moon's edge.

A simulation tool built from a JPL software library picks out events that geometry and lighting allow. Fed into the orbit-fitting process beside radio data, those timings cut sideways position uncertainty by as much as half. Timing precision mattered most in sensitivity tests. Mission planners gain confidence for keeping station and locating impact flashes.
arxiv-2509-04377:
Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata and six co-authors trim the memory cache that slows long conversations with language models in a 2025 research paper. Models store attention states for earlier tokens in a KV cache, speeding later generation. As chats lengthen, that cache swells into a memory bottleneck. Their method, PagedEviction, prunes the cache block by block in a structured way that respects the paged memory layout of the vLLM serving system, without touching its core attention code.

Three Llama instruction models were tested on the LongBench suite of long-document tasks. Memory use improved while accuracy beat pruning baselines on long-context work. Serving systems could host longer conversations or more users on the same hardware.
arxiv-2509-04577:
N Marchili and sixteen co-authors summarize twenty years of radio monitoring of blazars with two Italian telescopes in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Blazars are galaxies whose relativistic jets point almost straight at Earth, causing extreme flickering across timescales. Causality turns that flickering into size information about the emitting regions, and multi-frequency watching reveals different jet zones. The Medicina and Noto telescopes have tracked forty-seven blazars monthly since 2004 at several radio frequencies, continuing today at two of them.

The archive now holds about twenty-one thousand flux measurements. Basic analysis tools characterize the variability and preview the science inside. Radio behavior can then be tied to gamma-ray output, locating where the highest-energy radiation originates.
arxiv-2509-04877:
Students and teachers are adopting tools such as ChatGPT in software engineering courses before course plans have settled rules. Maryam Khan, lead author with two co-authors, report a pilot study in a 2025 paper. They mine hundreds of GitHub projects, reading README files and issue discussions for known motivators and demotivators around large language model use.

Engagement, process understanding, and programming help appear often as motivators. Plagiarism and intellectual property concerns dominate the demotivators, followed by security and over-reliance worries. Some expected concerns, such as evaluating learning outcomes, never appear. The study is the first empirical step toward a framework for careful integration.
arxiv-2509-05277:
One sensor driving across a bridge may be enough to map the bridge's vibration patterns, Dhiraj Ghosh and two co-authors argue in a 2025 structural engineering paper. Bridges need regular health checks, but fixed sensor networks are costly to install and maintain.

The moving sensor records acceleration as it crosses, under both known shaking and unknown random traffic. From frequency data the team extracts natural frequencies and damping, then rebuilds mode shapes, the patterns of motion, using smooth building-block curves. For traffic loading they add a statistical method that handles road roughness through a vehicle and bridge interaction model. Numerical tests show accurate shapes at fine spatial detail.
arxiv-2509-05477:
Different mathematical pictures of the same deformed quantum rules may describe the same physics, Sebastiano Segreto and Matteo Bruno examine in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Generalised uncertainty principle theories modify the basic commutation rules, suggesting a smallest measurable length, but each algebra admits several realisations.

The authors first define what counts as a quantum theory of this type, then give conditions for two realisations to be unitarily equivalent, meaning linked by a map that preserves all predictions. They construct that map explicitly for two widely used realisations and check matching results on a harmonic oscillator and a falling particle. One case where equivalence fails hints that a classic uniqueness theorem may not extend.
arxiv-2509-05577:
Ring-like algebraic invariants of families of Jacobians are studied by Younghan Bae and three co-authors in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. A Jacobian packages the line bundles on a curve, and its compactified version sits over the moduli space of stable marked curves used throughout geometry.

The authors show the cohomology ring of a universal fine compactified Jacobian depends on the stability condition chosen, answering a question of Pandharipande. Yet the ring also degenerates through the perverse filtration to an intrinsic ring that does not depend on that choice. Their tools include support theorems and a new Fourier theory for abelian fibrations. Double ramification cycle relations on the universal Picard stack also enter.
arxiv-2509-05777:
Zhihao Lin and Zhen Tian survey how game theory guides decisions for self-driving cars that must react to other road users. Their 2025 review covers scenario-based methods, where cars plan against drivers and pedestrians whose moves are uncertain. Game-based simulators let these strategies be tested safely and at scale before any road trial.

The review walks through settings from highway obstacle avoidance and ramp merging to roundabouts, unsignalized crossings, and autonomous racing. For each setting it compares how studies adapt the standard game model and what those choices do to performance. Learning-based versions, the authors find, handle varied conditions better than older simulation approaches. They close by naming the limits of current work and directions where scenario-based decision-making still needs research.
arxiv-2509-06077:
Notable counting polynomials are taken apart into classic number sequences in a 2025 paper by Francis Atta Howard, the first of a series. The paper studies partition functions and their algebraic and counting structure, giving precise splittings using Dobinski numbers, Bell numbers, and moment generating functions. A new match involving the Kurepa factorial is developed to probe the Kurepa conjecture.

The closing part turns to physics. Howard examines effects tied to Kurepa factorials, occupation numbers, and the Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein distributions, the counting rules for the two great families of particles. The algebraic traits built earlier shape those connections, linking pure counting with statistical mechanics.
arxiv-2509-06277:
Teaching a music generator to forget specific training material is explored in a 2025 paper led by Jinju Kim with four co-authors. Text-to-music systems can absorb copyrighted creations, raising legal and ethical exposure. Machine unlearning promises an opt-out: remove a dataset's influence without retraining and without wrecking performance.

The authors apply existing unlearning methods to a pretrained text-to-music baseline and measure how well the material is forgotten while quality survives. Their early results, from ongoing research, map the challenges specific to music, where style and melody entangle across works. The analysis is offered as a foundation for unlearning in generative music systems.
arxiv-2509-06577:
Ranking colors so image-processing tools can work on color pictures is approached through voting theory by Marcos Eduardo Valle and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. Mathematical morphology offers powerful tools for images, but they need an ordering of pixel values. For color and richer images, no agreed best ordering exists.

Voting supplies the model: each candidate ordering acts like a voter, and the Condorcet ranking orders elements by how often they win head-to-head comparisons. That ideal ranking is costly, so the authors train a machine learning system to learn a simpler reduced ordering that imitates it. Early computer experiments confirm the learned ordering works well enough to define morphology operations for color images. The approach turns a social-choice idea into a practical image tool.
arxiv-2509-06677:
Radio faintness in distant star-forming galaxies is explained by energy losses to the cosmic microwave background in a 2025 astronomy paper led by I. H. Whittam, with fifteen co-authors. Radio emission tracks star formation without dust blocking the view. At high redshift, though, the background glow of the early universe grows far stronger and can drain energy from radio-emitting electrons.

Using about two hundred thousand Lyman-break galaxies at early cosmic times, the team stacked radio observations from the MIGHTEE survey to measure their average brightness. At a fixed ultraviolet brightness, radio output falls as redshift rises. That decline matches the predicted effect of inverse Compton scattering off the microwave background. Rival explanations, like different stellar mass mixes or evolving dust, are discussed, but the authors judge scattering the most compelling cause.
arxiv-2509-06777:
Information that cannot reach distant nodes in a graph gets a new delivery scheme from Kushal Bose and one co-author in a 2025 machine learning paper. Graph neural networks pass messages between neighbors, but bottlenecks squash those messages, a flaw called oversquashing. Rewiring the graph distorts its meaning, and widening channels adds parameters.

Instead of updating every node at each layer together, their framework updates only a batch of nodes chosen by centrality, letting information travel sequentially rather than being compressed all at once. Theory shows the method's sensitivity fades more slowly with depth than standard message passing. Applied to eight graph classification benchmarks, including two long-range ones, it produced notable gains on several datasets. The framework works with existing models rather than replacing them, which makes it easy to adopt.
arxiv-2509-06977:
A deep learning model that acts differently on different hardware is a deployment risk, and Zehua Li measures that drift in a solo 2025 paper. Models run on CPUs, graphics chips, and compiled runtimes, and results can split between backends. Li proposes a configuration-first setup to test the fit between backends in a systematic way.

Experiments are split from code through YAML setup files, covering both library-level and whole-repository models. A three-tier checking protocol tests tensor-level closeness, activation alignment, and task-level metrics. Across several hundred checks at many tolerance settings, about seventy-two percent of runs passed, with mismatches concentrated at stricter thresholds. Detection models and compiled backends drifted most, often through post-processing that is not deterministic. Fixed adapters and selective fallbacks greatly improved agreement without major speed loss, offering a repeatable method for dependable deployment.
arxiv-2509-07077:
Sebastian Cespedes, Senarath de Alwis, and Fernando Quevedo link quantum decoherence to the growth of entropy in the early universe in a 2025 paper. Decoherence is the loss of quantum phase links when a system gets tangled with its surroundings. The second law says total entropy must grow, and the pair of ideas should fit as one.

They start with a toy case: one qubit that gets tangled with its surroundings, where entropy growth tracks the fade of the off-diagonal parts of its state. They then turn to the cosmos, where the split is set by the horizon during inflation, the fast stretch of the young universe. In that case the off-diagonal parts do not fade in the way some past work took for granted. Yet, in a more full open-system view, the tangle entropy still grows step by step while the stretch lasts.
arxiv-2509-07377:
Chris Hone and 5 co-authors apply semisimplification functors across modular representation theory in a 2025 paper. Representation theory studies how abstract symmetry groups act on vector spaces, and modular cases, where the arithmetic wraps around a prime, are especially intricate. Semisimplification is a process that discards negligible parts to reveal a cleaner core structure.

Motivated by a functor from Lie superalgebra theory, the team builds new functors for finite groups, refining the cyclic group Brauer construction and categorifying the Glauberman correspondence. For degenerate categorical Heisenberg actions, their functors commute with the action and give concrete forms of periodic equivalences first found by Henke and Koenig. The results also yield branching rules, which describe how representations split when a symmetric group shrinks to a smaller one. The work ties several deep strands of algebra into one toolkit.
arxiv-2509-07477:
Doctors hesitate to trust AI diagnoses they cannot inspect. Patrick Wienholt and 4 co-authors built MedicalPatchNet to answer that concern, in a 2025 research paper. The system classifies chest X-rays. It cuts each image into separate patches, classifies every patch on its own, then combines the verdicts. Each patch's contribution stays visible, so no separate explanation tool is needed.

Trained on more than two hundred thousand CheXpert images, the model matched a strong standard network's accuracy. On a localization test set, its highlighted regions matched real pathology more often than a popular heat-map method. The authors released code and training scripts publicly. Built-in explanations like these can reduce shortcut learning, where models latch onto irrelevant clues, and help clinicians trust AI support.
arxiv-2509-07977:
Jesse C. Hoke and 8 co-authors link two kinds of signatures in twisted trilayer graphene in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Stacking three graphene sheets with small twists creates flat electronic bands where electrons interact strongly. Many experimental signatures of those interactions appear, but how they connect to each other, and to superconductivity, has stayed unclear.

A scanning single-electron transistor maps local thermodynamic behaviour across a region where the twist angle changes smoothly, alongside transport measurements. Gapped states and correlation features are tracked against the changing angle and band structure. Connecting local probes with global behaviour should help physicists decide which microscopic ground states the material chooses, a step toward understanding its superconductivity.
arxiv-2509-08077:
Tal Agranov and 3 co-authors show that living groups can spread themselves with rare evenness in a 2025 physics paper. Most random crowds clump and thin out. Hyperuniform systems do not. Their density stays far more even than chance allows, even at large scales. The team's model starts from work on long-lived states in biology.

In the model, each member fights for a shared resource. That fight feeds back on the group as a whole. Over time it guides the group to a sharp edge state. There, each life span grows without bound. Spread out in space, the model then shows the even pattern. A coarse, fluid-style theory of the same rules matches the team's simulations well.
arxiv-2509-08377:
A thin circular barrier sorts Landau levels by how much each state touches it, proves Masahiro Kaminaga in a solo 2025 mathematical physics paper. Electrons in a magnetic field organise into Landau levels with heavy degeneracy. A circular delta interaction, an infinitely thin ring of potential, lifts that degeneracy according to each state's overlap with the ring.

Starting from a known matching equation in terms of Kummer functions, the author isolates one Landau level from the rest of the radial spectrum. An exact asymptotic formula gives the energy shift, with an explicit boundary weight that decays factorially. The analysis also tracks the crossover to a hard-wall barrier. Precision results like these anchor models of quantum dots and rings, where circular barriers are real device features.
arxiv-2509-08577:
Z. M. McIntyre and 1 co-author present a loss-tolerant way to make many Bell pairs at once in a 2025 paper. Bell pairs are linked quantum states shared between distant registers. They are a key resource for quantum networks and distributed computing.

The phase of a light pulse encodes a qudit, a multi-level quantum unit, using cat states that mix light and matter. If a photon is lost in transit, a parity check can detect it. Single-qubit rotations then correct the damage in a fixed way. The scheme fits both optical and microwave circuit setups. It offers a practical route to parallel entanglement generation.
arxiv-2509-08677:
Truong Thi Hien and 3 co-authors study Cohen-Macaulay properties of powers of edge ideals for weighted oriented graphs in a 2025 paper. An edge ideal encodes the edges of a graph in algebra. Cohen-Macaulay is a strong regularity property for such objects.

For symbolic powers, the property holds for all powers exactly when the underlying graph is a disjoint union of complete graphs. Ordinary powers for exponent at least two are also fully characterized. A criterion tells when ordinary and symbolic powers coincide. The work is theoretical algebra. It connects graph structure directly to the behavior of ideal powers.
arxiv-2509-08877:
A. L. Chernyshev studies quantum escapism on the honeycomb lattice in a 2025 paper. Quantum fluctuations can stabilize magnetic phases that classical theory would not allow, or expand phases beyond their classical range. A minimally augmented spin-wave theory is used to map those effects.

Two classic spin one-half models on the honeycomb lattice are examined in detail. In one case, fluctuations replace spiral phases with several collinear phases and extend others. Results agree closely with large numerical renormalization calculations. The author discusses use for other models and other order types. The paper presents the method as simple, versatile, and powerful for quantum magnets.
arxiv-2509-08977:
Binh Huy Nguyen and 1 co-author study how symmetry shapes averaged traits of random small scale structures in a 2025 paper. The RVE method takes one sample cell and treats it as a stand in for a whole material. Heat flow traits are the test case here.

A cell's own symmetry can break the true group symmetry and skew the traits it gives. The pair derive rules for when the mean tensor and its spread stay fixed under a symmetry group. Post steps with projectors then force the hoped for symmetry back in. Large FFT based runs on fiber materials back the claims. The steps cut spread with no bias, in theory.
arxiv-2509-09177:
Hanyi Mao and 3 co-authors propose FSPO for length fairness in sequence level reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. Methods that clip importance weights for whole sequences use a fixed range. That range systematically reweights short versus long responses and distorts training.

FSPO clips the sequence log ratio with a band that grows with the square root of length. A formal length reweighting error measures fairness, and small error gives a directional guarantee for updates. Empirically, clip rates flatten across length bins and training stabilizes. Gains over baselines appear across model sizes and datasets, largest on one Qwen model. The fix is simple and general.
arxiv-2509-09377:
Nitin Bartwal and 1 co-author investigate approximation by neural network operators in Lp spaces in a 2025 paper. Lp spaces collect functions whose p-th power is integrable with respect to a measure. The setting uses a general measure over a hypercube, in one or many dimensions.

Uniform approximation for continuous functions and Lp approximation theorems are proved for neural network type operators. Error bounds are given in terms of K-functionals, which measure smoothness. Logistic and hyperbolic tangent activation functions are verified to satisfy the theorem hypotheses. Implementations for continuous and integrable functions are shown for Lebesgue and Jacobi measures on a square. The work is approximation theory.
arxiv-2509-09577:
José Julian Díaz-Pérez and 1 co-author solve a two-walker puzzle exactly in a 2025 statistical physics paper. Each walker drifts along its own channel with uneven left and right step rates, and the pair can swap places at a set rate. The authors compute the full joint chance of finding the walkers at any two sites at any time, a rare exact handle on a system out of equilibrium.

Two crossovers appear in the motion. First the walkers pass from independent wandering to a swap-ruled regime, then the channels blur until both circle the same spot. A lasting directional unevenness between channels also survives. The authors suggest uses from motor proteins trading loads to traders swapping roles in order books.
arxiv-2509-09677:
Akshit Sinha and 4 co-authors argue in 2025 that progress in language models looks slower than it really is because tests stay too short. A tiny lift in one-step accuracy, repeated over many steps, compounds into a far longer task a model can finish without slipping. Long jobs therefore fail mainly through execution slips, not through missing knowledge or planning skill, once both are handed to the model.

Given the facts and the plan, larger models still complete many more turns than small ones with near-perfect single turns. Accuracy per step decays as jobs lengthen, partly because models condition on their own earlier errors and repeat them, an effect sheer size does not cure. Extra thinking time eases that trap and stretches single-turn execution much further.
arxiv-2509-10077:
Simen Storesund and 3 co-authors propose a brain-like way to find shortest paths in this 2025 paper. Classic algorithms such as Dijkstra's need a global view of the network and steps no real neuron could perform, while reinforcement learning adapts too slowly to match animal behavior. Their alternative runs on local spike messages inside a spiking neural network, with realistic delays.

Neurons that get a certain paired signal earlier than expected shorten their own delay. That timing squeeze then travels backward from target to source, marking the best route. The authors prove the method converges and test it on random spatial networks, where it finds all shortest paths using timing alone, with no central control.
arxiv-2509-10177:
Sudeb Ranjan Datta and 3 co-authors let a black hole disk and its corona trade energy in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The two trade until both sides balance. In a two-phase flow, the corona's heat and the disk's glow feed each other. That bookkeeping sets a floor. Below that floor, the X-ray spectrum cannot soften. A plain slab corona struggles with hard states seen in X-ray binaries. That gap pushed the team to model the exchange in full.

Their Monte Carlo code is called MONK. It now runs the two-way talks inside general relativity. An albedo dial sets how much light the disk reflects. The rest is swallowed and added as heat. The team iterates to a global truce. Faster spin hardens the spectrum. A hotter corona does the same. Higher albedo does too. A firm floor holds for a fully covered disk.
arxiv-2509-10277:
Thomas Fromentèze and 3 co-authors grow mechanical materials the way living tissue grows, in this 2025 paper. Living things build complex working structures without a central plan. The authors adapt Turing's reaction-diffusion idea, with direction-sensitive diffusion, so that small building blocks emerge on their own with stiffness and direction properties set in advance.

A database links the growth settings to the resulting elastic behavior, worked out by standard averaging methods. No repeated optimization loop is needed. As a proof, they grew a mechanical cloak, a structure that hides a defect from passing forces by steering them around it. Tests confirmed they could set local stiffness and direction separately, a step toward bio-inspired materials that design themselves.
arxiv-2509-11077: Lev Borisov and Zengrui Han revisit a result from algebraic geometry in this short 2025 paper. Hanlon, Hicks, and Lazarev had built resolutions of the structure sheaves of toric substacks using certain line bundles on the surrounding toric stacks. Borisov and Han supply a new proof of that construction which they describe as substantially simpler than the original argument, making the result easier to check and to use.
arxiv-2509-11277:
Hiroshi Ishikawa wrote this 2025 paper on the basics of quantum theory, with no co-authors. The topic is a clash of two pictures. In one, a watched system jumps between energy states. In the other, its change is smooth. Ishikawa seeks an account that holds both at once, trial by trial.

He recasts each jump sequence as a set of claims. Each claim says which energy states are filled. Chain operators give each claim its odds. A selection rule then filters the claims. It keeps only those with well-defined joint odds for a given state. Claims that clash, the kind behind known paradoxes, are thrown out. The usual demand that operators commute is not imposed. The scheme captures firm links between jumps in one trial. One link says a state is filled by one thing only, much like Boolean logic. Standard odds still come out right.
arxiv-2509-11477:
Anton T. Than and seven co-authors show a quantum field theory simulation on a hybrid quantum computer. This 2025 physics paper faces a cost problem. Boson fields are costly on plain qubit machines. Their encodings are bulky. Their endless state space must be cut off, and errors grow with time.

The team's trapped-ion device stores qubits in the ions' inner states. Bosons live in the ions' shared motion. Gates act on each part and between them. No encoding overhead or cutoff is needed. They simulated a one-plus-one-dimensional Yukawa model out of equilibrium. The model simplifies interacting nucleons and pions. Occupation odds for fermions and bosons were measured. High boson states filled from an empty start, and the device tracked them well.
arxiv-2509-11677:
J. S. Alvarado, M. Hoballah, and E. Voutier report early measures of the proton's inner makeup. This 2025 nuclear physics paper uses deeply virtual Compton scattering. A photon is produced as an electron scatters off a proton. The process is a prime channel for generalized parton distributions. Those tie partons' momentum shares to their places in the nucleon.

Data came from the CLAS12 detector at Jefferson Lab. The team detected the electron and the photon only. Conservation laws rebuilt the third particle. Machine learning helped select the events. Beam spin asymmetries and cross sections were measured. The leaner selection boosted counts and widened the covered phase space. It gave the first CLAS12 measure of this observable at very small momentum transfer.
arxiv-2509-11777:
Mikhail Kulyabin and 7 co-authors release a dataset of synthetic user feedback from an industrial automation forum in a 2025 paper called UXPID. Customer forum posts hold rich product experience insights, but the text is unstructured and domain-specific. It is also rarely labeled well enough for steady study.

The dataset holds thousands of synthesized, anonymized feedback branches drawn from a public forum. Each record bundles multi-post comment threads with metadata. A large language model marked them for user experience insights, expectations, severity, sentiment, and topic. Because the records are synthetic, privacy and licensing barriers that block real forum data are sidestepped. The resource supports training and testing transformer models for issue spotting, sentiment work, and requirements extraction in tech support settings.
arxiv-2509-11977:
Powers of polymatroidal ideals, and the syzygies that pile up as the powers grow, occupy Antonino Ficarra and one co-author in a 2025 algebra paper. Homological shift ideals capture those syzygies, and the question is how orderly their behavior becomes asymptotically.

The authors prove that the first homological shift algebra over the Rees algebra is generated in degree one, a tidy answer for the first layer. They conjecture the i-th shift algebra is generated in degrees up to i and confirm that in many significant cases. A strong persistence property is established for the first shift ideals, and the chain of associated primes is shown to grow as conjectured for i equal to one and for many families. Componentwise polymatroidal ideals keep their structure under the first shift as well.
arxiv-2509-12077:
Pictures, not just strings of symbols, can be the input a machine reads, and Yvo Ad Meeres with one co-author unify the theory of such picture automata in 2025. Their device works on directed acyclic graphs, into which two-dimensional inputs are first encoded.

The encoding does the heavy lifting. One family of encodings, fixed by input size alone, captures exactly the languages of returning finite automata, boustrophedon automata, and online tessellation automata, three classic picture recognizers. Shrinking a string to a simple directed path leaves only regular languages. Let the encoding depend on the symbols themselves, however, and the same DAG machines recognize some context-sensitive string languages and outrun tessellation automata in two dimensions.
arxiv-2509-12177:
Eight pinpoint objects with oddly narrow emission lines may be an entirely new population. Haojing Yan and two co-authors report them in 2025 from James Webb Space Telescope data. The objects turned up in three wide survey fields. Their redshifts fall between about 3.6 and 5.4.

Each object is barely wider than the telescope's own point spread function. In the sharpest bands, each spans under a kiloparsec. Yet their oxygen and hydrogen lines blaze with huge equivalent widths. Their line widths run only a few hundred kilometers per second. Two identities compete for these objects. At least one spectrum fits an active galactic nucleus. That would make them a new breed of faint, nearly hostless type 2 AGN. Most energy distributions instead fit young, low-mass, star-forming galaxies, caught in a first compact stage.
arxiv-2509-12277:
Skin lesion photos alone miss facts a doctor would use, like the patient's age and the true size of the spot. Mehdi Yousefzadeh and seven co-authors build GraphDerm in 2025, a classifier that fuses the image, a millimeter scale read from an embedded ruler, and patient metadata into one population graph.

Lesion and ruler masks come from trained segmentation networks, and real-scale shape measures follow from the calibrated images. Patients become nodes linked by similarity, and a graph network classifies each lesion. On standard ISIC collections the graph scores far above an image-only baseline, and a sparser graph using a quarter of the links keeps nearly all of that gain.
arxiv-2509-12377:
Random shocks with heavy jumps drive many real systems, from prices to climate, and equations perturbed by such Lévy noise need quantitative error bounds. Jorge González Cázares and one co-author derive convergence rates in 2025 for multivariate equations driven by Lévy processes over short times.

Their bounds measure the gap between two solutions in the uniform Wasserstein distance and are written directly in terms of the drivers' characteristics. When both drivers sit in the small-time stable domain of attraction, the bounds yield rates in probability. For additive noise they sharpen into clean distance convergence, using two couplings of the jump parts to reach sharp rates.
arxiv-2509-13177:
Salvatore Esposito and 6 co-authors present ROOM, a simulator for generating photorealistic medical data sets for bronchoscopy, in a 2025 paper. Continuum robots, flexible robots that bend continuously, are advancing bronchoscopy by accessing complex lung airways. Their development is limited by a lack of real-life training and test settings, since real data are hard to collect for ethical and safety reasons.

ROOM leverages patient CT scans to render multi-modal sensor data at medically relevant scales. That data includes color images with real-life noise and light reflections, metric depth maps, surface normals, optical flow, and point clouds. The authors validate the generated data on two canonical tasks for medical robotics, multi-view pose estimation and monocular depth estimation. The system shows diverse challenges that leading methods must overcome to transfer to medical settings.
arxiv-2509-13277:
Sunit Das, Akash Adhikary and three co-authors show in 2025 an odd-in-field longitudinal conductivity in magnets that break time symmetry. Normal metals give even response at small fields. Broken time symmetry allows a linear leading term.

Semiclassical theory yields closed forms for both directions. Berry curvature and orbital moment drive the effect. Point-group rules match Hall rules for the longitudinal case, while transverse rules differ. Large-field oscillations hold both parities. Valley graphene checks peak near band edges and track magnetic order with heat. Recent odd resistance in magnetized graphene is explained.
arxiv-2509-13377:
Federico Girotti and Alessandro Vitale study when quantum paths clean up into pure states, in the hard case of endless spaces, in a 2025 paper. In quantum theory, a mixed state can grow pure as it is watched step by step. For spaces of fixed size, past work tied that cleanup to dark subspaces, parts of the space the watching does not touch.

The pair show, with a class of clear cases, that the old rule fails once the space is endless. They go on to prove that the new effect in their cases is the sole new thing that can block cleanup in such spaces. The root cause, they show, is a lost compactness trait of the set of projections. For a part of endless models, though, the old rule still holds.
arxiv-2509-13877:
Bochao Kong and Ji Zeng prove a covering bound for the permutohedron in a 2025 combinatorics paper. The permutohedron is the polytope whose vertices are all reorderings of the numbers from one to n. All its vertices lie on one obvious hyperplane. There, the coordinates sum to a fixed total. The question is how many other hyperplanes it takes to cover every vertex.

The pair show that at least n hyperplanes are needed when n is odd. At least n minus one are needed when n is even. A more general version was known from Pawlowski. Their proof is shorter and different. It also yields an algebraic criterion for permutohedra built from arbitrary distinct real numbers. The criterion tells when the full count of hyperplanes is forced.
arxiv-2509-13977:
Irkhin computes thermal corrections in low-dimensional magnets in a solo 2025 paper. Heisenberg ferro- and antiferromagnets in one and two dimensions cannot order at finite temperature. Yet they keep strong short-range order. An effective magnetic moment captures that order, and it shrinks as the sample warms. Extracting that shrinkage cleanly from infinite spin-wave sums is the technical challenge.

Irkhin applies Riemann zeta function regularization to pull out the thermal corrections. The method assigns finite values to divergent sums through the zeta function. The one-dimensional ferromagnet recovers the familiar square-root-of-temperature spin-wave law. That matches spin-wave theory and published Monte Carlo runs. The opposing chain instead follows a generalized incomplete Riemann function. Its temperature profile for correlation behavior is distinct.
arxiv-2509-14277:
Shahjalal and five co-authors present HQCNN in 2025, a hybrid quantum and classical network for sorting medical images into classes. Medical image sorting is hard because labelled scans are few, classes are uneven, and disease patterns can be subtle.

Their network pairs a five layer classical image backbone with a small quantum circuit of four qubits, the basic units of quantum computing. The circuit adds state encoding, entanglement and a Fourier inspired attention step, which weighs image parts by pattern. On six standard medical image sets the hybrid beat classical and quantum baselines in the reported tests. Scores were strongest on cell and organ image sets, and the model also held up on a noisy breast image set.
arxiv-2509-14477:
Thales Sales Almeida and three co-authors introduce Ticket-Bench in 2025, a multilingual benchmark for task oriented AI agents. Agents increasingly book and buy through function calls. Success depends on accurate calls under realistic language and cultural conditions, which current tests largely ignore.

Ticket-Bench simulates football ticket purchases in six major languages, from Portuguese and English to French and Italian. Local teams, cities and user profiles replace naive translation for realism. A wide range of commercial and open models were tested for function calling accuracy and consistency across languages. Reasoning oriented models are among those compared in the results. The benchmark exposes how much agent skill drops, or holds, when language and locale change together.
arxiv-2509-15577:
Jaeyoung Kim leads a team that rewrites fetched text so a language model can use it better. Search backed systems fetch pages, then write answers from them. Fetched pages may be on topic yet lack what the answer needs. Past rewrite tools miss this point: they chase topic match, not true usefulness for the answer.

Their method, R2U, learns what usefulness means by watching rewriting and answering together. It scales that watch to build firm training signals. A rewrite is scored by how much it lifts the answer's quality. Those scores then tune the rewriter in two ways. On many open question sets, the method beats strong rivals. The gain comes from grading use, not just match.
arxiv-2509-15777:
Haoran Xu leads a team that finds the patch commits that fix security flaws. Open source projects fix flaws in code commits, but spotting which commit is the fix is slow by hand. Past auto tools lack accuracy and travel poorly across projects. The team first study the field's tools closely to learn what works.

Their study yields four lessons, from the worth of shrinking the search space to the edge of trained meaning over complex builds. Guided by those lessons, they build a two stage tool. Version based filtering first narrows the candidates. A large language model then votes over several rounds of dialogue to pick the patch. The design aims at accuracy with speed.
arxiv-2509-15877:
Josef Dick and Friedrich Pillichshammer study how evenly point sets fill a cube. The star discrepancy gauges that evenness: low values mean a fair spread. Its inverse asks how many points a target evenness needs in a given dimension. That count is known to grow only linearly with dimension, but all proofs fail to give an explicit point set.

The pair analyze unions of lattice point sets built from polynomials, each shifted at random by a digital rule. They prove such unions, random or complete, hit the linear bound for the inverse count. The proof leans on a concentration inequality, so it is not fully constructive either. Still, it narrows the open problem with concrete families.
arxiv-2509-16477:
Giant eruptions from other stars could strip the air from nearby planets, yet those eruptions are nearly impossible to see directly. Nuri Park, Evgenya L. Shkolnik, and Joe Llama use the Sun as the one test case, linking flare brightness to the mass and energy of the eruptions that follow. They extend a known X-ray link into far-ultraviolet light, using data from three space missions across two full solar cycles.

Far-UV flare peaks track eruption mass, energy, and speed in clear patterns. Those patterns let astronomers estimate unseen eruptions on Sun-like stars from flares alone. Such estimates feed straight into judging exoplanet air loss.
arxiv-2509-16577:
Antonio Tarizzo, Mohammad Kazemi, and Deniz Gündüz work on learning over wireless links in a 2025 paper. Many devices can train a shared model and send updates through the air at once. The air channel adds the updates up on its own, which saves time. Plain analog sending, though, is hurt by noise and fading.

The team design digital codes that are learned along with the task. A learned decoder cleans the summed signal with several smart steps. A shared codebook is tuned from end to end. Their design works at far lower signal quality than the best prior method. It also holds up across models and uneven data splits.
arxiv-2509-16977:
Petros Georgoulas Wraight and co-authors read handwriting with very few labels in a 2025 paper. Handwritten text tools usually need large labeled sets to train. Archives and small collections cannot supply them. Their method uses optimal transport to match word images to text labels in a principled way.

Starting from a tiny labeled seed, the system labels confident matches. It then retrains on the growing set and repeats. Tests on low-resource benchmarks show clear accuracy gains. Archives could digitize rare scripts and personal papers without years of hand labeling. That opens fragile collections to search and study while the originals stay safe.
arxiv-2509-17177:
Bowen Qin leads a large team of co-authors on a 2025 arXiv findings report from the FlagEval project. The report shares early results from tests of large reasoning models, the systems built to work through hard questions step by step. The team states that its test set was kept free of contamination, at least to a fair extent, so scores should reflect real skill.

The questions used in the tests can be checked on their own, with no human grading needed. They cover both text-only problems and visual problems that call for reasoning from images. Alongside the report, the team releases ROME, a benchmark for vision language models. ROME probes whether a model can reason from visual clues. Links in the paper point to the benchmark, the test data, and later updates.
arxiv-2509-17277:
Mandip Goswami, writing alone, releases a small data set of synthetic alert sounds in a 2025 arXiv paper. Earcons are the short beeps and chimes that interfaces use to signal events. Researchers who study them need sound clips that are free of rights claims and quick to reuse.

The set, called BeepBank-500, holds several hundred clips made from recipes rather than recordings. Each recipe sets the wave shape, pitch, length, loudness shape, and wobble, plus a choice of three echo settings from dry to room-like. The release packs studio-grade audio files, a rich table of signal and spectrum facts, and two small baseline tasks. One baseline sorts clips by wave family, and the other guesses pitch. The audio is dedicated to the public domain, and the code is shared under an open license.
arxiv-2509-17377:
Hannah Bansal, Kemal Kurniawan, and Lea Frermann test whether logic solvers make language models sturdier reasoners. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses first-order logic problems and counterfactual variants of them. A variant changes one predicate or swaps the roles of two constants, a small edit that flips the right answer.

Past work showed language models often break on such variants, as if they lean on surface patterns. The team couples models with a symbolic solver and checks whether that neurosymbolic mix holds up better. Across model sizes, the mixed systems were indeed more robust, but they scored worse overall than pure neural systems. A new hybrid that adds chain-of-thought prompting improved matters, yet still trailed plain chain-of-thought. The authors close with open directions rather than a verdict, a fair map of a live trade-off.
arxiv-2509-17577:
K. L. Kozlov and B. V. Sorin study how to compactify a topological group through its enveloping semigroup. Their 2025 arXiv paper follows Ellis's functional approach. When a group sits inside the homeomorphisms of a space with pointwise convergence, and the action is well behaved, its closure yields a compactification with a semigroup structure.

These Ellis compactifications are right topological monoids that also respect the group's action on itself. The authors compare them with the Roelcke compactification and pin down the uniformity behind each Ellis one. They describe the proper cases for concrete groups: permutations of a discrete space, automorphisms of an ultrahomogeneous chain, and automorphisms of a linear order, each in its natural topology. The paper organizes a scattered theory into a usable map for topologists.
arxiv-2509-18077:
B Jego and 3 co-authors ask how a galaxy's place in the cosmic web shapes its star birth. Their 2025 study uses the SIMBA sim of the universe, from early time to now. Past work found galaxies near web strands tend to be heavier and more shut down, but that may just reflect a changed mix of galaxies.

To isolate the web's own effect, they study star-forming galaxies only. Each galaxy's gap to the nearest strand is mapped in 3D. Early on, galaxies near strands formed stars faster and drew more gas. Today the trend bends into a V shape with distance.
arxiv-2509-18177:
George Correa de Araujo, Helena de Almeida Maia, and Helio Pedrini build fake scenes to test if AI models grasp place words. Their 2025 frame, Scrapbook, deals with base ideas: what an object is, where it sits, and how it relates to a second object. Big sets of varied questions probe each idea on its own.

Current models did well at naming and counting objects. They stumbled on place facts, and on questions with extra limits. One model gave clashing answers and smooth but wrong ones. Others leaned toward yes answers and tripped on shapes. The frame gives a way to map such gaps.
arxiv-2509-18277:
O Cakirli and 3 co-authors study five paired stars where one partner pulses as a beta Cephei star. Their 2025 paper uses crisp light data from the TESS satellite, plus sharp spectra from ground scopes. Such pairs are rare test beds, since eclipses pin a star's mass and size with care.

Light curves and speed curves, fit as one, give mass, radius, heat, and metal mix for each part. Air traits come from split spectra and a sampling fit. Placed on a star-life chart, each part's state is checked against track models. Pulse tones were found in all five systems, which adds benchmarks for star theory.
arxiv-2509-18377:
In meetings, transcripts often credit words to the wrong speaker. Xinlu He and five co-authors built a system that lets users fix those errors live, with help from a language model. Their 2025 paper describes in-meeting speaker correction driven by short bits of human feedback. The system pairs live speech recognition with speaker labeling.

After each segment, the system shows brief model-written summaries to help users spot key speaker errors. A fix updates the transcript and also enrolls the speaker's voice for later lines. Several checks help pin down which fix the user meant, since speech, model, and user inputs can all err. The team also built a model-driven simulator to test the flow at scale. On a standard meeting test set, speaker error fell sharply versus the live baseline. A small user study pointed to ways to smooth the experience.
arxiv-2509-18677:
Stars glow in X-rays from their hot outer layers, and that glow shapes the planets around them. Takuma Shimura and five co-authors study single F-type stars in this 2025 paper. They picked 33 stars with rich X-ray data by matching two large catalogs. Burst-heavy stars were left out so the sample reflects calm, typical behavior.

The team measured plasma temperature, emission strength, and X-ray brightness for each star. Hotter plasma came with stronger emission, a pattern also seen in cooler stars. The F-type values sat within bounds familiar from G-type dwarfs like the Sun. Activity also tracked the Rossby number, a spin measure, in the same way as for G stars. Upper bounds on emission and brightness held for single stars but not for binaries. The authors conclude F-star coronae can be read with G-star frameworks.
arxiv-2509-19177: Yana Mokanu, writing alone, studies random processes driven by Lévy-type noise in multi-dimensional space. The question is ergodicity in total variation: does the process's distribution settle toward a fixed invariant measure, forgetting its start? The process is tied to an integro-differential operator with unbounded coefficients, a harder case than standard ones. The paper also describes the speed of convergence to that measure and gives examples. The abstract is brief, so this summary stays at that level.
arxiv-2509-19777:
Solving elasticity on fractured, mixed-material bodies strains ordinary equation solvers. Sabit Mahmood Khan and Yashar Mehmani build a preconditioner, a helper that makes those systems far easier to solve. Their two-level design splits the domain into subdomains and learns local basis functions on each. The coarse space built from those functions carries the global behavior.

The high-order twist lets subdomain interfaces deform, unlike a rigid-interface predecessor. Mortar spaces handle the bending and twisting that real joints undergo. The method targets domains of arbitrary shape and material contrast, fractures included. Fast elasticity solves feed into reservoir, geothermal, and structural modeling. A preconditioner that respects local physics can turn overnight runs into routine ones.
arxiv-2509-19877:
Working out how electrons act in a material takes heavy math, and the standard route is slow. Shi Yin and three co-authors train a deep network, NextHAM, to guess the key matrix fast. Their trick starts from a cheap first draft of that matrix, built from the start charge. The draft guides the network at the input and seeds its answer at the output.

The network also respects the rules of three-dimensional turns, with learned fixes on top. New kinds of atoms and new shapes are what break such tools, so the team widens the training data too. A fast, broad tool could screen new battery and catalyst materials at scale. One model for many materials, not one per family, is the goal.
arxiv-2509-20277:
Code written by language models can quietly import security risks, and Xiaofan Li and Xing Gao map those risks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their focus is the software supply chain: the external components and build pipelines inside modern products. Model flaws like fabrication and stale training data can plant threats in both places.

The authors catalog three categories covering eleven potential supply-chain threats. Some let attackers hijack software or workflows outright. Others plant hidden weaknesses that grow over time. They built a tool that generated more than four hundred thirty-nine thousand test prompts from real online questions. Four popular models from the GPT and Llama families all showed the threats persisting. The paper proposes a confirmation-based prompting defense and a warning middleware to reduce the danger.
arxiv-2509-20377:
Retrieval systems sometimes hand a language model documents that hurt more than they help. Tomoaki Isoda proposed filtering those documents by the model's own self-knowledge in a 2025 arXiv manuscript called SKILL-RAG. The author later withdrew the manuscript, judging the project incomplete and planning no revised version. The text remains of record as a withdrawn preprint.

The method trains the model, through reinforcement learning, to state what it knows and does not know. That self-knowledge then decides which retrieved documents are worth keeping. Filtering works sentence by sentence, dropping irrelevant parts while preserving useful ones. Experiments on two open models reported better answers with far fewer input documents. Because the work was withdrawn, its claims should be read as unvetted rather than established.
arxiv-2509-20577:
Not every question deserves the full depth of a giant model. Sampurna Roy and five co-authors route inputs through depth-specialized experts in a 2025 arXiv paper. Standard transformers spend identical computation on trivia and on hard logic. Their design, DS-MoE, splits experts by reasoning depth: shallow pattern matching, composition, inference, memory, and self-supervision.

A learned router assembles a custom chain of experts for each input, activating only what the complexity warrants. Training and testing used the Pile, a large mixed corpus of papers, law, code, and web text. Against uniform-depth transformers, the system saved up to sixteen percent of computation and ran thirty-five percent faster. Accuracy on multi-step reasoning rose by about three percent. Routing choices double as readable reasoning chains, adding transparency.
arxiv-2509-21477:
Reconstructing ocean vertical velocity from surface data is hard when observations are incomplete. Yuan Gao and 5 co-authors tackle that Earth science problem in a 2025 paper. They first build KD48, a high resolution ocean dynamics benchmark. It derives from petascale simulations and expert driven denoising. Standardized, analysis ready benchmarks have long been missing in this field.

Their reconstruction paradigm, VISION, rests on dynamic prompting. A visual prompt is generated on the fly from whatever observations are available. It encodes both data availability and the physical state of the ocean. A state conditioned prompting module injects that prompt into a universal backbone. The design aims to handle missing data, the core obstacle in real ocean observations.
arxiv-2509-21777:
Big online services usually split search and recommendation into a retrieve step and then a rank step. The split causes mismatched tuning and extra upkeep. Vianne R. Gao and thirteen co-authors present SynerGen in this 2025 paper, a single generative model that does both jobs. Earlier generative models merged the steps but often favored one job over the other.

SynerGen is a decoder-only Transformer trained on records of user behavior. One training goal serves retrieval, and a mixed pointwise and pairwise goal serves ranking. Inside the shared model, search signals improve recommendation and recommendation signals improve search. A new way of encoding time helps the model use when things happened. On standard benchmarks for both tasks, SynerGen beat strong rivals, showing one model can serve both kinds of access.
arxiv-2509-22077:
Bert Mulder, Ad Lagendijk, and Willem L. Vos present a better way to smooth noisy measurements in this 2025 paper. Experiments often need features like spectral peaks, with their centers, widths, and heights, plus rates of change, all read from data clouded by noise. Common smoothers fail when feature widths vary strongly across a dataset. The authors modify a classic method, Whittaker-Henderson smoothing, to balance features and noise locally.

Their key addition is a set of adjustable weights, tuned by cross-validation, that let the smoothing strength vary along the data. On synthetic optical data for a nanostructure reflector, the method recovered a pulse's timing distortion while cutting noise by a large factor, exposing buried detail. The paper also gives a general framework for unevenly sampled data, jumps and kinks in the data, edges of data ranges, and smoothing in several dimensions.
arxiv-2509-22277:
Max Hugen, Bob Krekelberg, and Alison Hsiang-Hsuan Liu study firefighting on graphs, a game where fire spreads along edges and firefighters protect one vertex per round, choosing without knowing the future. On trees, a simple strategy is known to be nearly optimal. Their 2025 paper asks what changes when the graph has cycles. Cycles, they show, hand the adversary real power: the algorithm and the ideal solution may cut different cycles, leaving them playing on different boards.

Even on a tadpole graph, one cycle with a tail, they prove no deterministic online strategy can guarantee a good competitive ratio. They then give a matching strategy for graphs with at most one cycle, and extend it to cactus graphs, where many cycles appear but barely touch. A variant where firefighters arrive in pairs changes the picture completely: the problem becomes constant-competitive.
arxiv-2509-22377:
Yasmina Kheddache and Marc Lalonde test whether GPT-4o can spot false claims that mix text and images. False posts spread fast online, and a model that reads both words and pictures could help flag them. The pair built a tuned prompt and a clear frame for the checks. Images and text were first shrunk to fit the model's input limits.

They set six scoring rules and let the model rate its own confidence. Tests ran on five data sets, from politics news to social posts. Runs were repeated to check if grades stayed stable. The results map where GPT-4o does well and where it fails.
arxiv-2509-22577:
Zach Hunter, Matthew Kwan, and Lisa Sauermann prove that the permanent of a random matrix almost never hits any fixed value. The permanent sums products over all permutations and is notoriously hard to compute. For matrices whose entries are independent and not too concentrated, earlier bounds left room for clumping. The team shows the chance of any one value drops exponentially with matrix size.

Their proof also covers the determinant, giving a new route to a classic result of Kahn, Komlós, and Szemerédi. As a payoff, sign matrices of each size take exponentially many distinct permanent values. That settles a problem posed by Ingram and Razborov.
arxiv-2509-22977:
Surajit Bera, Jorge Kurchan, and Marco Schiro extend the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a toy system of fermions with random links. Their version couples those fermions to a disordered bosonic system with its own glassy behavior. The bosonic side can sit in many metastable states, each with a rugged energy landscape. Within each state, the fermions act in SYK-like ways, but with distinct couplings.

The coupling makes the quantum spin-glass phase more stable. It also slows the bosonic dynamics from fast decay to a much slower fall. On the liquid side, the fermion dynamics change sharply. The hallmark critical SYK behavior washes out there.
arxiv-2509-23077:
Wearable activity models decay when a new wearer shows up with distinct movement patterns. Reza Rahimi Azghan and 6 co-authors build CLAD-Net to learn continually without forgetting. Each new subject is a new task in sequence. Labels are scarce and uneven in human studies, which compounds the problem. CLAD-Net pairs a self-supervised transformer with a supervised CNN.

The transformer acts as long-term memory across body sensors, learning without labels. The CNN classifies activities and learns by knowledge distillation, which guards old skills. On PAMAP2 data, final accuracy passed ninety-one percent. Forgetting stayed under nine percent, beating replay and regularization baselines.
arxiv-2509-23177:
Non-Hermitian superconductors can host spectral patterns with no Hermitian counterpart. Chuo-Kai Chang and 4 co-authors map a one-dimensional lattice that holds every internal symmetry allowed. The lattice mixes nonreciprocal hopping, onsite dissipation, and s-wave pairing in an SSH-type frame. Pseudo-Hermiticity plus sublattice symmetry constrain the spectra. Several regimes appear as parameters move.

Real spectra, purely imaginary spectra, and complex flat bands all show up. Majorana zero modes emerge when a transverse field suppresses the skin effect. Uniform dissipation proves essential to keep those modes stable. A winding number built by Hermitianization matches the gap closings. Phase diagrams tie the invariant to the zero modes.
arxiv-2509-23377:
A moving sea floor over uneven terrain launches pressure waves that bounce before surface waves form. Ravindra Pethiyagoda, Santu Das, and Michael H Meylan model that process in the time domain. Linear water wave theory for a compressible ocean frames the math. Fourier transforms and eigenfunction expansions solve it in steps. The team claim first detailed views of the pressure bounce and the acoustic-gravity waves that follow.
