The reward directly punishes wordiness while still rewarding correct answers, so agents learn when speaking helps and when silence is smarter.

Across seven reasoning benchmarks, the trained systems set new best scores while using only a fraction of the tokens of rival methods. Habits such as strategic silence emerged on their own during training. The result is a practical plan for agent teams that stay affordable at scale.
arxiv-2510-22577:
Light field microscopy captures a whole volume in one exposure, helping neuroscientists film living brain activity. Feng He, Guodong Tan, Qiankun Li, Jun Yu, and Quan Wen tackle weak reconstruction methods for a large field version of that tool in a 2025 paper.

They build XLFM-Zebrafish, a large benchmark dataset and test suite for this imaging style. Their learning task hides some camera views and predicts them, teaching angle aware structure with less labeled data. A new loss checks that predicted volumes, when passed through the known optics, match real projections. Their method improves a standard quality score by several percent over baselines.
arxiv-2510-22677:
Entangled photon pairs, called Bell states, are basic building blocks for quantum communication and sensing. Netanel P Yaish, Samata Gokhale, and Avi Peer demonstrate in 2025 a way to generate, manipulate, and detect polarization entangled Bell states at photon rates far beyond normal detectors.

Ordinary photodetectors handle only about a million to ten million photons per second, while bright sources produce far more. Their nonlinear interferometer acts as an ultrafast quantum detector, avoiding that electronic bottleneck. They process states at roughly five hundred billion photons per second, about five orders of magnitude above standard methods, limited only by the optical bandwidth of the source.
arxiv-2510-22977:
Chenlong Yin and four co-authors ask whether stronger reasoning makes language model agents invent tools that do not exist. Builders often train agents to think first and then act, yet newer models seem to hallucinate more as they reason better. No prior study had tested that link in a controlled way for tool use.

The team built SimpleToolHalluBench, which checks two failure modes: no tool is present, and only decoy tools are present. Their tests support the worry that reasoning gains can raise tool hallucination. The benchmark gives builders a way to measure the trade-off before agents act in real settings.
arxiv-2510-23577:
Zhongyi Yu and six co-authors tackle temporal graph link prediction: guessing which nodes in a changing network will interact next, given their history. Real interaction streams are lopsided — a few pairs account for most events, and gaps between events vary wildly. Standard models encode time poorly under that lopsidedness and tend to forget pairs that interact only now and then, exactly where predictions are hardest.

Their framework, TAMI, attacks both problems. A log time encoding squashes long and short gaps into a more balanced scale, and a link history aggregation step keeps each target pair's past from fading. Existing top temporal graph networks can plug into TAMI without redesign. Across thirteen classic datasets and three newer benchmark sets, TAMI steadily improved the models it wrapped, in both settings where test nodes were seen before and where they were new. The code is public.
arxiv-2510-23677:
Wisdom Boinde and two co-authors study quiet patterns in the Lights Out puzzle, now in many colors. The classic puzzle is a grid where pressing a square flips its light and its neighbors' lights. A quiet pattern is a set of presses that changes nothing in the end, a kind of self-canceling combination. Here each square can sit in one of p states, where p is prime.

The authors show how to grow quiet patterns from small grids into grids p times larger, an evolution step across scales. Using elliptic curves, they prove a reverse step, de-evolution, also exists for most primes. They further describe every way to press a grid so that only five squares — the fewest possible — end in a nonzero state. The work links a recreational puzzle to deep tools from number theory.
arxiv-2510-23977:
Yohan Abeysinghe and six co-authors present SynCast, a neural weather model for forecasting air pollution, built to catch the spikes that ordinary models miss. Particulate pollution is a leading health risk, and episodes driven by wildfires, city haze, and dust storms are exactly when warnings matter most. Standard forecasting losses underweight those rare extremes, so models smooth them away.

SynCast fuses weather and air composition data on a regionally adapted transformer backbone, then refines its output with a diffusion-based sampler. Training draws on the harmonized ERA5 and CAMS datasets. Domain-aware objectives, informed by extreme value theory, force the model to respect the tails of the distribution. The result is sharper forecasts across particle sizes, with the gains under extreme conditions and in hard-hit regions, at no cost to global accuracy. The authors offer the system as a foundation for next-generation air quality warnings.
arxiv-2510-24177:
L. M. Pismen reviews theories of nematodynamics, the flow and orientation of nematic materials such as liquid crystals, and argues they are inadequate. Existing theories link how the nematic alignment turns to how the material flows, often by assuming the system stays near equilibrium. Pismen proposes a different basis for that link.

His approach rests on a local symmetry: rotating the nematic alignment and the flow together leaves the physics unchanged. Within a vector based theory with a variable modulus, this symmetry sets how energy passes between alignment and flow through antisymmetric coupling. The method avoids false instabilities when no active input is present, without needing near equilibrium assumptions.
arxiv-2510-24377:
Hedieh Abdollahi measures the half light radii of dwarf satellite galaxies of Andromeda, working alone. The data come from the Isaac Newton Telescope monitoring survey of Local Group dwarf galaxies, taken with the Wide Field Camera between 2015 and 2018 in two filters. The analysis sits inside a larger hunt for long period variable stars in these galaxies.

Abdollahi derives surface brightness and number density profiles for each system and fits them with exponential, Plummer, and Sérsic models. The resulting radii agree well with published values but show subtle differences between models and systems. Accurate sizes help compare the Andromeda satellites and support the variable star study.
arxiv-2510-24477:
Johanna Hartke reviews how planetary nebulae can trace accreted stellar populations in massive galaxies, working alone. Planetary nebulae are glowing shells shed by dying stars, and they serve as spatial and kinematic markers in nearby galaxies. This mini review focuses on their role in tracing halo and intracluster light assembly in galaxy groups and clusters within one hundred megaparsecs.

Hartke links characteristic nebula metrics, such as the alpha parameter and the luminosity function, to shifts between in situ and accreted stellar populations. Results from nearby systems are set against integral field surveys that measure nebulae and stars together. She closes with upcoming instruments and remaining observational challenges.
arxiv-2510-25177:
Kazuhiko Seki, the sole author, studies how a heat grade warps the shield that ions form near a charged wall in a fluid. In the classic view, that shield fades in a set smooth way. Heat grades push plus and minus ions in unlike ways, an effect called the Soret drift, so the shield shifts.

Seki adds a swap entropy term for each ion kind, then solves the broad shield rule in closed form for one like case. In a rim case, the fall turns to a power form. A work shield length grows with heat, so the hot side shields less and the cold side more. That length also sets the wall's charge hold.
arxiv-2510-25377:
Charlotte Myin and Benoit Mahault study flocking mixtures. Their 2025 physics paper studies nonreciprocal matching effects. Flocking describes groups moving jointly like birds. Mixtures contain two species or types here. Nonreciprocal means influence is not mutual equally. Even weak nonreciprocity can reshape collective actions.

They mix runs with continuum formula study. A binary Vicsek model supplied the runs. Nonreciprocity destabilizes the ordered flocking phase, they find. That happens across much of the phase diagram. For aligning populations, one species condenses into bands. That band travels within a liquid of others. For anti-aligning effects, both form polar clusters. Those clusters show large-scale chaotic changes. Both cases produce demixing of species overall. No repulsive effects are needed for demixing. Their theory shows the instability is generic.
arxiv-2510-25677:
Hasan Akgul led four co-authors presenting ZK-SenseLM. Mari Eplik, Javier Rojas, and Aina Binti Abdullah helped. Pieter van der Merwe completes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper makes wireless sensing verifiable and secure. A large-model encoder processes Wi-Fi channel information. Optional radar or RFID inputs are also supported. Policy tokens tie radio features to human meanings.

End-to-end zero-knowledge proofs attest inference integrity. Masked spectral pretraining with phase consistency trains encoder. Selective abstention reduces unsafe actions under distribution shift. A calibrated head abstains when confidence is low. The risk-coverage operating point is bound into proofs. A four-stage proving pipeline structures attestation. Feature commitment, threshold binding, and time binding occur. PLONK-style proofs show the network produced logged actions. Tamper and replay attacks are rejected by proofs. Activity, presence, and respiratory tasks were evaluated. Scores and calibration improved across tasks.
arxiv-2510-26277:
Kang Chen leads six co-authors in a study of internal signals that reveal when a language model answer is likely right. Standard ensemble methods sample several answers and score them by output probabilities, entropy, or self evaluation, yet those external signals can be poorly calibrated after post training. The authors instead inspect neuron activations inside the model during generation.

They find that correct responses activate far fewer unique neurons than incorrect ones, and that correct responses agree more strongly across samples, while incorrect ones diverge. Their Neuron Agreement Decoding picks candidates by activation sparsity and cross sample agreement, using only internal signals. It can predict correctness within the first thirty two generated tokens and supports early stopping.
arxiv-2510-26677:
Ronan Paugam, with five co-authors, presents an algorithm that tracks wildfire behaviour from space in near real time. The tool, FCI-FireDyn, uses the Flexible Combined Imager on the Meteosat Third Generation satellite, which scans the full disk every ten minutes. From those scans it builds fire arrival time maps, rate of spread, and burnt area growth.

Paugam and the team combine threshold-based detection in the mid-infrared with space-time interpolation to rebuild the fire front's progress, at fine scales in both space and time. They test it on three large fires in Portugal, Greece, and France from the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Final burnt areas stayed within twenty percent of reference data sets. The algorithm also caught speed-up phases that came before peaks in fire power, a sign of its use for live monitoring.
arxiv-2510-27477:
Swarang Joshi checks how well computer word meanings match human ones for compound words, in this 2025 study. A compound joins two words, like sunflower, and readers weigh which part drives the meaning. Two human ratings matter: dominance, which part leads, and transparency, how far the whole follows from its parts. Joshi compares both ratings with model scores.

The models are GloVe, which gives each word one fixed vector, and BERT, which shifts vectors by context. Helper measures cover word association strength, frequency, and predictability. BERT's scores matched human composition far better than GloVe's. Predictability ratings forecast transparency well in both human and model data. The findings clarify what drives compound reading and how to model it.
arxiv-2511-00177:
Hiba Ahsan and Byron Wallace test whether sparse autoencoders can reveal and mitigate racial bias in language models used in healthcare. Models may spuriously rely on patient race when predicting, worsening existing disparities. They identify autoencoder traits in Gemma family models that correlate with Black individuals, checking when those traits activate on reasonable inputs such as clear demographic terms.

The study then assesses whether those traits can be controlled to reduce biased associations with stigmatizing concepts. Health AI readers get a concrete audit technique. Finding the internal traits tied to race is a first step toward models that use clinical facts instead.
arxiv-2511-00477:
Aditya Parikh, Sneha Das, and Aasa Feragen audit age bias in medical image segmentation, where models outline structures in scans. In breast cancer segmentation, models perform worse for younger patients, a gap usually blamed on denser breast tissue. The team audits the MAMA-MIA dataset and quantifies the bias in its automated labels, uncovering a biased ruler effect: flawed validation labels can misstate a model's true bias.

Controlled experiments then test where the bias comes from. It does not stem from label quality sensitivity, nor from an imbalance in case difficulty counts, and balancing training data by difficulty fails to close the gap. Younger cases appear intrinsically harder to learn. Training on biased machine-made labels teaches and amplifies the disparity, a warning for automated annotation pipelines.
arxiv-2511-00677:
Robert Ghrist and Cassie Ding rebuild persistent homology with a new yardstick: precision instead of scale. Classic persistence tracks how topological features are born and die as geometry grows, summed up in barcodes. Working over the p-adic integers, the authors define arithmetic barcodes for network sheaves, where each bar marks the precision level at which a cohomology class stops lifting through finer and finer approximations.

Their central Digit-SNF Dictionary shows hierarchical precision data from maps between successive levels encodes exactly the Smith normal form exponents of the coboundary operator. For rank-one sheaves, loop holonomy fixes bar lengths through p-adic valuation, and stability holds under small shifts that respect precision. Torsion becomes the signal, not a nuisance, with uses from quantized consensus to sensor synchronization.
arxiv-2511-00877:
Yuanceng Xu, Li Li, and Wei-Jia Li look inside anti-de Sitter black holes in holographic axion models, which describe strongly coupled materials that break translation symmetry. They strain these solids by shearing them and ask what happens to the black hole interior.

Shear, they find, always removes the inner Cauchy horizon. The bridge like structure inside collapses there, the geometry turns sharply anisotropic, and the interior heads toward a spacelike singularity. For power law axion potentials, strong shear can also create a domain wall with a scaling region near the boundary and a Kasner style epoch near the horizon. Deeper inside, the dynamics settle into anisotropic Kasner behavior, sometimes alternating between epochs as the singularity nears.
arxiv-2511-00977:
Kristiyan Sakalyan and colleagues introduce NicheFlow, a generative model for tracking how cell neighborhoods change over time in tissue. Spatial transcriptomics can now map gene activity across tissue slices at several time points, but most models follow single cells and miss how whole local communities develop together.

NicheFlow treats each local neighborhood as a point cloud and learns how both cell states and their positions evolve between slices. It combines optimal transport with variational flow matching to make that inference. On data sets ranging from embryonic development to brain development, the model recovers both the large scale tissue layout and the local mix of cell types. That offers a way to study development and disease as moving ecosystems, rather than isolated cells.
arxiv-2511-01077:
David McCoy, Yulun Wu, and Zachary Butzin-Dozier argue, in a position paper, that progress in large language models should be measured as capability per unit of resource, not by scale alone. They criticize what they call scaling fundamentalism, pointing to environmental costs and widening inequality in who can afford to build models.

Their framework uses gradient influence patterns to guide where resources go. In transformers, a small share of parameters carries outsized influence. They argue that updating only high influence parameters beats full tuning per unit of resource. Simple gradient norms can find those parameters cheaply. Pairing parameter selection with data selection multiplies the gains. They propose gradient blueprints, shared metadata about which parameters matter, to spread the method.
arxiv-2511-02077:
Jucheng Shen and Yeonju Ro work on speeding up a newer kind of language model, the masked diffusion model, which reveals text in blocks rather than word by word. Popular fast decoders unmask many tokens at once when confidence passes a fixed global threshold. The authors show confidence actually swings strongly from block to block and step to step, while different inputs in one dataset follow nearly identical confidence paths.

Their method, One-Shot Dynamic Thresholding, calibrates thresholds on a single sequence and reuses them for later inputs at almost no extra cost. On question answering, maths, and coding benchmarks it improved the balance between accuracy and speed, raising throughput by roughly a quarter to a half depending on the task.
arxiv-2511-02177:
Asma Miled, Trong Tam Nguyen, and fourteen co-authors improve how films of a promising solar-cell material are made. The material is CsPbBr3, an all-inorganic perovskite valued for stability, but its starting chemicals dissolve poorly, so smooth thin films are hard to grow from solution. The team instead recrystallised films under high pressure and compared them carefully with usual films.

At an optimised pressure of 300 bar (three hundred times atmospheric pressure), the films came out smooth, free of pinholes, and single-phase. Their roughness stayed below a nanometre, and thickness was set by the starting concentration. Grains and crystallites grew larger, light emission strengthened with a lower excitation threshold, and stability under light rose. Heating experiments traced the expected sequence of crystal phase changes, matching single-crystal behaviour.
arxiv-2511-02277:
Giorgos Sfikas, Konstantina Nikolaidou, Foteini Papadopoulou, George Retsinas, and Anastasios Kesidis revisit a unfashionable choice for representing three-dimensional rotation. Estimating an object's pose from an image often calls for a probability distribution over poses, not a single answer, because symmetry and projection can make several poses plausible. Normalizing flows can model such distributions, but they need a parameterisation of rotation, and Euler angles, the classic choice, are usually dismissed for their known shortcomings.

The authors ask whether that dismissal is deserved in this setting. They explore building the flow model on Euler angles and compare it against a model built on a more complex parameterisation, weighing several aspects of usefulness. The paper's contribution is the head-to-head examination itself: whether the simple, well-understood angles can serve pose estimation better than their reputation suggests.
arxiv-2511-02777:
Antonio Oroz, Matthias Niessner, and Tobias Kirschstein present PercHead, a model that rebuilds a 3D head from one photo and allows separate edits to shape and look. Both tasks are ambiguous, since many heads could explain the same image. Their 2025 paper rests on a new perceptual loss built from the vision models DINOv2 and SAM 2.1.

Unlike pixel-level losses, the new loss judges images by deep visual understanding, giving cleaner guidance in fine detail areas. It can replace standard losses directly. The model uses vision transformers, trains on multi-view and in-the-wild photos, and reaches state-of-the-art quality on new views, even at extreme angles. For editing, a segmentation map steers shape while a prompt or photo sets appearance, all through an interactive interface.
arxiv-2511-02977:
Fuming Yang, David Nott, and Anne Presanis offer a way to spot when data sources in a combined model disagree. Evidence synthesis pools several sources to estimate hard-to-measure quantities, but shared parameters can hide conflicts between sources, or between data and model. Their 2025 framework uses score discrepancies, checks built from model scores, extended into the latent space of hierarchical models.

In simulations on an exchangeable model, the method caught between-source inconsistencies well. The team then applied it to an influenza severity model, where it added information beyond standard deviance checks. Because the framework is general, it can travel across fields that pool evidence, from health to policy. The authors present it as a flexible tool for judging consistency in Bayesian synthesis.
arxiv-2511-03077:
R. Khorrambakht and six colleagues plan robot actions by imagining their outcomes in a learned visual world model. Copying human demos task by task transfers poorly and needs constant resets. Their 2025 system, WorldPlanner, instead learns from a few hours of unstructured play data. It builds an action-conditioned video model, a diffusion sampler for candidate actions, and optionally a reward model.

A Monte Carlo tree search then plans long action sequences inside the imagined world, and a simple predictive controller executes the plan on the real robot. The action sampler curbs the world model's hallucinations during planning. On three real robot tasks of varied difficulty, planning beat behavior cloning baselines by a clear margin on a standard manipulation test set.
arxiv-2511-03177:
Takumi Anzawa studies a Lie algebra tied to adjoint multiple zeta values, a variant of numbers formed by nested sums. Earlier work by Jarossay found algebraic links among those values and asked whether a certain scheme matched a known double shuffle group. Anzawa sharpens that question by adding a set of adjoint conditions.

Within the sharpened frame, Anzawa builds the Lie algebra that the adjoint double shuffle links define. The build leans on parity results due to Hirose to fix the algebra's shape. Lie algebras encode how symmetries fail to commute, so pinning this one down clarifies the hidden structure behind the values. The result moves a long-standing comparison between two formal objects closer to a firm answer.
arxiv-2511-03277:
Yi Ouyang and Chenhao Zhang prove a version of a classic slicing result for spaces built over real closed fields. Bertini-type results say that a well-chosen flat cut through a shape tends to keep its good traits. Here the trait at stake is being formally real, which ties algebra to whether sums of squares behave as signs demand.

Their test turns on a global section and whether it keeps one sign across the space. When the cut set carries a formally real generic point, the section cannot change sign, and the reverse holds under extra conditions. As a result, an open range of surface cuts keeps both formal reality and wholeness for shapes of dimension at least two. The work extends a core tool of geometry into the real closed setting.
arxiv-2511-03377:
Jonas Cederlof and Sara Roman track how job hunting changes across a spell without work, using two point four million monthly activity reports. The reports log applications, interviews, and other search steps in fine detail. A design that follows the same spell over time separates true change from the shifting mix of who remains jobless.

Raw effort seems to rise with spell length, but that rise reflects who stays, not how one person behaves. Within a spell, effort stays flat and drops sharply just before a new job starts. Near benefit exhaustion, effort falls by about a tenth, likely as program duties crowd out search. Callback rates fall month by month, with only a small share tied to the spell itself.
arxiv-2511-03577:
Antoine Aspeel, Antoine Girard, and Thiago Alves Lima turn approximation error from a nuisance into a preview signal for nonlinear control. Controllers often steer a simpler over-approximation of a hard system, then treat the gap as an unknown disturbance. The authors note the gap depends on the input itself, so it carries usable information about what comes next.

Policies that read both state and that error are called informed policies. Turning such a policy back into a valid input for the true system becomes a fixed-point problem. Existence follows from a classic theorem, and efficient solvers cover affine and general nonlinear cases. Using error as preview could tighten control of constrained systems like robots and power converters.
arxiv-2511-03877:
Kimia Kazemian is the lead author among twelve authors introducing lead-lag forecasting as a named problem and releasing two large benchmark datasets for it. On social and collaborative platforms, early signals such as views, likes, pushes, or stars often precede later outcomes such as citations, sales, reviews, or forks by months or years.

One dataset links arXiv accesses to citations for about two point three million papers; the other links GitHub activity to forks for about three million repositories. Curation details are documented, lead-lag structure is verified statistically, and parametric and non-parametric baselines are benchmarked. The release gives forecasting researchers a shared testbed that avoids survivorship bias.
arxiv-2511-03977:
Michael Warnock, David A Hague, and Vesna F Mitrovic give an exact expression for how a semiclassical two-level quantum system responds to arbitrary periodic driving. Standard Floquet calculations truncate an infinite matrix, which can discard interference detail and create artefacts for quantum sensors and control.

Using a star-resolvent formalism with the path-sum theorem, the team derive an exact series for transition probabilities from a compact kernel that encodes the whole drive. Expansion uses a non-harmonic Fourier basis built from divided differences of complex exponentials, with coefficients from products of generalized Bessel functions. An analytic formula of this kind can support sensor and control design without truncation error.
arxiv-2511-04077:
Spela Vintar and Jan Jona Javorsek compare word associations from humans and large language models for emotionally loaded cue words. Human associations reveal the mental lexicon but shift with personal experience, emotion, and cognitive style, and associative leaps between distant concepts can drive creativity.

Overlap between human and model associations proved moderate. Model responses tended to amplify the emotional charge of the stimulus word, and they were more predictable and less creative than human responses overall. The comparison suggests current models mimic associative behaviour only partly: they lean harder on affect and safer links, while people range wider and stranger in the connections they offer spontaneously.
arxiv-2511-04177:
Claire Yang, Claire Jie Zhang, Maya Cakmak, and Max Kleiman-Weiner show that a helpful personal assistant can quietly harm bystanders in shared environments. Catalog evidence carried a shorter, different title; the arXiv record gives When Assisting One Disempowers Another, and that record governs. A bystander never consented to be affected, yet the assistant's choices still shape their options.

Bystander disempowerment is formalized and its terms pinned down: trouble arises when an assistant steadily picks actions that raise the user's power at the bystander's expense. In a gridworld test suite, between roughly a quarter and almost all generated environments showed the effect, hinging strongly on the assistant's aim and capability.
arxiv-2511-04377:
Saikat Panja, writing alone, introduces Fatou and Julia sets for word maps on groups and polynomial maps on algebras, bringing the basic split of complex dynamics, tame versus chaotic behaviour. It enters algebraic settings where it had no established form. Two concrete families anchor the definitions.

For groups, the power map on the general linear group over complex numbers is analysed. For algebras, polynomial self-maps of matrix algebras induced by single-variable monic polynomials are studied. Explicit descriptions of both Fatou and Julia sets are pinned down in each case. No wandering Fatou component exists for the matrix pairs considered, echoing a classical rigidity phenomenon from one-dimensional dynamics in a new home.
arxiv-2511-04677:
Joaquin Tarraga-Moreno leads eight authors on interconnection networks for post-exascale machines. AI, simulation, and analytics workloads push supercomputers toward mixed, tightly packed designs. More accelerators per node cut data movement but strain the links between them.

Bottlenecks appear both inside nodes and between them when components share network resources. The authors survey scalable designs for both levels of connection. High-bandwidth memory and storage trends raise the stakes for balanced communication. Their analysis targets machines where compute keeps growing faster than the wires that feed it, a central planning problem for data centers.
arxiv-2511-04777:
Dawn Virginillo and two colleagues formulate power grid restoration with frequency dynamics included. Recent blackouts and system splits have pushed operators to recheck their restoration plans. Restarting islands have low inertia, so static plans can hide dynamic dangers.

Their optimal power flow formulation restores the network step by step with switching choices. A brute-force tree search validates the static version's switching rules for global optimality. On the IEEE nine-bus model, the static plan's best sequence breaks dynamic limits. The dynamic version avoids those violations, showing why restoration planning must respect frequency behavior, not just final flows.
arxiv-2511-04977:
Heng Er Metilda Chee and co-authors define a new task: judging how close two stickers are in meaning. Stickers are a common form of visual chat, but their signs are varied and sly, so machines find them hard to compare.

The team built Triple-S, the first test set for this task, with 905 human-marked pairs of like and unlike stickers. Old vision and mixed models did poorly on it. Their new General Sticker Encoder learns strong sticker vectors and leads on new stickers, plus on tasks like mood sorting and sticker search.
arxiv-2511-05177:
Mathias Lundteigen Mohus and co-authors introduce associative poisoning, a way to attack generative models through their training data. Past data attacks either wrecked output in a broad way or needed control of training, which limits their real-world reach.

Their method twists fine traits of what a model makes, by planting linked examples, with no grip on the training run itself. Models like Stable Diffusion and ChatGPT are the kind of target in view. The work shows a sly risk for firms that train on scraped data, and it points to checks that could catch planted links.
arxiv-2511-05577:
An Vuong and co-authors test whether vision-language models can predict the properties of polymers when fine-tuned for the job. These models shine at tasks like visual question answering, but their worth in materials science is still unclear. Separate models are often trained for each property, which raises cost.

The team built a multimodal polymer data set and turned it into instruction-tuning pairs. Their fine-tuned models, adapted with a low-cost method called LoRA, beat single-mode and baseline approaches. Using both image and text inputs helped rather than hurt. The authors argue one fine-tuned model can serve many property tasks, cutting the cost of deployment and upkeep.
arxiv-2511-06077:
Lin Guan leads a team describing how Douyin, the short-video platform, recommends clips using ten thousand past actions per user. Recommenders gain from long behavior histories, but reading them usually costs too much time and money at billion-user scale. Their system runs in full production traffic.

Three ideas make it fit. Cross-attention from the candidate video to the history replaces history self-attention, cutting the cost from quadratic to linear. A request-level batching scheme shares each user's encoding across their candidate videos. And training on shorter windows still generalizes to far longer ones at run time. Gains grew steadily as history length and model size scaled, echoing scaling laws seen in language models, while latency budgets held.
arxiv-2511-06577:
Kaoru Ohno and Yutaka Okabe revisit a subtle point in the theory of boundary critical phenomena, answering a recent calculation with their own decades-old one. A 2020 study of the O(N) model in half-space expanded a boundary anomalous dimension in powers of one over N but could not sum its series. Even so, its numbers matched the authors' simple 1983 formula.

Here the authors show the newer series is exactly equivalent to their original expression. One final formula in the 2020 paper, written with two generalized hypergeometric functions, cannot give the right values, so corrected versions are derived in appendices. Full derivations for ordinary, special, and extraordinary transitions appear, including cases the earlier paper left unwritten.
arxiv-2511-06677:
Swetha Rani Kasimalla and colleagues build realistic fault data for microgrids dominated by inverters, where genuine fault records are scarce and lopsided. Rare inverter failures and extreme line faults are exactly the cases a diagnosis system must catch, yet they barely appear in training data. A detailed simulated microgrid first generates a broad spread of internal and external fault scenarios.

Their generative model, F2GAN, sharpens its generated data with feedback on means, spread, links between traits, and feature matching at several levels. Classifiers trained only on the synthetic data performed strongly on real faults. A hardware-in-the-loop test bench tied to a real-time simulator reported perfect accuracy in live trials.
arxiv-2511-06977:
Youjie Xu, Steffen J Schmidt, and Nikolaus A Adams propose new ways to transform temperature profiles in compressible turbulent channel flow so they collapse onto the universal law of the wall. Velocity transformations for compressible flow are well studied, but a settled temperature counterpart has been missing. Their derivation analyzes the momentum and energy balance in the overlap layer, accounting for the mixing length model, the work of the body force, and the turbulent kinetic energy flux.

Two transformations result, of Van Driest type and semi-local type. Tested against direct numerical simulation and wall-resolved large eddy simulation data, the semi-local version collapses data better in the viscous sublayer and buffer layer. Total error stays below two percent for most isothermal-wall cases. The work also identifies a multi-layer structure in the kinetic energy flux that enables simpler approximate transformations.
arxiv-2511-07177:
Cédric Aïd studies how valuations extend across algebraic field extensions when the Axiom of Choice cannot be used. Valuations extend notions like divisibility and size on fields. Their extensions govern much of algebraic number theory and geometry, but standard proofs often lean on choice principles to guarantee maximal ideals exist. Working choice-free makes every existence claim earn its keep.

Aïd proves that each extension of a valuation matches exactly one maximal ideal in the relative integral closure of the valuation ring, and that every such ideal arises this way. In the case of a finite field extension, he proves those maximal ideals exist without using choice. The paper ends with an elementary proof of the fundamental inequality, a basic relation bounding the extensions' invariants, showing core valuation theory survives this way.
arxiv-2511-07677:
Feyisayo Olalere and colleagues separate voices for children who struggle to hear in class. Classrooms mix chatter, echo, and several talkers, and children voices resemble each other more than adult voices, weakening the cues separation models rely on. Most assistive models train on adults in quiet, simple rooms.

A compact multi-channel network, MIMO-TasNet, is adapted for real-time use in hearing aids or cochlear implant setups. Low delay matters because late sound confuses lip reading and attention. Training and testing reflect real classroom acoustics and child speech. Better separation could decide whether a hearing-impaired child follows the lesson or loses it.
arxiv-2511-07977:
Jorge Mastache and Raul Henriquez-Ortiz study how decaying dark sector particles could distort the cosmic microwave background spectrum. The early universe glow is nearly a perfect blackbody, so extra injected energy leaves small mu and y type distortions. Their setting links dark matter to quantum chromodynamics through a decaying dark sector.

A unified framework handles fast and slow decays, plus particles moving at different speeds. Exponential, power law, oscillatory, and two step decays are compared across confinement scale, decay rate, and energy transfer values. FIRAS limits tightly restrict early injection, while planned missions could improve those bounds by several orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2511-08477:
Cosmin Ilie, Jillian Paulin, Andreea Petric, and Katherine Freese argue that supermassive dark stars and their remnants could solve three puzzles raised by JWST observations of the early universe. The telescope found ultra compact yet very bright early galaxies, compact dustless sources with strong Balmer breaks, and deepened the mystery of how the most distant quasar black holes formed so fast. Dark stars are powered by dark matter annihilation inside primordial gas clouds.

Such stars can grow by accretion into supermassive objects during cosmic dawn. The authors contend this single mechanism naturally accounts for the bright compact galaxies, the little red dot sources, and the seeds of early supermassive black holes. The proposal ties three separate observational surprises to one dark sector driven pathway.
arxiv-2511-08677:
Zhong-Zhi Xianyu and Jiaju Zang work on the mathematics of cosmological collider physics, where heavy particles present during inflation leave traces in the shapes of cosmic correlations. A key step mixes a heavy particle with the inflaton, and computing it means taking a folded, degenerate limit of a general interaction graph.

With a well-chosen change of variables, the authors derive new differential equations for generic tree graphs and solve them fully in analytic form. Taking folded and partial-energy limits at a vertex then becomes straightforward. Folded graphs turn out to involve functions of lower transcendental weight than their generic versions. As a showcase, the inflaton three-point function with three massive exchanges is written using a Kampé de Fériet function plus simpler hypergeometric pieces.
arxiv-2511-08777:
Michael Wilson wrote this theoretical physics paper on the infrared behavior of coupled gravitational and electromagnetic fields, and he later withdrew it from arXiv. The withdrawal notice names the author as the one who withdrew it, and arXiv lists no further reason, so the paper no longer stands as active research.

As submitted, the paper argued that a curvature decay rate of one over r cubed marks a universal threshold for Laplace-type operators on asymptotically flat spaces. Perturbations decaying faster were claimed to stay relatively compact, while decay at exactly that rate was said to create delocalized zero modes tied to gravitational and electromagnetic memory. Finite-difference simulations were offered in support. Readers should treat every claim here as withdrawn along with the paper.
arxiv-2511-08877:
Junichiro Niimi probes how language models memorize academic citations by asking GPT-4.1 to produce one hundred references across twenty computer science fields, then checking every field of every record against the truth. Citation counts serve as a stand-in for how redundantly a record appeared in training data.

Accuracy climbs with citation count in a log-linear way, with an inflection near ninety citations and saturation near twelve hundred, past which records come back nearly word-perfect. Memorization is layered: titles and first authors are recalled first, venues and numbers need far more repetition, and publication years are essentially never learned. Even famous records can be blended together when titles and authors overlap. The picture is of memory as a gradient, not a switch.
arxiv-2511-08977:
Zihua Wang and eight co-authors improve how large vision-language models learn from the handful of examples placed in their prompt. In-context learning lives or dies by which demonstrations get picked, an NP-hard selection problem where random or similarity-only choices waste the context or skew it.

The framework, Coreset-based Dual Retrieval, rests on a finding that samples inside a diverse subset deliver higher expected mutual information. A cluster-pruning step builds a diverse coreset that still hugs the query, and a dual retrieval mechanism performs global selection from it without giving up efficiency. Across experiments the method lifts in-context performance well above random, similarity-based, and information-score baselines. The authors offer it as a practical answer to a selection problem every practitioner of few-shot prompting faces.
arxiv-2511-09077:
Yan Li and three co-authors name a new kind of wave: the Painlevé soliton, a soliton riding on the background of a Painlevé wave inside an integrable system. The naming follows the older elliptic soliton, a soliton on an elliptic wave background, and the building leans on symmetries that earlier methods left unused.

Nonlocal residual symmetries drive a symmetry splitting method that builds the new waves in full. Extended Painlevé II solitons are built for the Korteweg-de Vries equation, the classic model of shallow water waves. Extended Painlevé IV solitons follow for the Boussinesq equation, another classic of water wave theory. The letter format keeps the account tight, aimed at the integrable-systems community, who track how solution families are laid out.
arxiv-2511-09277:
Sriganapathy Raghav, Boris Malomed, and Utpal Roy propose interferometers built from quantum droplets, self-bound states of ultracold atoms. Interferometers split a matter wave and recombine it, turning tiny phase differences into measurable signals. The authors study droplets in harmonic traps and in ring-shaped potentials.

In the trap, a Gaussian barrier splits the droplet coherently; in the ring, one or two barriers guide splitting and recombination. Transmission analysis finds barrier settings for balanced fifty-fifty splitting, and the atom imbalance after recombination reads out the relative phase. The trap design could serve as a tilt-meter and target detector, they suggest. The ring forms a compact rotation sensor of Sagnac type.
arxiv-2511-09477:
Andrew Hamara, Greg Hamerly, Pablo Rivas, and Andrew C. Freeman test whether planning can be done by simple vector arithmetic in a learned space. Instead of training policies or value functions, their system SOLIS learns an embedding where similar outcomes sit close together. A single global advantage vector points from losing regions toward winning ones.

Candidate actions are ranked by how well they align with that advantage direction, reducing planning to geometry. The embedding is trained with supervised contrastive learning on outcomes. In chess, SOLIS reaches competitive strength using only shallow search guided by the embedding, under constrained conditions. The authors suggest evaluation-aligned latent planning as a lightweight alternative to full dynamics models.
arxiv-2511-09677:
Pedro Dall'Antonia and four co-authors fix a lopsided exploration problem in GFlowNets, samplers that generate compositional objects in proportion to a reward. Easy-to-reach regions dominate training, while hard-to-reach high-reward modes get vanishing learning signal. Their fix borrows the logic of boosting from classic machine learning.

Boosted GFlowNets train a sequence of samplers, each targeting a residual reward that compensates for mass already captured by earlier members. The residual principle reactivates gradients in underexplored regions. Under mild assumptions, adding boosters can never worsen the learned distribution and typically improves it. On multimodal synthetic benchmarks and peptide design tasks, the ensemble explores far more evenly and diversely. Standard trajectory-balance training stays stable and simple throughout.
arxiv-2511-09777:
P. D. Marinos, T. A. Porter, G. P. Rowell, I. V. Moskalenko, and G. Jóhannesson model the faint glow of neutrinos and gamma rays spread across the Milky Way. Cosmic rays wandering the Galaxy collide with gas and light, producing this diffuse emission, and the GALPROP framework simulates that propagation. The authors build a set of realistic bounding models to bracket what the signal should look like.

They compare the predicted signals with IceCube neutrino data and LHAASO gamma-ray data at energies up to the PeV scale. Every model matched the neutrino data within uncertainties, and the results also fit expectations drawn from the gamma-ray side. The models give current best predictions for very-high-energy galactic neutrinos, useful for planning future searches.
arxiv-2511-10177:
Tishya Chhabra, Manisha Bajpai, Walter Zesk, and Skylar Tibbits test a geospatial foundation model on the practical job of tracing coastlines of small sandy islands. They curated and labeled 225 multispectral satellite images of two Maldivian islands and released the dataset publicly. On it they fine-tuned both sizes of Prithvi-EO-2.0, the earth observation model from NASA and IBM, using training subsets from five images up to 181.

Even with only five training images, the fine-tuned models delineated shorelines strongly, reaching an F1 score near ninety-four hundredths and solid overlap with hand labels. Larger training sets improved things further. The authors present the result as evidence of strong transfer learning, arguing such foundation models could support coastal monitoring in regions where labeled data are scarce.
arxiv-2511-10277:
Martin Braas and Lukas Esterle build game characters that can hold a conversation on ordinary consumer hardware. Big language models are too heavy, too slow, and too loose with a game's knowledge boundaries for non-player characters. Their system fine-tunes small language models into fixed character personas and attaches swappable memory modules that carry each character's conversational context and world knowledge, changeable at runtime without retraining.

Three open small models, from DistilGPT-2 up to a seven-billion-parameter Mistral instruct model, were trained on synthetic persona-aligned data and benchmarked on consumer-grade machines. The authors argue the modular persona-plus-memory design travels beyond games, suiting virtual assistants, support bots, and educational agents that need expressive, memory-rich dialogue at small scale.
arxiv-2511-10377:
Yukun Shi and eighteen co-authors report on building a prototype detector part for the CEPC. The CEPC is a proposed electron-positron collider planned for precise studies of the Higgs boson. Their piece is an analog hadron calorimeter, a forty-layer sandwich of steel plates and scintillator tiles read out by silicon sensors. The design follows the particle flow idea for rebuilding particles inside jets.

Before three beam tests in 2022 and 2023, the prototype passed electronic tests and cosmic ray checks to show it was ready. Data from those beam tests is still being analyzed. The work aims to sharpen understanding of hadron showers, validate the particle flow approach, and refine the design of the final CEPC detector.
arxiv-2511-10577:
Vishal Thenuwara and Nisansa de Silva present DESS, a system for fine-grained sentiment analysis that extracts triplets of an aspect, the opinion expressed about it, and the sentiment polarity. Getting all three right together is hard, especially when the relevant words sit far apart in a sentence.

DESS pairs DeBERTa, whose enhanced attention mechanism tracks context and word relationships well, with an LSTM channel that processes grammatical patterns, in a dual-channel design the authors carefully tuned. On standard datasets it improved F1 scores over current methods by several points, for both finding aspect-opinion pairs and assigning sentiment. Their analysis credits DeBERTa's attention for handling complicated sentence structures, suggesting that thoughtful upgrades of the underlying language model bring real gains.
arxiv-2511-10777:
Xiaxin Li and Arya Mazumdar speed up one-bit compressed sensing, a technique that recovers sparse signals from measurements reduced to a single bit each, just the sign of every reading. The narrower task they target is support recovery: finding which entries of the unknown signal are nonzero.

Existing methods keep the measurement count low but usually need decoding time that grows in line with the full signal length, which hurts at large scales. Borrowing ideas from group testing, the authors design schemes with sublinear decoding complexity and near-optimal measurement counts. They give exact recovery with a few more measurements, and an approximate version with a tunable error parameter. A probabilistic scheme whose error probability vanishes completes the set. Each scheme comes with explicit bounds on measurements and decoding cost.
arxiv-2511-11277:
D Kuiri, J H Correa, and their colleagues study how spin effects reshape a fingerprint pattern in tiny Josephson junctions, devices where current crosses a thin barrier between superconductors. Repeated Andreev reflections, where charges bounce and convert at the barrier, carve a subharmonic gap pattern into the conductance. That pattern is widely used to read off transport traits and the induced gap.

Spin-orbit coupling mixes spins and opens avoided crossings in the leads' energy bands, which then stamp strong reflection features onto the conductance traces. An external magnetic field shifts those features, and their visibility turns on the spin polarization of the bands. The analysis explains when each feature should appear.
arxiv-2511-11777:
Vinit Mehta, Charu Sharma, and Karthick Thiyagarajan review the fast-growing meeting point of large language models and three-dimensional vision for robots. Language brings reasoning and instruction following; 3D sensing brings spatial understanding. Together they promise machines that can be told what to do and can see where to do it.

Foundations of both fields are laid out, followed by sensing technologies, current methods, applications, and open challenges, with a focus on next-generation robotic perception. Hallucination, spatial grounding errors, and compute limits recur as obstacles. As a map of a young field, the review helps researchers see which combinations are proven, which are promised, and which remain wishful.
arxiv-2511-11977:
Aditya Khanna counts partitions whose dimension, the number of standard Young tableaux of that shape, is exactly two modulo four. Partitions with odd dimension were enumerated by McKay and characterized by Macdonald through the theory of 2-core towers, a layered decomposition of partitions by their two-core structure.

The same tower machinery is pushed one step further, to dimensions congruent to two modulo four. Explicit formulas are given when the binary expansion of n has no consecutive ones, and a recursive formula computes the count for every n. Parity and congruence questions about tableaux dimensions connect representation theory with elementary arithmetic, and each settled congruence sharpens the picture.
arxiv-2511-12377:
Samuel Wairimu and Leonardo Horn Iwaya audit the security and privacy of AI health chatbots on mobile phones. Such chatbots act as always-available companions for fitness, mental health and other services, offering tailored advice and early predictions. Those benefits come with a risk that sensitive health data may be mishandled.

The study examines sixteen chatbots found on the Google Play Store in three phases: manual inspection, static code analysis, and dynamic testing while the apps run. Findings include security flaws such as remote web debugging left enabled, privacy problems, and failures to meet store policy, including missing public privacy policies. The authors close with recommendations on data handling and design choices.
arxiv-2511-12577: Farook Rahaman, Bikramarka S. Choudhury and Anikul Islam study quantum wormholes. They are solutions of the Wheeler-DeWitt equation. The setting is Friedmann-Robertson-Walker cosmology. The solutions satisfy the Hawking-Page wormhole boundary conditions. The setup allows any factor ordering of the Hamiltonian constraint operators. Matter is given in one of two ways. It is either a perfect fluid, or a scalar field with a simple link to gravity.
arxiv-2511-12677:
Oliver Joergensen, Dominik Drexler, and Jendrik Seipp work on a memory problem in automated planning. Planners that search state by state must store every state they generate, and large tasks can flood memory. Tree databases, borrowed from model checking, can store each state in very little space, but they demand a large block of memory reserved in advance. The authors design a dynamic version that grows as needed, for both grounded and numeric planning variables.

They prove the dynamic version keeps the good properties of the static one. In tests on classical and numeric planning tasks, compression reached several orders of magnitude, often with negligible runtime cost. For planning researchers, that means bigger tasks become searchable on the same hardware. The paper pairs the new data structure with a careful comparison against other state compression techniques.
arxiv-2511-12877:
Yang Hou and five co-authors describe a new heating regime in periodically driven quantum systems. Driven many-body systems usually absorb energy until they reach a featureless infinite-temperature state. In Floquet superheating, heating starts at rare hot spots where a local fluctuation crosses a threshold. Their example uses a sharp spin-echo drive that barely heats low-energy states while thermal fluctuations open strong heating channels elsewhere.

The consequences are dramatic: prethermal behavior that lasts exceptionally long, and macroscopic measurements that split into two distinct groups rather than one. A simple theory based on a critical droplet size, balancing heat injected by the drive against heat flowing out, explains when hot spots grow. The authors present the mechanism as a new route to stabilizing non-equilibrium phases of matter, turning the heating problem of driven systems into a controllable, spatially structured process.
arxiv-2511-13077:
Li-Ming Cao, Long-Yue Li, and Xia-Yuan Liu compute what a black hole looks like when its spacetime is two Schwarzschild solutions glued along a shell. The Israel junction conditions govern such gluing. Light bending at the shell and the delay of light crossing it shape the image of a thin glowing disk, obtained by ray tracing. For a resting shell they identify three image signatures: a redshift cusp at the shell, a V shape in the transfer function. Photon rings that no longer match photon spheres one to one.

They then let the shell collapse. The spacetime passes from one photon sphere inside the shell, through a stage with two, to one outside, yet the images never show two separate photon rings. The shell's motion breaks the redshift factor. The study gives observers concrete features to test whether real black hole images hide a junction.
arxiv-2511-13277:
Jutta G. Kurth and Jean-Philippe Bouchaud derive the long-run distributions of an extended Chiarella model of financial markets. The model pits a saturating trend-following force against a pull back toward fair value. Both forces act with noise, so prices settle into steady patterns rather than fixed points.

In the small-noise, weak-feedback limit, both mispricing and trend follow single-peaked Gaussian curves. Slow trends change the picture and allow a split into two peaks when mean reversion is slow, with a critical point the authors pin down. They also correct two claims in earlier literature about when trend and mispricing distributions turn bimodal.
arxiv-2511-13377:
Amélie Canin and 5 co-authors present Haute Couture, a method that stitches James Webb Space Telescope spectral cubes into one uniform cube. The MIRI instrument's spectrometer yields twelve cubes with different views and resolutions, and their overlap zones often disagree on brightness. Stitching must fix both the resolution gaps and the flux mismatches.

Their algorithm treats the twelve cubes as parts of one large incomplete matrix and fills it with non-negative matrix factorization. A prior step jointly scales the cubes so overlaps agree as well as possible. Applied to Orion Bar data from the PDRs4All program, it produced a single cube at the best resolution across the full wavelength range.
arxiv-2511-13577:
Maxime Brazeau and 3 co-authors present a calibration method for microscope-coupled infrared spectrometers that measure faint light emission. Fourier transform tools can read weak sources, but microscope coupling, which eases capture from tiny objects, lacked documented setup steps. Their method leans on the known emissivity of hot doped silicon.

Applied to a newly installed commercial device, the method yielded responsivity and noise floor values inside the predicted range. The team demonstrated it with two detector types, covering both steady and modulated step-scan modes. Microstructure researchers gain a practical recipe for trusting absolute light numbers from such setups.
arxiv-2511-13677:
Angela F. Harper and 3 co-authors present an open-shell frozen natural orbital method that shrinks quantum chemistry calculations without losing control of accuracy. The method uses second-order averaged perturbation theory to pick which virtual orbitals matter, replacing the crude energy cutoff used on standard molecular orbitals. Open-shell states, with unpaired electrons, are the hard and important case.

Chosen orbitals drove steady convergence of correlation energies and, more tellingly, of singlet-triplet energy gaps as the active space grew. Tests ran from small molecules to a two hundred sixty electron iridium complex tied to phosphorescent materials. Quantum and classical solvers both benefited, with the large case nearing the measured gap as basis and space grew.
arxiv-2511-13777:
Pierre-Olivier Goffard, Hansjoerg Albrecher, and Jean-Pierre Fouque analyze how miners should split computing power among Pay-per-Share mining pools. Proof-of-work mining pays rarely and randomly while costs run constantly, so pools smooth income by paying per share of work. The pool manager sets both share difficulty and the management fee, which shapes what miners actually earn.

With a simplified wealth model for miners, the authors study the trade-off between handing risk to the manager and paying for that safety through fees. Allocation across pools with different difficulty and fee settings becomes a portfolio choice under uncertainty. The analysis gives miners and pool designers a principled way to weigh stability against cost in this reward system.
arxiv-2511-14077:
Yingjie Luo, Eduard P. Kontar, and Debesh Bhattacharjee improve estimates of the electrons that carry most of a solar flare's energy. Flares accelerate electrons that then radiate in X-rays, radio, and ultraviolet light. Because the electron spectrum falls steeply, the numerous low-energy electrons dominate the energy budget, yet they are the hardest to measure.

The authors apply a warm-target X-ray model with a kappa-form electron distribution to two well-observed M-class flares, using EUV data to pin down the hot plasma. The model constrains electron properties from a few to tens of kilo-electronvolts, even below the RHESSI instrument's threshold. Results show the approach holds up under uncertainties that earlier studies left unaddressed.
arxiv-2511-14377:
D. Alonso-López and 20 co-authors map magnetic fields in the Shapley Supercluster Core using the polarization of background radio sources. Faraday rotation grids trace magnetized plasma, and this region packs two galaxy clusters with two groups between them. The team combined POSSUM rotation data with Planck thermal measurements to pin down gas density and field properties together.

They detect excess rotation scatter across the region and infer average field strengths of a few microgauss in the groups and clusters. The scatter falls off with distance from the nearest system more gently than either semi-analytic models or cosmological simulations predict. That flat profile challenges current pictures of how cosmic magnetic fields are distributed.
arxiv-2511-14477:
Miao Shang and Xiaopeng Hong introduce Gaussian Spatial Transport for tasks that need point based density maps. In crowd counting and landmark tasks, each label is just a point in an image. Models must turn those sparse points into a full density map. Standard transport methods are slow because they solve a costly plan at each training step.

Their method uses Gaussian splatting to link image pixels to label points. From that link they derive a transport plan with a probability based formula. A new loss then guides standard network training. Tests on crowd counting and landmark tasks show strong results with much better training speed.
arxiv-2511-14677:
Divij Sharma, James M. Sullivan, Kazuyuki Akitsu, and Mikhail M. Ivanov report the first precise field-level measures of a bias tied to equilateral primordial non-Gaussianity. Many inflation models predict slight departures from a Gaussian pattern in the early universe, and the equilateral type is a hallmark of single-field models with extra interactions. The bias coefficient tells how halo and galaxy counts respond to that early pattern.

Measuring it is hard because its signal mimics ordinary scale-dependent bias. Working at the field level with effective field theory, the team extracts clean values for dark matter halos. Better control of this bias is a key step toward testing inflation with galaxy surveys.
arxiv-2511-14777:
Mahdi Samiei, Mahdi Mansouri, and Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah test whether language models can truly execute long procedural rules. Models shine on tasks labeled as reasoning, yet faithful step by step rule following is different. The authors use finite state machines as a minimal, fully interpretable probe. The model receives an explicit machine definition and must track state over many turns.

No world knowledge is needed, only exact application of transition rules. Turn accuracy and task accuracy separate local slips from full run success. The setup isolates where long horizon execution collapses. Results challenge claims of robust procedural reasoning. The benchmark gives a clean tool for measuring state tracking fidelity in future models.
arxiv-2511-15477:
Alessandro Cecconi, Michelangelo Bin, Lorenzo Marconi, and Rodolphe Sepulchre study contraction in excitable systems, using the Hodgkin-Huxley model of a neuron as their main case. Contraction means nearby states move closer over time, so small differences fade rather than grow. They ask when that property holds, with and without incoming synaptic pulses, and what it means for spike timing.

Without input, the model contracts in the range that matters for real physiology. With pulse inputs, contraction survives when input events stay sparse enough, and it is lost when the firing rate grows too high. Spike timings prove reliable exactly in the contracting regime, linking a math property to trust in timing.
arxiv-2511-15677:
Gerasimos Damigos, Achilleas Santi Seisa, and three co-authors present a streaming framework that sends robot LiDAR data in real time over a 5G network. LiDAR builds three-dimensional point clouds by timing reflected laser pulses, and robots often need that data processed at a remote edge server. Sending bulky point clouds without delay or loss is the central challenge.

Their system extends a low-latency transmission scheme to add Draco geometry compression, adjusting compression to the sensed channel capacity and network load. Encoding errors are kept within the accuracy robots need. Real experiments over a public 5G network across several kilometers of city preserved low delay and loss, while remote mapping algorithms validated the stream in practice.
arxiv-2511-15977:
Daniel Mas Montserrat, Ray Verma, and four co-authors make large genomic workflows for precision medicine run faster by managing memory per chromosome. One sample can span hundreds of gigabytes, and memory spikes, heavy disk use, and failures plague pipelines. Chromosomes differ greatly in memory demand, so fixed resource plans waste resources and stretch run times.

A symbolic regression model forecasts per-chromosome memory use, with a bias against over-allocation. A dynamic scheduler packs tasks like a knapsack problem using simpler forecasts. A static scheduler orders chromosome work to cut peak memory with no loss of speed. On tests in simulation and real pipelines, the methods cut memory overruns, balance load, and speed the full run.
arxiv-2511-16177:
Thomas Collignon and seven co-authors mitigate shared storage congestion in high performance computing with a control theory approach. Intensive tasks depend on fast data access, yet shared storage congestion causes unpredictable slowdowns and timeouts. Traditional stack tuning is workload specific and needs deep expertise. Their self adaptive controller regulates client side input output rates dynamically instead.

Only a small set of runtime load metrics feeds the controller. Implementation on a multi node cluster is tested under a representative workload. Total runtime falls by up to a fifth, and tail latency improves as well. Dynamic regulation generalizes better than static tuning, the authors argue. Stable performance matters as much as peak speed for shared scientific computing facilities.
arxiv-2511-16377:
Hrad Ghoukasian and Shahab Asoodeh design local differential privacy mechanisms whose main aim is fairness: each person randomizes their own sensitive attribute before sharing. The question is which randomization least distorts the data's fairness while keeping privacy.

For binary sensitive attributes the authors derive a closed-form optimal mechanism, and for multi-valued attributes they build a tractable optimization framework that finds the optimum. They also prove that, for classifiers that best balance discrimination and accuracy, cutting data unfairness necessarily cuts classification unfairness. Experiments across datasets and fairness metrics beat existing local privacy tools on fairness while holding accuracy near the non-private level, and the trade-off compares well with standard fairness fixes.
arxiv-2511-16977:
Hiroki Tateishi and eight co-authors store frequency-multiplexed photons in a quantum memory while preserving their nonclassical link to telecom partners. Quantum networks need this to distribute entanglement fast. Frequency multiplexing multiplies the rate, but it demands broadband pair sources and memories that speak the same spectrum.

Their source is a cavity-enhanced down-conversion device tuned to both visible and telecom wavelengths, producing photon pairs in a clustered comb. The memory is an atomic frequency comb in praseodymium-doped crystal, offering more than eighty modes. Filtering the main cluster gave about thirty-three effective modes, checked by matching counts. After storage the cross-correlation stayed strongly nonclassical. That shows cavity sources and rare-earth memories can be integrated toward scalable quantum networks.
arxiv-2511-17077:
Sarathchandra Khandavilli, Arno Förster, and Lucas Visscher develop a way to pull apart exciton couplings, the interactions that let energy move between molecules after light absorption. Their setting is the GW-Bethe-Salpeter method, a standard tool for computing excited states, recast so each molecular fragment can be examined on its own. Localized orbitals let them split an excited state into parts sitting on one fragment and parts shared as charge transfer between fragments.

Tests on ethylene and pyrene pairs reveal how truncating the excitonic basis and approximating couplings shift the computed energies. The team then applies the method to chlorophyll pairs, where slight shape distortions create weak charge-transfer asymmetries. The framework offers a practical route to reading excitonic behavior in large molecular assemblies, fragment by fragment.
arxiv-2511-17177:
E. N. Bulgakov and four co-authors work out the theory of a tiny spinning top made of light. Two counter-propagating, circularly polarized laser beams can trap a submicron spheroidal particle and drive it around the beam axis in a circular orbit. The authors derive equations linking the orbit's properties to the optical force and torque on the particle, showing the particle also spins around its own equatorial axis while it orbits.

Two regimes can occur. In one, the particle's own spin is far faster than its orbital motion; in the other, the two rotations lock together. The orbit can even run against the rotation of the light's electric field. Numerical simulations confirm the analysis. The results could guide nanoscale gyroscopes and techniques that sort tiny particles by shape.
arxiv-2511-17677:
Abu Kaisar Mohammad Masum, Naveed Mahmud, M Hassan Najafi, and Sercan Aygun build a hybrid model that joins the BERT language model with a small quantum circuit for text classification. Tuning BERT alone can be costly and sensitive to settings, and quantum methods have been tipped as a possible boost. Their system fine-tunes the combined model and tests whether the quantum part earns its place.

On standard benchmark sets, the hybrid scores on par with, and at times better than, purely classical baselines. It also adapts across varied data sets without a full redesign. The authors present the work as a feasibility study: early evidence that classical-quantum fine-tuning of pre-trained language models is workable and worth further testing at larger scales.
arxiv-2511-18077:
Dixi Yang, Anheng Wang, Chunming Wang, Hajime Tanaka, and Jiaxing Yuan show how swimming bacteria reshape the separation of two mixed liquids into distinct phases. Phase separation is well understood for passive mixtures, but motile bacteria couple their self propulsion to how they wet the boundary between liquids.

Experiments with a common bacterium in a polymer mixture, plus simulations, reveal spinning droplets, elongated chains, and branched clusters. Activity slows droplet coarsening through rotation driven repulsion, yet speeds it when the other phase is the minority. A biofilm protein acts as a wetting glue that clusters bacteria even in dilute suspensions.
arxiv-2511-18177:
Elias Lumer, Matt Melich, Olivia Zino, and six co-authors compare ways for language models to answer financial questions from regulatory filings, earnings reports, and similar documents. They contrast vector based retrieval, including an agentic version with hybrid search, against a hierarchical system that walks document structure without embeddings.

Across a large set of filings and a benchmark of questions, the vector agentic system wins most comparisons at similar speed. Two add ons help further: reranking retrieved passages with a cross encoder sharply raises retrieval quality, and expanding small chunks into larger context wins most comparisons at tiny extra cost. Production tradeoffs are discussed.
arxiv-2511-18277:
Yeji Song, Jaehyun Lee, Mijin Koo, JunHoo Lee, and Nojun Kwak present Point-to-Point, a method for editing video while keeping the original motion intact. Editors face a trade-off: change the subject and the movement warps, or protect the movement and the edit fades. Older motion codes either cling too tightly to the first layout or stay too vague. The team returns to point-based motion, tracking a few key points through the clip.

The catch is choosing which points matter without a human marking them. Their answer is anchor tokens, compact codes learned from a video generation model's prior knowledge that capture the essential point paths. Those anchors can be moved to fit a new subject, letting the edit follow. Wide experiments are reported across varied scenes.
arxiv-2511-18477:
Jing Rou Puah and Sasa Arsovski build a deep network that estimates three things about a star at once: its age, its lifetime, and its stage of evolution. Getting these values right is a long-standing problem in astrophysics. Their model feeds on two kinds of data from a large sky survey, spectra and brightness measures. The model splits its work across specialised parts: a simple network for numbers, and an image-style network joined with a vision transformer for spectra.

Three output heads predict the three targets, with stage sorted into five classes from hot stars to red giants. Labels come from standard stellar evolution tracks. The authors tune the design in three phases, balancing the joint loss. They report a final model that pairs low age error with physically realistic outputs, checked further by a dropout-based uncertainty method.
arxiv-2511-18977:
Xin Yuan and nine co-authors present FastForward Pruning, a faster way to decide how much of each layer of a large language model can be cut. Pruning shrinks models, but the best cut is uneven across layers, and searching for it with reinforcement learning is powerful yet prohibitively slow at this scale. Their core move is to decouple the search: a single-step learning framework optimises the policy apart from the separate problem of meeting the overall size budget.

A curriculum that starts with cheap, simple tasks and grows harder cuts the search cost further. Across three model families, the framework finds pruning plans that beat rival methods on the balance of size and performance. The work targets teams that must compress frontier-scale models on a realistic compute budget.
arxiv-2511-19077:
Surender Kumar, Markus Frohlich, Stefan Velja, and eight co-authors find why tiny platelets of two layered semiconductors lose their light emission so fast. That loss is a problem for light emitting uses of these strongly light interacting materials. Combining ultrafast laser spectroscopy with first principles calculations, they trace the sub picosecond decay of excited states to traps at the platelet edges.

The traps are bright hole states from metal orbitals, present even when edges are passivated with hydrogen. One compound shows more localized edge states than the other, and zigzag edges trap more than armchair edges. Platelet size decides whether edge trapping or slower core recombination wins, and the trapping states aid catalysis.
arxiv-2511-19177:
Alcino Cunha and Nuno Macedo address a common step in formal software work: choosing the best specification from several candidates. A specification states exactly what a system should do, and picking the wrong one wastes later effort. Their technique generates test cases that a user labels as wanted or unwanted, narrowing the field step by step.

Two solver-based algorithms are offered, one that guarantees the smallest test suite and one that trades that guarantee for speed. A prototype builds suites for Alloy specifications, a widely used modeling language. Tests on many problems show the exact method is practical often, while the faster one handles dozens of candidates.
arxiv-2511-19477:
Aram Vardanyan reports lessons from building and running a production browser agent, a system that operates a web browser on its own. Such agents promise autonomous web work but face severe reliability and security problems in practice. Vardanyan's central finding is that the model's raw capability is not the bottleneck: architectural decisions decide whether an agent succeeds or fails. Hybrid context handling, mixing accessibility tree snapshots with selective vision, and full tooling that matches human interaction, are among the choices he examines.

Security analysis of real incidents leads to a sharper claim: prompt injection attacks make general-purpose autonomous browsing fundamentally unsafe. He argues against building general browsing intelligence and for specialised tools with programmatic constraints, where safety limits are enforced by code rather than by the model's own reasoning. The paper is a field report for teams shipping agents.
arxiv-2511-19777:
F. Ciavattini, A. Della Corte, and C. Lucamarini attach a new invariant to pairs of points in a compact dynamical system. For each pair they build families of ever finer approximate chains, nested and without cycles. The order spectrum collects the countable order types reached as those chains tighten.

The spectrum does not depend on the chosen shrinking sequence and stays fixed under topological conjugacy, the standard notion of two systems being the same. It also refines Conley's partial order, a classic tool for sorting a system's long-run behavior. Order theory thus gains a sharper lens on dynamics.
arxiv-2511-20177:
Dai, Chen, Shu, and colleagues feed language-model world knowledge into sequential recommenders carefully. Their 2025 paper proposes GRASP for predicting users' next actions. Recommenders read past behavior to guess what comes next. Collaborative signals alone are often too thin. Language models add rich world knowledge about items.

That knowledge arrives with hallucinations attached, though. Prior work trusted model output far too readily. GRASP retrieves similar users and items as auxiliary context. Generation-augmented retrieval synthesizes helpful item descriptions. Holistic attention then weighs knowledge at several levels. Noisy guidance gets filtered instead of obeyed blindly. Two public benchmarks plus one industrial dataset were used. The industry set held one hundred thousand interactions. GRASP reached state-of-the-art results across diverse backbones. Gains held when paired with varied base models. The design deploys as a front-end feature module. Deployed systems can adopt it without surgery.
arxiv-2511-20277:
Zhang, Wu, Xu, Wu, Xu, Drew, and Niu speed up neural training by reading the whole landscape. Their 2025 paper introduces HVAdam, a full-dimension optimizer. Adam-like methods tune each parameter's step separately. Per-dimension tuning ignores the global loss shape. Valleys then trap training in slow zigzags.

HVAdam tracks a hidden vector across all dimensions. That vector captures the loss surface's trend direction. Updates align with the trend instead of fighting it. A restart strategy refreshes the trend estimate. Convergence is proved for convex and non-convex cases. Toy functions show it reaching optima fastest.
