Extra depth or context length hurt when the training budget could not support them. One caution stands out: rotary position embeddings, a hit in large models, did not reliably transfer to small ones.
arxiv-2512-21077:
Abhijeet Kale, Rohit Batra, and four co-authors let an algorithm decide which two-dimensional materials deserve expensive physics calculations. The prize is spin Hall conductivity, the efficiency with which a material converts charge current into spin current for spintronic devices. First-principles values come from density functional theory with tight-binding Hamiltonians and spin-orbit coupling, far too costly to run across the roughly two thousand candidate materials.

Active learning closes the loop: models trained on an initial twenty-four diverse systems nominate the most promising next calculations, and three rounds grow the dataset to forty-one computed cases. The best candidate found shows a conductivity nearly twenty-three times the initial round's champion. Feature analysis then explains the wins, pointing to orbital symmetry near the Fermi level, atomic species, covalent radii, and electronegativity. The dataset is public for the spintronics community.
arxiv-2512-21477:
Ethan Andersson and Valeri Frumkin show that topology, the mathematics of global shape, can steer a single moving particle. Topology usually controls waves spread across a system, giving robust transport in electronic and photonic materials. Whether it could direct one localized particle, coupled to the field guiding it, was largely unexplored.

Their test system is a walking droplet, a small oil drop that bounces on a vibrating fluid surface and is propelled by its own waves. By structuring the wave environment, the authors make band gaps exclude the droplet from whole regions. Edges guide its motion along chosen paths. Its orbital motion depends on chirality, through an emergent gauge structure in the wave field. Here global geometric design acts directly on a particle's path, not just on waves. The results suggest new ways to direct matter without pushing it locally.
arxiv-2512-21577:
Emmy Liu, Varun Gangal, and their co-authors argue that the many competing definitions of AI hallucination fold into one. Hallucination, in their proposal, is simply inaccurate internal world modeling that becomes visible to the user. A stated fact contradicting a knowledge base counts, and so does a summary contradicting its source.

Earlier definitions appear as special cases once two choices are explicit: which reference world model the output is judged against, and what policy decides when a mismatch counts as a conflict. The unified view forces evaluations to state their assumed reference world. It also separates true hallucinations from planning mistakes and reward errors, different failure modes needing different fixes. The authors connect the framework to HalluWorld, a companion benchmark that spells out its reference worlds completely for stress-testing models.
arxiv-2512-22377:
Sajjad Taravati introduces temporal Bragg gratings as a new class of optical amplifiers. These are layered photonic forms, periodic in space, whose refractive index is varied in time near the Bragg frequency. Through careful simulations, Taravati varies where the time-variation sits, in high-index or low-index layers, and how its frequency and amplitude change the gain spectrum and field behavior.

Both layer choices produced strong parametric gain, with high-index modulation giving higher gain at comparable depth. The gain peaks can be tuned across a broad frequency range, making the device frequency-agile. Amplification is asymmetric: below the Bragg frequency, far stronger modulation is needed than above it. In the extreme low-frequency limit, discrete sidebands merge into a broadband gain continuum.
arxiv-2512-22677:
Trung Hieu Giang and Ngoc Quynh Nguyen study what happens to a curved-shell model as the shell flattens into a plate. Their subject is the nonlinear shallow shell model associated with Donnell, Vlasov, Mushtari, Galimov, and Koiter, a classic description of thin curved forms under load. The question is asymptotic: do minimizing solutions of the shell model settle into the solutions of the corresponding plate model as curvature disappears?

The authors prove that they do, and their result allows general applied forces. That generality matters because the earlier reference result assumed the tangential components of the applied forces vanish, a key restriction. Removing it substantially widens the class of loading conditions under which the shell-to-plate limit is now justified.
arxiv-2512-22777:
Kasra Jalaldoust and Elias Bareinboim ask when knowledge learned in one domain can be carried to another by recombining pieces. Drawing on causal transportability theory, they picture a target predictor as a circuit assembled from causal mechanisms, each learned from source data. Two levels are defined: a single mechanism that transfers directly, and full circuits composed from several transferred modules, which can even predict labels no single source mechanism predicts.

The authors give conditions for learning such circuits from source data alone when the causal structure of both domains is known. They then loosen the requirements, adding a supervised adaptation scheme that uses a little target data and no explicit causal graph. The few-shot error ends up tied to the size of the smallest target circuit buildable from source modules. A gradient-based version of the circuit search behaves as the theory predicts in experiments.
arxiv-2512-22877:
Ju-Hsuan Weng, Jia-Wei Liao, Cheng-Fu Chou, and Jun-Cheng Chen benchmark how well image generators can be made to forget a concept. Text-to-image models sometimes produce harmful or copyrighted content, so erasure methods try to remove ideas. Nearly all testing, however, only attacks the model through text prompts. Real uses such as image editing feed information through other channels that can smuggle the erased concept back in.

Their benchmark, M-ErasureBench, tests erasure through text prompts, learned embeddings, and inverted image latents, under white-box and black-box access. Current methods hold up against prompts but mostly fail against the other channels. Erased concepts reappear at very high rates in the white-box case. The authors answer with IRECE, an inference-time add-on that finds the concept through cross-attention and disturbs the matching latents during generation, cutting reappearance while keeping image quality.
arxiv-2512-23077:
Saraswati Soedarmadji, Yunyue Wei, Chen Zhang, Yisong Yue, and Yanan Sui use vision-language models to discover reward functions for controlling simulated bodies with muscles. Musculoskeletal systems have hundreds of actuators, and nobody knows how to write a reward that turns a phrase like walking forward with upright posture into coordinated motion. People can judge movement by eye, though, and modern vision-language models can share that judgment.

Their framework, MoVLR, loops between control optimization and model feedback. A controller tries to move the body, the vision-language model assesses the resulting motion against the stated goal, and that assessment is converted into structured guidance that refines the reward. Through repeated rounds, rewards emerge that produce physically coordinated locomotion and manipulation in high-dimensional musculoskeletal models. The results suggest vision-language models can ground abstract motion descriptions in the implicit principles that govern real motor control.
arxiv-2512-23377:
Shuangyang Li and co-authors introduce faster-than-Nyquist signaling, a technique that packs symbols more tightly in time than the classic Nyquist criterion allows. Future wireless networks need far higher throughput, and simply widening the channel is not always possible. Faster-than-Nyquist signaling sends more symbols through the same resources by accepting controlled interference between them and untangling it at the receiver.

The article is a structured tutorial and roadmap rather than a single new result. It lays out the principles and theory, then presents promising results for coded faster-than-Nyquist systems. An application is integrated sensing and communications, where one waveform must both carry data and probe the area, an important function for next-generation networks. The authors close by mapping open research challenges, including receiver cost and interference control, and the directions they judge most promising.
arxiv-2512-23477:
Yao Ma, Yong-Liang Ma, and Lu-Qi Zhang model the matter inside neutron stars with a baryonic extended linear sigma model. A framework that includes baryons and the explicit breaking of chiral symmetry. Using a relativistic mean field approximation, they ask whether such a model can describe both ordinary nuclear matter and stars heavy enough to contain hyperons, particles with strange quarks.

The model reproduces hadron masses and nuclear matter properties near saturation density well. Matching the observed mass-radius relation of neutron stars, however, requires the pion-nucleon sigma term to take a value far from its measured vacuum range. The authors read this tension as a hint that the model's low-energy constants change with density, and they call for calculations beyond the leading-order mean field treatment.
arxiv-2512-23577:
Jing Fu Hu, Hang Lu, and Bao Yuan Sun ask how much dark matter a neutron star could contain without contradicting observations. A star with dark matter mixed in, alongside ordinary nuclear matter, would have different mass, radius, and tidal response. Recent measurements by NICER and the LIGO-Virgo gravitational-wave detectors make it possible to bound that hidden component.

The team built equations of state from twelve nuclear matter models plus a self-interacting fermionic dark matter model, then solved the two-fluid structure equations. For each model they found the largest allowed dark matter fraction, and noticed it correlates almost perfectly with the star's maximum mass. Turning that correlation into a probability statement, they bound the dark matter mass inside such stars at a level near a tenth of a solar mass.
arxiv-2512-24177:
Yun-Xuan Lu and four colleagues report a compact cold-atom source. It produces two species at once. The species are lithium-6 and rubidium-87. Such sources underpin work on quantum mixtures and molecules. Dual-species setups are traditionally bulky and complex. This design strings two-dimensional magneto-optical traps in series. Efficient Zeeman slowing works over a short distance.

The performance sets records. Lithium loading reached billions of atoms per second. The oven temperature stayed moderate. The rate was forty-four times higher than without the slowing light. Rubidium streamed in at a comparable rate. Its oven sat at room temperature. The whole vacuum system fits in a small volume. The science cell is included in that size. The authors offer the setup as a fast starting point. Double-degenerate mixtures and ultracold molecules are the targets.
arxiv-2512-24977:
Barna Zajzon, Younes Bouhadjar, Maxime Fabre, and others introduce SymSeqBench, a unified approach for creating and studying rule-based symbolic series. Sequential structure supports language, motion, and choice-making, and AI systems must learn it too. Their tools, including SymSeq, strictly create ordered symbolic data sets with known rules.

The approach is domain neutral while linking tasks to formal theories of computation and computability. Cognitive science and AI readers get benchmarks where the true rule behind a sequence is known, so learning can be judged exactly. Controlled symbolic series help split genuine rule learning from pattern rote recall.
arxiv-2601-00077:
Tailan S Sarubi leads five co-authors in reviewing how detector efficiency limits attempts to prove that nature is truly non-classical. Their 2026 article centers on the detection loophole: when detectors miss many events, classical hidden-variable models can fake quantum correlations. The review starts with the classic Bell setup and the efficiency thresholds tied to the CHSH inequality, then follows the path toward the first loophole-free tests.

Later sections move through other causal setups. An instrumental scenario turns out to share the Bell bounds for binary variables. In prepare-and-measure tests, losses weaken dimension certification and open security holes in quantum key distribution. A bilocality setup, using several independent sources, can relax the efficiency needed a great deal. For experimentalists, the review gathers scattered thresholds into one map of how good detectors must be before a non-classical claim can stand.
arxiv-2601-00477:
Mohammed Latif Siddiq and colleagues study what happens when autonomous coding agents act as teammates on GitHub. These agents now open pull requests that change production code on a large scale. The authors ask how such agents affect software security, how their security work is reviewed, and what early signals predict rejection.

Drawing on a dataset of more than thirty-three thousand curated agent-authored pull requests, they filtered for security work and verified the results by hand, confirming over twelve hundred security-related requests. They then compared acceptance and review speed across agents, programming ecosystems, and kinds of changes. Qualitative coding revealed recurring security actions and intents, and review metadata showed signals tied to rejection, giving maintainers practical guidance.
arxiv-2601-00977:
Katherine Bruce and three co-authors study, in 2026, two outbursts of a spinning neutron star that feeds on a companion. The star, SAX J1808.4-3658, pulses hundreds of times each second as it spins. It flared from July to November in 2019, and again in late 2022. Two space telescopes, NICER and NuSTAR, watched both flares. The team plot the full light curves from the NICER data.

Several thermonuclear bursts, flashes from fuel burnt on the surface, lit up during the flares. The team track how the light spectrum of two such bursts changed over time. They then fit the combined spectrum of both telescopes at once, a first for this star. Their best fit needs light reflected off the disk around the star. It pins the tilt of the system to about seventy-two degrees. A narrow feature at low energy also shows in the steady glow.
arxiv-2601-01577:
Dat and 3 co-authors present Hanoi-World, a world model meant to help self-driving cars plan ahead while staying safe. Learning by trial and error needs huge amounts of driving data and can latch onto pixel noise instead of meaning. Their model learns compact inner representations and predicts how they change, much like imagining a route before taking it.

A recurrent network supports long planning horizons while keeping response time workable. Tests used a highway driving package across several settings. The authors report the system forms driving plans with safety awareness and compares well with leading baselines on collisions. The approach targets data-light training for vehicle control.
arxiv-2601-01677:
Wildfires in western Canada have grown more destructive, and the record seasons of 2023 and 2024 caused heavy social and environmental losses. Zhengsen Xu and fourteen co-authors present a data-driven system for predicting wildfire risk that is designed to be trustworthy, reporting not just a forecast but also how confident the forecast is.

Trained on long sequences of weather, fuel, land, and human factors, the model beat existing time-series methods while staying cheap to run. Its explanation tools show temperature drivers dominating risk in both years, with moisture mattering more for regional contrasts in 2024. Maps of uncertainty reveal where predictions are least sure, helping managers judge where to act with care.
arxiv-2601-01877:
Variational quantum circuits are often made bigger to gain power, yet highly parameterized circuits train poorly and generalize worse. Jun Qi, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Pin-Yu Chen, and Min-Hsiu Hsieh explain why from the standpoint of the function class such circuits can express.

Using random matrix theory, they show a collapse. Sufficiently unstructured circuits fall into a universality class. There, outputs and gradients concentrate sharply. The expressible functions shrink to a narrow family of near-constant ones. The authors call this a simplicity bias. Barren plateaus are a symptom of it. Tensor-structured circuits escape the collapse because bounded tensor rank limits the randomness. The message for designers is that architecture, not parameter count alone, decides whether a quantum model stays trainable.
arxiv-2601-01977:
The compound GdRu2Si2 hosts tiny magnetic whirlpools called skyrmions, and a recently found high-temperature magnetic phase has puzzled researchers. J. Sourd and five co-authors probe a single crystal with sound: measuring how the speed of ultrasound changes in magnetic fields applied along two crystal directions.

Strong anomalies in sound velocity trace the compound's complex phase diagram, and the new phase proves fragile for fields along one axis but robust along the other. A Landau theory and a microscopic toy model reproduce the zero-field elastic anomalies across acoustic modes, letting the authors propose a magnetic structure for the mysterious phase. Sound, in effect, listens to magnetism reorganizing itself.
arxiv-2601-02077:
A gravity theory is modified only minimally. It carries dynamical dark energy. The framework is called w-dagger VCDM. It promises flexible cosmic expansion. The instabilities that plague many alternatives are absent. Artur Ladeira and three co-authors test that promise. They add a realistic neutrino sector. They also use the newest data.

The team combines three data sources. Planck satellite data is one. DESI baryon acoustic oscillations and DESY5 supernovae are the others. They bound the total neutrino mass below zero point one one electron volts. The effective number of neutrino species matches the standard model. Across every dataset combination, one signal persists. The data prefer a late-time dark energy transition. It crosses between quintessence and phantom behavior. The inferred Hubble constant rises as well. The Hubble tension eases substantially. No early dark energy is needed.
arxiv-2601-02177:
WiFi signals can identify a walking person by their gait without any camera, which sounds ideal for contactless authentication until several people are present at once. Oliver Custance, Saad Khan, and Simon Parkinson test a cheap option. Can ESP32 WiFi sensors separate multiple people's gaits? Six signal separation methods are evaluated. Seven scenarios run, with one to ten people.

Accuracy stayed moderate no matter the algorithm. It ran between about thirty-nine and fifty-six percent. The best method, non-negative matrix factorization, topped that range. Diagnostic measures showed feature spaces overlapping by ninety-seven to ninety-nine percent. Within-person signatures were unstable. Environmental sensitivity was strong. The bottleneck, the authors conclude, is the sensing hardware's quality and spatial diversity, not the algorithm, a bound with direct security and privacy implications.
arxiv-2601-02377:
Xinyu Huang and a large team survey security for robots controlled by large language models. Language control lets robots understand complex commands and carry out sophisticated tasks, but a bad output is no longer just harmful text. It can become a dangerous physical action, a gap the authors call the embodiment gap between abstract reasoning and the physical world.

The survey organizes attacks into a taxonomy covering jailbreaking, backdoor attacks, and prompt injection through several input channels. Defenses are sorted as well, from formal safety specifications and runtime enforcement to schemes where several models check each other. By mapping threats against defenses in one place, the review shows where text based protections fall short for embodied systems and where new work is most needed.
arxiv-2601-02477:
Harald Schmid, Felix von Oppen, Gil Refael, and Yang Peng define a quantum charger. An interacting quantum system that moves energy between two drives, and ask how fast it can charge as it grows. The figure of merit is charging power. With long range interactions inside the charger, a collective steady state charging mode appears whose power grows faster than the system size, beating the same number of independent, parallel units.

Using the driven Lipkin Meshkov Glick model and spin chains with power law interactions. They show the effect holds up to a critical size set by the breakdown of the high frequency regime. Optimal work output and reachable starting states are discussed. The effect could be tested in trapped ion experiments, and the authors present interacting driven systems as promising platforms for better energy conversion.
arxiv-2601-02577:
Alexander Roman and Jacob Roman present Orchestral, a light Python toolkit for building agents on large language models without being locked to one provider. Developers today choose between provider bound software kits that lock them in and sprawling multi package systems that hide control flow and make results hard to repeat. Tool calling across providers is messy in practice, with split interfaces, mismatched message formats, and uneven streaming behavior.

Orchestral defines one shared, type safe form for messages, tools, and model usage that works across major providers, removing manual format translation. Tool schemas are built from Python type hints. The design keeps the simplicity needed for scientific computing and production deployment, so the same agent code can move between providers while staying portable and reliable.
arxiv-2601-03377:
Edoardo Efrem Gervasoni and three co-authors rethink how treatment effects should be defined when randomized trials are emulated from observational data. The target trial framework emulates trials started at many time points and pools them for precision, usually assuming the treatment effect is constant over time. The authors argue that assumption hides real variation, especially because common effect measures are noncollapsible, so pooled numbers can mislead.

Their alternative is model-free and starts from the estimand: choose exactly which effect, in which population, is wanted, then estimate it with G-computation or inverse probability weighting. Estimands are proposed for different study designs. Applications to simulations and to real intensive care data on antimicrobial de-escalation show clearer, more reliable interpretation than the standard model-based approach.
arxiv-2601-03477:
Mehedi Hasan Shuvo and five co-authors build a driver behavior analysis system that values clear explanations as well as accuracy. Aggressive or distracted driving causes real harm, so models that flag risky behavior should show which factors drove each call. Earlier studies often skipped feature selection, the step of choosing which inputs matter, and lost both performance and clarity.

The team used a Kaggle dataset with nearly thirteen thousand rows and tested thirteen learning algorithms after cleaning and scaling the data. A random forest reached ninety-five percent accuracy. Using LIME, an explanation tool, they picked the ten most influential features and retrained. Accuracy dipped only slightly, to about ninety-four percent. Leaner models that people can inspect are easier to trust in safety work.
arxiv-2601-03577:
Ye Su and Yong Liu build a unified theory for Mixture-of-Experts models, the design that lets large language models grow by activating only a few expert networks per input. Two core practices, top-k routing and load balancing, work well but have rested on habit rather than proof. The authors derive both from a Bayesian view as optimal sparse approximation and prior regularization.

An information theory view casts the same tools as cutting routing confusion and raising channel capacity. Routing itself is shown to be a hard combinatorial problem, and the authors prove a coherence barrier: when experts look too alike, greedy routing cannot recover the best subset. Adding orthogonality, a geometric separation between experts, formally fixes that failure, giving designers a principled rule instead of folklore.
arxiv-2601-03977:
Parisa Poorhasani and Bogdan Iancu argue that cancer survival models should be trained for each stage apart. Models trained on all stages together can look better than they are and can hide how factors change with stage. The pair work with the SEER data set on colorectal, stomach, and liver cancers.

Poorhasani and Iancu build machine learning models that can be explained after training. They use SHAP and LIME, two tools that show which factors pushed a prediction up or down. The tools reveal how age, personal traits, and clinical factors matter in different ways by stage and cancer type. Such detail could help doctors plan care that fits the person and stage.
arxiv-2601-04177:
Haoran Su, writing alone, designs a traffic system that clears a path for emergency vehicles in crowded streets. Normal strategies cannot keep up as conditions change by the second. Su combines graph neural networks with multi-agent reinforcement learning in a two-level design suited to streets full of connected vehicles.

A high-level planner sets the global plan, while low-level controllers carry out the driving paths. Graph attention lets the system scale as the number of vehicles changes. Trained with a multi-agent policy method, the system cuts emergency travel time sharply against baselines and far more against uncoordinated traffic in simulations. Crash rates stay near zero, ordinary traffic keeps most of its efficiency, and extra studies support robustness across scenes.
arxiv-2601-04277:
Beier Luo and four co-authors tackle a side effect of post-training large language models in their 2026 arXiv paper. Models get better at tasks but worse at judging their own confidence, leaning toward systematic overconfidence. Earlier fixes matched a post-trained model's final output pattern to its pre-trained version, which the authors argue misses what changes during inference itself.

They separate two failure patterns: confidence drift, where final confidence swells while the underlying decision path stays much the same, and process drift, where that path itself wanders. Their method, Dual-Align, corrects both, matching final distributions and steadying the layers where paths split, by learning a single temperature value. Experiments are reported to cut calibration error toward a supervised benchmark while keeping post-training gains intact.
arxiv-2601-04377:
Dongqi Liu and eight co-authors argue that retrieval systems hand language models a pile when they should hand them a map, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation fetches passages to ground a model's answers, but standard pipelines present them flat and unordered, so the model misses how evidence connects across documents and struggles to synthesize it.

Their framework, Disco-RAG, builds discourse structure at two levels: trees inside each passage that capture its local organization. a rhetorical graph between passages that tracks how they continue, contrast, or support each other. Both feed a planning blueprint that conditions the final generation. On question answering and long-document summarization benchmarks, they report state-of-the-art results with no finetuning at all, which they take as evidence that structure, not just content, is what retrieved text was missing.
arxiv-2601-04577:
Jiachen Liu, Maestro Harmon, and Zechen Zhang dissect how breakthroughs happen, in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI research accelerates yearly, yet the intellectual moves behind strong papers — spotting the gap, importing an idea, reframing the problem — have never been systematically recorded. Their dataset, Sci-Reasoning, traces highly rated papers from the big machine learning conferences of 2023 to 2025 back to the predecessors each built on. Writing the reasoning link between them in structured form.

The pipeline mixes community quality signals with model acceleration and human verification. Across the corpus, fifteen thinking patterns emerge, and three strategies dominate, accounting for over half of all links: reframing around a gap, synthesizing across domains, and shifting the representation. The strongest recipes combine patterns, pairing gap-driven reframing with a representation shift, or cross-domain synthesis with one. The dataset is meant both for studying scientific progress and for training research agents on real reasoning trajectories.
arxiv-2601-05177:
Asmi Haldar and 3 co-authors doubt a stock test for a trapped state of quantum stuff in a 2026 paper. The state, called many-body localization, sets in when flaws trap a quantum set so it can not reach a calm, mixed state. Tests tend to track one bland mean: how fast a stamped mark on the set fades. The team say that mean hides rich acts at the scale of each site.

They zoom in on a chain of spins with strong flaws, and run the best class of runs on it. Site-by-site probes show peaks and rare acts at each spot. The bland mean wipes all that flat. A more keen test counts for more than a fine point. The trapped state is the hope of some quantum stores, ones that must hold facts safe from the churn of heat.
arxiv-2601-05477:
Valery Lunts and Olaf Schnuerer answer, in a 2026 mathematics paper, a structural question about constructible sheaves. Sheaves are tools that track local data on a space and how it fits together. The setting is a stratified topological space, meaning a space split into simpler layers.

The central question asks whether one derived category, built from constructible sheaves, matches another built from sheaves whose cohomology is constructible. Along the way, the authors establish basic facts about locally constant sheaves and about constructible sheaves themselves. Results of this kind matter because derived categories organize much of modern algebraic geometry and topology, and equivalences between them let results move cleanly from one framework to another.
arxiv-2601-05777:
Yaoqi Guo and 6 co-authors cut the running cost of software engineering agents in 2026 with an experience-driven early termination method called EET. Language-model agents that fix issues can burn money through unproductive iterations. Knowing when to stop is therefore as valuable as knowing how to continue.

EET extracts structured experience from earlier issue-resolution runs and uses it to decide when to stop during patch generation and selection. On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, across three representative agents, total cost reportedly fell by roughly a fifth to over a half, with almost no loss in resolution rate. Gains came from terminating about a tenth of issues early and using markedly fewer calls and tokens overall.
arxiv-2601-06077:
What is information worth to a decision maker? Aolin Xu defines that value rigorously in a 2026 paper covering perception, prediction, communication, and common sense. The definitions are decision-theoretic, meaning they measure how much each source improves choices, not just how much data it carries.

The quantities share key properties with Shannon entropy and mutual information, and reduce to them in special settings. One striking result: perception without prediction can have negative value, while prediction alone never does. The measures answer practical design questions for autonomous systems, such as which agent to observe first and how much it matters. Xu also notes possible insight for cognitive and neural science.
arxiv-2601-06277:
Markus J. Aschwanden and 1 co-author test a scaling law linking event energy and duration in astrophysical systems in a 2026 paper. Self-organized criticality describes systems that build up stress and release it in avalanches of all sizes, from solar flares to earthquakes. The fractal-diffusive version makes concrete predictions.

From four assumptions about dimensionality, fractal volume, diffusion, and energy, the model predicts duration grows with energy to a specific power. Two observational studies found exponents close to that prediction. Cases with a narrow range of durations gave much smaller exponents, but the authors show this tracks a truncation bias: limited time coverage distorts the fit. The spread in measured exponents is thus an observational effect, not a physical property of the systems.
arxiv-2601-06377:
An agent that chats for months needs a mind store that can grow and fix its own flaws. Ningning Zhang and 4 co-authors built HiMem for that need in a 2026 paper. Past stores have a hard time with change, scale, and self-fixes in long talks.

HiMem has two tiers. One tier holds tales of past chats, cut at points where the topic shifts or a surprise lands. The next tier holds firm facts, drawn from those tales in a few clean steps. The two tiers link by sense, so a search can jump from tale to fact and back. When new facts clash with old ones, a fix step heals the store. On long-chat tests, HiMem beat the main past tools on truth, fit, and thought, while its cost stayed low.
arxiv-2601-06477:
Bias can pin itself to a place, not just to a sex or a race. Debasmita Panda and 2 co-authors built a test set for that kind of bias in a 2026 paper. Their set, IndRegBias, holds posts from India in plain English and in mixed code-switch text. The posts mock or slight a home state or zone.

The set holds a large pool of posts from Reddit and YouTube, on hot themes of state pride and strife. Each post got a grade for how harsh the slight is, through a tiered mark plan. The team then tried a range of AI models in three modes: no coach, few-shot, and full fine-tune. The first two modes did a poor job of spotting the slight and its grade. Full fine-tune work did far better. The gap shows this bias needs its own tools, tuned to its own ground.
arxiv-2601-06677:
Zohaib Khan, Omer Tafveez, and Zoha Hayat Bhatti test small-model reasoning on a micro-budget in 2026. Recent reasoning advances typically rely on massive scale, they observe. They ask whether strong reasoning can be induced in small models instead.

Their models hold at most one and a half billion parameters. Training runs on a single A40 graphics card for under a day. They use reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for that training. Low-rank adapters keep the trainable footprint small and cheap to store. The paper frames this as plasticity against rigidity in adaptation. Small teams get a recipe for reasoning models without giant clusters. Results would matter for schools and labs with one good GPU.
arxiv-2601-06777:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Ali Lotfi and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers normalized difference layer. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Normalized difference indices have been a staple in remote sensing for decades. They stay reliable under lighting changes produce bounded values and connect well to biophysical signals.

Even so, they are usually treated as a fixed pre processing step with coefficients set to one. Which limits how well they can adapt to a specific learning task. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-06877:
Donghuo Zeng, Roberto Legaspi, and Kazushi Ikeda wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on chat agents that aim to persuade. A good agent of this kind shifts its plan to fit each user. It tracks how the mood and aims of the user change as the chat goes on. The team trains its agent with reinforcement learning, where the agent learns from rewards.

The method has three main parts. One part picks the next move from a set plan and pulls past text that fits the chat. A pull rule called Maximal Marginal Relevance keeps the text on point and fresh. A second part learns a sketch of the user. That sketch has 81 parts and mixes kinds of facts. A third part, named in the full text, ties the sketch to the plan the agent picks.
arxiv-2601-06977:
Zhengjie Xiong and Yangyang Xu wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a fast way to solve hard math tasks in parts. The way is called the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM. The tasks in view split into two blocks of choice. Each block has its own aim, and the aims add up to one shared aim.

Rules bind the two blocks as one. Some rules bend, in the sense that they are not straight lines. Some rules are straight and tie the blocks to each other. Tasks of this shape show up in real work. One case is how to share scarce goods or power across a network. A second case is machine learning with rules the model must obey. The paper gives a form of ADMM that fits this class of tasks.
arxiv-2601-07777:
Linda Albanese and colleagues revisit how a neural network model recalls patterns, comparing serial and parallel updating. Blume-Emery-Griffiths networks are fully connected models for pattern recognition and associative memory. They generalize the standard Hopfield network. Past studies treated them heuristically, mainly with the replica trick under a replica symmetric assumption. Their 2026 notes first rebuild that picture rigorously.

The rigorous route uses Guerra interpolation, a method from spin glass theory. With the existing picture secured, the authors can compare recall modes on firm ground. Serial recall updates neurons one by one; parallel recall updates them together. The difference can change what the memory retrieves. Statistical physicists studying neural networks are the readers. The work replaces heuristic confidence with proof for a classic model.
arxiv-2601-08277:
Yizhuo Rao and co-authors speed up particle-in-cell simulations by using matrix units on modern CPUs. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that these simulations spend most cycles on particle-grid interactions. Fine-grained atomic updates become a severe bottleneck on traditional many-core chips.

New CPUs add matrix processing units built for efficient outer-product operations. Matrix-PIC reshapes the particle-grid work to harness those units. Plasma and fusion researchers rely on particle-in-cell runs that can take huge compute budgets. Cutting the core bottleneck could shorten design cycles for devices modeled this way. The work shows a path to gains without moving to special accelerators.
arxiv-2601-08477: Francesco Dettori and co-authors envision verified empathy for therapy chatbots. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that conversational agents increasingly support mental therapeutic pathways. Empathy is a key non-functional requirement in such settings, with real societal impact. Current chatbot practice gives no systematic way to specify or verify empathy, though. The authors propose a framework joining natural language processing with formal verification. Verified empathy claims could help clinics and regulators judge whether a support bot behaves as promised with vulnerable users.
arxiv-2601-08677:
Serena Dipierro and three co-authors study flat fronts in a type of energy with long range pulls. Think of a wall that splits two states of a stuff. Far parts of the stuff still pull on the wall, and a wave like force acts on it at a set pace. The team asks if flat walls can be the best shape for such energy.

They show flat front forms do exist that give the least energy. They also show what shape the energy takes when seen from far off. At large scale it looks like a local wall cost with a slant that shifts by place. A reader in this math field gets two gains. Flat fronts are real in this long range case, and the large scale cost is now known.
arxiv-2601-09577:
MD Nazmul Alam Shanto, Md. Tanzeem Rahat, and Md. Manzurul Hasan speed up a classic string search. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies permutation pattern matching, also called jumbled or Abelian matching. The task: find a spot in a text where the letter counts match a pattern's counts exactly.

Letter counts are captured by the Parikh vector, one tally per symbol. The authors give linear-time detection under a Parikh budget, plus packing and disjoint selection variants. Jumbled matching shows up in bioinformatics and music search, where order is loose but content matters. Linear time keeps the method usable on very long texts.
arxiv-2601-09677:
Guillermina Senn and four co-authors scale up a hard image problem: sharpening pictures when the blur itself is unknown. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Bayesian semi-blind deconvolution at scale. In blind deconvolution, both the true image and the blur kernel must be guessed from the data.

Semi-blind versions use extra knowledge about the image or the blur to narrow the search. The Bayesian frame tracks uncertainty instead of betting on one answer. Scaling that care to large images is the paper's challenge. Sharper recovery matters in astronomy, microscopy, and medical scans.
arxiv-2601-09777:
An ALICE collaboration paper uses short-lived particles to probe the final stage of heavy-ion collisions. The 2026 arXiv paper studies the hadronic phase through how resonances spread in momentum and angle. Resonances decay so fast that their yields carry fingerprints of the medium they died in.

After the quark-gluon plasma cools, hadrons keep colliding for a while in a hadronic phase. New collisions can destroy resonance signals, while fresh reactions rebuild them. The balance shapes the yields physicists measure. The paper also uses resonances to probe the internal structure of exotic states. Together, the measurements test how matter behaves as it freezes out.
arxiv-2601-09977:
Rikizo Ikuta studies how light grains clash in groups of two and three. When two light grains meet, their clash rate drops in a known dip. That dip is the Hong Ou Mandel effect. More noise in the light tends to make the dip less sharp.

Ikuta asks if the same trend holds for three grains. He finds that it does not. In a circuit with a fair shape, the trend can break. Noise can shift the clash rate in a way that two grain tests would not hint at. The result warns that rules from two grain tests do not scale in a plain way.
arxiv-2601-10077:
Francesco Maria Iudica lifts a classic lift into p-adic form. The Cogdell lift maps cycles on Picard surfaces to forms on the elliptic side. Such maps link two worlds of forms. A p-adic form lets the map bend with a prime p.

Iudica gets more than one result. In part one, he lifts the adjoint Kudla lift. He uses a p-adic Kudla lift built in past work. The paper then works out what the lift yields. Maps of this kind aid the study of L values and cycles. They show how forms on one side cast light on the other side.
arxiv-2601-10277:
Evangelos Kolyvas, Alexandros Antonov, and Spyros Voulgaris speed up how blocks spread in a chain net. Chain nets have been built for over a decade. Yet their rate stays low. Each block must reach all nodes in the net. Slow spread caps the whole rate.

Nodes in such nets link at random. That random web adds lag. The team made SCRamble, a self tuning overlay. It reshapes links as the net runs. It seeks a web that spreads blocks fast. The work tests the overlay in sims of chain nets. A faster web could lift the rate cap.
arxiv-2601-10477:
Yu Wang and co authors cut city scenes by what places mean, not just how they look. A city holds homes, schools, parks, roads, and more. From a sky shot, plain tools can find built forms with ease. They can mark blocks, roofs, and water well. Social forms are more hard.

A school and an office can look the same from the sky. Their split is in use, not in shape. The team use sight and text thought to make that split. Their tool reads cues of use in the shot. It aims for maps that serve real city tasks, like plan and care work.
arxiv-2601-10877:
Ludovic Righetti and Vincent Boulanin ask whether open robotics innovation threatens peace and security. Open access to papers, software, and hardware is central to robotics. It lowers entry barriers, supports reproducible science, and speeds reliable system building. The same openness, they note, sharpens the dual-use risk built into robotics research.

Open tools lower the bar for states and non-state actors to build robots for military or harmful ends. The authors weigh that risk against the clear gains of openness. Their essay speaks to researchers, funders, and policymakers who must set the terms of sharing. It asks the field to face its security shadow without giving up what makes it thrive.
arxiv-2601-10977:
Haoran Xu proposes a scheme for parabolic equations that keeps solutions positive. Parabolic equations model heat, diffusion, and option prices. The scheme spreads wide, using a broad stencil, and it is built on the Feynman-Kac formula. That formula writes the solution as a conditional expectation over a diffusion process.

Rather than the usual compact Markov chain shortcuts, Xu approximates that expectation directly with the wide stencil. The design aims to be accurate and positive at once. Staying positive matters because negative values are nonsense in the models it targets. The scheme serves financial work, the author's home field, where prices must stay sensible.
arxiv-2601-11277:
Gauhar Abbas works through hadronic tau decays at higher orders in QCD. The 2026 preprint is an introduction-style work from IIT-BHU. QCD is the theory of the strong force in particle physics. Its strength is set by one key number, the strong coupling.

That number, alpha-s, rules strong dynamics at all energy scales. Tau decays give a clean place to measure it well. The tau is a heavy cousin of the electron. When it decays to hadrons, QCD shapes the outcome. Higher-order terms sharpen the link between data and alpha-s. The work sets out that link in step-by-step form.
arxiv-2601-11477:
Itauany do Nascimento Barroso and Hermano Velten model dark matter as a condensate. Their 2026 preprint adds a Kapitza potential to the setup. Bose-Einstein condensate dark matter is a studied alternative model. It casts dark matter as a vast quantum fluid.

A Kapitza potential was just realized in a lab BEC. That first realization drives fresh theory work on the system. The team asks what such a potential does in galaxies. Their focus is a core-tail structure in galactic halos. A dense core with a long tail is a known BEC trait. The Kapitza term may reshape that profile in testable ways. The work links tabletop quantum optics to galactic scales.
arxiv-2601-11977:
Ren He, Yinliang Xu, Jinfeng Wang, Jeremy Watson, and Jian Song forecast power prices in one shot while data stay private. Power forecasts use series with complex links across sites. Rules on privacy bar full data share between regions.

Past tools need much expert input and fail to move well to new sites. Pre-trained series models help, but their zero-shot skill on such tasks is weak. The team guide a set of expert models with extra input data. Their aim is a good first forecast with no site training.  A strong first call saves time for grid staff each day.
arxiv-2601-12177:
Amalendu Krishna and Subhadip Majumder build Kato's ramification filtration via the de Rham-Witt complex, with applications. They work on a regular scheme of positive characteristic that is F-finite. A simple normal crossing divisor marks the bad locus.

They define a filtration on the de Rham-Witt complex of the open part. Ramification gauges how wild maps behave near the divisor. A de Rham-Witt form links that gauge to cohomology. The work adds tools for arithmetic geometry in positive characteristic.  The filtration is built for divisors of that cross form.  The applications show the reach of the new filtration.
arxiv-2601-12377:
Haobo Xi and six co authors work on how a moving LiDAR unit keeps track of where it is. Their tool builds maps from small cubes called voxels. Good maps help the unit place itself with care as it moves. Past tools in this line fit planes with all points in a cube at once.

That all in approach can go wrong in a few ways. stray points can pull a plane off course. Large planes can be split when they should stay whole. Planes from distinct surfaces can also be merged by mistake. The team puts forward R-VoxelMap, which fits planes step by step in a recursive way. The aim is a more exact map and sharper placement.
arxiv-2601-12577:
Primate decision making gets a fresh look through deep recurrent reinforcement learning in work with no author named in the record. Decades of research have mapped the neural circuits behind primate choices in detail. Less is known about why those circuits exist in the first place. Theory holds that they evolved to maximize reward under hard conditions. Those conditions are noisy signals that change over time.

The work trains recurrent agents by reinforcement learning in such settings. It then checks whether primate like behavior emerges from that training. If it does, reward driven learning may explain why the brain circuits look as they do. That would tie mechanism to function in a clean way. The study sits between neuroscience and machine learning.
arxiv-2601-13077:
Sanghun Lee studies the shape traits of surfaces that end at a rim. The surfaces obey a calm rule called g stability, tied to how their null spread acts. That spread must stay at or above a fixed rim value set by a given map.

Lee proves two kinds of results. First, such a calm surface with a free rim can carry a metric with plus scalar curve and a least rim, if fit terms hold. The claim links calm shape to curve in a clean way. Such links help maths staff who study black hole rims and trapped surfaces. The paper adds care to a niche where shape, curve, and rims meet.
arxiv-2601-13377:
Diogo D. Carvalho, Luis O. Silva, and E. Paulo Alves teach a machine to learn how plasma bits hit, from phase space data. Far from balance, plasma hits and wave acts mix in hard, time shift, chance ways. Past work joined simulators that can be taught by gradients with reads of plasma phase space.

The new work grows that join. The learnt hit rule can shift with time. It can also span more than one instant, in an integro form. Such a rule fits a plasma whose back cloth shifts as it runs. For fusion and space plasma teams, a learnt hit rule from real reads beats a fixed guess.
arxiv-2601-13677:
Carsten Lüth and co-authors seek a reliable way to pick which images experts should label in 2026. In 3D medical image segmentation, expert labels cost much time and money. Active learning picks the most useful cases to label next. Yet past methods fail to beat even random picks, once random baselines are tuned for 3D data.

The team presents a simple method that at last beats that random baseline. A method that truly helps could cut labeling costs in a big way. Hospitals and labs could train strong models with far fewer expert hours. The result gives the field a firm base to build on.
arxiv-2601-13777:
Zvi Chapnik, Yizhar Or, and Shai Revzen compare ways to learn how a simple robot moves in 2026. Geometric mechanics shows how shape changes let a body move through its world. In high-friction settings, the whole interaction is captured by a motility map. The team built a physical robot just to test learning methods for that map.

Their robot has under-actuated degrees of freedom, fewer motors than motions. Its contact with the ground is hard to model by hand. They compare methods that learn the map from motion tracking data. Sample-efficient learning matters when each robot trial costs time.
arxiv-2601-13877:
Ignacio Santamaria and co-authors map a special set of matrices and use it for wireless design in 2026. The set holds matrices that are both unitary and symmetric. They characterize this manifold rigorously for the first time. They derive its tangent space and its geodesics, the shortest paths on it.

A geodesic parameterization through a real symmetric matrix follows. It yields a new Riemannian optimization algorithm with a rare trait. The method needs no adaptation parameter to be set by hand. The target use is BD-RIS systems, a new kind of smart radio surface.
arxiv-2601-13977:
Carlos D'Andrea and Alicia Dickenstein extend a classic vanishing theorem to toric settings in 2026. Residues appear in complex and algebraic geometry, in interpolation and duality. The first global vanishing result was the Euler-Jacobi theorem of 1835, for the projective plane. It says certain sums of residues must be zero.

Their toric Euler-Jacobi theorem carries that idea to toric varieties. They also study zeros at infinity, points where the pattern may break. Vanishing theorems act as checks that keep computations honest. A toric form suits the spaces used in modern geometry and physics.
arxiv-2601-14077:
Lars Reining and co-authors release a Python package for making two-tone test images in 2026. Mooney images are high-contrast, two-tone visual stimuli made by thresholding photos. They let researchers separate image content from image understanding. An ideal Mooney image looks unrecognizable at first glance.

After seeing the original template, the image becomes fully interpretable. That flip makes Mooney images valuable for studying visual perception. Their MooneyMaker package creates such ambiguous images in a standard way. Shared tools help perception labs compare results across studies. The pack makes the balance point easy to set and share. Labs can match their sets to a known scale and pool results with trust.
arxiv-2601-14177:
M. Voyer and Q. Changeat precompute aerosol traits to speed the study of exoplanet skies in 2026. The James Webb Space Telescope can record light across a wide range of colors. It can pick up the marks left by many kinds of cloud grains, from silicates to Titan tholins. Teams use retrievals to read such data and work out what floats in a planet's air.

The team gives ready grids of how these grains block, scatter, and bend light. Off-the-shelf grids make each new fit start much fast. Teams can pull a set at once and start a fit the same day. More worlds can then be checked in the same span of telescope time. The grids cover many kinds of dust and ice found in the sky.
arxiv-2601-14577:
Ariel Bruner and Mona Singh present a fast tool for metabolic modeling in this 2026 paper. Constraint-based metabolic modeling is the predominant framework for simulating cellular metabolism. Its central assumption is that metabolism operates at a steady state. In that state, the production and consumption rates of each metabolite are balanced. The assumption imposes linear constraints on the fluxes of biochemical reactions.

Many modeling tasks build on that linear frame, but they can still be slow or awkward. The team's tool, FBApro, is a fast, simple linear transformation. Its title says it serves diverse metabolic modeling tasks. Readers get a simpler way to run flux balance style studies of how cells route their chemistry.
arxiv-2601-14777:
Jiaxuan Liu, Yang Xiang, Han Zhao, Xiangang Li, and Zhenhua Ling build a movie dubbing system in this 2026 paper. Movie dubbing synthesizes speech from scripts, conditioned on video scenes. It requires accurate lip sync, so the voice matches the mouth. It also needs faithful timbre transfer, so the voice sounds like the actor. Character identity and emotion must be modeled properly too.

The team presents FunCineForge, a unified dataset toolkit and model for zero-shot movie dubbing. Zero-shot means it can dub a new actor or scene without retraining on them. The setting is diverse cinematic scenes, as the title says. Readers get tools and data for dubbing films across languages with the performance intact.
arxiv-2601-14877:
Miguel J. S. Martinho, Hamed Valizadegan, and co-authors put a vetting tool to work on data from the TESS space telescope. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses full-frame images from TESS. Those images hold light curves for millions of stars, not just a picked few.

A dip in a star's light can mark a planet crossing in front of it. But full-frame data makes these transit signals harder to check. False alarms are common. The team applies ExoMiner++ 2.0, a newer and stronger form of their vetting system, to sort real signals from noise.
arxiv-2601-15177:
Lorenzo Fernández Maimó, Alberto Huertas Celdrán, and co-authors manage a deep learning guard for 5G networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with anomaly detection, the spotting of odd traffic that may signal an attack. The system runs in a fog and edge computing setting.

Fifth generation networks push compute out to the network's edge. That spread-out design supports apps and data work close to the user. The authors study how to manage the detection system itself over time. The settings must adapt over time as the network and its threats change day by day.
arxiv-2601-15277:
Sahar Tahmasebi, Eric Müller-Budack, and Ralph Ewerth harden fake news detectors against mood tricks. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with misinformation, a pressing social problem. Sentiment has long been a useful signal for spotting fake news stories.

Detectors read which sentiments fake news carries, or use sentiment and emotion as features. That reliance opens a door to attack. A story's tone can be tweaked to fool the detector. The authors test large language models for robust detection under such adversarial sentiment attacks. The tests show how much a tone shift alone can sway a verdict.
arxiv-2601-15477:
Gaetano Ferraro and Michele Castellana study how proteins shape cell membranes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Biological membranes are active surfaces, not fixed walls. Proteins embedded in them can bend and reshape them. That shaping affects how the membrane works. Past studies covered small bends in depth, the authors note.

Many real processes involve strong bends instead. The pair therefore study the large-deformation regime. They look at how lipid membranes and protein inclusions act on each other there. Their tool is the finite-element method, a standard way to simulate such systems. The work speaks to cell biology at a basic level. It asks how the parts of a membrane push and pull when shapes change a lot.
arxiv-2601-15877:
Chahat Ahuja studies which lattice points can be seen from the origin in a 2026 arXiv paper. In the classic problem, sight lines are straight. The share of visible points is a known constant involving the zeta function. Later work generalized sight lines to monomial curves. There, the density takes a similar zeta form. Ahuja works with a broader family of polynomial curves. Visibility along curves asks whether a point is the first lattice point on its curve.

Families of curves bend the notion of a blocked view. Densities then depend on the curve family's shape. Such problems join number theory with geometry in a pleasing way. Exact densities are rare prizes. The paper extends a line of results that began with straight lines and grew one curve family at a time.
arxiv-2601-16277:
Nikita Nedelko weighs neutrino mass bounds from sky data with SPT views. His 2026 preprint joins SPT-3G views from 2018 with Planck lens data. It also adds low scale parts of Planck maps. The sum of neutrino mass sets how space form grew. DESI BAO bounds on that sum have drawn much note of late.

Nedelko asks if SPT plus Planck ease those DESI bounds. Joint fits can shift the mass sum that best fits all data. A shift would change what mass range teams take as firm. The work tests one data join against a hot claim. It stays close to the fits and their terms.
arxiv-2601-16877:
Eugene Gorsky and Anton Mellit link knot math to a famed coin space. Torus knots wrap a ring in a set braid. Their (n, n+1) type is the next twist past plain. A rich homology grades such knots in fine steps. Their 2026 preprint builds a straight bridge from that grade to diagonal coins.

Coins here are poly forms that stay fixed when swapped in pairs. The bridge picks out hook-shaped parts of that space. From it, the team reads how key classes act. Those acts form a Lie-type rule set on the space. Knot grades thus gain a new, plain face for work.
arxiv-2601-17277:
Mohammad Rifqi Farhansyah and co-authors present PingPong, a test set for code-switching talk. Code-switching means mixing languages in one chat. Most of the world does it each day. Yet few test sets show its true mess. PingPong holds natural multi-party dialogues that switch codes. It covers five language mixes. Some chats use three languages at once.

A fair test set shows where language models fail real users. Models that ace one-language tests can stumble here. PingPong gives builders a true target for mixed talk. It can guide training for chat tools in mixed-language homes and cities. The work fills a clear gap in how models are judged.
arxiv-2601-17577:
Emilio Barkett asks if language models form status hierarchies. Status orders rank people by respect and perceived skill. They shape schools, firms, and boards alike. Models train on human text full of such patterns. Barkett asks if models replay those ranks when agents interact. Multi-agent setups are where such dynamics would show.

If models sort each other by status, their group choices could skew. A high-status agent's word may count for too much. That would mirror a human flaw in machine teams. Early maps of the trait help designers counter it. The work joins social science with AI study. It treats models as social actors under test.
arxiv-2601-17777:
Xiaoyu Liu, Xiaoyu Guan, Di Liang, and Xianjie Wu study a clash that arises when language models learn many tasks at once. Fine-tuning is the step that adapts a trained model to new tasks. When tasks pull in different ways, gains on one can hurt scores on another. The authors call this the seesaw effect.

Their 2026 preprint argues that the clash comes from treating all model weights the same. Weights differ in how much each task needs them. The method in the title, DPI, uses that spread of needs to guide updates. The goal is tuning with less cross-task harm, so a model can learn new skills without losing old ones as fast.
arxiv-2601-18377:
Anna Bertani and four colleagues study why false claims about COVID-19 spread more in some lands than in others. The flood of false claims has been called an infodemic, and it can slow the work of health staff. The team asks which traits of a land track with that risk.

They draw on posts from Twitter across three years and on facts from a group of rich lands. The facts cover pay, school, health, and work, grouped into a set of broad signs. With math tools that shrink many signs into a few, they trace how the links shift as the health crisis goes on. The work points to social roots of false claims, not just to bad posts by a few people.
arxiv-2601-18477:
Giuseppe Destefanis and six colleagues audit how tests of bug-guess tools are run and shared. Such tools learn to flag parts of code that are apt to hold flaws. In this field the main proof is a run on real code, so the worth of a claim hangs on how that run was planned and told.

The team look for weak spots in that chain. A run can leak facts, pick a kind test set, or skip the facts a reader needs to check it. Each flaw can make a weak tool look strong. Their audit aims to lift the bar for what counts as proof. That would help teams trust the grades they read and pick tools with more care.
arxiv-2601-18577:
Sangwon Jang and five colleagues teach a video tool to check and fix its own work as it builds each clip. New video tools can make fine clips, but their moves often break the laws of how stuff moves. A ball may float, or a cup may pass through a desk. Past fixes call in a judge tool or train the tool on more clips. Both paths cost a lot and still miss fine slips.

Their plan lets the tool sample a clip, grade its own moves, and sample again with the grade in mind. The loop needs no new training and no judge from out-side. A self-check loop could lift the truth of moves in clips for film, ads, and games. It could also cut the cost of each good clip.
arxiv-2601-18677:
Y. A. Rouzoumka and five colleagues build a radar tool to spot weak marks in a loud, rough sea of noise. At sea, waves and rain make a noise that does not act like the plain noise of maths books. A weak mark, such as a small boat, can drown in that noise. The team train a smart tool on the noise alone, with no marks in the training set at all.

A mark then shows up as a thing the tool did not learn to build. That is the trick: what does not fit the noise must be a mark. The team add steps that clean the noise first and blend the call with a known strong test. Their blend aims to catch faint marks that old tests miss. Sea radar that sees more could save lives and catch crime at sea.
arxiv-2601-18777:
Abhishek Divekar and Anirban Majumder fix a flaw in the use of language models as judges of search worth. To grade a search tool takes a large set of human grades on which hits count. That cost has pushed teams to let models grade in the place of folk. But model judges lean: they may prize long hits, or hits in their own style. A lean judge makes the search grade lean too.

Their plan uses a small set of true human grades to fix the lean of a large set of model grades. The fix blends the two in a way backed by stats. A fixed grade could let teams trust cheap model grades at scale. That would cut the cost of search tests a lot. It rests on a small, dear set of human truth to keep the whole firm.
arxiv-2601-18877:
Sarah Blunt and five colleagues chart how the tilt of the paths of big far worlds spreads. Each such world runs on a path that is more or less stretched, from a round ring to a long loop. The shape of that spread holds clues to how the worlds were born and how they were stirred since. The team use a clean set of finds made by one long hunt that read the wobble of stars.

They fix the counts for the worlds the hunt would miss, so the spread is fair. They work out how oft big worlds show at each mass, span, and path stretch. The counts rise with span for both light and heavy big worlds, out to a wide span. In that fair set they find a bump in path stretch at a set mark for the heaviest worlds.
arxiv-2601-19377:
Nicolas Fintzi and Jean-Lou Pierson compute how inertia tweaks the drag on droplets in a slow flow. A sphere like droplet moves through a uniform stream, and the flow pushes back. They work in the dilute limit, few droplets, and at low but nonzero Reynolds number, where inertia just starts to count.

Using the reciprocal theorem, they get the force and its first and second moments on the droplet. Those moments set the rheology, how the whole suspension flows and thickens. Sprays, emulsions, and microfluidics all live in this regime, so exact drag laws feed many designs.
arxiv-2601-19877:
Gunnar Birke and four colleagues design a numerical method for wave propagation on awkward grids. Cut-cell meshes arise when a grid is sliced by a curved boundary, leaving tiny sliver cells. Standard time stepping is forced into tiny steps by those cells. A domain-of-dependence stabilization fixes this by widening the stencil where cells are cut.

Their scheme preserves energy: the discrete energy is either conserved or dissipated, never spuriously created. Space is handled by a discontinuous Galerkin method and time by an explicit Runge-Kutta scheme. The test problem is the linear wave equation. Energy control plus large stable steps make simulations near complex boundaries practical. Such meshes appear in engineering and geophysics alike.
arxiv-2601-20177:
Si-Wei Dai and five colleagues extract parton fragmentation functions using a physics-informed neural network. These functions describe how a high-energy quark or gluon turns into the particles seen in a detector. Accurate versions are needed to predict many strong-interaction processes, and they must be drawn from experimental data.

Standard fits assume a fixed formula shape and then evolve the result across energy scales. The neural approach instead builds the known physics into the network itself. That could give more flexible fits with fewer shape assumptions, and sharper predictions for collider experiments that test the strong force.
arxiv-2601-20277:
Feng Yuan, Jingsong He, and Yi Cheng study a stem structure that appears when three solitons interact in the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili II equation. A stem is a localized feature that links the corners of two V-shaped wave forms. In a resonant three-soliton interaction, stems vanish and reconnect as the waves pass through each other.

The authors focus on stems of variable length in this resonance. Such wave patterns model shallow water and plasma waves, where solitons keep their shape after meeting. Knowing how stems form and reconnect helps predict the extreme waves that can arise when several wave trains cross.
arxiv-2601-20777:
O. Ly studies a purely magnetic route to spin currents with rich harmonics. The 2026 paper is about spin pumping, a basic way to move spin through a material. In its standard form, spin pumping gives a simple response at the driving frequency alone. Recent work showed that spin-orbit coupling can break that limit. It can drive strongly nonlinear spin and charge currents.

Ly asks what magnetism alone can do, with no spin-orbit help. The paper pursues high-harmonic spin pumping by a magnetic route. Harmonics are responses at multiples of the drive frequency. Rich harmonics would give engineers more knobs for spin-based devices. The study adds to the basic physics of how spin moves and can be shaped in magnetic materials.
arxiv-2601-21177:
Xin Peng and Ang Gao speed up a key step in flow-based sampling of physical systems. Their 2026 paper presents Flow Perturbation++, a multi-step unbiased Jacobian estimator. Continuous normalizing flows can sample the Boltzmann distribution without bias. Their growth in high dimensions is capped by one cost. Jacobian determinants need as many backward passes as there are dimensions. That cost grows fast with system size.

Stochastic estimators cut the cost but add bias. The first Flow Perturbation method is unbiased yet noisy. Flow Perturbation++ uses multi-step estimates to tame that noise. It keeps the estimator unbiased while it calms the variance. Sound Boltzmann sampling underlies free-energy work in chemistry. A faster, honest estimator widens what can be simulated. The gain is real speed with no loss of trust in the numbers. That mix is rare in this field.
arxiv-2601-21477:
Tobias Schmidt and Kai Cui extend mean-field control to agents linked by sparse networks. Mean-field methods tame huge multi-agent systems by treating the crowd as a smooth average. Classic versions assume every agent interacts with every other, which real networks rarely do.

The authors build a framework for large sparse graphs, where each agent has only a few neighbors. They connect local limit theory to graph neural networks through the statistics of each neighborhood. That bridge lets control methods scale to road networks, power grids, and robot swarms, where links are few but the system is vast.
arxiv-2601-22577:
G. G. L. Nashed and A. Eid explore wormholes held open by holographic dark energy in a modified gravity. A wormhole is a tunnel through space that a traveler could, in theory, cross. Their 2026 preprint works in a gravity where curvature and matter's trace jointly set the rules.

Holographic dark energy, drawn from a bound on information, serves as the tunnel's source. The team check what tunnel shapes the math allows. Such work tests how far modified gravity can go. It is theory at the edge of the known. Each sound shape sharpens the debate.
arxiv-2601-22677:
Yizhou Liu and five co-authors propose a way to tell dark matter kinds apart by the glow of cosmic filaments. The standard model says filaments — the web that links galaxies — are clumpy. Their 2026 preprint notes that warm dark matter, offered to fix small-scale snags, makes smoother, plainer filaments.

Mapping Lyman-alpha glow along filaments could show which picture is right. A clean test between rival dark matters is rare and prized. The work gives observers a target to aim at. It ties a faint glow to a deep question.
arxiv-2601-22977:
Lei You asks how to tell whether an AI model is truly new, or just a copy in disguise. AI has grown into ecosystems of base models and specialized adapters. Telling real novelty from redundancy is now a governance problem, since claims of novelty drive money and trust.

The framework audits uniqueness with in-silico quasi-experimental design, a statistical setup run inside the system. It probes how models behave under controlled changes. A fair novelty test could guide buyers, regulators, and builders judging a crowded model market. In-silico experiments make the audit repeatable, letting the same behavioral test run across many models and adapters.
arxiv-2601-23077:
José de Jesús Bernal-Alvarado and David Delepine fix a mismatch at the heart of epidemic forecasting. Standard models like SIR, SEIR, and SIRS track how many people are ill at once. But real reports count new cases per day, a flow, and fitting stock models to flow data goes wrong.

That mismatch can shrink predicted peaks by as much as half. Their universal pre-processor converts the data properly before fitting, across all three model types. Cleaner inputs mean forecasts that health officials can trust more. Peak underestimation is the costly symptom named in the study, the error that leaves hospitals unprepared at the worst moment.
arxiv-2602-00077: Francisco Martínez and María P. Frías set out an automated method for forecasting single variable time series with regression trees and their ensembles, bagging and random forests. The paper covers autoregressive design and recursive forecasts, choice of lag traits, trends, and seasonal patterns. Tests show accuracy on par with established statistical tools such as exponential smoothing and ARIMA. The authors also describe public software that implements every proposed strategy, so readers can run the full method rather than rebuild it from scratch.
arxiv-2602-00277: Omkar Salpekar and colleagues train LLMs on 100000 GPUs with fault tolerant hybrid shared data parallelism. Synchronous training stalls when any GPU fails, since all units must stay healthy at once. Their FT-HSDP design treats data parallel replicas as fault tolerance units. When a failure hits, only the replica holding the failed GPU or server goes offline and restarts. Other replicas keep training, aided by a fault tolerant all reduce protocol for gradient exchange.
arxiv-2602-00377: Zhaochen Hong and Jiaxuan You introduce DecompressionLM, a deterministic, zero shot concept graph system. Probing methods rely on set queries, limiting work to known concepts. It discovers what models encode without set queries or shared state. It targets three limits: coupling that loads frequent prefixes, decoding that suppresses long tail concepts, and scale limits from sequential exploration. Using Van der Corput sequences with arithmetic coding, it enables fixed, parallel generation without shared state. Across two model families, activation aware quantization expands concept coverage by 30 to 170 percent.
arxiv-2602-00477: Zhexiong Liu and Diane Litman tackle revision generation, where a text must show what its writer truly intends. Few-shot language-model methods falter when several intents tangle, while fine-tuning on intent-based prompts needs large labelled sets that the revision field lacks. Their Intention-Tuning method works layer by layer, picking a subset of layers to learn intents and passing what they learn on to revision writing. On small revision sets it proves both strong and cheap to run, beating several lightweight fine-tuning baselines.
arxiv-2602-00677: Arul Pandian B and colleagues describe GBD-DART, a new small radio telescope array at Gauribidanur. It targets bright pulsars and solar transients between 130 and 350 MHz. The array uses 64 short dipoles in a checkerboard layout. Opposite pairs are combined for dual-polarised operation. One tile is fully commissioned. It already runs in transit-observing mode. It has detected strong pulsars and solar flares over seven months. The backend limits instantaneous bandwidth to 16 MHz. The array is also a low-cost training platform for radio astronomy.
arxiv-2602-00777: Xuan Ai and colleagues present HyLRA for fast long-context inference, where attention's squared cost and Key-Value cache memory bottleneck large language models. Sparse attention with rigid patterns or harsh pruning fails to balance speed and accuracy. Layer profiles reveal two traits: some layers need full attention to avoid feature distortion, while consecutive layers share many critical tokens. Tests show throughput gains of 6% to 46% with similar performance and under 1% accuracy loss, beating leading sparse attention methods.
arxiv-2602-00977: Pengyue Yang and colleagues judge language model answers from the shape of activity, not from token odds alone. Their Structural Confidence frame reads mixed signals from a model's final-layer hidden-state path, blending spectral, local-variation, and shape traits. These traits catch stability patterns that odds and sentence embeddings miss. Tests across four benchmarks, FEVER, SciFact, WikiBio-hallucination, and TruthfulQA, show strong results against baselines on AUROC and AUPR. Unlike sampling methods that need many runs plus a helper model, this frame needs one deterministic forward pass.
arxiv-2602-01077: Haopeng Li and co-authors speed up diffusion transformers with PISA, a sparse focus plan that keeps the whole view. Block-sparse focus drops weak blocks to save time, but that bites hard at high sparsity. PISA notes weak-block scores hold a steady shape, so it can guess them well with block-wise Taylor math, not junk them. Strong blocks get exact math, the rest get good guesses, giving near-full focus at less than square cost. Video and image tests show speed gains with top quality kept.
arxiv-2602-01177: Ayanava Dasgupta and co-authors tie privacy, steadiness, and broad use in quantum learning in one frame. Learning runs are cast as quantum tools with mixed classic-quantum outputs, and losses as observables. Under a sub-Gaussian rule, a steadiness gauge caps the mean broad-use gap, and quantum Renyi gaps give a high-chance bound. In a trusted handler case, quantum differential privacy caps leaked info and yields a privacy-to-use pledge. For shady handlers, a new admissibility rule keeps privacy and full info use in tune.
arxiv-2602-01477: Pietro Carlotti and co-authors give a new reading of evidential deep learning. They prove its training amounts to amortized variational inference inside a hierarchical Bayesian model built on pseudo-likelihood. That lens exposes a flaw: standard evidential learning mixes epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, breeding steady overconfidence on OOD inputs. Their fix, Density-Informed Pseudo-count EDL, splits prediction from uncertainty size. It gauges the conditional label distribution apart from the marginal input density. The split keeps evidence in high-density regions while pulling OOD predictions toward a uniform prior.
arxiv-2602-01777: M. Arashi and colleagues treat gradient as a high dimensional estimation where theory shows mini batch gradients are inadmissible. They build an estimator that shrinks noisy mini batch gradients adaptively, pulling them toward a stable estimator from momentum. Shrinkage intensity comes from an estimate of noise variance using optimizer statistics.
