arxiv-2603-00877: Grewal and four colleagues rework flow-based design tools so they can steer protein and molecule search with sound variational methods. Their Active Flow Matching acts on endpoint spreads along the flow, letting gradient guidance push toward strong candidates while keeping these search and sampling methods rigorous. On tight-budget online design tasks, the forward form rivals the best known methods while balancing search and use of known wins.
arxiv-2603-01077: Hamzi, Owhadi, and Vaidya extend kernel methods for Koopman modes from fixed systems to random systems. Noise turns transport from first-order wave-like to a second-order smoothing type. Ray paths then give way to Feynman-Kac chance pictures for all three kernel builds. They prove the kernels match under an even-spread rule and build a point-fit plan with error bounds splitting fit error from sampling error. Mild noise can steady math, tested on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and curved systems.
arxiv-2603-02077:
Ming-Hao Liu, Christophe De Beule, Alina Mrenca-Kolasinska, and colleagues extend a scalable graphene model to strained sheets. Their 2026 work builds on a tight-binding model that speeds quantum transport simulations in the Dirac regime. Strain, from stretched or bent lattices, is vital for graphene device design yet costly to simulate at scale.

The scaled model carries over to strained graphene once displacement fields are scaled correctly. In-plane displacements scale with the factor itself, while out-of-plane ones scale with its square root. Under those rules, the long-wavelength theory stays invariant, the team proves. Extensive simulations check the laws through pseudomagnetic fields and local density of states. Pseudo-Landau levels and hybrid levels under real magnetic fields follow, plus transport through a strain barrier like a recent experiment.
arxiv-2603-02177:
Gilles Weymann-Despres, Léo Vacher, Michael Jones, and colleagues study sky polarization patterns in this 2026 paper. Maps of the early universe are blurred by glow from our own galaxy. One glow type, synchrotron light, comes from fast electrons in magnetic fields. Sorting its light into two pattern families helps separate galaxy glow from ancient signals.

That sorting step is not local, so it can make simple spectra look complex. The authors build a compact way to track how each pattern's spectrum bends with frequency. In toy and template skies, plain pattern strengths gained the most fake complexity. Two spin-preserving views kept clear meaning with only mild distortion. The team also gives tests, using three frequency bands, for whether one simple law fits the data.
arxiv-2603-02277:
Rahul Marchand, Art O Cathain, Jerome Wynne, and colleagues test whether language models can escape software sandboxes in this 2026 study. AI agents now run code, edit files, and use networks on their own. They usually work inside containers, sealed boxes meant to contain harm. The team built a safe benchmark that measures breakout skill directly.

The benchmark hides a flag outside the box, in a setup with no known flaws. Flaws are then added across setup errors, excess privileges, kernel bugs, and runtime gaps. When flaws existed, models found and used them to break out. That result shows why such tests are needed before trusting sandboxes. Sealed boxes must keep proving they can hold stronger models.
arxiv-2603-02377:
Edward Krock, Mughaid Ali, Haizhong Weng, and colleagues find new Brewster angles in thin films in this 2026 physics paper. The Brewster angle is where reflected polarized light hits a minimum. It arises from the contrast in refractive index between two materials. The classic result covers only the electric dipole part of the light's response.

Splitting the response into multipole parts reveals more such angles. Magnetic dipole and both quadrupole terms have their own Brewster angles, for both polarizations. Their equations show the moments must turn real-valued at those angles. Applied to a thin silicon nitride film, the theory uncovers a hidden interference effect. Magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole terms must cancel to reveal the angle there. Some new angles appear only in a narrow wavelength range.
arxiv-2603-02477:
Mubarak Olaoluwa and Hassen Drira recognize human motion from skeleton data in this 2026 paper. Skeleton sequences live in curved, non-Euclidean spaces, unlike flat image grids. Geometric deep learning is built for exactly such data. Their network, E2E-GNet, processes motion end to end in that curved setting.

A geometric transform layer sharpens the split between different motions. A special activation then projects the data onto a flat space for classification. Projection can distort skeleton shapes and blur key cues. A distortion-aware layer limits that damage during training. Tests across five data sets in three domains beat rival methods at lower cost. Ablation studies confirm each new layer pulls its weight.
arxiv-2603-02777:
Bhavesh Valecha, Jens-Uwe Sommer, and Abhinav Sharma study how long chain molecules drift inside a bath that pushes them in waves. Many living systems steer motion with chemical signals that change over time. The authors model ideal Rouse polymers sitting in a self-propulsion wave field that varies across space and time.

Through simplified analysis backed by simulations, they find the response depends on chain length and shape. Long chains, rings, and star-shaped chains ride the wave, drifting along with it. Short chains and fully connected nets drift the other way, against the signal. Because shape alone flips the direction, designers could steer soft materials by choosing polymer topology rather than changing the bath.
arxiv-2603-02977:
Prezemysław Górka and Mauro Sanchiz settle a question about averaging behavior in spaces of rough-smooth functions. Their 2026 paper studies Hölder spaces, whose members are functions over a metric space whose wiggliness is capped by a chosen exponent. The weak Banach-Saks property asks whether some subsequence of any weakly converging sequence has averages that converge in norm.

The answer they prove is no, in full generality. For every infinite metric space and every allowed exponent, the Hölder space fails the property. A single clean counterexample regime thus covers all cases at once. Such negative results map the limits of compactness-style arguments in function spaces, steering later work away from dead ends.
arxiv-2603-03477:
Robin Silber and four colleagues develop the theory of a third-order optical effect in magnetic nickel films. Light reflecting off a magnetized surface twists in ways that encode the magnetization, the Kerr effect. Second-order versions are well known; the team recently reported the first systematic sightings of the cubic version, which grows with the cube of magnetization, in one nickel orientation. Their 2026 paper supplies the detailed theory.

A third-order magneto-optic tensor, described by two independent parameters in cubic crystals, completes the surface response up to third order alongside the known linear and quadratic tensors. Full Kerr equations are derived for both face orientations of cubic nickel. Eight-directional measurements on real films, interpreted through transfer-matrix simulations, extract the parameters for each orientation. The cubic anisotropy proves far more pronounced in the second orientation, showing a threefold in-plane pattern.
arxiv-2603-04177: Thillen and others ask whether language models can generate human-level code refactorings, introducing the CodeTaste benchmark. Results show a clear gap: agents implement well-specified refactorings well but often fail to discover human refactoring choices given only a focus area. A propose-then-implement split aids match, and choosing the best-aligned proposal before implementation yields further gains.
arxiv-2603-04277: Chen and colleagues restore scale for drones that lose GPS and camera metadata. Five leading vision language models misjudge area badly, with median errors above 50 percent. Their tool, VehAnchor, reads ground sample distance from vehicles seen in aerial images. It estimates typical car pixel length from oriented boxes by kernel density estimation, then converts it with a pre calibrated reference. On DOTA the median error is 6.87 percent across 306 images, and with segmentation downstream area error falls sharply.
arxiv-2603-04477: Yanhua Zhao classifies activity from smart insole sensors with a circular dilated CNN. Pressure, accelerometer, and gyroscope sensors monitor gait and posture without intrusion. Her model reads 160 frame windows with 24 channels across pressure and inertial axes. Accuracy reaches 86.42 percent on standing, walking, sitting, and tandem, tested on unseen subjects. An XGBoost model scores slightly higher, but inertial sensors drive much of the discrimination. The approach suits embedded real time use.
arxiv-2603-04777: Yamamoto and colleagues demonstrate body-scale NFC networking for ultra-low-power wearables. NFC suits low-power wearables, but its short range limits use to point-to-point interactions. Their system widens NFC reach around the body for surface-to-multipoint communication with sensor tags. Meander NFC expands a clothing-based networking area to body scale while reading small tags. A meander coil creates a confined inductive field along textiles, ensuring robust coupling. The picoRing approach extends range between ring and wristband nodes by optimizing coils for middle-range NFC.
arxiv-2603-05077: Amrita Goswami and team use viscosity as a smoking gun for complex making in concentrated electrolyte answers, where speciation is hard to measure yet strongly affects answer traits. Runs and tests show viscosity reveals how much complexation occurs in concentrated aqueous answers. Stretching the atomistic Madrid-2019 force field to model FeCl2, they compare FeCl2 and MgCl2 answers. The seen viscosity gap reflects more complexation in the former, steady with recent X-ray absorption and neutron scattering tests.
arxiv-2603-05177: Tim Wittenborg and team present the SWARM-SLR AIssistant, a unified method for automating systematic literature reviews. It pairs the ordered SWARM-SLR method with a helper built around agents that brings research tools as one through a modular interface, supporting conversational guidance and keeping data stored. A single tool registry lets developers annotate and register tools alone with a shared metadata schema, easing the tool-test bottleneck. An early test shows better usability, though leanness, access, and being open to check need balancing before fully scalable automation arrives.
arxiv-2603-05277: Anders G Frøseth stretches his wealth-tax neutrality method along two dimensions. First, portfolio neutrality survives stochastic volatility and Epstein-Zin utility but breaks under HARA. Second, four channels break neutrality for implemented taxes even under CRRA. They are non-uniform test, inelastic-market price effects, progressive thresholds, and endogenous labour supply. Each channel is formalized, calibrated to the Norwegian tax where possible. The progressive threshold's tax shield lifts risk-taking near the exemption boundary. The method tests Saez-Zucman and French minimum taxes, the latter above EUR 100 million.
arxiv-2603-05577: Chazaridis and team propose DKSD-AE, a structured autoencoder combining Koopman operator learning with per-example norming, splitting speaker moves from content moves. Human speech carries language content and traits of the speaker, and checking needs speaker representations steady across content and nuisance factors like ambient noise. Current methods often depend on labeled data, text guidance, or large ready-made models, limiting growth and use. Across many data sets, DKSD-AE matches or beats top base models while keeping high content error rates, with far fewer settings no text guidance.
arxiv-2603-05777: Raghunadhan and team tackle quantum network scanning with limited watching. Unknown link settings must be found from path reads, so the authors design a cyclic plan for any shapes. They build a learning frame on fixed points, with a Werner guess tool. It ties whether links can be found to the rank of the meeting table linking paths and links. Monitor placement and reading giving become a tuning problem holding both traits. Two integer coding kinds are tested on star and tree nets, with the cost-capped version spreading load.
arxiv-2603-05877: Buchele and colleagues present MSS, an algorithm determining the radii and positions of spheres filling a given volume. In granular materials, MSS generates particles for discrete element method simulations of complex-shaped particles, with each particle represented by a set of spheres collectively approximating its shape. This particle shape representation is often called the multi-sphere approach. For a given number of spheres, MSS approximates the target shape more closely and more cheaply than other discrete element multi-sphere generators reported in the literature.
arxiv-2603-06177: Cascella and colleagues study finiteness conditions on skew braces, from finite non degenerate Yang-Baxter solutions and structure skew braces. They examine lambda f braces and the subclass whose additive group is FC, finding finite conjugacy resemblance with an FC center analog. Through skew braces, they test whether elements sit in a finite decomposition factor, marking infinite solutions behaving like finite ones. They prove that for a sub skew brace with both groups of finite index, the indices coincide and it holds a strong left ideal of finite index.
arxiv-2603-06277: Wang shows that polynomials of degree at least 2 with an attracting cycle pulling at least two critical points in the connectedness locus are not combinatorially rigid. This holds when the map has no indifferent cycles at all. In one key case, connected Julia set hyperbolic polynomials are combinatorially rigid exactly in the disjoint type case.
arxiv-2603-06677: Tang and team address chart data smarts, where methods handle shallow reading and factual question-answering but not the complex reasoning deep research requires. Two snags: training reward clash and data gradient conflicts, and evaluation limited to factual recall. For training, PRPO tunes in parallel across reward sides with capability splitting across data types, untangling clashes. For testing, MCDR-Bench applies the error one-off principle, turning soft assessment into objective error spotting via set error injection. Jointly they advance chart deep research through joint training and fair testing.
arxiv-2603-07177: Ramanandraibe and colleagues give a unified way to build multi-cycle codes of any size r over a finite field. The method uses r-D prime units built as tensor products of one-variable ones, mixed with multi-D cyclic orbits. That link ties combo and algebra views as one and yields a natural poly basis. It also gives an optimal product bound past the BCH and Reed-Solomon bounds. A building recipe is shown, shown with optimal 3-D codes.
arxiv-2603-07577: Ferrari and colleagues deploy partly guided anomaly detection on a high-speed drug Blow-Fill-Seal line. Manual inspection varies by worker and old vision pipelines prove rigid for variable output. Their generative adversarial model with a residual autoencoder and dense bottleneck trains only on nominal samples and flags anomalies via rebuild gaps. Heatmaps give both sorting and spatial maps, with high scores inside a tight capture time slot.
arxiv-2603-07877: Lin and colleagues answer a question posed in a recent book by Brezis and Mironescu on Sobolev maps to the circle. They show the least mass among area-minimizing integral rectifiable currents with a given boundary equals the infimum of areas among smoothly immersed submanifolds sharing that boundary. This holds when the boundary itself bounds a smooth submanifold. The note settles the book's stated proposition in the affirmative.
arxiv-2603-07977: Liu and colleagues scale machine learning interatomic potentials by testing Mixture-of-Experts and Mixture-of-Linear-Experts designs inside the DPA3 framework. They probe routing strategies and expert designs. Sparse activation combined with shared experts brings substantial gains, and nonlinear expert formulations beat linear ones when shared experts are present. Element-wise routing consistently beats configuration-level routing, while global routing often turns numerically unstable. The resulting element-wise model beats all DPA3-based baselines across the OMol25, OMat24, and OC20M benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-08077: Benescu and colleagues ask whether large language models can judge relevance better than embedding similarity in information retrieval. Similarity gives a short-sighted view of relevance, they argue, while language understanding and reasoning could capture what a passage truly offers. They compare LLM-based relevance judgment systems against neural embedding retrieval systems on the TREC-DL 2019 passage set, and find no noticeable improvement at first. Digging deeper, they analyze how reasoning itself shifts the comparison between the two approaches.
arxiv-2603-08277: Irwin and colleagues study how dynamic stall shapes aerofoil optimisation for curvilinear blade kinematics. The study uses a cyclorotor in hover, typical of vertical-axis turbines and cycloidal props, as its test case. Two-dimensional unsteady RANS simulations coupled with Kriging shape the design, which is then tested with force measurements and PIV. Results improve through suppression of leading-edge vortex shedding during the primary thrust peak.
arxiv-2603-08677: Xiran Yang and colleagues sample rare excited-state paths with a deterministic, time-reversible dynamics. Excited-state motion is costly and often random, blocking standard path sampling. Their NATPS method builds on MASH hopping, secures the reversibility and balance that path sampling needs, and yields reactive path sets far cheaper than brute-force runs or forward-flux sampling.
arxiv-2603-08777: Ignacio Salgado-Linares and colleagues simulate thermal Hall transport with semiclassical spin dynamics. Computing the conductivity from live energy-current links plus energy magnetization is fiddly, so they lay out the linear-response recipe with care. They apply it to a chiral magnet and to a Kitaev magnet in a field, beating the plain non-interacting picture and giving experiments a benchmark.
arxiv-2603-08977: Henry Li Xinyuan and colleagues factor speech content away from speaker timbre with a simple linear method. Their Universal Speech Content Factorization learns a universal speech-to-content map by least squares, then derives speaker-specific transforms from a few seconds of target speech. As a zero-shot voice conversion system it rivals methods needing far more target data or extra neural training.
arxiv-2603-09177: Allen W. Shafter fits modern relations between the decline times t2 and t3 for a large sample of novae drawn from a recent compilation. Fits run in both directions to handle the asymmetry of least squares, which only shrinks residuals in one variable. Within the uncertainties, one relation simplifies to a plain proportionality, with t2 about half of t3. The pair of formulas lets observers convert between the two decline measures in either direction.
arxiv-2603-09577: Onur Günlü establishes randomized distributed function computation, where a sender transmits just enough for a receiver to produce a randomized function of the input. As a form of semantic communication it resembles remote source coding, and privacy constraints fit it naturally, since they usually demand a random step. Strong coordination metrics give local differential privacy for every input sequence. That holds even when sender and receiver share no common randomness, and shared randomness can cut the rate hugely.
arxiv-2603-09777: Anisa Khatun reviews recent ALICE results on photon induced processes when heavy nuclei at the LHC just miss each other. Run 2 work covers vector meson output, nuclear breakup and proton emission in lead on lead events. Early Run 3 data add open charm and named hadron output from photon nucleus hits. Plans for the tau magnetic moment with a future ALICE 3 close the survey.
arxiv-2603-09877: Changyao Tian and colleagues present InternVL-U, a compact unified model that understands, reasons about, generates and edits images. Such models usually trade strong image making against strong reading of meaning. InternVL-U pairs a multimodal language model with a separate image generation head, keeping the two visual roles apart. Built with data rich in meaning, the small model beats unified rivals several times its size.
arxiv-2603-09977: Shi Chen, Aleksey Cherman and Robert D. Pisarski ask whether hot QCD has a conformal manifold in the chiral limit. New lattice hints suggest the chiral transition may be second order for two or more massless flavours. An 't Hooft anomaly at general imaginary chemical potential narrows the possible critical behaviour to three minimal scenarios. Their favoured one lies beyond Ginzburg Landau theory, with a line of fixed points tied to baryon density.
arxiv-2603-10177: Simon Frisk, Austen Fan and Paraschos Koutris present K-Join, a parallel join algorithm built from vertex covers and the HyperCube primitive. Parallel join processing aims to evaluate queries with minimal data transfer between machines, and the best possible method stays open. Their novelty is choosing HyperCube shares as a linear combination of several vertex covers. The resulting load follows a new hypergraph measure that matches or beats all leading algorithms.
arxiv-2603-10277: Erin Carson and Xinye Chen propose using graph neural networks to estimate the condition number of sparse matrices far faster than classic numeric routes. Their graph features cost little to build, scaling with the nonzero entries plus the matrix size. One scheme predicts the costly inverse-norm part without forming the inverse, while the other predicts the whole condition number at once. Tests on one-norm and two-norm cases show large speedups, and the approach can extend to other norms, with code made public.
arxiv-2603-10377: Md Muntaqim Meherab, Noor Islam S Mohammad, and Faiza Feroz propose Causal Concept Graphs for language models. The aim is to show not just where concepts sit, but how they drive each other during stepwise reasoning. Sparse autoencoders supply interpretable latent features, and differentiable structure learning recovers causal edges between them. A new Causal Fidelity Score checks whether graph-guided interventions move outputs more than random ones. On three reasoning benchmarks with GPT-2 Medium, their graphs beat tracing and ranking baselines by a wide margin, staying sparse and stable.
arxiv-2603-10577: Marta Sumyk and Oleksandr Kosovan test whether vision-language models can audit computer-use agents, software that carries out desktop tasks from plain instructions. Five models judged task success from an instruction and the final screen state, across three benchmarks on macOS, Windows, and Linux. The study scored accuracy, calibration of confidence, and agreement between models. Leading models were accurate and well calibrated, yet all slipped in complex or mixed settings, and even the best disagreed a lot. Auditing itself, they argue, needs reliability checks.
arxiv-2603-10877: Ayan Sengupta and coauthors present ARMADA. This framework distills knowledge from large vision-language models into smaller language-only models. It can use closed black-box teachers too. Standard distillation assumes teacher and student share a modality. Older multimodal routes need costly teacher pre-training. ARMADA instead aligns the models without changing the teacher. It was tested across twenty-five tasks. Those tasks span understanding, reasoning, and instruction tuning. It lifts student scores. It also challenges the idea that a vision teacher cannot strengthen a text model.
arxiv-2603-11177: Shyam Balaji proposes a single origin story for all of dark matter, the universe's baryon asymmetry, and a detectable gravitational wave background, all from ultra-slow-roll inflation. The sharp braking of the inflaton during that phase seeds primordial black holes as dark matter. It also sets up spontaneous baryogenesis through a derivative coupling, tying black hole abundance to baryon yield. Flat tails allow high-scale inflation with a small tensor window, while steep tails force a far lower scale. Gravitational wave observatories can break that degeneracy.
arxiv-2603-11377: Leandro Gomes builds inhomogeneous cosmological models that look uniform to those inside them, yet decelerate everywhere while looking like accelerating ones. The matter is an ensemble of massive particles, almost like dust, reacting to local tidal forces as a thick fluid would. The models extend the standard homogeneous cosmology. Over large scales, backreaction from the local gravitational potential mimics a running dark-energy term. Luminosity distances then imply acceleration, even though the true expansion slows. The effective equation of state can be tuned widely.
arxiv-2603-11477: Chen and Botta present rt2gtfs, an open-source Python package that rebuilds bus timetables from real vehicle data. Most access studies trust printed schedules, as if buses ran exactly on time. Delays and disruptions make real travel times swing widely, though. rt2gtfs pulls high-frequency vehicle location feeds from the UK Bus Open Data Service. It matches live positions to scheduled trips and stops, then infers true arrival and departure times. The output is a corrected GTFS bundle, ready for routing and access analysis at national scale.
arxiv-2603-11677: He and Lim argue that human-agent collaboration needs foresight, not just control. Today's users approve or fix single agent actions to cut immediate risk. They get no view of what those choices cause later, so they must guess later effects in their heads. The pair propose simulation-in-the-loop: users and agents explore simulated futures together before any decision lands. Trying paths in simulation turns reactive fixes into informed exploration. It also helps users surface hidden constraints and preferences along the way.
arxiv-2603-11877: Xu and co-authors review silent speech interfaces, systems that decode speech intent without sound. Normal speech interfaces lean on the acoustic channel, which brings noise, privacy, and impairment problems. The review sorts sensing by where signals are tapped: brain oscillations, muscle activity, articulator motion, and active probing. It then tracks a shift toward language models as strong priors that resolve sparse, drifting biosignals. Modern systems, the authors note, now near the word error levels real use demands.
arxiv-2603-12077: Kupriyanov, Lazarev, Roschin, and Werner widen flow shop scheduling through recursive functions. One recursive frame can hold six extensions of the classic problem at once. Three function types do the work: one tied to machines, one adjusting processing times, and one guarding feasibility. The authors lay out how these functions stack and how objectives take recursive form. General rules and properties for such functions follow. Simple cases then show how to phrase new problems ready for branch and bound.
arxiv-2603-12677: Shuxin Liu and co-authors improve knowledge editing in language models by joining its two stages. Locate-then-edit methods first plan a target representation, then fit parameters under constraints. Uniform regularization in the first stage can shrink strong requests too much and weak ones too little. Their MetaKE casts both stages as one bi-level problem. A structural gradient proxy passes downstream feedback upstream without costly backpropagation. Experiments showed a better trade-off between accuracy and editability than strong baselines.
arxiv-2603-12777: Shahnoor Ali and co-authors present a quantum code-division scheme for multiuser quantum key distribution on a shared channel. Chaotic phase shifters encode and decode states from many senders at once. Signals are combined through a beam splitter network, then split back at the receiver. Matched chaotic shifters let each pair recover its state and form a secret key. The authors derive input-output relations for any user count. They then rate key performance under collective attacks and varied noise.
arxiv-2603-12877: Karma Dajani and Niels Langeveld characterize when two alternate base transformations share the same invariant measure. Each transformation switches between two maps: one scales by a real base and folds modulo 1, the other does the same with an integer. The pair of systems is indexed by its base and integer choices. The authors find all pairs for which the absolutely continuous invariant measures coincide. The result settles exactly which parameter choices give the same long-run behavior.
arxiv-2603-12977: Yijun Quan and co-authors achieve exact federated continual unlearning for ridge heads on frozen foundation models. Deleting a user's data on demand is required by the right to be forgotten. Prior federated methods settle for rough reconstruction or costly retraining. With a ridge head, the optimum rests on two additive summary statistics. Their protocol streams add and delete requests in fixed-size messages. The server head then matches centralized retraining exactly, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2603-13077: Yihang Zhou and co-authors rebuild rooftop wind fields from sparse sensors with learning methods, for drone and air mobility safety. Rooftop flows bend, split, and vary by direction, which makes sparse reads hard to fill in. Wind-tunnel data trained Kriging and three deep models for comparison. Deep models beat Kriging on image and error scores by wide margins. Mixed-direction training helped far more than single-direction training. Sensor placement tuned by decomposition methods added robustness under small shifts.
arxiv-2603-13377: Ivan Svatko and co-authors ask what deep learning models really learn from bioimaging data. Representation learning gave big gains for natural images, but microscopy may differ. Their study covers cell culture and tissue imaging, two widely used data types at key scales in biology. Simple baselines, even untrained models and structural representations, matched top methods in many test settings. That result shows common benchmark metrics can mask a lack of high-level biological features. Close comparison with baselines helps show where models are strong or weak.
arxiv-2603-13877: Liakopoulos and co-authors test deep learning for scribe verification in Chinese manuscripts. The task is to judge whether two fragments share the same writer. Models include Siamese and triplet networks, in both convolutional and transformer forms. Two datasets are used: the Tsinghua Bamboo Slips and a subset of a Chinese calligraphy collection. A MobileNetV3-based Siamese model with contrastive loss ranks best or second best on accuracy and ROC area for both datasets.
arxiv-2603-13977: Christiansen and Lin introduce new variants of Regge finite element metrics with a stronger trace property. In their construction, the trace operator maps onto a space of continuous scalar functions. Scaling those functions by the identity tensor returns a metric in the same element space. The metrics can use high-order polynomials and splits such as Clough-Tocher or Worsey-Farin. Sketched uses include general relativity, incompressible elasticity, and conformal geometry.
arxiv-2603-14077: Nguyen and co-authors improve eye feature extraction from event camera streams with a model called AISSM. Event density swings hard as gaze behavior changes, and fixed models lose accuracy at those shifts. AISSM adjusts how much weight goes to current data versus recent history. A companion network estimates signal-to-noise ratio and event density to set that balance. A new training trick speeds learning. Tests show the system beats the best prior models for event-based eye features.
arxiv-2603-14577: Nabhaan and co-authors tune edge device settings online with the CORAL method. Edge inference setups with equal throughput can differ twofold in power draw. Finding the lean setup by hand takes exhaustive profiling per model and device. CORAL searches live, with no offline profiling step. It uses distance covariance to catch nonlinear links between settings and metrics. Power budgets and throughput goals are handled as joint targets. On two Jetson devices, CORAL hits 96 to 100% of the best found settings, they report.
arxiv-2603-15077: Del Popolo and co-authors test modified gravity with the luminosity-temperature relation of galaxy clusters. They build a semi-analytic model with angular momentum, dynamical friction, and shock heating, then check it against simulations and data. Two theories get tested: f(R) gravity and the symmetron model. Massive clusters stay screened and match standard cosmology. Low-mass groups below about 1 to 2 keV show steeper slopes under modified gravity. The authors report these models fit the observed relation better than standard cosmology.
arxiv-2603-15177: Bell and co-authors study when a map of a free semigroup can be split into two smaller maps. A free semigroup is built from a finite alphabet, with strings joined in sequence. A map that cannot be split counts as irreducible, much like a prime number. They show this trait is real and nontrivial for maps that keep rank fixed. They give a test that tells split maps from unsplit ones. They also study divisibility between maps, non-unique splits, and what incidence matrices reveal.
arxiv-2603-15477: Laayoun and Missaoui study mean field games whose state paths stay inside a bounded region, as if reflected at the wall. They prove that an equilibrium exists for this class. A penalty method, paired with relaxed controls, builds it from games with free dynamics. Under a mild smoothness condition, a mimicking step yields a Markovian equilibrium. Extra convexity gives a strict one. In the general case, relaxed solutions are approached by strict controls on penalized systems.
arxiv-2603-15777: Yang and co-authors study a writing tool that guards student thinking in real classrooms. AI writing aids can scaffold argument skills, yet class use stays little studied. The team deployed the VISAR tool in an undergraduate writing course. Forty-nine students used it across three sections over two semesters. Logs, drafts, surveys, and interviews tracked how features were used. Students chose planning and targeted generation supports on their own. Such use paired with better argument quality and concept grasp. Gains in critical AI literacy also appeared.
arxiv-2603-16177: Baek and co-authors test a simple training strategy called specialized pretraining. The idea is to repeat a small domain dataset during pretraining, not save it for finetuning. They test it on ChemPile, MusicPile, and ProofPile. The method improved domain skill and kept general skill after finetuning. It also cut the tokens needed for a target score by up to 1.75 times. The authors derive scaling laws to pick the best repeat count.
arxiv-2603-16377: Paul and co-authors examine age predictors through generalization, bias, and causal lenses. Such predictors often fail on new data when outside traits intrude. Race, gender, or tissue can act as confounders. The team discusses learning representations that stay invariant to those traits. They test an interpretable neural model built on adversarial learning. Mouse gene data illustrate how the model behaves. Results match a known drug study, but causal claims stay limited.
arxiv-2603-16877: Cheng and co-authors build a retrieval augmented system that answers questions on long financial reports. Analysts struggle with 10-K filings that can exceed 100 pages. The system mixes full text and semantic search, then adds an optional reranking stage with a cross encoder model. Tests used the FinDER benchmark, with 1,500 queries in five groups. With reranking, correctness for high scoring answers rose to 49.0 percent, up from 33.5 percent without it. Fully wrong answers fell to 22.5 percent, down from 35.3 percent in baseline runs.
arxiv-2603-17377: Rozenfeld and Laufer Goldshtein add uncertainty bounds to sound source localization. Most methods give only a point guess, with no sense of trust. Their conformal approach builds regions that should hold the true source spots. One variant knows how many sources are active, and the other counts them first. Tests on simulations and real recordings kept the promised coverage, they report, across echo levels and setups.
arxiv-2603-17477: Xie proposes a structure-preserving scheme for the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, a core model of magnetization dynamics. The method pairs a Crank-Nicolson step with an implicit Gauss-Seidel fractional iteration. It runs first-order in time and second-order in space. The scheme stays stable and keeps vector length exact, he reports. Those traits ease the theory behind the method. Tests in one and three dimensions confirm accuracy and stability.
arxiv-2603-17677: Kim and Ye add adaptive guidance to retrieval-augmented masked diffusion models. Retrieved text can clash with what a model already knows, and noise then hurts output. Their ARAM framework needs no training and tunes the guidance scale during denoising. It reads the signal-to-noise ratio of the shift that retrieved context causes. Strong evidence gets more weight, while weak or noisy context gets damped. Knowledge-heavy QA scores beat strong RAG baselines, they report.
arxiv-2603-17777: Krenkel and co-authors push a Remeika-series superconductor to a quantum critical point with disorder. The material hides a charge-density-wave transition under its superconducting dome. Electron irradiation at 2.5 MeV adds point-like, nonmagnetic disorder in fine steps. Resistance shifts from Fermi-liquid form toward a clean linear law as dose grows, they report. Long-range wave order dies at the top dose. They place the critical mix between x of 0.75 and 0.85.
arxiv-2603-18177: Barrass and co-authors present CRG, a hybrid decomposition method for stochastic unit commitment with combined-cycle generators. Combined-cycle units add many binary variables and mode constraints to grid scheduling. CRG splits linear parts with Benders steps and integer combined-cycle parts with Dantzig-Wolfe steps. New valid inequalities tighten the lower bound in a clear way. On a 935-generator FERC dataset, CRG beat Benders alone past 20 scenarios and scaled past Gurobi memory limits.
arxiv-2603-18277: Steinbring and Ng review holographic quantum foam and present observational evidence tied to GRB221009A. Quantum fluctuations make spacetime foamy at amounts set by the holographic principle. The foam predicts a dark sector whose quanta follow infinite statistics, not fermion or boson rules. Blurring of distant point sources is the key test proposed. The record-bright burst's follow-up data match the widened point-spread function the foam predicts.
arxiv-2603-18377: Yu and co-authors introduce PlanTwin, a privacy-preserving planning layer for cloud-assisted LLM agents. Cloud planners normally see raw local state, including code, files, and credentials. PlanTwin projects the real setting into a de-identified abstract graph that keeps planning structure. The cloud works only on that twin through a bounded interface, while a local gatekeeper enforces budgets. On 60 tasks, sensitive items stayed fully hidden with under 2.2% utility loss.
arxiv-2603-18577: Chen and co-authors build MedForge to catch fake medical images and explain each verdict. Text-guided editors can now add or remove lesions in real scans. MedForge-90K holds realistic edits across 19 diseases, with expert reasoning notes. The MedForge-Reasoner marks suspect regions first, then gives its verdict. Extra training aligns its grounds with expert checks and cuts made-up evidence. Tests show top detection accuracy with explanations that match expert review.
arxiv-2603-18677: Di Santi and Florida set out metrics that separate AI help from AI dependence. Amplification means the pair does better while human skill stays intact. Delegation means the human hands reasoning over to the machine. Four metrics track gain, dependence, reliance, and skill drift over time. NetLogo simulations span three reliance regimes and many atrophy settings. No baseline setup reaches positive joint gain, even with zero skill loss. Gain appears only when a direct interaction term lets retained human skill feed the output.
arxiv-2603-18877: Xu and Wang compute strong decay widths for pseudoscalar hidden-charm tetraquark states. QCD sum rules, built on quark-hadron duality, supply the hadronic couplings. Vacuum condensates up to dimension five enter the QCD side. Two states with mixed diquark-antidiquark structure are treated. The Zc minus state gets a total width near 326 MeV. The Zc plus state comes out near 92 MeV. Error bars stay within a few MeV in both cases. The results give targets for searches for these exotic states.
arxiv-2603-19777: Shu and co-authors present early galaxy findings from the FATHOMER survey with the FAST telescope. The pilot drift scan covered 60 square degrees over 28 hours in 2021. Two source-finding methods gave consistent lists of hydrogen galaxies. The team measured line widths, flux, and hydrogen mass for each find. They report 702 galaxies with redshifts below 0.09. Of these, 331 were already known from ALFALFA. Another 77 have no optical match and may be dark or faint systems.
arxiv-2603-20177: Kaasik and Quilis study whether one metric space can have every other as a Lipschitz quotient. In the separable case, they adapt a classic construction to get such a universal space. The compact case turns out the opposite: no universal compact space exists. Their proof uses the curve flat index, an ordinal gauge of curve structure complexity. Lipschitz quotients cannot raise this index on compact domains. Yet compact spaces exist with arbitrarily high countable index values.
arxiv-2603-20277: Perkins and Zhang study electricity markets where customers face firm budget limits. A budget caps the total a user can pay, price times quantity. Yet prices emerge from market balance, which makes the welfare problem hard to define. They show a natural dual-ascent method reaches one unique competitive balance under budgets. That balance solves a convex welfare problem with a spliced utility function. They give the spliced form in pieces and test it on examples.
arxiv-2603-20377: Bailey and co-authors apply their radiating Bondi flow theory to forming giant planets. In core accretion, late growth depends on gas falling in from the disk. Older models treat this inflow as adiabatic, ignoring the planet's own glow. Paper I showed such feedback can suppress accretion by orders of magnitude. Here, planets in smooth disks see accretion cut by ten to a hundred times. The cut applies inside about 10 AU and weakens for gap-opening planets. Time-dependent simulations confirm the effect is stable and robust.
arxiv-2603-20677: Ommi and Estaremi characterize nuclear weighted conditional expectation operators between L^p spaces. These operators blend averaging over a sigma algebra with a weight function. The paper gives full tests for when such an operator counts as nuclear. The tests link the weight and the underlying measure structure. One sharp result follows for non-atomic measure spaces. In that case, the only nuclear operator of this type is the zero operator. The work sits in operator theory on function spaces.
arxiv-2603-20977: Monterde studies local uniform mixing in continuous quantum walks on weighted graphs. Local mixing at a vertex means the walk can be made near a state whose entries all have equal size. He derives necessary conditions from the spectral and combinatorial traits of the graph. These include a bound that links all entries of each eigenvector, and a cap on vertex degree for Laplacian based walks. The conditions rule out local mixing for many graph classes. Almost all planar graphs and trees have a vertex where it fails.
arxiv-2603-21177: Baroian and Berger speed up GRPO training by replaying high-signal prompts. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards spends most compute on rollouts, and many prompts teach nothing. Prompt Replay keeps a buffer of prompts with near even pass rates, where the learning signal is strongest. Only prompts are reused, not trajectories, so training stays on-policy. On math benchmarks, the method cuts zero-variance prompts and speeds early accuracy gains, though final accuracy converges with the baseline.
arxiv-2603-21377: Mabrok presents HamVision, a framework for medical image analysis built on the damped harmonic oscillator. The oscillator's phase space gives three representations: position for feature content, momentum for boundary and texture gradients, and energy as a parameter-free saliency map. For segmentation, energy gates skip connections while momentum adds boundary detail at each decoder level. For classification, the three are pooled into one feature vector. Across ten benchmarks, the segmentation head sets state-of-the-art Dice scores on four data sets with few parameters.
arxiv-2603-21477: Borges and co-authors address a detection problem in thin elastic plates: finding a hidden supported cavity from far-field wave patterns. The plate obeys the biharmonic flexural wave equation. They derive a reciprocity principle and factor the far-field operator under supported boundary conditions. Range properties of that operator justify both linear and direct sampling methods. Numerical tests with noise, sparse data, and multiple scattering show both methods recover the cavity's location and convex hull, with direct sampling cheaper and steadier.
arxiv-2603-21877: Lu and co-authors improve reinforcement learning for reasoning models by tuning prompts alongside the policy. When every rollout of a hard question scores the same, the learning signal collapses, worst on hard items. Their P2O method mines those hard samples and evolves reasoning prompts for them with GEPA. Good trajectories are then distilled into the model under the plain question, so no prompt is needed at test time. A mask filters extreme ratios during distillation. Gains reached 8 points over GRPO on average, and 16 on hard contest sets.
arxiv-2603-21977: Okoyomon and Goebel turn power flow prediction on radial grids into a sequential path problem. Classic solvers scale poorly, and global models often fail on new grid shapes. Their BOOST-RPF method splits a radial network into root-to-leaf paths and learns local voltage drops with boosted trees. Three variants predict raw voltage, the drop from the parent node, or a physics-shaped residual. Its parent residual variant won on two benchmark grids, beating analytic and neural rivals. The method scales linearly and keeps accuracy on unseen feeders.
arxiv-2603-22077: Bracci-Testasecca and co-authors study the two-dimensional Heisenberg spin glass with a semiclassical expansion. At leading order they get a quadratic spin-wave Hamiltonian. They then examine whether its excitations spread out or stay localized. Around magnetically ordered states, low-energy waves are delocalized. Around spin-glass ordered states, they stay localized, though weakly. The split traces back to how spin-rotation symmetry breaks in the base model. The authors conjecture that adding interactions between the waves restores the hydrodynamic picture and favors ergodic behavior.
arxiv-2603-22277: Scholtz and co-authors test what shapes the broad line profiles of active galactic nuclei. Some claim the Little Red Dots show exponential profiles from electron scattering in an ionized cocoon. The team fits spectra of 32 nuclei across these groups. Exponential fits are not the best in about 60 percent of cases. Lorentzian and multi-Gaussian shapes do as well or better. The authors show stacked or layered broad lines can look exponential on their own. So scattering need not dominate the profiles.
arxiv-2603-22477: Cottrell and co-authors introduce STORM, a model for spatial transcriptomics data that tackles three problems at once. Gene maps tied to tissue spots suffer batch effects, mixed cell signals, and missing readings. STORM aligns slices of differing shape by matching their physical patterns, not raw grids. It factors the data into a shared latent space that stays readable, unlike black-box deep models. Tests show top results on batch integration, cell-type separation, and filling in unmeasured genes.
arxiv-2603-22577: Hugglestone and co-authors present STRIATUM-CTF, an agent framework for solving capture-the-flag security challenges. Language models handle code well but falter on long, stateful attack chains. Their system plugs tools for inspection, decompilation, and debugging into one protocol, so the agent keeps a steady context. They entered the system in a live university contest in late 2025. It won first place against twenty-one human teams. Log analysis shows the shared tool protocol cuts made-up steps compared with plain prompting.
arxiv-2603-22677: Zhu and Li present MuQ-Eval, an open-source score for the quality of AI-made music. Common metrics score whole sets of clips, not single clips, and match human views poorly. MuQ-Eval trains light prediction heads on frozen features from the MuQ model. Training uses expert ratings for clips from 31 text-to-music systems. The simplest version matches human scores well at system and clip level. Tests show the encoder choice matters most. Models tuned on just 150 clips still give usable scores.
arxiv-2603-22977: Baktash and co-authors build DariMis, the first dataset for Dari misinformation detection on YouTube. Dari is spoken by tens of millions yet lacks research coverage. The set holds over nine thousand hand-labeled Dari videos. Labels cover information type and harm level. The two dimensions prove linked: false content often carries medium or high harm, true content rarely does. A pair-input encoding of title and description boosts recall for false content. A Dari-Farsi tuned model gives the best test scores.
arxiv-2603-23177: Schumm and Stiller rethink self-sovereign identity principles from the viewpoint of the actors involved. Centralized identity systems face steady security and privacy problems. Prior work gathered identity principles but left the user view thin. The authors split combined requirements into 24 simple quality requirements. Each is mapped to the actor who owns it: data owner, issuer, verifier, or system. A dependency model then shows how actors rely on each other. The result is a first structured model for such system design.
arxiv-2603-23277: May, Simpson, and Michael build a leaner model for spatial data with many outcome classes. Their reduced-rank multinomial model ties class effects to a few shared latent factors. That cuts the parameter count while keeping links between classes. Standard samplers break under this setup, so they design a Gibbs sampler with Laplace-based proposals. Simulations check how to pick the rank and how well the proposals work. Applied to tree species in the Blue Ridge Mountains, the model scales well. It predicts single species, species unions, and area totals.
arxiv-2603-23377: Teknowijoyo and three co-authors re-examine odd magnetic signals in LK-99 family materials. Copper-doped apatite samples made by hydrothermal routes show repeatable anomalies below room temperature. Some readings hinted at vortex-glass behavior like that in superconductors. The team tests that idea with DC and AC magnetization plus memory effects. The signals instead fit glassy freezing of interacting magnetic clusters. Chemistry checks blame covellite, a copper sulfide phase that lurks in these mixed samples. The work warns that phase mixes can fake superconducting signs.
arxiv-2603-23677: Gul and three co-authors detect out-of-distribution images without any training. Most detectors read only the last layer of a network before its output. The team show mid layers carry just as much signal for spotting odd inputs. Their method pools features from block after block and averages them per class into prototypes. A test image scores by its cosine closeness to the nearest prototype. Odd images sit far from all of them. Across standard benchmarks, the fusion lifts detection and cuts false alarms.
arxiv-2603-23877: Hwangbo and co-authors report early carbon monoxide and dust signals in the Type Ib supernova 2024rbc. At 62 days after explosion, near-infrared spectra show the first CO overtone band on a dust continuum. This is the first CO seen in the ejecta of a Type Ib supernova, they state. Light-curve fits give a nickel mass of 0.07 solar masses and an ejecta mass of 1.7 solar masses. Their CO fit implies a temperature near 4040 K. Dust fits give 910 K and a small dust mass.
arxiv-2603-23977: Chen and co-authors present CHONN, a neural network design based on electrical circuits. Many networks shape their features by loose heuristics, which limits modeling of data with built-in dynamics. CHONN treats feature change as a latent potential process. Single Kirchhoff Neural Cells give stable first-order updates. Chained cells build higher-order dynamics inside one block. Tests cover operator learning, long-horizon forecasting, and ImageNet-1K recognition. The circuit design improves structural fidelity, rollout stability, and visual learning, they report.
arxiv-2603-24177: Song and co-authors use deep reinforcement learning to find better ways to create magnetic skyrmions. Skyrmions must survive thermal noise for use in spintronic devices. The trained agent searches over dynamic paths of magnetic field and temperature. For Fe3GeTe2 monolayers, its path beats fixed-temperature field sweeps in success rate. The skyrmions it makes also live longer, thanks to their round shape and equilibrium size. The authors trace the gain to low dissipated work along the learned path.
arxiv-2603-24277: Sezik and co-authors compute a state-dependent visit probability for run-and-tumble particles. The visit probability gives the chance a particle first reaches a point by a given time. Past work ignored the internal state that drives the motion. The authors track that state during first passage. They use Doi-Peliti field theory in one dimension. They also derive the total span covered by right- or left-moving particles, and compare with Brownian motion results.
arxiv-2603-24477: The Cursor Research team reports on Composer 2, a model built for agentic software engineering. Training runs in two phases. Continued pretraining first deepens knowledge and latent coding skill. Large-scale reinforcement learning then sharpens end-to-end coding, with stronger reasoning and coherent multi-step work on long tasks. Training runs inside the same Cursor harness used in deployment, with matching tools and realistic tasks. A new benchmark drawn from real problems in large codebases, including Cursor's own, shows a major accuracy jump over earlier Composer models.
arxiv-2603-24877: Sivaraman and co-authors reflect on AI data science systems that support reasoning through transparent intermediate artifacts. End-to-end AI tools can run complex analyses, but users struggle to weigh alternatives or reformulate problems. Drawing on two medical data science systems, the authors find success came from deliberately designed intermediates. Readable query languages, concept definitions, and input-output examples helped users judge analytical choices. Users could refine their questions and add their own knowledge despite opaque model internals. The authors invite the HCI community to design such artifacts deliberately.
arxiv-2603-24977: Zhou and co-authors ask how odd superconductivity grows out of the Fermi arc state in underdoped cuprates. That state lacks a full Fermi surface, so the standard BCS picture may not apply. The team solves a model built for such arcs and folds the arcs into the BCS rules in exact form. They find a new effect that pushes the transition temperature down. Their results match key lab facts: a dome-shaped peak with doping, low stiffness, and a gap far above the BCS limit.
arxiv-2603-25377: Dai and co-authors train speaker naming and speech transcription as one joint job. Big audio-language models can diarize and recognize speech end to end. But telling voices apart lags, since chat data is scarce and no loss targets speaker traits. Their GLSC-SDR adds speaker classification to the training mix. Clustered speakers give global labels, and re-encoded cluster members give fine local ones. On three meeting sets it matches or beats simulation-fed and multi-encoder rivals, with no large real chat corpus.
arxiv-2603-25977: Chau Loo Kung and co-authors present a transformer built for diffusion MRI of the brain. Diffusion signals depend on direction and strength, which standard models handle poorly. Their design adds a new position code, called D-RoPE, for diffusion space. It lets one model capture space, direction, and weighting together. The model handles any number of diffusion directions. After masked pretraining, its features transfer across scan protocols. On mild brain impairment classification, finetuned features beat baselines by six percent, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-26077: Zhou and co-authors ask whether a passing satellite can destroy the stellar bar of a Milky Way-like galaxy. Bars are common, yet many galaxies lack them. The team runs N-body and hydro simulations of collisions with a round intruder. Mass ratios of 1:3, 1:5, and 1:15 are tried. Most hits barely weaken the bar or change its pattern speed, they find. Only off-center, steep, retrograde hits destroy bars. Hits along the minor axis weaken bars more than hits along the major axis. Gravity, not gas, drives the damage.
arxiv-2603-26377: Taye builds a thermodynamic account of why heartbeats per lifetime stay near constant in warm-blooded vertebrates. The product of resting heart rate and max lifespan sits near one billion cycles, a pattern noted since 1908. He treats the adult body as a steady state far from equilibrium and links entropy output to heart rate. Tests on 112 species give a log slope near minus one, as predicted. A four-part multiplier then explains why some clades drift from the shared value.
arxiv-2603-26477: Castorene and co-authors test how a Heisenberg-Kitaev magnon system performs as a Stirling-cycle engine. They use linear spin-wave theory on a medium that also carries Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. The DM term keeps the spectrum symmetric, giving even caloric responses and balanced engine efficiency. Bond-dependent Kitaev exchange instead warps the magnon density of states in a lopsided way. That warp enables both direct and inverse caloric effects, and Kitaev-driven cycles reach far higher efficiency, marking these magnets as tunable energy platforms.
arxiv-2603-26577: Esseldeurs and co-authors weigh two sources of gravity waves inside stars that host a companion. Convection stirs waves from within, while tides from the partner excite their own set. The team models the energy and angular momentum each wave type carries. They scan stellar masses and life stages to find which source wins where. A key aim is how a companion reshapes angular momentum flow in the host's radiative layers. The balance shifts with the star's state and the tide's strength.
arxiv-2603-26777: Tu and co-authors present BHCast, a framework that forecasts black hole plasma motion from one blurry image. Event Horizon Telescope images show structure around a black hole but not how the plasma moves. Simulations can show motion, yet they cost too much for direct inference. A neural model turns the still frame into future frames, super-resolving as it rolls forward with a multi-scale loss. Tree models then read spin and viewing angle from traits like pattern speed in the forecast movie.
arxiv-2603-26877: Akerib and co-authors push pulse shape discrimination in the LUX-ZEPLIN dark matter detector. The liquid xenon detector hunts weakly interacting massive particles. Its main tool against background is the charge-to-light ratio. Pulse shape adds a second handle on electronic recoil events. The team rebuilds photon timing to form a prompt fraction measure. That alone cuts background leakage to 15 percent, and to about 5 percent for one xenon process. Combining both tools halves the false positive rate for large pulses.
arxiv-2603-27277: Vogel and co-authors present Codebase-Memory, a knowledge graph system that helps language models explore code. Coding agents usually reread files and grep repeatedly, burning thousands of tokens per query. Codebase-Memory builds a persistent Tree-Sitter graph over the repository instead. It parses 66 languages with parallel workers and call-graph traversal. Impact analysis and community discovery enrich the graph further. Across 31 real repositories, answer quality reached 83 percent versus 92 for file exploration. The graph route used ten times fewer tokens. Graph-native queries matched or beat the explorer outright.
arxiv-2603-27477: Jahanzeb and co-authors describe a new setup for timing electron release. Light pulses can free electrons from atoms in attoseconds. The dual-sideband RABBITT method reads those tiny delays. Their rig pairs an extreme ultraviolet source with an infrared probe. The probe runs at 1200 nanometers. Active control holds timing steady to 45 attoseconds. Sideband signals swing with the driving field's phase. The team reports those swings in detail. The rig opens fine tests of photoionization delays.
arxiv-2603-27577: Peng and co-authors turn camera views into text for indoor navigation. SOL-Nav splits each RGB-D view into a grid. Each cell yields semantic, color, and depth notes. Those notes join the spoken instruction as pure text. A pretrained language model then plans the route. No large visual pretraining is needed. Tests on R2R and RxR benchmarks look strong. Real-world runs confirm the approach works. Model size and data needs both shrink.
arxiv-2603-27677: Kounatidis and Malikopoulos control plants safely when dynamics stay unknown. Only an approximate model is on hand. Pontryagin's principle sets up the model-based problem. A cost term punishes mismatch with the real plant. Shared Hamiltonian minimizers let model control stay optimal. The key is keeping control-relevant structure, not full dynamics. An online method learns Hamiltonian gradient factors from path data. Robotic cruise control tests confirm the idea.
arxiv-2603-27877: Weck and co-authors release HumMusQA, a hand-written music question set. Audio-language models need tests that probe real listening. The set holds 320 expert-written questions. Musically trained curators validated each item. Six top audio-language models face the benchmark. Robustness to unimodal shortcuts is also checked. Focused manual curation beats mass generation here. The dataset targets deep music comprehension.
arxiv-2603-27977: Wang and five co-authors propose SARL, a way to train reasoning models without labeled answers. Instead of scoring only the final answer, SARL maps the steps of each response and rewards sound reasoning structure. On math tests it beats earlier label-free methods and even some methods trained with true answers, with large gains on AIME25. On open-ended WildBench tasks it also leads prior label-free methods and a preference-based rival.
arxiv-2603-28077: Cheng and five co-authors propose a way to entangle a superconducting qubit with a squeezed cavity state. A parametric drive on the cavity makes the system follow an anisotropic Rabi model in a squeezed frame. Using high-order time averaging, they derive the resonance conditions for a three-photon process. A slow sweep of the cavity frequency then steers the pair into a maximally entangled state. Simulations confirm the scheme is accurate and robust.
arxiv-2603-28977: Pearce and D'Oh Nym propose a SETI search based on advanced civilizations cooking food with starlight directly. They define the Flavor Zone as the best distance from a star for cooking food. A toy model, the Digiorno-Like Object, sets the zone by package directions. They study how orbit affects cooking times and paradigms for such objects. They then test if current technology could detect these objects in their zones. Their result is blunt: such objects are not detectable with current technology. They add that no one should ever try.
arxiv-2603-29077: Turdubaeva and Lee propose a Generator-Interpreter framework for emotion reading in language models across cultures. Past work focused on interpretation and ignored the cultural background of whoever expresses the emotion. Their framework captures both expression and reading. They test six language models on an emotion task with data from 15 countries. Results vary with emotion type and context. Alignment between the two sides matters, and the expresser's country of origin has the stronger effect. They call for culture aware emotion modeling to improve fairness and robustness.
arxiv-2603-29377: Liu and co-authors show how altermagnetism and doping can boost d-wave pairing in the Hubbard model. Altermagnets have no net moment but split spins by momentum. That setting can suppress long-range antiferromagnetism while keeping strong spin fluctuations. Their strong-coupling analysis yields an anisotropic t-J model. Exchange effects lift singlet d-wave pairing and promote triplet p-wave pairing. Mean-field results show the d-wave channel grows under small anisotropy. Monte Carlo simulations confirm a mixed d-plus-p state at stronger anisotropy.
arxiv-2603-29677: Eisenhardt and co-authors build a test frame for pitfalls in multimodal active learning. Models that mix text, image, and sound face special traps. Some inputs go missing, and some modes are harder than others. These traps never arise with a single mode. Their frame isolates each trap with synthetic datasets. Clean isolation allows fair tests of query methods. Models kept leaning on one mode and neglecting the rest. No query method fixed that imbalance. Two real datasets confirmed the pattern.
arxiv-2603-29877: Maier and co-authors build a math model of chained extract-transform-load processes. Thread counts tune throughput in each ETL phase. But random per-record times and chain bottlenecks complicate that link. They model the chain as a controlled discrete-time Markov process on a graph. Mean throughput rises with threads but with shrinking gains. A flow balance rule ties threads, throughput, and mean time. Heavy-tailed random times complete the model. It gives a sound simulator for resource control work.
arxiv-2604-00277: Betteti and Laurenti build hybrid energy-based models for learning port-Hamiltonian dynamics with proven stability, expanding safe designs through absorbing invariance. Unlike classical Lyapunov theory, this property allows richer designs. They extend the theory to nonsmooth units via Clarke derivatives and derive rules for radial growth without bound, exposing an expressivity trade-off in standard models. A hybrid design with a moving visible layer and static hidden layers proves absorbing invariance and extends the proofs there, tested on deformed multi-well and ring systems with altered metrics.
arxiv-2604-00777: Krekels and colleagues show negative differential heat conductivity can arise in a purely linear system, without nonlinear interactions in the connecting medium. They couple one end of a harmonic chain to a bath of overdamped thermal particles and the other end to a standard Langevin bath. As the temperature gap grows, the steady heat current falls to zero. The effective damping scales inversely with the square of the particle bath's temperature.
arxiv-2604-00977: Hao and team propose FP-DRL, a reward-based learning method. It models policy with flow matching and tunes the entire return spread, rather than cutting returns to a mean. Standard policies built as plain Gaussians struggle with many-peaked spreads, capping reach of optimal answers in multi-answer problems. Flow matching fits complex spreads fast, and a spread model guides many-peaked policy updates better, with state-of-the-art results on most MuJoCo control tasks.
arxiv-2604-01577: Takashiro and colleagues study out-of-sample transfer where models train on short runs but must operate over much longer spans under bounded memory. They focus on a fast-slow looping setup where a state is kept across inputs rather than reset each step. For each input, the model runs weight-shared updates with a looping core, then carries the state forward. Steady latent loops improve out-of-sample transfer over looping, state-space, and attention rivals. Tests spot state-tied shifts and feature-wise bent mixing as parts.
arxiv-2604-01777: Li and colleagues propose GardenDesigner, a framework encoding aesthetic principles for Jiangnan gardens, a Chinese style now valued as assets for film, games and tourism. Manual modeling leans on experience and takes much time. GardenDesigner uses a chain of agents. Terrain and road agents apply water-centric terrain and pathway rules. Asset agents choose and arrange objects under aesthetic and cultural constraints. GardenVerse expert garden knowledge supports arrangement. A Unity interface lets non-experts build gardens from text in one minute, and evaluations find outputs diverse and pleasing.
arxiv-2604-01977: In 2026, Garg and colleagues automate flaw detection rule writing with RuleForge, an AWS system. In 2025 over 48,000 flaws were published, beyond manual handling. RuleForge turns Nuclei templates for CVE details into JSON patterns spotting malicious HTTP requests exploiting flaws. It uses a language model as judge on sensitivity and specificity, scoring AUROC 0.75 and cutting false positives by 67 percent against test only checks. A five by five plan with five candidates and up to five refinements each, plus feedback loops, drives improvement, and extensions cover raw sources and multi event workflows.
arxiv-2604-02177: Brahmbhatt, Ganesh and Avraamidou speed up distributed model predictive control by dropping iteration. Their FACET method computes explicit control laws offline for each subsystem with multiparametric programming, then explores critical regions by facet properties to target the search. Control matches centralized methods while cutting average compute time by 98 percent against classic iterative control and 42 percent against earlier iteration free versions. The gain suits real time control under tight latency limits.
arxiv-2604-02677: Kumar and three colleagues study how plural language-model help shapes human thought. Two trials with 562 people covered math and writing. In math, an expert helper plus peer-like agents that flag common errors gave the best unassisted post-task scores. In writing, help raised essay quality, while a pair of role-specialized helpers kept more idea diversity than one generalist helper.
arxiv-2604-03177: Journeaux and colleagues pin down how dysprosium-162 atoms respond to light near the 530-nanometer line, a quantity trapping designs must know precisely. Using the strong spin-dependent light shift near that line, they measure the background scalar and vector polarizabilities in the ground state. The values match atomic-structure calculations and clarify nearby transition contributions for emerging tweezer platforms.
arxiv-2604-03377: Niu and colleagues propose ViBA, a learning framework that trains visual matching continuously from raw video without labeled poses or depths. It combines tracking, depth-based outlier filtering, and differentiable bundle adjustment jointly refining camera poses and feature spots. Tests cut translation error 12 to 18 percent and keep over 90 percent localization accuracy on unseen sequences, at real-time speeds.
arxiv-2604-03577: Zhao, Liu, and Wei propose a way to fully and deterministically tell apart any high-dimensional Bell states using ICO. Older schemes separate bit and phase information in turn, but their approach uses gravitational ICO as the sole tool. No matter the dimension, broad Bell states are told apart by tuning built-in local single-qudit gates and reading each qudit. The causal structure survives, allowing a damage-free reader over two rounds.
arxiv-2604-03677: Yoshinari Fujinuma and Keisuke Sakaguchi unlocked a missing skill in masked diffusion language models, which build text by cleaning up masked passages in both directions. Standard tuning masks only answers, so the models could not fill gaps inside a prompt; masking prompts and answers together during tuning fixed that. Model-filled prompts matched or beat hand-written ones and carried across models.
arxiv-2604-03877: Hope McGovern and colleagues compared what language models know about narrative analogies with what they say when asked. Models handle analogies well when surface and structure cues line up, but falter when the link hides below the surface. Probing internal representations beat prompting for rhetorical analogies in open models, while both scored low on narrative analogies. The gap between knowing and saying thus depends on the task, and prompting may not reach stored knowledge.
arxiv-2604-03977: Tingfei Li and Shuanghong Li studied matrix-element statistics in the disorder-free Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a solvable cousin of the usual SYK model. Its Hamiltonian uses 4-body interactions of Majorana fermions with constant couplings, hence disorder-free. For operators built from products of n Majorana fermions with n at least 4, off-diagonal matrix elements fit a generalized inverse Gaussian distribution. That contrasts with the Fréchet fits found in the Lieb-Liniger model, advancing eigenstate thermalization studies.
arxiv-2604-04077: Md Motaleb Hossen Manik and Ge Wang built ADAPT, an agent-based testbed for decentralized scholarly publishing. Journals face submission overload, reviewer fatigue, uneven evaluation, opaque governance, and manipulation, while AI tools usually aid single steps under central control. ADAPT treats journal management as a closed-loop control system with author, reviewer, and rotating editor pools steered by policy-level control. Tests across surges, drift, disagreement, and collusion showed bounded, interpretable responses under stress.
arxiv-2604-04177: Jason Chan, Robert Gaizauskas, and Zhixue Zhao argued that logical soundness is an unreliable yardstick for neurosymbolic fact-checking with language models. Such systems translate claims into logical formulas and check whether they follow validly from verified premises. The authors showed that sound conclusions can still mislead, since human inferences often diverge from strict logic. Drawing on cognitive science and pragmatics, they offered a typology of such cases and urged using models' human-like reasoning tendencies to validate formal outputs.
arxiv-2604-04277: Al-Shareeda and colleagues test whether machine learning can pick error-checking settings for vehicle-to-everything links in 5G networks. Their agent chooses check polynomials and coding rates on the fly, learning from rough signal feedback, burst interference and deep fades. Learning helps most at low to moderate speeds, cutting undetected errors by up to 50 to 70 percent against greedy selection in weak-signal conditions. At speeds from 180 kilometres per hour up, fast channel changes weaken learning and shrink the gap between policies.
arxiv-2604-04377: Shibata and Bannai study compression via substring equation systems, which encode strings as solutions to substring-equality and character-assignment constraints. They show every string has such a system of size on the order of chi, the smallest suffixient set size. This settles chi's reachability, an open problem. They prove computing the smallest system's size is NP-hard and inapproximable within one plus epsilon. The smallest bidirectional macro scheme size lies between the smallest system size and four times it. The two schemes thus match up to a constant factor.
arxiv-2604-04577: Shinde, Maan and Bera characterize compact, steep-spectrum radio sources using Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey images. The team studies 171 compact candidates between declinations -40 and +41 degrees, compact at 147 MHz in TGSS but undetected at 1.4 GHz in NVSS. Characterization identifies 66 compact sources, 87 non-compact, diffuse or resolved sources, and 18 sources detected in neither RACS nor NVSS, implying far steeper spectral indices. Of the 66 compact sources, 38 have spectral indices steeper than -1.5. The work shows many sources went undetected earlier with incorrect spectral limits from poor NVSS imaging in the Galactic plane.
arxiv-2604-04777: Galindo-Silva compares areas either side of colonial borders in sub-Saharan Africa to study how colonial rule reshaped religion. Areas under French and Portuguese direct rule show markedly more Christian adherence than areas under British indirect rule, while old faiths hold on more under indirect rule. Neither mission presence nor pre-colonial politics explains the break. The evidence points instead to the break-up of the old social order: where direct rule eroded rigid hereditary structures, Christianity, which bypassed those bounds, spread to fill the gap.
arxiv-2604-04977: Baird and Moin propose predicting multi-vulnerability attack chains in software supply chains from bill of materials graphs. Supply chain breaches often stem from cascaded interactions among vulnerable parts, yet bill pipelines usually treat scanner findings as single per-CVE records. Their new approach learns attack chains through graph learning driven by bill data. It treats bill structure and scanner outputs as a dependency-constrained evidence graph, not a flat list. CycloneDX bills become graphs whose nodes capture components and known flaws, joined by typed links.
arxiv-2604-05077: Islam and three co-authors propose a feature-aware privacy framework for graph learning in metal additive manufacturing. Metal printing enables vital parts, but quality checks depend on sensor streams containing private process data, limiting sharing. Current defect-detection models treat melt-pool observations as independent samples, ignoring layer-wise couplings. Conventional local differential privacy degrades utility by injecting even noise across all feature dimensions. Their system combines a graph attention network with feature-aware noise, preserving utility while protecting private details.
arxiv-2604-05177: Hajaiej and Su find the best constant in the Gagliardo-Nirenberg rule for the nonlocal Laplacian. Old methods cannot apply straight, since smoothness results for the tool seem hard. The authors build a new method proving the best constant comes from the ground state answer of the rule, and giving the best constant itself.
arxiv-2604-05277: Bachard and four colleagues use semantic embedding to learn how molecular swarms act, giving richer traits for tuning such systems. The swarm uses microtubules, pushed by surface kinesin motors, with DNA tags for control. Adding that tag link to a microtubule model, mined semantic atoms match expected acts. Splitting each frame shows well the expected effect of outside control values. These results help explain simulated tests, making them surer for building lab systems.
arxiv-2604-05677: Sorge and three colleagues design dynamic control allocation for a dual-tilt hexarotor that tilts each propeller on its own.
