A top controller sets the needed wrench while an allocator imposes first-order actuator dynamics and uses spare capacity, modeling saturation head-on. Simulations back the scheme and probe how tilt-angle shapes sway results.
arxiv-2604-05777: Keßler and three colleagues show simple social cues can transmit model-based representations without mind-reading. In reinforcement-learning simulations, a naive agent watching an expert copies actions or boosts values, converging toward expert representations. Model-based learners gain most from social exposure, learning faster with more expert-like representations.
arxiv-2604-06077: Becker, Rouzé, and Salzmann build the first rigorous framework for Gibbs sampling in bosonic many-body systems, where infinite-dimensional models had lacked matching complexity results. They show physically relevant bosonic models have gapped dissipative generators, so thermal states can be prepared efficiently when the gap scales well with mode count. For Bose-Hubbard models inside and beyond mean-field theory, the generators keep a positive gap and converge exponentially to the thermal state. The work yields a qubit algorithm whose runtime grows polynomially in mode count and inverse gap.
arxiv-2604-06177: Hu and seven colleagues build WebExpert, a web agent for specialized fields like finance, biomedicine, and pharmaceuticals, where queries drift and evidence runs noisy. It retrieves sentence-level experience with topic merging and rule distillation, induces light facets such as time, region, policy, and industry from supervision, and plans with preference learning plus a coverage goal. At run time an experience gate steers decoding toward active facets. Across four benchmarks it beats the strongest browsing baseline by up to 3.6 points on exact match while cutting page hops.
arxiv-2604-06377: Balasubramanian and eight colleagues transfer post-trained capabilities across models without retraining. Their Master Key Hypothesis says capabilities are directions in a low-dimensional subspace, transferable through linear alignment. UNLOCK contrasts Source activations with and without the capability, aligns the direction to a Target model, and applies it at inference. Chain-of-thought transfer from the 14B Qwen1.5 model to its 7B sibling gains 12 percent on MATH. A direction from Qwen3-4B to Qwen3-14B lifts AGIEval Math from 61 to 71 percent, beating post-training's 68 percent. Success depends on pretraining.
arxiv-2604-06477: Kim and ten colleagues build a reflection-to-action system for rumination and recurring regrets. Grounded in Transtheoretical and Gross's emotion-regulation models, they study self-reflection tech bridging thought and action. In a 15-day field study, voice diaries kept regrets and wishes, plus WhatIf-Planning. People split into free-form and Gross-guided groups. Their system operationalizes Preparation to bridge Contemplation and Action; evidence shows effects on coping flexibility and emotion regulation. Coping flexibility improves significantly, with the Gross-guided group generating more alternatives and implemented plans.
arxiv-2604-06677: Nath and Suzuki study a simpler stellarator of round coils. Tilted ring coils make the twist steering plasma, while symmetric coils cancel the vertical field. Field-line tracing reports clear nested flux surfaces, and DESC gives the vacuum edge balance. Tuning coil size and tilt angle cuts particle drift and lifts alpha-particle holding. Beside W7-X and LHD on the Gamma-C proxy, its D11 is low, and orbit runs for 100 eV protons and alpha particles show good holding.
arxiv-2604-06877: Dubbeling, Huisman, and Şakar add range-checked value types to the VerCors program verifier. These predicate subtypes cap what values a var can hold, giving a neat way to state range rules. Their approach writes specs by itself from subtype rules and mixes several subtypes for one var with ease. A strict mode for overflow checks demands that every sub-part also stays within the stated subtype. A trial build now runs inside the VerCors verifier.
arxiv-2604-07177: Tajwar, Wuhrlin, and Anand ask how well real-time 3D Gaussian splatting, a way of rendering scenes from soft 3D blobs, runs on modest edge hardware. Rather than testing many devices, they throttle one strong graphics card to mimic weaker tiers, then measure frame rate and power across scenes and settings. The results map the trade-off between speed and energy, hinting at what standalone headsets and thin clients can realistically handle.
arxiv-2604-07277: Gan and five colleagues speed up online training of Android agents, where slow emulators make each step costly. Current methods learn from one action per visited state, wasting the effort spent reaching that state. Android Coach instead samples several actions for a single state, guided by a learned critic that scores actions. A process reward model plus a group-wise advantage estimate keeps the critic honest, yielding success gains of 7.5 and 8.3 points on two benchmarks and 1.4 times the training efficiency.
arxiv-2604-07977: Padilha and Anjos model oblique shocks in massive star clusters as a primary accelerator of cosmic rays up to the knee of the energy spectrum. Their model combines supernova and collective wind shocks, stressing how the shock obliquity angle sets the maximum particle energy. Oblique shocks greatly raise acceleration efficiency, letting particles reach multi-PeV energies depending on rigidity. The preferred model reproduces the all-particle spectrum and composition seen by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory. It reads the knee as a sequence of rigidity-dependent cutoffs.
arxiv-2604-08177: Collmann, Nimr, and Fettweis present a least squares method for estimating phase-locked loop noise parameters from spectra. In current MIMO mobile systems, phase noise can seriously impair performance, so accurate modeling is needed for compensation. At a phase-locked loop output, phase noise is simulated and commonly shown as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, whose spectrum fits a multi-pole model. The method estimates oscillator constants and PLL bandwidth from a measured spectrum. Applied to the MAX2870 and MAX2871 PLL chips, it provides estimates.
arxiv-2604-08577: Jin, Hu, and Paschalidis harden reinforcement learning from human feedback against small prompt shifts that can wreck multi step reasoning. Their DRTO method pairs token level feedback learning with distributionally robust optimization, building ambiguity sets over span losses to stress difficult response segments. Tests show steadier behavior under distribution shift, gaining 4.4 percentage points on MATH-500 with smaller gains on LiveCodeBench over standard token optimization.
arxiv-2604-08677: Chilarescu studies the steady state of a general Bond type endogenous growth model in which both sectors use distinct CES production functions, where CES means constant elasticity of substitution. He proves that in this general setting, saddle path stability cannot be claimed. The short paper focuses on steady state properties alone, leaving the stability question settled in the negative for this class of models.
arxiv-2604-08977: Flores and four colleagues test the assumptions behind active learning for translation when only a handful of examples can be labeled. Active learning picks samples to annotate by optimizing informativeness and diversity. Yet recent work found it no better than random sampling on language generation with 100 to 500 samples. They show neither informativeness nor diversity tracks test performance in this setting. Instead, the order of training samples and their interplay with pretraining data matter more, so future methods for very few samples must account for those factors.
arxiv-2604-09377: Hui Liu, Zou, Chen, Jie Liu, Wang, and Li address task-aware language model routing with multi-level task-profile-guided data synthesis for cold-start scenarios. Large language models vary substantially in performance and cost across tasks and queries, motivating routers that select models for user cost-performance trade-offs. Existing routers generalize poorly in cold-start settings where in-domain training data is unavailable. The authors build a hierarchical task taxonomy and diverse question-answer pairs approximating test-time queries, then introduce TRouter, modeling cost and performance.
arxiv-2604-09577: Leviathan and twelve colleagues show that a modern language model, properly prompted and tooled, can robustly generate custom interfaces, not just text. Until now, generative UI remained a promise, with model output arriving as a static markdown wall of text. Ignoring generation speed, human judges overwhelmingly prefer the generated interfaces to standard markdown output. The results trail human experts yet match them in at least 50 percent of cases. The team also releases PAGEN, a dataset of expert-crafted examples for judging future generative interfaces.
arxiv-2604-09677: Fokoué, Babbitt, and Levental complete a trilogy linking ant-colony choices to machine learning, showing stochastic gradient descent is isomorphic to colony learning. Pheromone updates match weight updates, with evaporation matching learning rates, colony fitness matching flipped loss, and recruitment waves matching backprop passes. Plasticity also maps across: trail reinforcement, evaporation, abandonment, and new trails mirror potentiation, depression, pruning, and neurogenesis. Simulated colonies learn like neural networks on similar tasks.
arxiv-2604-09777: Macrie and 45 co-authors present observations of Type Ia supernova 2023qov spanning a year around peak. JWST spectra at 276 and 363 days show dust emission near 400 Kelvin cooling by about 75 Kelvin, the first unambiguous detection of dust in a normal Type Ia supernova. The emission fits carbonaceous dust within one light year, near a ten-thousandth of a solar mass. No active dust creation appears, suggesting an infrared light echo from old circumstellar dust. Nebular line profiles suggest uneven, layered ejecta and a double-horn argon structure indicating a toroidal enhancement.
arxiv-2604-10077: Purkayastha, Banerjee, Llados, and Pal rebuild damaged document text with DocRevive, a single pipeline for a problem later document tasks depend on. It combines optical character recognition, image analysis, masked language models, and diffusion models. The pipeline spots text, flags damage with a damage detector, and fills gaps with an inpainting model. A diffusion module then blends the restored text back in, matching font, size, and alignment. A synthetic set of 30,078 degraded images sets the benchmark, and a new metric judges repair quality.
arxiv-2604-10177: Li, Lin, Hsieh, and Huang study piecewise-stationary restless bandits, where each arm evolves as a Markov chain but rewards shift across unknown segments. Their modular framework plugs any bandit solver into change detection and fading exploration, adapting to shifts of unknown count. They measure excess regret from exploration and detection against an oracle restarting the solver at true change points. They prove regret grows roughly like the square root of mixing time times segments times arms times horizon. Simulations show near-oracle regret, beating solvers that ignore change.
arxiv-2604-10477: Li and four colleagues test magnetar field shapes against X-ray polarization curves. They pit a plain dipole spin model against a version with a first order twist tweak. Both magnetars fit a dipole led shape, with no strong global twist called for. The twisted model gains only slightly for one source, with a Bayes factor near 3.3. For the second source the gain is nil, so viewing angle plus source traits seems to drive the varied polarization.
arxiv-2604-10777: Shenoy and three colleagues address uncertainty in imaging photoplethysmography, which recovers pulse waves from facial video pixels. Current methods perform well on benchmarks but never sample solutions at test time, blocking uncertainty analysis for clinical use. Their RIS-iPPG method models recovery as an inverse problem, building paths from camera pixels to true signals via flow and score vectors, then sampling the likely wave. A regularization linking residual flow predictions in adjacent time windows further improves recovery. Tests on three datasets show superior rebuild quality and uncertainty estimates.
arxiv-2604-11177: Sharma and three colleagues benchmark how traces, called thought streams, affect video scene understanding. They test Gemini 2.5 Flash and Flash Lite configurations on scenes from 100 hours of video. They ask: does more thinking help, where do gains stop, and what do models think about? They introduce metrics: Contentfulness, Thought-Final Coverage, and Dominant Entity Analysis. Contentfulness rates scene content; Thought-Final Coverage rates outputs; Dominant Entity Analysis names subjects, actions, and settings. Quality gains from thinking plateau, with improvement in the first few hundred tokens. Flash Lite offers best value.
arxiv-2604-11277: Govindarajan and Sadanandan update the holomorphic modular bootstrap with a recent exact S-matrix result inside the modular linear differential equation setting. Using allowed exponents modulo one, they obtain admissible solutions for all such equations with up to six characters. The equations have Wronskian index below six and one accessory parameter with effective central charge at most 24. They then single out solutions with good fusion rules, called tenable. Where possible they identify the conformal field theory and, in unitary cases, the modular tensor category class.
arxiv-2604-11477: Liu and Chen propose out-of-money reinforcement learning, aligning coding agents through live markets, not human or AI feedback. Human and AI feedback induce sycophancy, and test environments invite evasion. They deploy agents where capital depletion acts as a negative gradient. A 20-month study traces from a sycophantic baseline to a liquidity-aware design. It is a strict test-driven workflow with a state lock tied to 95 percent code coverage. In a 94-day window it posted Sharpe near 2.06. The authors stress these results do not prove investment alpha.
arxiv-2604-11677: Billand and ten colleagues ask whether little red dots are a class. JWST dots are read as active nuclei and hosts with masses. Using a LRDness metric of compactness, V-shape, and Balmer strength, they study 48,000 photometric and 5,000 spectroscopic galaxies over 750 square arcminutes. Shape tracks morphology with no clear transition. H-alpha strength rises with sharpness and compactness. The nitrogen deficit is global to compact metal-poor galaxies. Only the 3 percent most extreme dots show a Balmer break above 3, and all galaxies share a Balmer decrement trend, suggesting one origin.
arxiv-2604-11777: Capistrano-Filho and Nascimento develop a framework for the fifth-order Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation in a mean-zero Sobolev scale. A local high-order feedback on the periodic variable yields a five-halves derivative gain, driving regularity spread and a unique continuation property. From an observability inequality for the adjoint system they obtain exponential decay of the nonlinear closed-loop equation for small initial data. With this plus the Hilbert Uniqueness Method and a fixed-point step, they get local exact controllability near the origin.
arxiv-2604-11877: Sehayek and Craig study how higher symmetry structures constrain axion effective field theories. Higher-group and non-invertible symmetries set limits on the energy scales where different symmetries can emerge at low energies, guiding guesses about ultraviolet physics. In axion theories coupled to abelian and non-abelian gauge bosons, with or without charged matter, they clarify these emergence limits. The limits are universally met by anomaly inflow onto topological defects, while in perturbative ultraviolet completions they prove supererogatory, given the wide separation of scales.
arxiv-2604-12077: Belda and five colleagues introduce a version of multiscale orthogonal decomposition, for optimal modes per band. Old filters cause spectral overlap and demand a full eigenvalue problem per band. The new approach swaps time-domain filters for compact masks with disjoint supports, splitting scales into a block operator. Each band needs a system sized by active bands, not the full size. Tested on synthetic data and cylinder-wake PIV at Reynolds number near 5,000, it recovers modal shapes and singular values while cutting cost by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2604-12377: SungHo Kim and three colleagues tackle Korean language models, which usually split text into subwords. Subword splitting misses how each Korean character is built from smaller jamo units. Their SCRIPT module injects that subcharacter structure into existing models. It needs no architecture change and no retraining from scratch. SCRIPT lifts every baseline tested on Korean understanding and generation. It also reshapes embeddings to capture grammar patterns more cleanly.
arxiv-2604-13177: Prabhu and nine colleagues show quantum computational displacement sensing with a superconducting circuit joining a qubit to an oscillator. Instead of estimating a sensed displacement and then classifying it, their protocol uses tuned quantum circuits before and after sensing. It maps the binary class label directly onto the qubit's ground or excited state. Circuits with up to 24 entangling gates and 38 free parameters gain accuracy with depth, beating conventional sense-then-classify protocols by up to 15 percentage points on some tasks.
arxiv-2604-13277: Ahmad studies comprehension debt, the gap between what a team knows about its codebase and what it must understand to maintain it. GenAI tools spread through software work, and he asks how they feed that debt. Drawing on 621 reflective diaries from 207 students over eight weeks, he identifies four debt accumulation patterns: black-box code acceptance, context-mismatch debt, dependency-induced atrophy, and verification-bypass. One mitigating pattern uses GenAI as a comprehension scaffold for deeper understanding, and he argues the debt lives in team cognition rather than code itself.
arxiv-2604-13377: Gracia and Lahijanian ask if refining uncertain MDP models can reach the best controller with no error left. Their method turns a nonlinear stochastic system into an uncertain MDP, builds a controller with guarantees by robust dynamic programming, then refines the model until it is near best. Theory gives a sufficient condition, vanishing ambiguity, that ensures the process reaches the best result in the limit and finishes in finite time. Set-valued MDP models meet it, while interval MDP models do not.
arxiv-2604-13477: Cai, Peng, and Zheng study photon counts for a driven single-molecule system with spectral drift from nonequilibrium outside shifts. Using generating functions and the stochastic Liouville equation, they analyse shifts under shifting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise and random telegraph noise. In the slow tuning limit, brightness and shifts depend on those effects early but become free of them later. In the fast tuning limit, neither line shape nor Mandel's value depends on those effects, owing to rapid settling.
arxiv-2604-13577: Yoshida proves new lower bounds for testing whether a directed graph has cycles when each query reveals only a vertex's outgoing neighbors. Any one-sided tester needs roughly n to the two-thirds power queries, improving the prior n to the five-ninths bound. A two-sided tester still needs about the square root of n queries. For tolerant testing, he shows a linear lower bound by reduction from bounded-degree three-colorability.
arxiv-2604-13677: Jafari, Nguyen, and Liu measure how comfortable pedestrians feel when a mobile robot passes them on a sidewalk. Safety studies often track collisions, but comfort is a feeling, and it is hard to quantify. In one-on-one trials with volunteers, reported comfort correlates moderately but significantly with motion variables such as closest distance and time to collision. A composite predictor using all variables performs best, with an odds ratio of 3.67, meaning a pedestrian it flags as comfortable is nearly four times more likely to be comfortable.
arxiv-2604-13777: Li and six colleagues tackle unlearning in large language models without a forget set. Models may memorize sensitive or copyrighted text, and standard unlearning asks users to supply the material to forget, which is hard to audit and risks leaks or abuse. Their MAGE framework needs only a light anchor naming the target entity. It probes the model, builds a weighted local memory graph, then synthesizes scoped supervision. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks, its self-made supervision matches external-reference supervision while preserving overall utility.
arxiv-2604-13877: Xiao and nine colleagues propose Scalable Quantum Molecular Generation, a variational circuit sampling graphs from priors. Each heavy atom gets three qubits; one two-qubit bond register is reused for bonds, an atom-no-reuse, bond-reuse design with linear scaling. Classical decoding maps measurements to graphs with constraints. At eight heavy atoms, GPU state-vector runs up to 45,000 times the CPU; GPU tensor-network up to 2,200 times. Tensor-network simulation reaches 40 atoms exactly, where state-vector methods fail. The architecture handles de novo generation, linker design, and scaffold decoration.
arxiv-2604-13977: Niklaus and colleagues ask how to synthesize high-quality pretraining data, testing prompt design, generator size, and source data in controlled trials over one trillion tokens. Structured formats like tables, math problems, FAQs, and tutorials beat curated web baselines, while generators larger than 1 billion parameters add nothing. Their FinePhrase set holds 486 billion tokens of rephrased web text and cuts generation costs up to 30 times.
arxiv-2604-14377: Szyszko and Birowska show atomic arrangement, not just mix, steers the electronic and optical traits of two-dimensional molybdenum-tungsten-sulfur alloys. Stability and energy track composition, but band-edge splitting, valley shape, effective-mass direction dependence, and optical selection rules shift with layout. Even without spin-orbit coupling, band edges split at the K point throughout the range. Separated conduction bands open extra optically active transitions beyond the usual A and B excitons. Hole masses at the valence-band top vary with direction as local symmetry breaks.
arxiv-2604-14477: Żukowska, Stammer, Schiele, and Fischer ask whether useful mechanistic circuits can be found in vision transformers through computational graphs. Edge-based circuits, defined by links between model parts, exist for language models, but vision work so far uses neuron-based circuits that show what is encoded, not how signals route. Their Automatic Visual Circuit Discovery method recovers class circuits for classification, circuits behind typographic attacks in CLIP, and circuits that steer harmful behavior right. Insightful, actionable edge-based circuits can thus be recovered from vision transformers, the team concludes.
arxiv-2604-14577: Mata-Cervera, Porras, and Shen unveil the spin field around optical vortex lines, where intensity vanishes and phase is undefined. Gauss's law dresses these dark threads in pure longitudinal polarization, with the polarization plane tilting and winding around them. The spin field unifies textures and defects: a point defect of undefined spin sits inside a meronic texture spanning half the spin unit sphere. The structure does not spread in travel, localizes far below the light wavelength, and shows strong anisotropy, revealing hidden transverse-spin topologies in scalar vortex beams.
arxiv-2604-14777: Zhao, Qi, Li, Fan, Li, and Wei give field-tunable nanofluidic transport a formal footing built on Poisson-Boltzmann theory. Their map of confined electric double layers under external fields yields a framework for tunable transport, with the ionic transistor treated in depth. The framework reproduces observed conductivity-concentration scaling and explains polarity-switching devices. It also predicts one basic thermodynamic limit for electrostatic modulation: 60 millivolts per decade. The authors call the framework accurate and broad, able to cover a wide range of ion transport in confined spaces.
arxiv-2604-14977: Lebon, Lindberg, and Altafini find the smallest set of control input nodes and an output feedback law for complete disturbance decoupling of coupled oscillator networks. The networks sit near stable phase-locked sync. Applied to swing dynamics of power grids near sync, decoupling means shielding node subsets from outside disturbances with batteries adding or drawing active power. Simulations on the IEEE New England 39-bus system show the method yields minimal control placement with effective disturbance rejection while keeping closed-loop inner stability.
arxiv-2604-15177: Formenti and colleagues study how hard it is to predict fungal automata, rules applied alternately vertically and horizontally. They cover all freezing totalistic one-dimensional radius-1 rules, most predictable with nondeterministic logspace methods, leaving one nonlinear rule open. They also examine the freezing majority rule, proving prediction turns P-complete at radius 1.5. The paper maps a model where simple local rules still hide sharp complexity jumps.
arxiv-2604-15577: Peysakhovich and Berman show that reward-weighted classifier-free guidance can act as a policy improvement operator for autoregressive models, tilting sampling toward a reward without retraining. The method approximates tilting by the Q function, letting new reward functions be optimized at test time, demonstrated on molecular generation. Distilling the guided policy back into the base policy as a warm start then speeds standard reinforcement learning convergence.
arxiv-2604-15977: Hoffmann and Kryszkiewicz study how nonlinear power amplifiers distort massive MIMO signals under realistic channels. Most work assumes linear front ends, but energy-saving hardware pushed to its limits behaves nonlinearly, especially for OFDM. The authors first characterize the distortion under standard models, then show 3D ray tracing exposes those models as inaccurate. They propose a statistical model for signal-to-distortion ratios using the generalized extreme value distribution, plus a learning model. The learning-based power allocation gains about 12 percent median user throughput over a fixed operating point.
arxiv-2604-16077: Baseilhac and Ben Aribi compute a limit of quantum hyperbolic invariants for the figure-eight knot complement. They show the real part of this semi-classical limit is rigid. It does not depend on the chosen holonomy representation. It equals either 0 or the hyperbolic volume divided by two pi. Which value occurs depends on a parity condition on logs of holonomy eigenvalues along the canonical longitude. They also survey general features of these invariants.
arxiv-2604-16177: Beltrame and six colleagues present the winning entry in the CVPR2026 NTIRE challenge on removing shadows from images. Their three-stage pipeline refines predictions step by step, combining colour appearance with semantic guidance and geometric cues from depth and surface normals. A contraction rule keeps reconstruction error from growing across stages, and their final ensemble topped the hidden WSRD+ 2026 test, taking first place overall.
arxiv-2604-16377: Choudhury, Maurya, Kuwar and Buduru address a forensic question: which language model wrote a given piece of code. Their GoCoMA framework combines two signals, the stylistic fingerprints of the code itself and image-like views of compiled artifacts that capture lower-level byte patterns. Those signals are fused inside a curved, hyperbolic space before being mapped back for a final attribution decision. On two open benchmarks, the combined approach beat both single-signal and flat-space rivals under identical testing rules.
arxiv-2604-16477: Brossard gives a constructive proof of Rice's theorem and the halting problem from Hilbert's Tenth Problem undecidability. Unlike classical proofs, which use the law of excluded middle twice, his proof works in intuitionistic logic with neither diagonalization nor self-reference beyond MRDP. The key is two witnesses. For each Diophantine polynomial, a pair of programs acts as negative and positive witnesses when solvable. Both diverge when it is not. A decider for the property would decide solvability, a contradiction. Halting undecidability follows as a corollary, formalized in Rocq.
arxiv-2604-16577: Brery and colleagues explore multilevel networks with dual-stage feature fusion for activity recognition. Combining convolutional, memory and hybrid networks exploits matching strengths, but layout matters. Their two-level design uses late fusion of first-level outputs plus intermediate fusion across both levels. Testing 15 architectures on two public benchmarks, both fusions beat late fusion alone. The best configuration also beat baseline models, proving the approach for activity recognition.
arxiv-2604-16677: Chen and colleagues open ReconVLA, a trusted guarded model for cautious, failure-wise robotic control. VLA models map visual views and language orders to smooth action chains, but give no tuned trust. ReconVLA applies conformal prediction to action token outputs of ready bots, giving uncertainty scores tied to running quality and task success. It extends conformal prediction to robot state space, catching oddballs and unsafe states before failures occur. In sim and real robot trials, guarded guesses improve failure foresight and reduce fatal errors without new training.
arxiv-2604-17077: Bordignon and Minelli study elliptic Dedekind sums, Sczech's generalization of the classical sums to complex lattices. They prove the normalized sums follow a Gaussian limit distribution, meaning their values spread like a bell curve. The result describes these sums' behavior at large scales. They also settle a conjecture due to Ito.
arxiv-2604-18177: An, Kadhe, Thakur, DeLuca, and Patel propose STaD, a framework for exposing compositional skill gaps in large language models. Aggregate benchmark scores hide which reasoning skills a model lacks and how to fix them. STaD generates controlled task variations that add structured, step-by-step support, a technique called scaffolding. Tests on six models across three reasoning benchmarks reveal distinct failure points and skill gaps for each model.
arxiv-2604-18377: Pandharipande, Petersen, Schmitt, and Wood reprove an odd cohomology invariance for general compactified Jacobians. Pagani and Tommasi defined smoothable fine ones hinging on degree and stability rule, yet Migliorini-Shende-Viviani showed those counts ignore both choices. The authors give a direct counting proof by summing shares of single edge strata. An appendix adds a rule for equivariant isomorphism and a non-equality result in the Grothendieck ring.
arxiv-2604-18477: Ali and Murad present MS-RCGR, a lossless code that turns life-science sequences into multi-scale shape traits. Older codes lose information or miss scale structure, but ratio-based math plus layered k-mer breakdown preserves full strings. The system serves three styles of analysis: classic machine learning on shape traits, vision models on made images, and hybrids pairing protein language vectors with shape traits. Tests on lab-made DNA and protein data across seven classes show steady gains, best when language vectors join the new traits.
arxiv-2604-18677: Yamamoto and Hambye ask whether the ultrahigh-energy neutrino recently caught by the KM3NeT telescope could have come from decaying or annihilating relics of the early universe. Such a source would concentrate the signal near one energy, easing tension with other experiments that saw nothing. Their calculation also predicts a possible imprint in the cosmic microwave background, testable in future observations.
arxiv-2604-19177: Kang, Mao, and Ma propose a nonparametric conditional independence test for continuous spaces. It splits samples into tables. They condition on order stats. This stays valid without stratum sizes growing to infinity. It yields handy statistics with a known null distribution. Tests show reliable error control with small samples. An Uber case study shows it can test and spot association, with summary stats capturing strength and direction.
arxiv-2604-19377: Qiu and colleagues compare the energy costs of AI-powered sixth-generation Internet of Things networks under central and spread-out designs. Training models and sending data drive much of the energy use, so tuning them matters for green design. The study first models energy use for both designs, then tests a setup in German railways using sensor data for predictive maintenance. Spread-out models keep predictive accuracy near 90 percent while cutting total electricity use.
arxiv-2604-19877: The SLAM Labs team releases Super Apriel, a 15-billion-parameter language-model supernet whose every decoder layer offers four mixer choices, from full attention to gated delta variants. Any layer-by-layer placement can switch between requests without reloading weights, giving many speed presets from one checkpoint. Recommended hybrid presets run markedly faster at decoding while retaining 77 to 96 percent of quality, and the shared checkpoint also enables draft-free speculative decoding.
arxiv-2604-20277: Li and four colleagues use machine-learning molecular dynamics to watch sliding in ferroelectric MoS2 moiré superlattices. Heat alone drives layers to slide near 1 m/s at 300 K, as a broad drift of the pattern rather than stiff motion of the whole bilayer. With relaxed constraints the slide follows a near barrier-free path matching the drift, defying the small rigid-slide barrier. Sulfur gaps flip sliding to pinning, with just 0.1 percent sulfur gaps enough to turn long-range sliding into local wobbles, holding beyond small twist angles.
arxiv-2604-20577: Ikhwantri and Marijan propose a graph diagnostic framework for assurance cases, linked arguments that justify system claims with evidence. In regulated domains cases support compliance and safety standards. Their framework handles link finding between argument parts and graph sorting for provenance, telling model from human cases. They compile a dataset of assurance cases as graphs of nodes and edges. Graph neural networks score ROC-AUC 0.760 on link finding and F1 94 out of 100 on provenance tests. Yet explanation methods show only moderate faithfulness, leaving a gap between reasoning and argument structure.
arxiv-2604-20777: Simionato and five colleagues offer a method that gauges long-term treatment effects and residual lifetime value change in short multi-cohort tests under user learning. Even with short- and predicted long-term metrics, a treatment's effect on staying may be missed. To estimate time-varying treatment effects, they offer an inverse-variance weighted estimator that pools multiple cohort figures. Their framework tests steady-state impact and residual user value within a trial. Empirical results show better precision in gauging long-term treatment effects and residual lifetime value change.
arxiv-2604-21277: Jindi Guo, Chaozheng Huang, and Xi Fang test whether multimodal language models can rebuild masked text from visual context alone, without explicit questions. Their MMTR-Bench spans 2,771 samples across languages and target lengths, covering documents and webpages in single- and multi-page form. A level-aware scoring protocol handles the diversity. Representative models struggle, most at sentence- and paragraph-level reconstruction, showing the benchmark probes layout understanding, visual grounding, and knowledge integration rather than instruction following.
arxiv-2604-21477: Run Hao and Zhuoran Tan probe security pitfalls in Model Context Protocol tool servers, where third-party tools expand supply-chain risk. Their MCP Pitfall Lab models developer pitfalls as reproducible scenarios validated from traces, not agent self-report, and introduces a semantic bill-of-materials enriching component inventory with security-relevant tool semantics. Across 2,579 validator-completed runs over four models, attacks succeed 31.9 percent of the time overall, with multi-modal injection strongest at about 39 percent. Hardening cuts BOM-backed findings from 27 to 16.
arxiv-2604-21977: The Euclid Collaboration presents AstroVink, a vision transformer classifier for finding strong lens candidates in Euclid imaging. The base model, trained on mock systems and labelled non-lenses, recovers 88 of 110 lens candidates within the top 500. After the Q1 release yielded about 500 lens candidates, the model was retrained on high confidence candidates and new negatives. The retrained network recovers all 110 systems, at one lens per about 5 checks. Applied to the Q1 selection of 1.08M targets, it identified eight Grade A and 26 Grade B new lens candidates.
arxiv-2604-22077: Za'ter and Hodge present a test of time series foundation models, transformers, and deep learning baselines for solar, wind, and load forecasting. It uses the ARPAE PERFORM dataset for the Texas grid. Eight capabilities are assessed, including zero-shot performance, fine-tuning efficiency, multivariate input and output handling, horizon sensitivity, new-site tests, odds forecasts, and context window effects. Models evaluated include TimesFM, Chronos Bolt, MoiraiL, MOMENT, Tiny Time Mixer, Temporal Fusion Transformer, PatchTST, TimeXer, LSTM, and CNN.
arxiv-2604-22177: Song and seven colleagues propose UniME, a two-stage method for brain tumor segmentation with missing MRI modalities. Stage 1 pretrains a single ViT Uni-Encoder with masked image modeling, building a unified representation robust to missing modalities. Stage 2 adds special CNN Multi-Encoders to extract high-resolution, multi-scale, fine-grained features. Fusing these features with the global picture yields precise segmentations. On BraTS 2023 and BraTS 2024, UniME outperforms previous methods under incomplete multi-modal scenarios.
arxiv-2604-22277: Lee and Lee run a careful test with 127 people on how agreement among several AI agents sways human judgement. The test used three set-ups: majority, minority and diffusion. Majority consensus sped up opinion change and raised self-belief. That pattern matches social-proof and bandwagon effects. Minority pushback slowed change and encouraged more thought. People followed three paths, reinforcing, aligning or oscillating, based on how independent they judged the agents to be. The authors argue that agreement structure itself, apart from content, can bias trust in AI systems.
arxiv-2604-22677: Suarez-Roman, Serrano, and Gandica unveil scale-invariant online interaction patterns in social movements across three massive mobilisation events. Online platforms host movements, leaving network traces that show how information, participation, and coordination emerge and evolve. From Twitter hashtag data, they build co-occurrence networks and apply degree-thresholding renormalisation. These linked social events show self-similarity at peak mobilisation times. Those critical points show modular-to-nested shifts, in co-occurrence and bi-partite networks, peaks in user participation, and clustering spectrum collapse across network scales.
arxiv-2604-22977: Dolatkhah and three colleagues frame combined operating room planning and scheduling as a mixed integer programming model, placing mandatory and elective surgeries across rooms and days under overtime and surgeon limits. A column-building algorithm solves large instances, boosted by a hybrid reinforcement learning and genetic algorithm method for initial columns. Tests on made-up and real Naples hospital cases show average quality gaps under 1.5 percent, beating previous methods. Under 20 percent surgery duration swings, a 120-minute buffer gives the lowest overall cost.
arxiv-2604-23077: Tamm and Aljanaki test nine pretrained audio backend models for music recommender systems, a use case music information retrieval papers rarely explore. They test the models with five recommendation methods, including nearest neighbors, a shallow neural network, contrast multi-modal projection, a hybrid model, and BERT4Rec, in hot and cold-start scenarios. Pretrained representations show a large performance gap between old retrieval tasks and music recommendations. The findings suggest backend models capture musical information differently by task, laying groundwork for further study.
arxiv-2604-23277: Zhou and eight colleagues compress long LLM contexts without training, using structural graph priors to pick a compact sentence set. A sparse hybrid sentence graph joins mutual k-nearest-neighbour semantic edges with short-range sequential edges, and clustering extracts a topic skeleton. Sentences are ranked by task relevance, cluster representativeness, bridge centrality, and cycle coverage, then a budgeted greedy pass with redundancy suppression emits the context in original order. Tests on four datasets match strong extractive and abstractive baselines, with larger gains on long-document benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-23377: Takemura, Inoue, and Nishino formalize reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic learning, where a system obeys logical constraints yet learns the wrong link between concepts and labels. They prove a discrimination condition is necessary but not sufficient for ruling shortcuts out, then give a verified algorithm that checks whether constraints pin down the intended mapping. They also classify the hardness of detecting, counting, and repairing shortcuts, and validate the method on eight benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-23477: Lin and colleagues build SEMA-SQL, a system that answers plain-language questions by mixing ordinary database operations with language-model reasoning in one declarative framework. It generates hybrid queries, optimises them by rewriting costly language-model steps, and batches semantic joins so cleverly that language-model calls fall by 93 percent there. Experiments on established benchmarks show large gains in what such queries can express.
arxiv-2604-23577: Guo, Wu, and Yiu present RouteNLP, a closed-loop router that sends each language-model query to the cheapest tier that can handle it well. A difficulty-aware router, confidence-calibrated cascading, and a loop that distils lessons from escalation failures work together to cut cost. In an eight-week enterprise pilot, inference costs fell by well over half while acceptance stayed high and worst-case latency dropped sharply.
arxiv-2604-23677: Bal, Ekiz, Kahya, and Zorba study stationary solutions in the small-speed-of-light expansion of general relativity, where the field equations become more tractable for explicit construction. The stationary sector splits into strong-gravity and weak-field branches, richer at next-to-next-to-leading order. They build exact vacuum solutions in both branches, including rotating and quadrupole-deformed geometries, showing the full theory admits a richer stationary sector than a simpler truncation.
arxiv-2604-23777: Perkkola, Meijer-van de Griend, and Nurminen present an architecture-aware method for exact unitary gate synthesis on superconducting quantum hardware. Tightly integrated with a recursive block decomposition, it makes hardware-aware choices at each recursion level through greedy qubit mapping, adaptive Gray code selection with swapping, and a heuristic cutting long-range CNOT ladders. It cuts CNOT counts by over a third on two test devices and runs over 500 times faster than rivals.
arxiv-2604-24077: Chen and four colleagues push back on a conjecture about the Perron vector of graphs. A classical bound caps the squared weight of any independent set at one half, and Gregory conjectured a gap tied to chromatic number and size. Odd cycles already break that conjecture, and the authors give an exact formula for the gap in terms of spectral radius and a Rayleigh quotient. They then build graphs whose gap shrinks exponentially fast, ruling out any universal polynomial-style lower bound.
arxiv-2604-24177: Sasaki reviews recent work on low-lying scalar mesons and glueballs. He proposes a new scalar nonet classification with f0(980) and a0(980) as the lowest states, and names f0(1500) as a primary glueball candidate. Production yields in heavy-ion collisions agree across statistical, coalescence, and S-matrix frameworks. Treating glueballs as topological solitons yields a spectrum matching lattice QCD and experiment, with f0(2470) read as a tightly bound glueballonium explaining its long lifetime.
arxiv-2604-24277: Joia Neto and three colleagues resolve a conflict between operating system timekeeping and uninterruptable trusted computing on microcontrollers. Trusted Execution Environments isolate Secure and Non-Secure software sharing interrupt controllers, and real-time systems need SysTick interrupts for timekeeping. Trusted services require atomicity against the Non-Secure side, blocking SysTick handling. Their Secure-driven sync lets the Secure World measure time and credit the Non-Secure RTOS with missed ticks before re-enabling interrupts. The approach restores consistent time across worlds with no RTOS changes and little runtime overhead.
arxiv-2604-24677: Tokka proves a local limit, as vertex count grows without bound, for uniform random bipartite planar maps that are d-regular, for every d at least 3. The proof uses a bijection between maps and blossoming trees from earlier work. After showing the associated decorated trees converge locally, he extends the bijection to infinite trees and transfers convergence to planar maps. The limit object is one-ended and recurrent under the simple random walk, almost surely.
arxiv-2604-24777: Boumali and Chargui separate results that follow directly from a bounded thermal weight from those needing extra phenomenological input. The discrete Boltzmann factor regularizes the canonical weight on a lattice and caps allowed energy. For Hawking radiation, they study the discrete Bose-Einstein factor, showing luminosity suppression and thermal shutoff near the cutoff. They build a discrete work functional with an exact Jarzynski-type identity. The Crooks relation does not collapse to work alone. Standard continuum expressions return smoothly as the bound parameter tends to zero.
arxiv-2604-25177: Wright improves results of Fouvry and Radziwiłł on unbalanced convolutions. He treats sequences supported on comparable ranges, with one sequence equidistributed for small moduli, and sharpens the ranges for the convolution parameters. One improvement widens the range of the length parameter, and another widens the range of the modulus. To prove the new bounds, he improves a result of Bettin and Chandee on trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions for denominators with a fixed factor.
arxiv-2604-25577: Xu and five colleagues recast online fair re-ranking as trade in an attention market under Walrasian equilibrium, with fairness as a taxation cost. Their review of online methods across 20 settings finds sharp performance gaps. Seeking the equilibrium equals gradient descent on a ranking manifold built by the market. They propose ManifoldRank, an online algorithm that adjusts gradients to fit the manifold for each setting. On the supply side it adds a fairness correction with costs, while on the demand side it predicts a further correction from ranking scores.
arxiv-2604-25677: Martínez-Fernández and three colleagues study coherent deeply virtual Compton scattering on helium-4, going beyond leading power in the theory. Hard exclusive reactions on light nuclei expose the quark-gluon makeup and support three-dimensional imaging of these systems. The authors include kinematic corrections at two subleading orders plus next-to-leading-order corrections to the leading amplitude in the strong coupling. They show these contributions are essential for describing the data precisely, yielding the first tomographic image of helium-4 at the quark-gluon level.
arxiv-2604-25777: Zheng and five colleagues present SpecFed, a way to speed federated inference for large language models. Federated use mixes outputs across workers, but autoregressive decoding needs frequent full-model passes. Workers must also send full token probability distributions, which dominate latency. SpecFed enables parallel processing through speculative decoding, plus a top-K scheme that shrinks transmissions, with two server-side rebuild strategies. The authors bound rebuild error and two kinds of bias. Tests show high fidelity with much lower communication cost.
arxiv-2604-26477: Tao and three colleagues rechecked multi-objective optimization claims for quantum solvers with GPU-based quantum-annealing-inspired algorithms. Past studies reported quantum wins but left out the heavy pre- and post-processing costs of real quantum solvers. The inspired algorithms, which draw samples by chance like quantum hardware, made candidates about one hundred times faster than the quantum processors studied. End to end, they also beat top classical solvers, making them the best of the lot on the MO-MaxCut suite so far.
arxiv-2604-26577: Nakao and Takemoto benchmarked language-model safety for robotic health attendants against 270 harmful instructions across nine prohibited categories. The mean violation rate across 72 models was about 54 percent, with over half the models above 50 percent. Plausible-sounding requests like device manipulation and emergency delay proved harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones. Proprietary models were far safer than open-weight ones, with medians near 24 percent versus 73 percent. Medical fine-tuning gave no overall safety gain, and prompt defenses helped only modestly.
arxiv-2604-26677: Ye and six colleagues make wave vortices around a tiny hole with a small, adjustable setup, using water waves in a lab. Type-II vortices differ from ordinary vortices with phase gaps and appear naturally in island ocean tides, for example around New Zealand, Madagascar, and Iceland. The team pairs a wobbling dipole island with a single plane wave and measures phase structure, topological charge, and angular momentum of the wave. Vortex birth and handedness follow the relative phase between source and wave.
arxiv-2604-26777: Cassanelli and nine colleagues report IQUEYE at Gemini South, a fast photon counter based on avalanche diodes that times photon arrivals to sub-nanosecond per hour accuracy. Built for intensity interferometry, it now covers ultra-fast astronomy: optical pulsars, millisecond pulsars, and fast radio bursts. Brought to the roughly 8-metre Gemini South dish as a visitor instrument, it gained about an order of magnitude in sensitivity. There, the team observed giant pulse emitters and millisecond pulsars for over 40 hours within a week.
arxiv-2604-26877: Aggarwal and Vaidya study entropy solutions for nonlocal conservation laws whose flux depends on nearby values in space and on past states in time, giving the system memory. They build a convergent finite-volume approximation, prove existence and uniqueness of the entropy solution, and track the limit as the time-memory window shrinks. That passage shows a memory-to-memoryless effect, converging to the memoryless nonlocal law, with rate estimates derived. The approximations stay asymptotically compatible with that limit, in a general setting without convexity restrictions on the kernels.
arxiv-2604-27077: Shigida, Hanin and Gromov introduce nuGPT, a new parameterization of the Normalized Transformer, showing learning rate transfer over width, depth, and token horizon in extensive empirical tests. nGPT itself trains fast without weight decay or learning rate warmup. Yet despite hyperparameters scaling with model size, it shows no transfer across model dimension and token horizon. The authors combine numerical experiments with alignment exponents and revisit the muP approach to hyperparameter transfer and modify it. The outcome is a parameterization designed to restore the transfer nGPT lacked.
arxiv-2604-27377: Qi-Dong Chen and four others give an account of bound-state resonances for Schwarzschild-de Sitter holes, extending work on Schwarzschild holes. They derive the characteristic equation and closed-form energies for resonances, recovering the Schwarzschild spectrum when the cosmological constant vanishes. Schwarzschild holes support infinitely many resonance levels, but de Sitter counterparts support only finitely many, which caps the oscillatory domain and blocks infinite delocalization. They find delocalized half-bound states at discrete values of the cosmological constant, a feature absent for Schwarzschild holes.
arxiv-2604-27677: Huang and seven colleagues offer PuzzleMark, a tough watermarking method for code data sets. To reduce leak risk, it picks carrier snippets by code complexity, choosing highly fit snippets for marking. It replaces the old co-occurrence pattern with a novel joining pattern through variable name joining, placing watermarks to fit the code while keeping design simple. Checks use Fisher's exact test under black-box settings, reaching 100 percent success with zero false alarms and tiny performance impact.
arxiv-2604-27877: Bärlin offers a fresh route to damping estimates for self-similar answers of hyperbolic relaxation systems in one dimension. Such bounds anchor stability proofs for relaxation profiles, with or without subshocks, by closing nonlinear stability arguments. He lifts the Mascia-Zumbrun and Yang-Zumbrun estimates from square-sum to sup-norm bounds, and widens the square-sum case to non-symmetric settings. His path is far simpler, skipping Kawashima-type estimates and pseudo-differential tools, and it opens a general stability theory for shock profiles under spread-out disturbances.
arxiv-2604-27977: Moussa and colleagues present D3-Gym, a set of test tasks for agents doing real science work. Hundreds of tasks from real research code bases come with plain instructions, setups that run, sample answers and auto scoring that matches human marks closely. Training on runs from these tasks lifted scores on a science-agent test, closing much of the gap to top closed systems.
arxiv-2605-00577:
Junxiang Yao and 3 co-authors study how supercurrents cross a half-metallic ferromagnet, a solid magnetic in only one spin channel. In such joins, triplet correlations are believed to carry the current over long distances, with all spins aligned. Their strips are made of a manganite film with superconducting contacts, building on earlier work that found strong currents across more than a micron.

The team varies strip length and width, hoping for tidy trends in the critical current. Strong currents appear throughout, but no simple pattern emerges, which they blame on build settings they cannot yet control tightly enough. They then test platinum interlayers between the ferromagnet and the contacts. The results look good: sharp switches and true zero-resistance states at two-micron spacing, with hints that wider gaps should work. The interlayer seems to help make the triplet pairs at the boundary.
arxiv-2605-00677:
Lixing Li asks whether language models that prove theorems in Lean are truly reasoning, or pattern-matching against memorized training material. To find out, Li built the Obfuscated Natural Number Game: the classic Natural Number Game, a gentle introduction to formal proof, with every identifier renamed. The renamed world is a closed, zero-knowledge environment where semantic cues from pretraining are stripped away, leaving only local axioms and definitions to reason from.

Li calls the skill under test architectural reasoning: synthesizing proofs purely from a domain's own rules. Every model tested paid a latency tax under obfuscation, taking longer to think. Robustness then split the field. General chat models lost accuracy without their semantic crutches. Reasoning-oriented models, including dedicated provers, held their accuracy despite the missing cues. The benchmark offers a quantitative way to tell genuine reasoning from recall, which matters for automated theorem discovery.
arxiv-2605-00777:
Venkata Pushpak Teja Menta tackles a flaw in speaker encoders used for multilingual voice cloning: the same voice can score differently when it speaks in a different script. Tests on Western-accented voices in English, Hindi, Telugu, and Tamil show clear drops for two standard encoders. The gap is much smaller for Indian-accented voices, so the failure depends on accent.

Menta presents LASE, a small added head placed over a frozen WavLM model. Training pairs a voice-identity loss with a reversed loss that hides language from the embedding while keeping speaker cues. LASE brings the cross-script gap close to zero on both test sets and matches a strong baseline in diarisation while using far less training data.
arxiv-2605-00977:
Michael Zhang, Elise Wang, Charlotte Whatley, Seth Strickland, and Dylan Bannon build tools to open medieval English legal records to wider study. Millions of handwritten pages record the start of a legal system now widespread, but most early records use highly abbreviated medieval Latin that only a few dozen scholars can read. The team constructs a dataset of several thousand lines across nearly two hundred criminal and civil cases.

Their open-source pipeline segments lines and recognizes handwriting, reaching solid word accuracy despite the small training set and abbreviation challenge. Post-processing with a language model and then a large model correction raises accuracy further. A transformer OCR system guesses too freely, the authors find. The pipeline powers a public web portal for scholars and students.
arxiv-2605-01077:
Hugo Abonizio, Filipe Rocha Lopes, Roberto Lotufo, and Rodrigo Nogueira teach a language model Brazilian healthcare knowledge drawn from official clinical guidelines. Brazil's Unified Health System relies on guidelines covering diagnosis, treatment, dosage, and monitoring for a huge population. Yet current models recall this guideline-specific knowledge poorly. No benchmark tested it in Brazilian Portuguese. The team adapts a fourteen-billion-parameter model to close that gap.

From nearly two hundred such rules they generate synthetic training data in rephrase, article, and question-answer formats using several generator models, then apply continual pre-training and reinforcement learning. Two new benchmarks test true-false clinical assertions and open-ended questions. Their best model beats much larger commercial systems on both, and ablations show generator diversity and reinforcement learning are critical.
arxiv-2605-01177:
Naotaka Ukai builds one shared theory for two models that look unrelated: a noise-removal model used in image work, and a phase-field model of how grain boundaries move in materials. Both models are systems of parabolic equations whose coefficients depend on the unknown solution itself. Past work linked the two areas only by changing the equations into a pseudo-parabolic form with an extra energy-loss term, which altered the models. A shared theory for the models in their true parabolic form stayed open.

Ukai defines a new kind of solution, called an energy dissipative solution, that keeps the energy-loss behavior inside the parabolic form. The main result states clear conditions under which such solutions exist. That settles the open problem and gives both fields one firm base for harder questions that span image work and materials science.
arxiv-2605-01577:
Mélodie Andrieu and Léo Vivion present a proof of Rauzy's conjecture from 1983, a question about the pattern structure of endless words over a three-letter alphabet. The background is a classic theorem. For two letters, the Sturmian words are exactly those with independent letter frequencies and the lowest possible abelian complexity. That complexity counts letter tallies in blocks and is fixed at two.

Rauzy had asked whether the three-letter case could mirror that picture, with constant abelian complexity of three and independent frequencies. Andrieu and Vivion prove it cannot: no endless three-letter word has both traits at once. The negative answer closes a forty-year question about how the binary theory extends, and it rests on detailed analysis that the published version refines further for the d-letter case. Word combinatorics gains a firm boundary where a hoped-for family simply does not exist.
arxiv-2605-01977:
Alain Blanchard reviews how cosmology changed from the first Astro and Cosmo Moriond meeting in 1981 to the present. He starts with the classic Big Bang picture, resting on expansion, early element formation, and the cosmic microwave background. From there he traces the path to the current model, in which dark matter and dark energy dominate a flat, accelerating universe.

Key steps include COBE's finding of background fluctuations, supernova evidence for faster expansion, and Planck's precision measures. Blanchard also covers current tensions, such as the Hubble disagreement, and prospects from surveys like DESI. He calls the shift Big Bang 2.0, because explaining the cosmos now needs physics not yet in hand.
arxiv-2605-02177:
Seyed Morteza Emadi asks a quantitative question about Pearl's causal hierarchy, which ranks observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries as distinct levels. Knowing answers at a lower level, how many extra bits are needed to specify answers at the next level up? Emadi formalises that gap through description length, the Kolmogorov complexity of a causal model's answers to a class of queries.

His main construction gives causal models on many binary variables whose observational distribution is cheap to describe, while single-variable intervention answers can need a quadratically larger description. For models with bounded parents and fixed building blocks, he proves an upper bound that makes the construction near optimal in the dense case. A rooted-tree construction extends the picture.
arxiv-2605-02277:
Lei Zhu and colleagues present CECOR, a system for correcting factual errors in text that need multi-step reasoning. Factual error correction revises a claim so it matches external evidence. Past methods do well on single-hop claims but treat claims as single units, so they struggle when a fix needs evidence from several sources. Paired training data are also scarce.

CECOR breaks a multi-hop claim into clear reasoning steps and injects controlled errors to synthesise training pairs, a decomposition and injection scheme. A two-stage learning plan joins supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning to raise accuracy and robustness. Evaluations reported in the paper show gains on compositional correction, where locating a semantic error inside a reasoning chain is the hard part.
arxiv-2605-02777:
Rufeng Chen and four co-authors present a diffusion-based planner for offline safe reinforcement learning, where the safety budget can change at deployment. A policy trained offline must respect a cost limit that may vary between episodes, or even within one. Diffusion planners generate flexible paths, but their usual guidance pits reward against safety as rival gradients, making compliance unreliable.

The authors recast the task as sampling paths from a distribution where the budget fences the allowed region and reward ranks paths inside it. Their method conditions cost-free guidance on the limit, while reward guidance refines return. A relabeling step reshapes reward targets so reward chasing does not quietly raise cost. A first-order analysis shows the relabeling suppresses that drift at sampling time.
arxiv-2605-03077:
Melody Xuan Lim, Zexi Liang, Gabriel Alkuino, Jason Z. Kim, Itay Griniasty, Teng Zhang, Paul L. McEuen, and Itai Cohen show how tiny machines can act on their own. One shared driving field powers them all. Most micro machines so far just follow outside fields step by step. They have no internal choice about what to do next.

The team designs energy landscapes with several stable states. The machine's own state then picks its response. One device holds two stable shapes under one magnetic field. A two-part device moves its surroundings. A third turns one input into motion and adapts to pushes from other machines.
arxiv-2605-03177:
Timothy J. Krogmeier, James Bradley, Anthony W. Schlimgen, and Kade Head-Marsden study how competing spin-pair pathways shorten coherence in molecular qubits. At low temperatures, nuclear spin interactions cause pure dephasing, and the noise can come from pairs inside the molecule, in its surroundings, or split across both.

Using an electronic-structure enhanced, non-Markovian method, they link measured dephasing times to single spin pairs for two qubit candidates with varied ligands and solvents. Knowing which pairs dominate points to concrete design changes. The work builds a workflow for raising coherence times where spin-spin dephasing rules.
arxiv-2605-03377:
Rishi Raj Sahoo and Subhankar Mishra present GRAFT, a global explainer for graph neural networks. It says which input features drive a network's class predictions. Past global tools highlight recurring subgraph shapes. But none summarize attribute influence across a whole class.

GRAFT picks diverse exemplars first. It then computes gradient-based scores and sums them into per-class feature profiles. A language model turns those profiles into short rules. Across datasets and architectures, the method captured model-relevant features. It also supported bias checks and feature-efficient transfer. A human study rated the rules for accuracy and use.
arxiv-2605-03477:
Mohammad Aghaie and Shao-Ping Li show that self-interaction limits on ultralight dark matter also constrain its couplings to ordinary matter. The two are usually probed separately. Yet matter couplings must generate self-interactions through quantum loops, linking the bounds.

They apply astrophysical and cosmological self-interaction limits. Strong limits on linear couplings to neutrinos follow, ruling out much of the range targeted by oscillation experiments. Quadratic couplings to electrons and light quarks are also capped. In places, those limits beat equivalence principle tests. Cosmic sensitivity to repulsive self-interaction becomes a strong indirect probe.
arxiv-2605-03577:
Ashley Hai Tung Tan, Christian Wolf, and four co-authors measure how the brightness of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei varies over time. These are feeding black holes in nearby galaxies, fainter than the ones most earlier studies used. The team analyzes 246 such objects at low redshift from a galaxy survey, using eight years of ATLAS telescope light curves.

They build an ensemble structure function, a measure of how much brightness changes with time gap. Its slope grows with black hole mass, and its size falls as luminosity rises. No break appears in the curve, and spectra twenty years apart suggest variation keeps rising over decades. Extinction, they argue, does not explain the Seyfert subtypes.
arxiv-2605-03677:
Wenjin Hou and fifteen co-authors propose Uni-OPD, a unified framework for on-policy distillation, a post-training method that merges specialized expert models into one student model. Distillation on the student's own generated states works well in practice, but the conditions for reliable improvement were poorly understood. The authors identify two bottlenecks: too little exploration of useful states, and unreliable teacher supervision.

Their dual-perspective recipe balances training data so the student explores informative states it generates itself. On the teacher side, an outcome-guided margin calibration keeps token-level guidance consistent with final rewards, separating correct from incorrect paths. The framework covers both language and multimodal models, tested across five domains and sixteen benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-04077:
Zhiyuan Zeng and ten co-authors examine a quiet design choice in GRPO-style reinforcement learning for language models: how token-level policy gradient terms are combined within each sampled group. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is now central to improving reasoning and code generation, and the aggregation rule turns out to carry its own bias. Sequence aggregation and token aggregation fail in opposite ways.

Token aggregation couples a response's sign to its length, while sequence aggregation downweights longer responses without saying so, through equal weighting of sequences. The proposed Balanced Aggregation computes token-level means separately within positive and negative subsets, then combines them with sequence-count weights. Experiments on two Qwen models and two training sets, evaluated on six reasoning and coding benchmarks, showed more stable training and better final performance.
arxiv-2605-04177:
Hoffmann Muki and Olukunle Owolabi test whether large language models label conflict events fairly. They compare four general open models and two models adapted for African conflict news against ACLED, a checked data set of events in Nigeria and Cameroon.

The general models often turned real battles into attacks on civilians, while the adapted models were much more even on that measure. Yet all models still favoured state actors over non-state actors in the same tactical setting, and wording tied to place could shift the labels. The results warn against using such tools without close human checks.
arxiv-2605-04977:
Raphaël Delécluse, Hazem Wannous, and Laurent Guimas report a competition on recognising people from overhead cameras while protecting privacy, held for ICPR 2026. Top-view images from RGB-depth cameras hide faces and other identifying detail by design. The released dataset holds eighty-six identities filmed by four synchronised overhead depth cameras.

Entrants faced three tracks: matching within colour images, within depth images, and across the two kinds. Results ranked colour easiest, then depth, then cross-modal matching hardest. The organisers release the dataset, scoring scripts, and documentation, establishing a repeatable benchmark for top-view and depth-based person recognition research.
arxiv-2605-05177:
Xuefeng Liu presents a numerical algorithm giving explicit two-sided bounds on eigenvalues of Schrödinger operators with singular potentials on unbounded domains, in two and three dimensions. Such operators model atoms and molecules, with Coulomb-type attraction as the key example. Liu stresses that every constant in the bounds is derived in closed form from the mesh, the potential, and named inequalities, rather than fitted.

The method truncates the domain, then pairs a standard conforming method for upper bounds with an enriched nonconforming finite element construction for lower bounds whose gap closes as the mesh refines. Experiments cover single and two-centre Coulomb potentials in two dimensions and the hydrogen atom and its molecular ion in three.
arxiv-2605-05277:
Bogdan Minko, Sabrina Sadiekh, and Evgeniy Kokuykin present GLiNER Guard, a single encoder model that handles both safety moderation and personal data detection for production language model systems in one pass. Operators need both tasks under strict speed and cost limits. Autoregressive moderators are accurate but expensive, while light encoders are fast but weaker, forcing an awkward trade-off.

The family includes compact models for high-throughput serving and a larger Omni variant for stronger moderation. Under dynamic batching on one high-end graphics processor, the compact model served requests far faster than its predecessor at sub-second tail latency. The authors also release a span-level benchmark for personal data detection in full pipelines.
arxiv-2605-05477:
Marcos C. de Oliveira shows that an ordinary quantum walk can produce correlations stronger than quantum theory normally allows. The walk itself is standard, a coin-driven walk on a line with nearest-neighbor steps. The post-quantum ingredient enters only in how the coin is prepared at the start, through an extended preparation step.

That setup can push Bell test values past Tsirelson's bound while respecting no-signaling in the observable statistics. The preparation can be mimicked in the lab at extra sampling cost. Coarse position measurements, though, can hide the effect almost completely, separating existence from what experiments can actually see.
arxiv-2605-05577:
Optimizers like Lion and Muon normalize gradient momentum through a linear minimization oracle, and they train large models well. Won-Jun Jang and Si-Hyeon Lee set out to speed up that family without paying for extra gradient evaluations. Earlier variance-reduction tricks accelerated these methods but cost too much computation.

Their approach, LMO-IGT, transports gradients implicitly to cut variance cheaply. They also unify the theory across constrained and unconstrained settings, introducing a stationarity measure called the regularized support function. The new measure bridges gradient-based and oracle-based viewpoints, clarifying when these optimizers can be trusted to converge.
arxiv-2605-05777:
A commercial language model behind an API will not show its internals, so how unsure it is stays hidden. Huizi Cui and four co-authors estimate that uncertainty by distillation. Their method trains a small proxy model to mimic where the black-box model's outputs concentrate, using a generation-discrimination setup with adversarial alignment.

The proxy learns the high-quality regions of the big model's output distribution. Its disagreement patterns then serve as a real-time uncertainty signal, without repeated sampling of the expensive model. The target application is flagging likely hallucinations before users act on them.
arxiv-2605-05877:
Yuchen He and three co-authors build a discrete optimal transport framework for studying simulated annealing. Annealing searches for good states by slowly cooling a random process, and sharp guarantees on its speed have been scarce. The team define a generalized discrete Wasserstein distance and a matching notion of action for paths of probability measures on graphs.

With those tools, the error of annealing is controlled by the action of its cooling path. They apply the result to two classic physics models, the mean field Ising model and the q-state Potts model. In both cases the annealing dynamics reach a set error within a polynomial number of steps. Symmetry reduces each analysis to a low dimensional projected chain.
arxiv-2605-05977:
Yinbo Yu and six co-authors present an online defense against backdoor attacks in deep reinforcement learning. Backdoored agents act normally until a trigger pushes them toward an attacker's chosen behavior. Older defenses hunt for triggers from reward oddities, then fine tune the model, which is costly and weak against complex triggers.

BehaviorGuard watches behavior instead of triggers. The authors find that backdoored policies shift their action distributions in a steady way, leaving traces in the tails even with no trigger present. A new metric reads that drift and suppresses backdoor actions while the agent runs. Tests across benchmarks and attack types, in single and multi agent settings, beat prior methods on both effect and speed.
arxiv-2605-06077:
Pierre Marion and Yu-Han Wu argue, in a position paper, that diffusion model generalization needs fresh theory. Unlike supervised learning, a diffusion model that fully memorizes its training set would copy it rather than create novel samples. Past explanations lean on capacity limits, quirks of optimization, or architecture biases, but how these interact stays unclear.

The authors urge the field to stop asking only why models fail to memorize. The better question, they say, is what a model actually learns before memorization sets in. They support the stance with an empirical study of diffusion models trained on CIFAR-10 images. Their findings are distilled into concrete open questions for future theory.
arxiv-2605-06177:
Jinge Wu and ten co-authors release BioMedArena, an open source toolkit for building and fairly evaluating biomedical research agents. Comparing such agents today is unreliable, since the same model on the same benchmark reports different scores under different harnesses and tool sets. Rebuilding a comparable setup for a new model can take weeks of custom engineering.

The toolkit separates six layers of evaluation, from benchmark loading to scoring, and exposes 166 biomedical benchmarks and 75 tools in nine families. New models, benchmarks, or tools plug in through a few lines of adapter code. It also ships reference agent harnesses and context strategies that users can equip on any backbone. Equipped backbones beat prior best results on eight representative benchmarks by about fifteen points on average.
arxiv-2605-06277:
Benoit Sehba studies the shape of the parameter sets that govern embeddings between weighted Bergman-Orlicz spaces. These analytic function spaces are indexed by weight exponents and growth functions, and knowing exactly when one space embeds continuously into another is a structural question. The note asks whether the admissible parameter regions have clean geometry, such as convexity, that analysts can exploit.

For a fixed pair of growth functions, Sehba shows the set of admissible weight exponent pairs is convex, under log convexity conditions on the inverses. He then fixes the exponents and proves the matching collection of growth function pairs is log convex under a natural interpolation of inverses. Interpolated embeddings between the spaces follow from those results. The findings give embedding theory for these spaces a tidy geometric form.
arxiv-2605-06377:
Philip Jordan and Maryam Kamgarpour study learning Nash equilibria when several agents act in a Markov game they can only partly observe. Earlier work needs centralization or shared information, and its costs grow exponentially in the number of players. They focus on games where state transitions are independent but rewards still couple the agents.

Their independent learning algorithm lets each player use only its own actions and observations, with no communication, yet the players jointly reach an approximate equilibrium. Finite history windows suffice under a filter stability assumption. The method yields quasi-polynomial sample and computational complexity for this class.
arxiv-2605-06477:
Pranav Mantini and Shishir K. Shah introduce GeoStack, a framework for adding knowledge to vision-language models without erasing what they already know. Training a model on a new domain usually causes catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills. GeoStack instead composes separately trained domain experts into one unified model.

Geometric and structural constraints on the adapter space protect the base model's knowledge. The authors also prove a weight-folding property that keeps inference cost constant no matter how many experts are added. Tests on multi-domain adaptation and class-incremental learning show strong retention. The approach offers a modular path for models that must keep accumulating skills over time.
arxiv-2605-06877:
Giansalvo Cirrincione and Adriano Fagiolini control mechanical systems whose friction depends on a hidden, finite memory. For Euler-Lagrange systems like robot arms, unobservable friction state breaks the Markov property, so standard adaptive control laws can lose their guarantees.
