In muon catalyzed fusion, a muon glues hydrogen isotopes together until they fuse. The leftover alpha particle often captures the muon. That sticking wastes the catalyst.

Collisions already free some stuck muons. The authors add a field assisted stripping channel and ask when it helps. Their rate network follows each stripped muon through slowing, capture, escape, and decay. A simple product of three probabilities governs the gain. One term is a hard no-go test: impossible recycling targets are excluded on paper. Benchmark scans found a best case worth chasing. Fusion yield per muon rose from about one hundred thirteen to about one hundred fifty seven. Escape, not stripping, is the true bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-07177:
When a meteoroid strikes the Moon, the flash lasts a blink, and slow cameras smear its story. Giancono and co-authors film those flashes at high speed in this 2026 arXiv paper. Observations came from the Zadko Telescope in Western Australia at two hundred to two hundred fifty frames per second. Standard surveys manage only a fraction of that rate.

Four confirmed impacts were resolved in detail. Their light curves showed complex shapes that simple exponential decays fit poorly. One flash was caught simultaneously by a slower fifty frame system. The slow record missed how fast the brightness truly fell. That gap suggests the slow camera smeared the brief vapor plume into the longer cooling glow. Across events, the initial flash energy varied far less than the total energy. The two also showed no statistical correlation. The vapor burst and the cooling ejecta may be physically separate acts.
arxiv-2606-07377:
Van der Meer and co-authors inject two kinds of error into a quantum error-correcting code to see which hurts more, in this 2026 arXiv experiment. Quantum error correction protects information by spreading it across many physical qubits, here using a bit-flip repetition code on a superconducting transmon processor. Theory predicts coherent errors, systematic over-rotations that add up in phase, damage logical quality differently from stochastic errors, which strike at random. Simulations with a free-fermion simulator quantified the expected difference for code sizes three and five.

The team observed no such gap in fidelity for either code size. That null result is the finding, and the authors propose an explanation. Drifts in qubit frequencies may inject phase noise that effectively randomizes the planted coherent errors. If so, real hardware noise blurs the theory distinction. The work advances understanding of how such errors behave in real hardware.
arxiv-2606-07577:
Sun, Li, Yang, and Zhang compress the memory of audio-visual language models so hour-long videos fit on one GPU, in this 2026 arXiv paper on OmniMem. Models that watch and listen accumulate tokens and key-value cache linearly with video length, exhausting memory in streaming use. Existing compression treats every token alike, ignoring the imbalance between plentiful video tokens and sparse audio tokens. OmniMem allocates memory by modality, managing visual and audio contexts separately, and selects which cache states to keep by perturbation awareness, favoring informative, non-redundant entries.

Budget-aware fine-tuning teaches the model to consolidate information into memory it retains. On 3 long-video benchmarks, using 2 audio-visual model families, OmniMem beat training-free compression baselines by 2 to 4 points of accuracy under identical memory budgets. Fine-tuning added another point or 2. The work targets deployment: continuous streams, fixed memory, and no permission to reprocess the past.
arxiv-2606-07677:
Ding and co-authors model how risk factors group diseases together, using electronic health records, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard models often treat each disease separately or hide their reasoning inside black-box predictors, which leaves rare diseases poorly estimated. The team instead uses a Bayesian hypergraph, a structure where one link, called a hyperedge, can join a whole set of diseases that share a risk pattern.

A repulsion prior, a built-in preference against near-duplicate groupings, keeps the discovered pathways distinct, and the Bayesian setup reports uncertainty for each grouping and each risk factor's influence. On simulated data and the UK Biobank, the method recovered stable, readable pathway structure and stayed well calibrated. Rare diseases gained the most, because borrowing strength from related conditions improved their estimates while prediction stayed competitive with standard approaches.
arxiv-2606-07777:
Rahmattalabi and co-authors rebuild a workhorse optimisation tool for the scale of modern ad and content platforms, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Matching millions of users to thousands of items reduces to huge linear programs, solved again and again as inputs drift. Existing GPU solvers run out of memory on production instances, CPU solvers are slow, and answers jump around between runs, churning downstream decisions.

Their solver, written natively in PyTorch, shards the problem by columns across a GPU cluster and fuses core operations into custom kernels. Communication stays minimal, one reduction of item-level values per round, so performance scales near-linearly as GPUs are added. To calm the run-to-run jitter, the solver uses ridge-regularised problems, with a dial that provably bounds how much the answer can drift between consecutive solves. Adding new constraint families is also cheaper than in schema-bound CPU solvers.
arxiv-2606-07877:
Borah, Augenstein, and Mihalcea ask whose norms a language model follows when culture and preference collide, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A user who values honesty may ask whether to correct a coworker publicly, where local norms favour indirect feedback. Earlier research studied cultural alignment and personalisation separately, leaving the trade-off unmeasured.

Their PACT framework presents models with such dilemmas and records which side wins. Models vary widely in how rigidly they enforce cultural norms. Country context shifted behaviour by about eight percent, dwarfing age at one percent and gender below one percent, and instruction tuning moved models unevenly. A five-country human study found culture-following is driven mainly by the scenario's country, with lowest agreement when participants judged their own culture: pluralism within cultures. Models matched the majority human choice but captured the spread of answers poorly, the best correlation with human distributions being only about a quarter.
arxiv-2606-08077:
Mengyuan Sun and co-authors teach language models to write grading rubrics that actually separate good answers from near-misses, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rubric-based judging is attractive, but rubrics models write for themselves lag human criteria on hard cases. The diagnosis is an objective mismatch: self-generated rubrics describe what a good response looks like, while effective criteria must discriminate between close candidates.

Their framework, Support Vector Rubrics, borrows the max-margin idea from support vector machines. It mines contrastive features from preference pairs into a rubric bank, learns a selector and global weights, and refines the bank by probing hard negatives. On RubricBench the method narrowed the gap to human reference rubrics from about twenty-four points to about zero point three points, beating strong self-rubric and judge baselines. The learned bank transferred across judge models without retraining, and stayed competitive with dedicated reward models.
arxiv-2606-08277:
Harry Zhang, Gorlo, and Carlone give robots a way to know which of their memories to distrust, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long-running robots keep a spatio-temporal memory of their surroundings, often as scene graphs with written descriptions attached to objects. Those captions are noisy and inconsistent across viewpoints, yet existing systems treat them as an oracle. The authors introduce object-level semantic uncertainty, a score measuring how much an object's captions scatter across views.

Their system, UQ-DAAAM, uses the score to actively refine uncertain objects under a fixed query budget. It chooses high-quality views and merges the new captions into a single description. Objects whose captions agree across viewpoints score as resolved, while scattered captions mark objects needing another look. The authors also derive probabilistic guarantees showing that high uncertainty reliably signals description problems.
arxiv-2606-08377:
Xefteris studies scheduling with help from a possibly wrong prediction, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The problem is restricted assignment. Jobs must be scheduled on machines, and each job can run only on a specified subset of machines. The goal is to minimize the makespan, the finishing time of the last job. In the learning-augmented setting, the algorithm receives a predicted assignment that may even be infeasible. The error, called moved-load, is the total volume that must be reassigned to reach an optimal feasible schedule.

Two guarantees come from a single prediction. First, an algorithm whose ratio degrades smoothly as error grows, keeping a worst-case guarantee. Second, given only an estimate of the optimal makespan, a repair procedure converts estimates into schedules. The point is to use a forecast when it helps and to stay safe when it does not.
arxiv-2606-08677:
Chitayat, Daigle, and Regeta study when families of derivations behave tamely, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A derivation on an algebra is a linear map obeying the Leibniz product rule, the algebraic shadow of differentiation. A derivation is locally finite if every element generates a finite-dimensional space under repeated application. The authors study conditions under which a Lie subalgebra of derivations, a family closed under the commutator bracket, is locally finite as a set.

As an application, they show that for a quasi-affine variety, any finitely generated solvable Lie subalgebra of derivations of its coordinate ring that consists of locally finite derivations is itself locally finite. Moreover, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, such an algebra is integrable. It comes from an action of an algebraic group, turning infinitesimal symmetries into global ones.
arxiv-2606-09177:
Nasereldin pins down why a classic coordinate trick in general relativity breaks once the universe has a cosmological constant, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Weyl coordinates give the general form of a static, axisymmetric vacuum spacetime by tying the orbits' area to a harmonic coordinate. That identification works in Ricci-flat vacuum. With a nonzero cosmological constant the construction stops being available, and the folklore is imprecise.

From the generalized static axisymmetric line element, he derives the reduced field equations. The result is sharp: the canonical Weyl choice for the area function is locally admissible if and only if the cosmological constant is zero. The Kottler metric, a black hole with a cosmological constant, gives the simplest example of the equation the area function must obey. The moral: the obstruction is not staticity or axisymmetry, it is that the area function is no longer harmonic.
arxiv-2606-09277:
Xinyue Huang, Hansheng Xu, and colleagues show a layered crystal's surface polarity depends on a stacking coin flip: odd or even layers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nb3Cl8 forms a breathing kagome lattice: niobium atoms trimerize into triangles, breaking inversion and mirror symmetry in each layer and generating an out-of-plane dipole. Stacked layers cancel dipoles in pairs, antiferroelectrically, so surface polarization follows layer parity.

Using Kelvin probe force microscopy, mapping surface electrostatic potential, the team visualized layer-dependent polarization in flakes: a pronounced odd-even oscillation. They also found intralayer polar domains: local reconstructions of the kagome network flip the surface dipole, creating ferroelectric-like configurations the parity rule would not predict. Interfacing monolayer molybdenum diselenide with the crystal, the textures modulate the neighbor's exciton emission via band alignment and charge transfer. Layer parity becomes a design knob: count layers, program the interface's optical response.
arxiv-2606-09377:
Sergei Vorobyov and Eugene Ilyushin tackle the memory wall that limits formal verification of neural networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Verification proves that a network behaves safely for every input in a region, not just tested examples. Standard bound-propagation tools keep all weight matrices on one graphics processor, so large networks simply do not fit.

The authors adapt two training techniques to the alpha-beta-CROWN verifier. Tensor parallelism splits both weights and bound matrices across processors, roughly halving peak memory with two devices, though bounds loosen as more zones are split. Fully sharded data parallelism splits only the weights and reassembles each layer on demand. That route produced bounds identical to the single-device baseline while cutting baseline memory by eighty to ninety percent on wide networks. It also completed a full safety proof for a large CIFAR-100 ResNet benchmark network.
arxiv-2606-09577:
Yuling Shi and her co-authors argue that judging doubt in code models needs tools built for code, not borrowed from prose, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A code model that stays silent when wrong is a real risk.

Code breaks in ways prose does not. One bad token can kill a whole program. The plan in the author's mind and the typed code can each drift from the other. And code, unlike prose, can be run. The team builds one doubt axis for each trait: token entropy, pseudo-code agreement, and behaviour agreement across runs. Across five code models, their blend lifted the AUROC score from about sixty-nine point six to seventy-seven point six. AUROC gauges how well a score sorts right from wrong output. One cheap axis matched the best costly rival while running over three times faster.
arxiv-2606-09677:
Dohwan Kim and Jung-Woo Choi add a one-step polish stage to multi-microphone speech separation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sharp separator models score well on lab metrics yet can sound strained to human ears. Pure generative fixes sound more natural, but they need many steps and run slowly. The team's MeCo corrector aims to keep both wins.

MeCo learns a mean flow field, the average drift that maps a rough split straight onto clean speech in a single step. A new training scheme, Data-Space Optimization, shapes that one leap. One loss punishes errors over long jumps, tuned to what listeners prize. A second loss grades the end point by signal fidelity. In tests, MeCo reached top scores for both fidelity and listening quality. The wins held in matched rooms and in fresh ones, with only slight added cost.
arxiv-2606-09777:
Hong Li and a large team build a teaching rig that lets people show robots how touch and force feel in this 2026 arXiv paper. Contact-rich tasks hinge on grip force and tactile cues. Yet force sensors and touch sensors clash in handheld gear, and pricey force gauges block scale. Their AetheRock is worn on the arm and gathers all three streams at once.

At the fingertip sits a small gel touch sensor that is simple to make. A pressure pad rests where the human finger grips. A custom board and a snug kit round out the rig. On the software side, ForceVT learns from force and sight to steady touch readings. Touch sensors drift as gels wear or vary by build, and ForceVT is built to shrug that off. Real trials showed the rig gathers data with strong efficiency.
arxiv-2606-09877:
Juan M. Huerta keeps a compiled knowledge wiki fresh while its source stream never stops in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wiki systems pre-load a corpus into a model's cache for fast, grounded replies. They presume the facts stay put. In live domains they do not: news breaks, pages change, and a stale wiki misleads. Huerta frames the job as a race against a perfect-foresight rival, scored by regret.

His lever is a materiality score, a forecast of how much each new item will matter to one entity. High scorers get pinned into the wiki before any query asks. Proofs cap the regret growth, with forecast error the lone domain term. Two fields test the frame. In finance, wild price swings flagged the key items among seventy-six thousand news pieces. On Wikipedia, edit speed played the same role. Both runs held regret near flat.
arxiv-2606-10177:
Lee and his team build a visual tool to help experts check the evidence behind language model answers in food science, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction. Graph retrieval-augmented generation lets models answer from structured knowledge graphs, but retrieved data can be irrelevant or conflicting, so human checking remains necessary in evidence-focused domains. A formative pilot study mapped the challenges of verifying complex, multi-layered retrieved evidence. Their system, VArify, visualizes that evidence as a file-directory-inspired tree.

The tree supports simultaneous exploration of relationships between evidence groups and hierarchies within them. A user study with six food science experts and students found the system helps users distinguish the model's internal parametric knowledge from external graph-sourced evidence. The display also helped experts spot inaccuracies inside the underlying knowledge graph itself, leading to more calibrated trust in model output.
arxiv-2606-10277:
Shi and colleagues propose a lightweight way to adapt wireless foundation models to many tasks at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper on wireless machine learning. Their Routing Adapter for Feature Composition treats hidden states from different Transformer depths as a reusable pool of multi-level features. A small task-driven network generates layer-wise aggregation weights for each task.

Each downstream task then receives its own mixture of low, mid, and high-level wireless features through weighted summation, without modifying the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on four representative wireless tasks show the adapter consistently outperforming conventional adaptation baselines. It does so while adding fewer than fifty thousand parameters, a tiny fraction of the backbone's size. The design gives one shared model many task-specific faces, which matters for deployment on infrastructure where storing a fine-tuned copy per task is impractical.
arxiv-2606-10377:
Lan and Yang analyze what happens when random projections compress both sides of a regression problem at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistical learning. Their bidirectional scheme applies separate random projections to the sample dimension and the feature dimension of an ordinary least squares problem under a fixed design. It then studies the estimator built from the doubly compressed data.

They develop an expected excess loss bound for the bidirectional estimator and compare it with the established bound for one-sided projection. The gap is quantified in terms of the compressed feature dimension and a constant scaling with the compression ratio. That constant can even be negative when the sample compression is mild, meaning bidirectionality can help. The analysis guides practitioners who must shrink both the number of samples and the number of features, common in distributed and privacy-sensitive regression.
arxiv-2606-10477:
Park and co-authors speed up privacy-preserving statistics in this 2026 arXiv paper, presented at the ACM Symposium on Applied Computing. Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data it cannot read, but it is slow. One costly operation is the inverse square root. Its speed depends on a trade-off between polynomial approximation and bootstrapping, a noise-resetting step, and the best balance shifts sixfold between libraries and hardware. The HE-DAP framework profiles each environment and picks the balance automatically.

On the Lattigo, HEaaN-CPU, and HEaaN-GPU platforms, HE-DAP accelerates the encrypted inverse square root by up to 2.35 times over a fixed configuration. Gains reach 1.96 times on Lattigo and 2.18 times on the CPU platform. Accuracy stays high, with mean relative error at or below a tiny bound the authors report. Tuned settings also speed four statistical operations end to end, with precision retained.
arxiv-2606-10577:
Li and colleagues reframe robot navigation as tool use in this 2026 arXiv paper on embodied artificial intelligence. The task is vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments: a robot follows spoken instructions through an unseen building, with no route graph and no task-specific training. Earlier systems funnel the model through a learned waypoint predictor proposing a few nearby points, shrinking its choices. AgenticNav instead hands the model three tools: pick a target pixel in the camera view, query exact depth at chosen pixels, and recall past views via a compact map.

On the R2R-CE benchmark the harness sets the best reported zero-shot results for its backbone model, and it generalises in real-world trials. Ablations credit the pixel action tool most, with depth queries and memory adding further gains. Failure analysis is candid: 88.9 percent of simulation failures are the model's own decision mistakes.
arxiv-2606-10777:
Hoarau asks whether a model's uncertainty merits trust in this 2026 arXiv paper. Classical calibration checks its stated probabilities against reality. Second-order models output a distribution over chances, whose spread is read as epistemic uncertainty, the model's ignorance. Nothing in that check tests whether the spread is honest. Hoarau defines epistemic calibration: the spread must match the scatter of predictions around the truth. It is stronger than the classical notion, exposing failures standard metrics miss.

To measure it, the paper defines the Expected Epistemic Calibration Error and proves the measure tracks the true error soundly. Across many methods, near-equal predictive scores hide big differences on this criterion; on vision tasks, DropConnect and MC-Dropout calibrate best. It depends sharply on assumptions: Bayesian logistic regression is perfectly calibrated where its linear premises hold, and poorly so on complex real data. For high-stakes deployment, uncertainty needs an audit too.
arxiv-2606-11177:
Sheng offers a unifying framework for equilibrium quantum many-body theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Methods for many interacting quantum particles at equilibrium differ not only in accuracy but in what they explicitly represent. Some keep the full state; others keep reduced summaries and reconstruct the rest through functionals or closure rules. Sheng recasts every method as an encoder mapping states to retained variables.

The identity encoder gives the full-state representation. A many-to-one encoder gives a reduced one, whose value labels a fiber, the set of states compatible with it. His central principle is sharp. An exact decoder for a task exists precisely when the task is constant across each fiber. Otherwise the theory must add structure, a variational principle or closure, to select the needed content. Static moments and imaginary-time correlation functions become restrictions of one readout functional to different probe families.
arxiv-2606-11277:
Yang, Bin, Yang, and Chen tackle a weakness of generative models in physics in a 2026 arXiv paper: extrapolation. Models trained over finite ranges of time, settings, or geometries often produce unphysical predictions outside the training range. Their framework, LAPG, guides a diffusion model with the principle of least action, enforcing physics during inference rather than only in training.

LAPG pairs a conditional score-based model with an action-derived physical guidance score. First the learned model generates an in-range proposal. Then an action-based prior refines it toward the target condition, turning least action into a differentiable correction. Tests cover free fall, conservative and dissipative spring-mass dynamics, interacting point vortices, and potential flow over parameterized airfoils. Across temporal, parameter, and geometric tests, LAPG reduced phase drift, preserved decay, captured vortex motion, and improved airfoil lift response versus training-time physics-informed baselines.
arxiv-2606-11677:
Makoto Nakashima proves a probabilistic formula for a heat equation with a point defect in this 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical physics. The operator studied adds a Dirac delta interaction, an infinitely concentrated kick at one point, to the ordinary Laplacian, which governs diffusion and quantum motion. Such point interactions model very short-range forces in three dimensions.

Feynman-Kac formulas express solutions as averages over random paths, turning analysis into probability. Nakashima constructs, for each positive time and starting point away from the defect, a probability law on path space plus a normalising factor. The solution is that factor times the expected value of the initial data at the path's end. Building the path law is the hard part, because paths must feel the single-point interaction correctly despite almost never hitting the point exactly.
arxiv-2606-11777:
Ziyi Chen, Jinyu Zou, Jinhua Gao and Gang Xu extend topological physics to quasicrystals in this 2026 arXiv paper. Topological charges, whole numbers derived from the Berry phase, a geometric phase quantum states accumulate, organise many exotic states of matter. Quasicrystals have ordered but never-repeating patterns, and their topological charges had not been systematically worked out.

Using group representation theory, the mathematics of symmetry, the authors derive all allowed charges for two-dimensional quasicrystals and the matching low-energy models. In an eightfold-symmetric example they demonstrate a charge of four. That is far beyond the unit charges of ordinary Weyl points, and unreachable in periodic crystals. They then show how to see such charges in photonic quasicrystals, where light plays the role of electrons. Circling the charge once makes the field pattern wind a matching number of times.
arxiv-2606-12077:
Yifan Wang and three colleagues cluster time series without training a network in this 2026 arXiv paper. Grouping time series by shape is hampered by a trade-off: matching methods compare every pair, a quadratic cost, while deep learning methods need expensive iterative training. Their framework, MSRGC-Net, sidesteps both costs.

A training-free reservoir computer, a fixed random recurrent network read out at several scales, extracts multiscale temporal features without any backpropagation. Granular-ball computing then models the data distribution with adaptive regions, producing compact anchor graphs instead of full pairwise comparisons. A consensus step aligns the features across scales and fuses their added information, from brief local patterns to long-term links. Tests on standard univariate and multivariate benchmarks show the method outperforming state-of-the-art approaches at low computing cost. Tests confirm each component contributes, and plots show the design sharpens cluster separation.
arxiv-2606-12277:
Chak and Anderson warn that a good model's favorite clues may not be the phenomenon's real clues, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Biologists often train a deep network, read off which genes it found important, and conclude those genes drive the disease. That logic fails if other equally accurate models rely on entirely different genes. The authors build a method that hunts for such alternative models: new networks scoring like the originals while differing as much as possible in their context-aware traits.

On the METABRIC breast cancer dataset, the method produced three alternative models. Their gene-importance profiles were entirely disjoint from those of ten baseline runs, sharing no top genes. Accuracy did not suffer for the difference. A single model's feature ranking therefore cannot certify a biological conclusion by itself. This search for rival interpretations should be a standard step before any insight is claimed from model traits.
arxiv-2606-12977:
Fei and colleagues present a fingerprinting method for text-to-image diffusion models that resists collusion attacks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Model fingerprinting embeds a user-specific ID into a model's outputs so leaked copies can be traced to their source, guarding the developer's intellectual property. The authors reveal a flaw in current methods: several buyers can collude, combining their copies to remove or obscure the fingerprints.

Their method encodes the fingerprint bit string into the coefficients of a personalised normalisation module built into the model, so the fingerprint can be read back from any generated image. The anti-collusion mechanism is based on lossless function-invariant parameter transformations. Each shared copy yields identical outputs alone, but averaging or merging copies degrades generation quality, making colluded models unusable. The same machinery lets developers mark fresh copies by re-tuning the module instead of retraining.
arxiv-2606-13277:
Sánchez-Ferrera and colleagues present ProtoX-AD in this 2026 arXiv paper, a method that detects and explains anomalies in time series data. A family of methods alters normal training data in known ways and trains a classifier to recognise each change. Unusual classification errors then flag anomalies, but the flag alone says nothing about what kind of fault occurred. ProtoX-AD adds prototypes, typical patterns stored inside the model, so each detection comes with an interpretable profile.

The model learns internal representations shaped by each change, alongside the prototypes, and flagged points are explained by the prototypes they resemble. This lets users distinguish distinct anomalous profiles instead of receiving an alarm. The framework supports careful study of how the choice of changes affects accuracy and explanation quality. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show detection performance. The prototype explanations remained informative across those tests.
arxiv-2606-13377:
Shihang Pan, Blasi, and Haack show that current noise can reveal hidden degeneracies in open quantum systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. The dynamics of such systems are governed by a Lindbladian, an operator whose eigenvalues set decay rates and oscillation frequencies. At an exceptional point, two eigenvalues and their eigenvectors merge into one, a distinctly non-Hermitian phenomenon. These points were previously identified mainly through short-time behaviour, such as transient currents. Steady-state average currents, the long-run flows, generally show no direct trace of them.

The authors derive general expressions for current correlation functions, which measure how fluctuations at two times relate, inside the Lindblad framework. They show exactly how exceptional points change those correlations as the time delay varies. An example with two interacting qubits coupled to two reservoirs makes the effect concrete. There the steady-state noise clearly separates overdamped, underdamped, and exceptional regimes.
arxiv-2606-13477:
Tianyi Ma and colleagues release SupraBench in this 2026 arXiv paper, the first benchmark for language models in supramolecular chemistry. This branch of chemistry studies host-guest assemblies, molecules that bind each other through non-covalent forces rather than shared electrons. Designing such systems is slow, with days of verification per candidate pair. Language models promise a fast alternative and perform well on some molecular binding tasks. Yet no benchmark tested them on the reasoning tasks of the field, such as predicting binding affinity.

Built with domain experts, SupraBench covers four core tasks: binding affinity prediction, selecting the top binder, identifying the solvent, and describing a host-guest pair, plus a vision-based task on molecular identification. The team releases a corpus of 16 million tokens from the field's literature. The resources let researchers measure where models reason about non-covalent binding and where they pattern-match.
arxiv-2606-14377:
Jos Zuijderwijk and colleagues offer a 2026 arXiv study of government openness in the Netherlands. Freedom of information laws let citizens request official records, but agencies can still slow or limit disclosure in practice. The authors ask whether public response data can reveal such transparency-impeding behavior, meaning habits that quietly block openness.

From earlier research the team lists nine recurring blocking patterns and builds measurable indicators for six of them. They test the indicators on a Dutch dataset holding over fifteen thousand request dossiers and nearly one hundred forty thousand documents in total. Interviews with researchers, journalists, and civil servants confirm the signals are readable and useful for choosing investigations, comparing agencies, and guiding oversight work.
arxiv-2606-14477:
Rosario and a large collaboration present a JWST survey of dust near active galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. Seyfert galaxies host feeding black holes whose heat lights up surrounding dust. The James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared instrument images the central few hundred parsecs, the galaxy's inner region, with resolution and depth beyond ground-based tools across nearly the whole mid-infrared range.

This GATOS paper explains the survey's aims, data reduction, and methods for separating nuclear from extended emission, then compares dust structures with stars, ionized gas, and molecular gas. The team concludes that resolved dust heated by the active nucleus is widespread among Seyferts, reaching a few hundred parsecs out and often outshining the wider star-forming disk. Even after correcting for emission-line contamination, the mid-infrared dust tracks the ionized gas closely.
arxiv-2606-14577:
Müller and a large team demo a cooling method for atoms in space in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dual-species atom sources in orbit could test the universality of free fall. They could also probe other quantum physics. But they need clouds that expand extremely slowly. The team proposes trap-quenched collimation. It excites collective modes inside the trap before release. It fits atom-chip setups already in use.

The team used NASA's Cold Atom Laboratory on the space station. They demoed the method on a rubidium condensate. Careful control of the release gave free expansion times up to seven hundred milliseconds. The measured expansion energy matched about seventy-eight picokelvin. Modeling suggests roughly fifteen picokelvin along two axes. Theory for a potassium-rubidium mix predicts joint collimation. It would meet the needs of a free-fall test at the target precision.
arxiv-2606-14677:
Rennela builds a fast way to check if two quantum error models match in a 2026 arXiv paper. An error model lists each fault's odds. It also lists which detectors the fault trips and which readouts it flips. Chip builders use these models to reason about fault-tolerant circuits. Before now, checking that two models agree was done case by case, with no firm rules.

Rennela sets up a rule system with a sound math base. His rewrite rules always stop and never clash. So each model ends in one unique normal form. That form can be found in near-linear time. The result is the first fixed test for model match with firm backing. It settles full decoder match exactly for non-adaptive pipelines. It also scales to partly adaptive circuits, like lattice surgery, with no blow-up in cost.
arxiv-2606-14777:
Yao and a large team release a vision-language model that speaks up on its own in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most large models are turn-based: they answer only when asked, even in video apps that feel interactive. The authors argue for a model present in the world like a person, watching continuously, deciding whether to speak or stay silent, and delegating hard problems to a background model.

Their open-sourced model, JoyAI-VL-Interaction, is an eight-billion-parameter vision-first system that decides each second whether to stay silent, respond, or delegate. They also release the full training recipe and a deployable system streaming live video into the model with pluggable speech, memory, and interface parts. Across six real-world scenarios, human raters preferred it by a wide margin over the in-app video-call assistants of two major commercial products.
arxiv-2606-15177:
Sun and coauthors present Gimbal, a 2026 scheduling system for serving mixture-of-experts language models. Such models route each token to a few sub-networks called experts. Serving splits work across engines, and two scheduling layers act alone. Front-end routers count requests, while back-end balancers watch expert use. The mismatch creates overloaded engines and expert hotspots under shifting workloads. Gimbal coordinates both layers with pressure signals from the engines.

Its dispatcher reads cache use, prefill work, backlog, and expert pressure before routing. A prefill-aware queue order with aging cuts blocking without predicting output lengths. For experts, Gimbal tracks which engine sends traffic to which expert. A heuristic guided by an optimization model places experts to cut load and traffic cost. Built on vLLM, Gimbal cut time to first token by about forty-three percent in tests. Time per output token fell by a third, and throughput rose.
arxiv-2606-15277:
Nguyen and coauthors guide federated graph recommendation with language model knowledge in a 2026 machine learning paper. Graph recommenders learn from user-item interaction networks, and federated training keeps raw data on user devices. The catch is that clients' data differ wildly, so their graph embeddings misalign. Averaging misaligned embeddings on the server loses the shared preference patterns. The authors let each client sum up its typical interactions into a compact semantic vector. A frozen language model produces those summaries from local patterns.

The server compares semantic vectors to find clients with related tastes. It then merges those clients' structural embeddings by choice, guided by the semantic match. Raw interaction data never leaves the client devices. On standard benchmarks, the method beat existing federated graph baselines throughout. Gains held across varied hyperparameter settings in their tests. The work shows semantic guidance can align federated recommenders without sacrificing privacy.
arxiv-2606-15477:
Cuji and coauthors present a Bayesian universal beamforming framework in a 2026 signal processing paper. Beamforming steers an antenna or hydrophone array's listening direction to pick one signal out of a noisy environment. Underwater channels are hostile: echoes bounce off surface and bottom, and motion adds Doppler distortion, so the best direction keeps changing. Instead of committing to one direction, the method keeps candidate directions and tracks odds over them.

Each branch produces its own output and error score. A Bayesian update, an exponential-weights rule for Gaussian noise, shifts weight toward the branch performing best. The output is a weighted blend, and the framework extends to broadband receivers with adaptive cleanup judged by the same errors. On recorded MACE trial data the receiver communicates reliably while mobile, with low detection error and zero observed bit errors. Soft spatial inference suits channels too fluid for any fixed pointing choice.
arxiv-2606-15577:
Peran and colleagues survey large language models as optimizers in 2026, sorting it into three paradigms. In direct optimization, the model itself searches for solutions through repeated prompting and heuristic generation. Tool-augmented work instead turns a problem stated in plain language into a formal specification for external solvers. A third paradigm has models create reusable algorithms that later run with no model calls.

Across the literature, direct methods are broadening toward full combinatorial solving but remain limited by reasoning capacity at scale. Tool-augmented systems score strongly on structured benchmarks, yet their accuracy hinges on correct formulation and on the tools at hand. Tool-creating work has produced notable algorithm finds, though reproducibility stays open. The authors argue tool-making is the most promising direction: for large families of similar problems, one costly creation pass beats fresh reasoning on every instance. Auditability still favours the tool-augmented route.
arxiv-2606-15677:
Vos and colleagues argue in 2026 that universities teach software testing under the wrong paradigm, and propose a redesign. Curricula treat testing as a rationalist exercise, prescribing methods and confirming expected outcomes, while real testing is empirical work under uncertainty. Students find the subject narrow and dull, and graduate unable to reason critically about complex, AI-laced systems.

The team proposes teaching testing as a whole professional task, using the Four-Component Instructional Design model to structure learning around complete tasks. Their P4TEST framework spells out the core competencies, epistemic moves, and habits of mind that testing involves, without fixing a process. Early learning tasks constrain and expose modelling choices; later ones demand that students build and defend their own models. The framework guides curriculum design and assessment. Planned experiments in bachelor and master programmes will test whether the redesign works in practice.
arxiv-2606-15877:
Bogdan argues in 2026 that fast-and-frugal heuristics and active inference describe the same computation, when an agent is unsure how precise its evidence is. Chain-of-thought prompting helps models on maths but hurts on planning and contested reasoning. The paper names meta-uncertainty about one's own evidence as the deciding property.

The free-energy-minimising policy under uncertain precision provably stops adding cues after finitely many high-validity ones, if the prior's tails are heavy enough. Under a descending-dominance condition on cue validities, that truncated policy is identical to Gigerenzer's take-the-best heuristic. This yields a falsifiable prediction: on such items, longer chains of thought should degrade answers. Bogdan builds a per-item meta-uncertainty score, validated by simulation recovery, plus a 79-frame benchmark and a pre-registered seven-model study.
arxiv-2606-15977:
Cârstea proves uniqueness for a finite-dimensional anisotropic Calderón problem in 2026, in dimension three and higher. The Calderón problem asks whether boundary measurements determine conductivity inside a body. Here it is a symmetric elliptic matrix field, polynomial within each cell of a known partition, and allowed to jump across cell faces. Anisotropy normally pins the answer only up to a coordinate change; the cell structure pins the answer down.

If the cells can be reached successively through enough flat interface patches, the local Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on one boundary patch determines every piece. The proof recovers one cell from flat-face data, then strips layers, using Runge approximation and unique continuation to carry the data across recovered cells. A stability theorem upgrades the result: recovery is Hölder stable on compact sets. For inverse problems, it shows structural assumptions buy genuine stability.
arxiv-2606-16077:
Jimenez, Kozachinskiy, and Opazo add a running-time requirement to a recent model of language generation in a 2026 theory note. Mistake-bounded generation asks a learner to produce valid new strings from a target language family with only bounded mistakes. The framework comes from Kleinberg, Peale, and Reingold. The note asks which families admit generators that also run in polynomial time.

Two basic families qualify directly: parities of variables, and conjunctions of literals. The main result covers monotone Boolean functions with polynomially many maxterms, a maxterm being a clause that rules out one corner case. That family includes every monotone function computed by polynomial-size decision trees. The proof is presented as a combinatorial game about writing numbers on a board. Open questions include non-monotone functions and closure under union.
arxiv-2606-16177:
Kim, Anderson, and Lu measure in 2026 how the quality factor of acoustic resonators depends on in-plane orientation. The devices are higher-order crossbar resonators, called XBARs, cut from 128 degree Y-cut lithium niobate on silicon. Designers usually orient them to maximize electromechanical coupling, which sets filter bandwidth. Whether orientation also changes Q, a measure of energy loss, was far less explored.

The team characterizes the A3, A5, and A7 modes across orientations from 10 to 170 degrees in a 500 nanometer film. Both Q measures show clear minima at 90 degrees to the x-axis. Average Bode Q values of 735, 204, and 59 fall to 66, 9, and 12 at 90 degrees in the reported data. Coupling shows the same angular pattern, dropping to zero at 90 degrees. Finite element results indicate the Q collapse there is not fully explained by power loss alone.
arxiv-2606-16277:
Lucey and co-authors report in 2026 that the Milky Way's inner stellar halo looks unlike the halos of simulated twin galaxies. The halo's star density drops with radius in a broken power law, with a break near 20 to 30 kiloparsecs. That break is usually blamed on star pile-up after the Gaia-Enceladus merger. The team tests this story against modern galaxy simulations.

They compare the measured profile, from 1 to 100 kiloparsecs, with 24 Milky Way-mass galaxies from the FIRE-2 and Auriga simulation suites. The simulated profiles fall off much more steeply inside about 15 kiloparsecs than the real one does. Breaks are rare in the simulations and never as strong as the Milky Way's. Of three simulated galaxies with clear breaks, only one owes its break to merger pile-up. The Milky Way seems to hold an in-situ part, stars born in place, that simulations miss.
arxiv-2606-16377:
Ferreira and co-authors compute in 2026 how hot, dense quark-gluon plasma responds to electromagnetic fields, pushing perturbation theory one order further. The plasma's static electromagnetic susceptibilities describe how it magnetizes and polarizes, inputs for modeling heavy-ion collisions. The team evaluates the leading hard correction, of order alpha-s, and the leading soft, resummed contribution, of order alpha-s to the three-halves power, within electrostatic QCD.

With both pieces included, the perturbative results agree reasonably with lattice QCD simulations at zero baryon chemical potential. The matching runs through lattice perturbation theory. The real payoff is reach: the formulas extend the susceptibilities to finite baryon density, where lattice methods fail outright because of the sign problem. That regime covers the intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions now probing dense matter. The authors also verify a claimed link between the leading temperature logarithm and the QED beta function.
arxiv-2606-16677:
Zens and Bijak forecast asylum applications in a 2026 paper written for the International Journal of Forecasting. Sudden surges in applications strain housing, processing staff and local services across Europe. Planners need not just a single expected number, but a distribution showing how bad the upper tail could get.

Their Bayesian model forecasts monthly applications for all twenty-seven European Union countries jointly. Latent application intensity is split into country-specific random walks plus shared common factors, with shocks that can be heavy-tailed or change in size over time. Using Eurostat data in a rolling out-of-sample test, joint models beat country-by-country forecasts, with the largest gains in the upper tail where preparation costs bite. No single specification wins everywhere, though. The best model varies by country, scoring rule and horizon, so agencies should match the model to the decision it supports.
arxiv-2606-16777:
Tianshenhong Sang and colleagues map a pair of brown dwarfs in a 2026 astronomy paper on Nu Ophiuchi. The star is bright enough to see with the naked eye and lies close by cosmic standards. Two brown dwarfs, objects between planets and stars in mass, orbit it in a six-to-one rhythm of orbital periods.

Earlier work knew the pair from the star's wobble, a flat view of the orbits. Joining radial velocity data with Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry, the team recovers the full three-dimensional layout. Both companions weigh in at roughly twenty-five Jupiter masses. Their orbital planes are tilted relative to each other, but stability tests over a million years cap that tilt at a modest value. In the best-fit layout the pair can stay locked in its six-to-one resonance. Rare pairs like this test formation theories.
arxiv-2606-17377:
Guan, Maity, and Tsiotras present a 2026 arXiv paper on shrinking huge decision problems by grouping states, without caring about geometry for its own sake. In a large Markov decision process, a good grouping should directly serve decision quality, the authors argue. Their abstraction merges states into regions that share one action distribution, trading a little optimality for a far smaller problem that planners can actually solve and replan quickly when conditions change.

For a fixed grouping, a performance guarantee separates the error from approximating values from the loss caused by sharing actions. Guided by that split, a multi-timescale learning method adapts the policy and a tree-shaped grouping together. Regions split or merge based on gaps between their action values, balancing performance against grouping size. Tests show strong state compression, better sample efficiency, and faster replanning than actor-critic baselines.
arxiv-2606-17577:
Ito and colleagues, of Honda Motor Company, present a 2026 arXiv paper on designing car front ends that protect pedestrians, using a foundation model to orchestrate the whole search. Crash safety is a hard place for data-driven shortcuts, since impacts involve nonlinear contact, material failure, and sudden state changes. Their workflow aims to cut evaluation from hours of crash simulation per design to seconds, letting stylists explore far more options before committing to full physics runs.

Four parts work together: a surrogate trained on crash simulations predicts leg injury scores and gives distribution-free uncertainty bands. An evolutionary search then finds diverse designs meeting user-set constraints on those scores. A morphing tool turns chosen parameters into smooth three-dimensional shapes, and a language interface steers the process. One bumper study produced dozens of safety-compliant alternatives in a single exploration.
arxiv-2606-17677:
Dong and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper with direct telescope evidence on what launches spicules, the thin jets that spray constantly from the Sun's chromosphere. Spicules may ferry mass and energy into the corona, feeding debates on coronal heating and the solar wind, but their trigger was unproven. One candidate is the eruption of microfilaments, tiny versions of the filaments whose blasts drive bigger solar jets. The sharpest solar telescope now flying was used to watch a quiet region at disk centre for the tell-tale pairing.

Thirty spicule events were caught rising from microfilament eruptions, the filaments far smaller than the minifilaments reported before. Small filaments produced single spicules; larger ones drove enhanced spicular activity, and some events twisted as they rose. The observations make the eruption mechanism hard to dismiss for these jets. Each confirmed trigger sharpens models of how the corona gets its supply.
arxiv-2606-17777:
Yagouti and colleagues study how clinical trials with several treatments can adapt as results come in, in a 2026 statistics paper. Response-adaptive randomization shifts new patients toward treatments that look better, which can help both ethics and efficiency. Most theory covered trials with just two arms, and work on many treatments stayed fragmented across specific methods.

The authors introduce one family of designs, called alpha-Rebalancing Targeting Strategies, that extends a known two-arm method. They prove that every design in the family shares key long-run traits: strong consistency, well-behaved estimates, and efficiency. A variant with forced exploration keeps sampling every treatment, even ones the target would drop. Simulations in a three-arm trial show how the variants behave in practice, guiding trial designers who want adaptation with solid guarantees.
arxiv-2606-18077:
Barman Ray and colleagues trap light together with charged particle pairs in an atom-thin layered crystal, in a 2026 photonics paper. Stacking two semiconductor monolayers, MoSe2 over WS2, creates a moiré superlattice that reshapes the electronic landscape. Inside an optical microcavity, the team strongly couples the cavity light to layer-hybridized excitons and to trions, excitons bound to an extra electron from deliberate doping.

The response refuses to behave monotonically. Screening by the dopant electrons and steady trion formation bend the oscillator strength in an unusual curve as density grows. The authors tie that curve to the moiré pattern steering where electrons collect. The trion polaritons that result move fast and far, with diffusion lengths approaching a hundred microns. Measured nonlinearities exceed those of similar systems studied before, hinting at strong optical switches from a single stacked bilayer.
arxiv-2606-18577:
Ito, Takeuchi, and Tsushima give a complete construction recipe for extremal curves of a special family over finite fields of odd characteristic, in a 2026 algebraic geometry paper. Van der Geer-van der Vlugt curves, built from linearized polynomials, matter to number theory and coding theory and connect to the geometry behind local Langlands correspondences. A curve is extremal when its count of rational points hits the theoretical maximum or minimum for its genus.

The input is simply a nonzero field element plus a linear subspace satisfying a trace condition, completing an odd-characteristic analogue of the authors' earlier characteristic-two construction. The key tool is the adjoint of a linearized polynomial. A particular factorization identity yields an explicit formula for the curve's L-polynomial, making it straightforward to decide whether a given curve is maximal or minimal rather than checking case by case.
arxiv-2606-18677:
Lee and the team tackle how tabular foundation models should manage memory when data arrive as a stream, in a 2026 machine learning paper. These models predict not by updating weights, but by conditioning on a context of past examples. That suits streaming under distribution shift. But the context is bounded, so someone must decide which examples to keep.

The authors develop a future-information view. It measures how much a retained context tells near-future queries. That yields three needs: preserve recent examples, retain uncertain ones, and remove redundant ones. Their policy Cure implements this, with entropy-gated admission and redundancy-aware eviction. Across seven data streams, Cure improved on classical stream learners by up to twenty-seven percent in relative terms. It stayed robust across foundation model backbones, and ranked first among context policies. The work repositions context management as the central design problem for streaming tabular prediction.
arxiv-2606-19377:
Williams and colleagues present Emyx in 2026, a fast all-atom protein generation model for computational enzyme design. Designing enzymes means generating proteins that scaffold catalytic residues and ligands. Current all-atom generators inherit expensive architectures from structure prediction. The authors argue much of that complexity is unnecessary for a generator, which conditions on sparse geometric constraints rather than rich evolutionary signals.

Emyx is a mid-sized conditional flow matching model. It concentrates capacity in standard transformer blocks, replacing heavy embedding stacks with lightweight conditioning and sparse links. An exact change of variables maps the flow matching interpolant into a leading noise-level framework, bridging training speed with top diffusion sampling methods. Despite being the smallest model tested, Emyx beats larger rivals on an enzyme design benchmark. It wins on success rate under strict scoring, structural novelty, scaffold diversity, and shape validity. Cheaper generation widens the search for working enzymes.
arxiv-2606-19977:
Bhautik Dhori, Deepak Upadhyay, and Prafulla Jha classify sliding-induced magnetic phases in two-dimensional square lattices in 2026. Altermagnets split electron spins without net magnetization and without relativistic effects, a combination prized for spintronics. Sliding one layer over another can switch valley-polarized states, but a full classification by spin-splitting type was missing. First-principles calculations, stacking theory, and spin-Laue symmetry analysis supply it.

A coupled quasi-altermagnetic state is proposed as a distinct subclass, with reversible type-IV spin splitting steered by interlayer sliding. Worked examples are the Lieb-lattice material Mn2WS4 and its Janus relative. Bands stay spin split at the zone centre even without spin-orbit coupling, and broken fourfold symmetry lets an anomalous Hall signal appear with reversible sign. Sliding becomes a design handle for spin-based devices.
arxiv-2606-20277:
Igor Chaban proves a symplectic duality for the constant term of the geometric Eisenstein series. His 2026 paper works over the function field of a smooth projective curve, for the general linear group and its mirabolic parabolic subgroup. The constant term is categorified by the cohomology of a quasimap space, which carries an action of a correspondence algebra whose commutative part is the ring of functions on the Coulomb branch.

A rank-one local system on the curve induces an action of the étale fundamental group on the Coulomb branch. The main result identifies the quasimap cohomology with the local cohomology of a natural vector bundle over the fixed locus, for a generic range of parameters. Dualities of this kind are the engine of the geometric Langlands program's recent progress, and the identification gives both sides a new computational handle.
arxiv-2606-20877:
John Meluso and three colleagues study artificial collectives in 2026, asking when teams of specialist or generalist agents do better. Many agents on shared tasks could tackle large problems in medicine or governance. Design advice abounds, but hard science of such teams is thin. Their tests use optimizing agents that vary in how broadly they read tasks.

Specialists read tasks narrowly. Generalists read them broadly. Specialist teams form sparse, centralized networks. Generalist teams form dense, spread-out ones. Network traits have small average effects. For specific task types, effects grow several times larger. The same design choice can help or hurt by task. Team design must match structure to task type.
arxiv-2606-21077:
Jerry Wang and four colleagues present OTTER in 2026, a red-teaming system that rewrites jailbreak prompts to evade toxicity filters on production language models. Many deployed systems rely on toxicity moderation as a primary defense. That defense assumes harmful intent correlates with toxic wording. Their work shows the assumption is brittle. Surface toxicity and adversarial intent can be separated by replacing as few as five tokens.

OTTER works as a black box through standard API access only. It evolves token replacements to lower toxicity while keeping attack intent. Tests on hundreds of standard attack prompts across four GPT models raise success rates sharply. A quantitative analysis of the toxicity and bypass relationship is also provided. Category breakdowns translate findings into hardening advice. Red-team evidence like this helps providers fix filters that screen words while missing meaning.
arxiv-2606-21277:
ADAC, presented in 2026 with no named personal byline, is a compiler that turns trained differentiable audio processors into real-time effects without hand translation. Such processors are usually tuned inside machine learning frameworks, then rewritten by hand in the FAUST signal processing language, an error-prone step repeated after every model change. ADAC lowers a trained model to a framework-neutral intermediate form and emits FAUST code directly.

The emitted code matches the source model's impulse response to within floating-point noise, including direct paths. During training, the model inside a running plugin is swapped after each gradient step, so the optimization loop stays audible to the designer. A stability certificate from the shipped parameters is checked before building, and a feedback delay network serves as the demonstration case.
arxiv-2606-21677:
Cole Dickerson, Wahab Khawaja, and Ismail Güvenç study how 5G networks can double as drone surveillance in 2026 without starving the communications they exist to serve. Integrated sensing and communication lets existing wireless infrastructure watch for small, maneuverable UAVs near airports and critical sites, but sensing and data traffic compete for the same resources.

Their shared-resource framework tracks how sensing waveform length, transmission rate, and beam allocation trade against throughput in a 5G new radio system. Adaptive sensing policies beat fixed reservations, preserving throughput under shifting load while keeping useful detection. When congestion peaks, software-defined sensor nodes borrow outside signals of opportunity for extra passive looks, sharply cutting tracking outages. Multistatic geometry, many transmitters and receivers, also sharpens position fixes and evens coverage over what a single site achieves.
arxiv-2606-22577:
Luigi D'Onofrio records an approximation criterion for Banach spaces in this 2026 functional analysis paper. Banach spaces are complete spaces with a norm, and a predual is a smaller space whose dual recovers the original. D'Onofrio studies spaces embedded into bounded sequences by a countable norming family.

The criterion identifies when the dual of the associated c0-subspace, the part whose coordinates vanish at infinity, equals a prescribed atomic predual. It holds exactly when bounded coordinatewise approximation by c0 elements is available. The formulation is a self-contained scalar version of a framework from D'Onofrio and four collaborators. The criterion is then applied to Lipschitz-free spaces, which encode the geometry of a metric space. For countable proper subsets of the half-line, gap coordinates identify the Lipschitz space with the bounded sequences. The c0-subspace coincides with Dalet's predual, making the identifications concrete.
arxiv-2606-22777:
Bang-Xian Han and Liming Yin generalize curvature comparison geometry in this 2026 paper. Alexandrov spaces carry a synthetic notion of non-negative curvature, defined by comparing triangles. Many interesting spaces, including some Finsler spaces where angles need not be symmetric, fall outside that classical setting.

The authors introduce a four-point comparison principle, the weak quadruple condition, satisfied both by Alexandrov spaces and by many spaces that are not infinitesimally Hilbert. Using it, they build a strainer theory for finite-dimensional S-concave Busemann concave spaces, whose tangent cones need not be metric cones. They show these spaces have constant integer dimension, satisfy a measure contraction property, and are rectifiable, with unique Banach tangent cones almost everywhere. The spaces also contain an open dense manifold part of full measure. Finally, the authors bound the size of the singular strata and construct natural stratifications.
arxiv-2606-22877:
Wenya Xie and colleagues build a long-horizon memory benchmark for AI assistants in this 2026 paper. An assistant should remember a user's attributes, habits, and preferences over months, updating them as jobs, routines, and tastes drift. Existing benchmarks use short, simplified interactions. They miss how real profiles change: parts evolve on different timelines, changes are driven by seasons and life events, and evidence is scattered across small actions in many apps.

Their benchmark, DynamicMem, is synthetic, since real long-term data is locked away by privacy. It constructs fifteen months of activity per user, averaging 2.2 million tokens and 1,772 grounded events across sixteen applications. Every recorded action reflects the user's profile at that moment, and each attribute must be inferred from behavioral traces rather than read off directly. Systems are evaluated at five quarterly checkpoints, testing whether memory keeps pace with a changing person.
arxiv-2606-22977:
Youxin Zhu and colleagues present StatABench in a 2026 paper on evaluating language models. Statistical analysis mixes subject knowledge with skilled tool use, so it is a stern test for these models. Earlier benchmarks covered only narrow slices of the field or used rigid formats. StatABench has two parts. Stat-Closed holds four hundred four questions across eighteen topics, in formats from multiple choice to practical problems. Stat-Open holds thirty open modeling tasks adapted from professional competitions.

Zhu and colleagues ran many models and agent frameworks through the benchmark. The strongest closed-track score came from GPT-5.1 at under seventy percent. The best open-source model scored lower still. On the open track, the top agent framework averaged a modest score under a judge-based grading protocol. The gaps point to weak tool-grounded reasoning and shaky method choices as the main barriers to reliable automated statistics.
arxiv-2606-23177:
Qi Li and colleagues make medical image segmentation show its uncertainty honestly in a 2026 paper. Segmentation models outline structures in scans, learning from human annotations. Those labels carry bias and vary between raters. Earlier methods that mimic each rater bury rater traits inside opaque hidden features, so their influence stays hard to analyze. The team's framework uses a Gaussian process in logit space. It splits each prediction into an image-based reference part plus rater-specific shifts, each described by explicit bias and variance values.

Li and colleagues test the method on a medical dataset labeled by several annotators. Modeling rater shifts explicitly improved how well the stated uncertainty matched reality, while accuracy stayed comparable to leading multi-rater methods. The learned bias and variance values also mirror real annotator behavior. That openness lets users see how individual raters move the final prediction.
arxiv-2606-23277:
Adam Štorek and colleagues control information flow through language models with a geometric method in a 2026 security paper. Language models now sit between sensitive data, often untrusted inputs, and privileged actions in agent systems. Prompt injections and confidential leaks are live risks. Information flow control offers a principled defense, yet tracking flow through a model itself lacked solid foundations. In an autoregressive model every input token can influence every output token, so naive tracking explodes. Their framework, GIF, uses the model's Jacobian and local output geometry to bound the mutual information between input spans and outputs.

Štorek and colleagues compute that bound on large models with automatic differentiation and low-rank approximation. A fully mechanized Lean 4 proof shows the bound is locally sound under stated regularity assumptions. Evaluations cover integrity and confidentiality tasks across prompt injection benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-23677:
Mukherjee and Shih show that averaging noisy biological patterns over time reveals a hidden large scale order, in a 2026 paper on pattern formation. Turing patterns, spots and stripes arising when chemicals react and diffuse at different rates, appear across living systems. Random noise can excite such patterns even where the deterministic system would stay uniform. Cells, though, often respond to accumulated signals over time, a fact most theory ignores.

The authors integrate the fluctuating configurations over time and study the variance of particle counts inside large windows. In the Levin Segel model they prove, and confirm in simulations, that this variance falls toward a fixed floor set by reaction kinetics as windows grow. The fall signals effective hyperuniformity, an unusually even large scale arrangement, appearing without any fine tuning. The ordered range widens hugely near the Turing instability, suggesting time integration is a general route to large scale organization.
arxiv-2606-23877:
Ottenhof and Lutellier build a bug detector that works at the level of individual cells inside Jupyter notebooks, in a 2026 paper on software engineering. Notebooks are graduating from quick prototypes to complex programs, and buggy notebooks on public platforms are rising fast. Their cell structure breaks ordinary tools: cells run in any order, and a file level warning is barely useful for finding a bug.

JupOtter combines three new pieces. A notebook specific way of splitting code into tokens preserves cell structure. A prediction technique flags buggy cells directly, rather than whole files. And OtterDataset provides over twenty one thousand notebooks labeled for cell level bug detection. JupOtter's F1 scores beat static analyzers and large language models on two of three datasets.
arxiv-2606-24677:
Madhulatha Mandarapu and Sandeep Kunkunuru argue that three fields maintain the same structure in separate silos. Time systems nest days inside months and years. Geography systems nest postcodes inside cities. Ontology systems arrange concepts in is a and part of hierarchies. Each field keeps its own index for its hierarchy. Yet all are subsumption posets with two recurring queries. One asks whether an item sits under another. The other rolls up a measure over all below it.

Their index, OEH, first probes the shape of a hierarchy. Trees get a nested set embedding, and low width directed graphs get a chain decomposition. Tested on five real hierarchies, OEH matches a two hop index on tree query speed. It uses half the space and builds six to seven times faster. Tests include a taxonomy with 1.3 million nodes. On high width graphs, though, two hop indexing wins.
arxiv-2606-24977:
A. Ballester, P. Pérez, and V. Pérez show that two classical theorems for skew braces come free from group theory. Skew braces are algebraic structures with two interacting operations, now central to several areas of algebra. Truman had proved Sylow and Hall theorems for finite skew braces directly. This short note takes a different route. Every skew brace yields a trifactorised group, a group splitting three ways into subgroups. The Sylow and Hall structure of such groups is already understood.

From that structure, Truman's theorems drop out as direct consequences. The argument replaces brace specific work with established results on factorised groups. A Cauchy theorem for finite skew braces also emerges naturally along the way. Ballester and colleagues thus tie the young theory of skew braces more tightly to classical finite group theory. Results proved once for groups need not be reproved for braces.
arxiv-2606-25477:
Ramsey theory promises that any finite colouring of a rich enough structure hides a large one coloured piece, and ideals measure how that promise can be localised. Julián Cano, Carlos Di Prisco, and Carlos Uzcátegui-Aylwin study Ramsey type ideals on the natural numbers in 2026. These are families of sets closed under subsets and unions that still force homogeneous sets for colourings, echoing classical theorems of Erdős and Rado, Nash-Williams, Galvin, and Ellentuck in ideal form.

New characterisations tie Ramsey ideals to partition properties and to convergence behaviour. Ideal versions of high dimensional Ramsey theorems are analysed, including colourings of barriers and of all finite subsets of the naturals. Between Ramsey and semiselective ideals the authors insert a new intermediate class, Galvin ideals, named for the lemma whose ideal form they capture.
arxiv-2606-25577:
Star forming galaxies line up on a tight relation between their mass and how fast they make stars, called the main sequence. Bernabé Cedrés leads the OTELO survey team in charting that relation for low mass galaxies in 2026 at three cosmic epochs, using different glowing gas lines as signposts at each distance. Nearly all the emitters found are low mass systems below ten billion suns. Fitting each galaxy's energy distribution yields its mass, infrared glow, and star formation rate.

The low mass main sequence they recover matches published relations closely, suggesting one sequence stretches into this little explored regime. One number refuses to agree: the turnover mass, where the relation bends, comes out higher at every redshift than in the literature. The team also warns that colour based selection misses many emitters and that missing infrared data can distort luminosity estimates.
arxiv-2606-25777:
A learner watching only correct sentences must eventually speak the language without inventing errors. Memory limits make it harder. Nicolas Flammarion, Chirag Pabbaraju, Hristo Papazov, Miltiadis Stouras, and Ola Svensson open a resource aware theory of this learning problem in 2026. The target languages are those recognised by small finite automata. The learner sees an adversarial stream of valid strings. It must settle on a hypothesis inside the target, missing few of its strings. With exponential space, exact identification is provable.

Under a tight memory budget the picture changes sharply. Their streaming algorithm uses polynomial space in the automaton's size. It converges with a bounded generation gap. Every string longer than about twice the state count is still captured. A near matching lower bound, reduced from communication complexity, shows large memory is unavoidable for smaller gaps. A crisp transition separates cheap generation from exact learning.
arxiv-2606-26077:
TaeHo Yoon and colleagues make a hard kind of proof easier to find. The proofs are called Lyapunov-style, after the Lyapunov functions they use. Each one builds a score that never goes up as an algorithm runs. The drop in the score gives a clean rate for how fast the method closes in on its goal. Most such proofs are found by hand, with templates or luck. Few certify that the rate is sharp.

Yoon's team turns a tight proof of a different sort into one of this style. A toolbox does the heavy lifting, with basic linear algebra, inside a live notebook. Users can run the steps on their own algorithm and see what comes out. The method pulls several known proofs under one roof. It also finds four new ones. One of them pins down a new best method for strongly monotone inclusion problems.
arxiv-2606-26277:
Dianjing Fan and colleagues turn raw web clicks into a read on customer intent for financial services. Banks see two disconnected worlds: anonymous visitors browsing before login, and known customers servicing accounts inside the app. Matching the two is hard, so web intent signals usually die unused. Their framework gives the clickstream two voices at once. A self-supervised Transformer compresses each session into a compact embedding for ranking tasks.

Interpretability gets its own pipeline. A language model drafts an intent taxonomy, which is then distilled into labels a production system can apply. Embeddings and labels together serve both scoring and human understanding. On a mobile homepage tile ranking task, top-one recall rises measurably with the session embedding. The dual design suits finance, where a recommendation must often be explained to regulators and customers alike. Clicks, read well, can follow a customer across the login wall.
arxiv-2606-26377:
Poojitha Thota and colleagues defend chatbots by checking both sides of a conversation: what the user seems to intend, and whether the reply would actually cause harm. Defenses that read only prompts or only replies miss attacks split across the two.

Specialist analyst agents judge intent and harm separately, with a judge agent resolving disagreements before any reply reaches the user. Across phishing, jailbreaks, prompt injection, cyber abuse, and harmful content, the joint check lifts average F1 score from 0.90 for the best single-sided defenses to 0.95, cuts attack success to about four percent, and halves false alarms on sensitive but benign requests.
arxiv-2606-26477:
Leonel Bixano and six colleagues examine the algebra behind the Lindblad equation. That equation governs open quantum systems, which leak energy and information to their surroundings. Closed systems evolve by simpler unitary rules. Open systems need dissipative terms, which describe the leaking. The authors ask what algebraic structure those terms require.

They represent the equation's operator in a new way. The dynamics then sit inside a closed algebra of Hermitian operators. An algebra is closed when combining its members stays inside the set. This algebra does not depend on the particular physical model. All model details enter through one set of coefficients. The framework yields recipes for building the algebra as systems grow. It also cuts the cost of constructing the full dynamics operator. A sample notebook for one quantum bit is included for readers.
arxiv-2606-26577:
Pouyan Navabi and Christos G. Takoudis present an active learning platform for saturation curves. Such curves rise from zero and level off at a plateau. They govern gas adsorption, enzyme behaviour, drug dose response, and atomic layer deposition, a chip-making process. Mapping a curve takes costly measurements, so each point must count. Standard curve-fitting tools can dip unphysically on sparse, noisy data.

Their platform uses Bayesian monotonic spline regression. Every fitted curve starts at exactly zero and never decreases. Bayesian means the fit carries explicit uncertainty, used to pick the next experiment. The plateau is fixed by a measurement at maximum exposure, not by a guess. The team benchmarked five distinct curve families, from classic adsorption to enzyme kinetics. One fixed model recovered every curve within measurement noise. No fitted curve ever violated the rising shape.
arxiv-2606-26977:
Shangtong Cao and six colleagues present CLIR, a fuzzing tool for the Cranelift compiler backend. Cranelift translates code to machine code for several processor families and is prized for speed. Testing it is hard: test inputs must obey strict strict form, sequences must be dense enough to stress the backend, and bugs must be traced across architectures. CLIR generates programs hierarchically to keep them valid.

A liveness-guided pass then packs more work into the test code. Liveness tracks which values are still needed, letting the fuzzer insert useful work safely. Diagnosis-guided tweaks carry findings across chip targets. The framework compares Cranelift against references, hunting bugs that could quietly corrupt built programs.
arxiv-2606-27077:
Güntert and Bosch compare what makes public transport trips feel good or bad in a big city and a rural town.
