Family barriers included weak family connection, relatives controlling health decisions, and gender inequality inside the household. Organizational, community, and policy barriers stacked above those. The authors argue that fixing clinics alone will not move elderly patients who are stopped first at home. Effective reform in rural Bangladesh must work on every level of the stack at once.
plos-pone-0358777:
Yan Zhu and four colleagues tackle a weakness in synthetic voices that must sound emotional, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Zero shot systems can copy a new speaker. Yet feelings often blur into the words. Their fix separates the two streams. Text meaning and emotional tone travel through parallel attention paths and merge only at a controlled gate, so neither corrupts the other during generation.

They also built a fine grained emotion space of sixteen classes, sorted from pitch and energy patterns in speech. During training, the system dwells on its hardest examples. Samples with unusually high loss get extra weight. Tested on speakers the system had never heard, using a standard emotional speech collection, it produced words with a low error rate and clean sound measures. The design targets expressive voices for media and assistance tools.
plos-pone-0358877:
Md Parvej Hussain leads a team of six measuring how a small start in life shadows children's nutrition across South Asia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The authors used recent demographic and health surveys from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and the Maldives. They matched children of low birth weight with similar children of normal weight. The total passed one hundred forty-seven thousand cases. Then they compared five forms of malnutrition.

About sixteen percent of the children had been born small. After matching, low birth weight was significantly associated with every form examined: stunting, wasting, underweight, having at least one form, and suffering several at once. The pattern held country by country with one exception, wasting in Bangladesh and the Maldives, where the link lost significance. The authors say preventing low birth weight itself, through maternal care, is the lever that moves all five outcomes together.
plos-pone-0359277: Santo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the microbes of the horse gut. They profiled the small compounds those microbes make along the whole digestive tract. Horses were fed in three ways: pasture, hay, or rations with added oats. Diet shapes the gut's chemistry, and those compounds affect the horse's health. The profiles give vets and owners a fuller picture of feeding effects.
plos-pone-0359577: Kotan and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on filling gaps in health data. Records often miss values, and the reason for the gaps changes what fix works. The team tested a method called CHIT, a cyclical hybrid approach, under three missing-data patterns. They used health data sets as the test ground. Honest tests of gap filling matter because filled values quietly shape later findings.
plos-pone-0359777:
David Calzada, Laura Martín-López, and Jerónimo Carnés published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, the house dust mite whose droppings trigger many allergies. The authors use genetic and microbiomics approaches to monitor the growth of mite cultures and the environmental influences on them.

Laboratories grow these mites to produce allergy test and treatment materials, so culture quality matters. Tracking both the mites' genes and their microbes can reveal why batches thrive or fail. Allergen manufacturers and researchers standardizing mite material are the readers for monitoring methods of this kind.
plos-pone-0360077:
Randa Al-Kharabsheh and Muayyad Ahmad built in 2026 a large scale artificial intelligence analysis to predict which neurology patients will return to hospital without planning to. Unplanned readmissions are costly and often signal that something in the first stay or the discharge plan went wrong. The authors use CHAID decision trees, a method that sorts patients into risk groups through a branching series of questions.

A decision tree has an advantage over many AI tools: doctors can read its reasoning and see which factors drove a prediction. If such a model proves accurate, hospitals could aim follow up calls, home support, and medication reviews at the patients most likely to bounce back. The work joins a wider push to make hospital prediction tools explainable.
pmc-10517477:
Alowais, Alghamdi, Alsuhebany, and co-authors survey how artificial intelligence is entering clinical practice. Health care is complex for patients, doctors, and hospitals alike. The authors argue that fast gains in these computer systems could improve care and daily life for patients if used well.

Inside, the review walks through where such tools can plug into medical work, from reading scans to easing routine tasks. It also weighs the care needed before hospitals trust them widely. For clinicians and students, the piece offers a broad, plain map of a fast-moving field and the choices it now forces.
pmc-13122077:
Yan-Bo Fu is first author on a 2026 randomized trial of a traditional Chinese herbal formula for leg artery disease. In lower limb arteriosclerosis obliterans, leg arteries narrow and harden, and reopening them by catheter often fails again over time. The formula, Danggui Sini Decoction, was added to standard care.

Thirty-eight patients at one hospital were split evenly between standard vessel reopening alone and the same care plus the decoction. At one month, overall success rates were alike, though quality of life improved more with the formula. At six months, the formula group had higher success and better vessel openness rates. The authors claim mid-term benefit and lower re-narrowing risk.
pmc-13196977:
John Owuoth and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study on new HIV infections in western Kenya. HIV rates in Kisumu County run over four times the national mean. The team enrolled adults with more than one recent sexual partner to measure how often new infections occur.

They followed 619 adults without HIV, testing them every three months for up to two years. Eleven new infections occurred over the follow-up span. The rate was lower than the team expected. Having four or more partners and forced sexual activity linked to higher risk in early checks. The authors credit prevention work, wider treatment, and regular counseling for the lower rate.
pmc-13197277:
Chernkhuan Stonsaovapak and colleagues wrote a 2026 review with network analysis on sensory cues for walking in Parkinson disease. Parkinson disease slows gait and shortens steps. External cues, such as lights, sounds, or touch pulses, can steady walking, but which type works best was unclear.

The team pooled thirty-three trials with more than eleven hundred patients. Touch-based and visual cues each raised walking speed versus control care. Visual, touch-based, and sound cues each lengthened stride. Rankings put touch cues first for speed and visual cues first for stride length. Both beat sound cues alone. The ranking gives clinics a clear order for choosing cue types.
pmc-13197477:
Christian Hoehne and colleagues ran a 2026 training study with a printed model for gum splinting. Periodontal splinting binds loose teeth to steady neighbors. Dental students need safe practice before treating patients, so the team built a low-cost printed jaw with movable front teeth.

Forty-three fourth-year students each made two splints in a crossover course, using two fiber materials in random order. Students rated the course good and highly relevant to real care. Felt readiness rose from poor before the course to good after it. Tooth placement accuracy did not differ by material or by session order. The cheap model offers repeatable practice under lifelike looseness.
pmc-13201077:
Yuuki Y Watanabe and colleagues tracked Greenland sharks after longline release in a 2026 study. Greenland sharks grow extremely slowly and mature late, so fishery bycatch could threaten them. Few studies had combined stress measures with long survival tracking in one species, so the team did both in Arctic waters.

They used hook timers, blood tests, motion sensors, and acoustic plus satellite tags. Blood stress markers sat within normal ranges for kin species. Released sharks swam faster with quicker tailbeats at first, then settled after about ten hours. Nine of ten tagged sharks survived past thirty days, with one tracked for years. Careful handling, they stress, keeps survival high.
pmc-13212777:
Yusuf Ilhan and Halil Goksel Guzel write in 2026 a letter to the editor responding to a study of surgery for colorectal cancer that has spread to the lungs. They praise the original work while arguing its treatment details need sharper reading in today's drug era.

Their main point concerns therapy given before surgery: the study reports older-style chemotherapy cycles but little about modern targeted drugs or immunotherapy. Tumour testing for a marker that predicts immunotherapy benefit was missing in many patients, which the writers call a serious gap. Since such drugs can change outcomes greatly for the small group who carry that marker, future reports should document regimens and testing fully.
pmc-13212877:
Xiangxiao Liu and a large team tackle in 2026 a threat to making fuel ethanol with blue-green bacteria: germs that invade the tanks and crash the batch. Germ killers and pH tricks tend to harm the fuel makers too, or fail when invaders mix.

The team wrapped the cells in alginate, a gel from seaweed. The gel lets air, light, and food pass, but blocks touch with the invading germs. Bare cultures died out fast under a mixed germ attack and made no ethanol at all. Wrapped cells kept growing and making fuel in the same tanks. Once rinsed and grown again, they got part of their output back, so the shield can be reused.
pmc-13213077:
Yoshiki Furumura and colleagues report in 2026 a rare emergency: a burst tangle of blood vessels in the thyroid gland that swelled an elderly woman's neck and squeezed her airway. Only one similar case had ever been published.

The 82-year-old patient's neck ballooned suddenly after she blew her nose, and breathing grew difficult. Doctors secured her airway early with a tube, then combined vessel-blocking radiology treatment with surgery to remove the lesion. She recovered completely. Imaging showed the abnormal vessels were fed by the upper thyroid artery. The authors stress airway first, then teamwork between radiology and surgery, when thyroid bleeding strikes.
pmc-13214077:
Timo Oosterveld leads a large team charting in 2026 how energy burn evolves in patients stuck in intensive care for ten days or more. Feeding such patients well requires knowing their expenditure, yet long-stay metabolism has been poorly mapped.

Across seven intensive care units in Europe and Australia, 433 patients contributed nearly twelve hundred calorimetry measurements. Average expenditure rose early, peaked near day ten, then declined, a pattern that held after statistical adjustment. A marker of protein breakdown climbed over the same first stretch. Grouping analysis found three trajectories, from low to high burners. The turning point matches the usual onset of persistent critical illness, a clue for tailoring nutrition.
pmc-13215177:
Christopher J. H. Smalley leads a large team asking in 2026 why two near-identical organic semiconductor crystals carry energy at wildly different speeds. The molecules differ only in their end groups, yet one moves excitons, packets of light energy, over a hundred times better.

Advanced electron techniques solved the crystal structures, including two forms of the slower material, and mapped defects inside its tiny crystals. Mixed crystal forms growing into each other created the defects, and spectroscopy tied them to nanoscale electronic changes. Computer modelling pinned the transport gap on rotational disorder among molecules. Managing such defects, the authors argue, is essential for better solar cells and electronics.
pmc-13215377:
Xiaowei Song and co-authors published a 2026 scoping review of frailty scores built from comprehensive geriatric assessment, including newer electronic versions. The review traces how these tools were developed, tested, and used across care settings.

Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, the team searched MEDLINE and CINAHL for English papers from 2004 to mid-2025 and kept 38 studies. The assessment-based index predicted death, hospital admission, and functional decline well across settings. Digital versions improved accuracy and fit into routine workflow, which supports wider use in hospitals, long-term care, and primary care. The authors still call for validation in more populations before routine adoption.
pmc-13215577:
Yujie Liu and co-authors report a 2026 study of how recalled parenting relates to social media addiction in Chinese university students. The team tested whether unmet interpersonal needs carry part of that link.

A survey of 1,766 students sorted parenting memories into supportive, distant, and harshly controlling styles. Students from the two harsher styles showed stronger feelings of burdensomeness and thwarted belonging, and those feelings were in turn tied to more addictive social media use. That path held for men but not for women. The authors suggest that warmer, less controlling parenting and care for belonging needs could lower digital dependence.
pmc-13215977:
Jean-Claude Stephan and co-authors report a 2026 case of sudden lung flooding after a routine anaesthetic reversal drug. A healthy 27-year-old man developed noncardiogenic pulmonary edema minutes after receiving neostigmine with atropine at the end of an appendectomy.

Before the breathing tube could be removed, his oxygen levels crashed, airway pressures spiked, and pink frothy fluid filled the tube, with chest imaging showing diffuse infiltrates in both lungs. Heart failure, fluid overload, suction injury, and allergy were each weighed and set aside using bedside ultrasound, the small fluid volume given, and normal allergy blood tests plus negative skin testing. He recovered fully after intensive care and was extubated twelve hours later. The authors present the link to neostigmine as a diagnosis of exclusion.
pmc-13217877:
Ohisa Harley and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study testing whether cheap blood-count inflammation scores can flag diabetic macular edema, the sight-threatening swelling that can appear even in early diabetic eye disease. Imaging catches it, but imaging is not everywhere.

Eighty patients with type 2 diabetes and non-proliferative retinopathy were split evenly by scan into edema and no-edema groups. Neutrophil counts ran significantly higher with edema, and two composite indices trended or reached higher values as well. A combined model using the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, the systemic immune-inflammation index, and body mass index discriminated moderately, with an area under the curve of 0.706. The authors present the panel as foundational evidence for a low-cost screening aid, not a replacement for scans.
pmc-13219077:
Fulya Mete Kalayci and colleagues examine which children with hypothalamic tumors go on to develop obesity in a 2026 study. Damage to the hypothalamus, the brain's appetite and hormone centre, can trigger rapid weight gain, but not every child with a tumor there becomes obese. Knowing which features travel with the outcome could focus prevention.

The study covered thirty-four children followed between 1999 and 2020, most often with optic glioma, pilocytic astrocytoma, or craniopharyngioma. Fifteen children, about forty-four percent, became obese, typically within three months of diagnosis. At diagnosis, obesity was linked to having had a skull-opening operation and to adrenal insufficiency and underactive sex hormone production. Once the analysis adjusted, surgical approach no longer predicted obesity, a caution the authors state. Insulin resistance and abnormal blood lipids clustered in the obese group. The study underlines how fast the weight gain arrives and how entangled it is with hormone deficits.
pmc-13219177:
Taissa Viana Damasceno and colleagues test an anesthetic combination for tambaqui, an Amazonian fish, in a 2026 aquaculture study. Fish are anesthetized to reduce stress and movement during handling and transport, and eugenol, the compound in clove oil, is standard. The team asked whether catnip oil, from Nepeta cataria, could work with eugenol for a gentler effect.

Three half-and-half mixtures were prepared, pairing eugenol with catnip oil, eugenol with corn oil, and catnip oil with corn oil. 288 tambaqui went through ten-minute baths at five concentrations. One experiment timed how fast fish were anesthetized and recovered, probing for synergy between the compounds, while a second recorded muscle and heart activity. A third used the blocker flumazenil to probe their action. The eugenol-catnip pairing gave muscle relaxation with minor cardiovascular disturbance, an easily reversed slowing of the heart, supporting it as a safe blend for this species.
pmc-13219977:
Molecular Medicine Reports retracts a 2017 article by Qun Xie and colleagues on Homeobox B9 and hypertrophic scar formation, in a 2026 editor's notice. A reader alerted the journal that the western blot data in two figure panels had already appeared in an article by different authors at different institutes, published in Molecular and Cellular Biology. Editorial analysis found that a histology panel in the first figure had been published before, by other authors, in Archives of Plastic Surgery.

Because data in the article had been published before its submission, the editor withdrew the paper from the journal. The authors were invited to explain the overlaps and gave no satisfactory reply, as the notice records. The editor apologizes to readers for the inconvenience. Notices stay attached to the article's record, so that anyone who finds the scar study through a database search also finds the warning that its data cannot be trusted.
pmc-13220577:
Xuanhe Tang and colleagues test whether a routine blood value at intensive care admission can forecast kidney injury after major aortic surgery in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Total aortic arch replacement is lifesaving surgery for a torn aorta, but acute kidney injury follows in half to seventy percent of cases and worsens survival. Lactate, the stress marker drawn on every ICU patient, was the candidate signal.

The study covered 356 adults operated on at Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital between 2021 and 2023, and 232 of them, sixty-five percent, developed kidney injury by criteria. Their admission lactate ran higher, a median of 3.90 against 2.10 in those spared, and risk climbed across lactate thirds. Adding lactate to a prediction model lifted its accuracy from 0.757 to 0.824 and improved how patients were reclassified between risk groups. The authors conclude a cheap, immediate lactate reading can sharpen early risk stratification and guide intensive care vigilance after this operation.
pmc-13221977:
Yidnekachew Degefaw Mazengiya and co-authors assess a World Health Organization costing tool for national antimicrobial resistance plans in Africa, in a 2026 review. The tool, launched in 2021, helps countries price their action plans, spot activities already funded, and size funding gaps. Focal points from fifteen African member states answered a questionnaire about using it.

Eleven countries reported raising funds with the costed data the tool produced. Costed plans shaped policy choices in seven countries and improved collaboration among funders and sectors. Challenges remained, notably thin domestic financing and donor priorities that clashed with national needs. The authors present costing as a catalyst for realistic budgeting and durable resistance programs.
pmc-13227677:
Maja Kovac writes a 2026 letter to the editor examining a randomised trial that compared two anaesthetic techniques for thigh-bone fracture surgery: peripheral nerve blocks and selective spinal anaesthesia. The trial's authors reported differences including more episodes of low blood pressure under spinal anaesthesia. Kovac questions whether the groups were truly comparable and whether the measurements support the conclusions drawn.

One concern is case mix: eighty percent of the spinal group carried high anaesthetic-risk grades, against a notably smaller share in the block group, which could itself explain extra blood-pressure drops. A second concern is repeated testing of block strength in sedated patients during surgery, a practice needing cooperation and unclear rationale. The letter asks for clearer reporting before superiority is claimed either way.
pmc-13231077:
Simge Seren Kirlioglu Balcioglu and colleagues review in 2026 links between body inflammation and brain structure in hard-to-treat depression. Some patients fail several antidepressant courses, and immune signals such as C-reactive protein often run high in that group. Brain scans in parallel work show changes in the hippocampus and in white matter wiring.

Most past work studied blood markers and scans apart, leaving their connection unclear. Newer thinking ties immune activity to the brain changes through shared pathways that may drive resistance to standard drugs. Sorting patients by both kinds of marker could create cleaner groups for trials. Targeted treatments aimed at the immune side may then be tested in the patients most likely to gain.
pmc-13231577:
Justin Berk and colleagues argue in 2026 for trial designs that let prisoners choose their treatment arm when they feel strongly. People in custody carry heavy illness burdens yet stay shut out of most clinical research. Fears about pressure and limited freedom, plus deep mistrust of medical systems, make classic random assignment hard to run fairly.

In a partially randomized preference trial, people with a strong preference take their chosen option. People without a strong view are randomized as usual, so cause and effect can still be estimated. The design also measures how much preference itself shapes results, and it may lift sign-up and completion rates. Similar gains could help other groups whose freedom to choose is limited.
pmc-13233577:
Eric D Kessel, Steve K Frey, and Hazen AJ Russell published a 2026 dataset paper describing a new digital terrain model for Canada. National water modeling needed one elevation grid covering the whole country, including lake bottoms and watersheds crossing into the United States. No such product existed, so the Canada1Water project built one from existing elevation sources.

The team merged high-resolution Arctic data and NASA elevation data with open-source depth measurements for lakes of ten square kilometers or more. Everything was aligned to one datum and projection, resampled to a grid of roughly twenty meters, and cleaned of voids and canopy errors. The result ships as stacked map files separating surface, ground, and lake-bottom terrain for use in water and groundwater models.
pmc-13233977:
Nien-Chu Shih, Joey A. Contreras, Wendy J. Mack, and Jeiran Choupan published a 2026 brain imaging study in healthy older adults. Perivascular spaces are fluid channels around small brain vessels that help clear waste, and sleep influences both clearance and brain connectivity. The team combined structural and resting scans with sleep questionnaires and cognitive tests from 512 participants in a healthy ageing cohort.

Enlarged spaces in the basal ganglia tracked with stronger connectivity in right temporal regions tied to memory, while spaces in a white matter region tracked with hippocampal and frontal connectivity. In early middle age, larger spaces in that region paired with stronger hippocampal connectivity and better cognition. Longer time in bed and better sleep quality in older adults also linked the basal ganglia pattern to connectivity. The authors suggest these channels mirror memory-network health.
pmc-13235177:
Parisa Gazerani offered in 2026 a hypothesis-driven view of how migraine and menopause together may mark vulnerability in the aging female brain. Migraine is far more common in women, and menopause brings large hormonal, metabolic, and immune shifts. The article gathers clinical, imaging, and mechanism evidence around that overlap. Its frame treats repeated migraine strain as interacting with estrogen-guided regulation across adult life.

Hormonal instability during the transition, followed by lasting estrogen decline, may reveal earlier hidden neural differences. Imaging and biomarker findings partly overlap with brain aging processes, yet results stay mixed across studies. Long-term thinking outcomes are not consistently tied to migraine in the studies reviewed. The author stresses migraine is not presented as a direct cause of degeneration. Testable longitudinal studies are proposed to settle whether migraine features signal later brain risk.
pmc-13235877:
Victor C.W. Tam and colleagues surveyed in 2026 trained laypeople in Hong Kong about what stops them from starting resuscitation at a cardiac arrest. Six hundred seventy-eight adults who had learned basic life support answered an online survey during the pandemic period. A planned behaviour model linked attitudes, social norms, and perceived control to stated intention to act. Perceived barriers were added to that model in two separate groups.

Barriers about personal performance tied strongly and negatively to perceived control over acting. Cultural barriers tied to attitudes and social norms, but not to perceived control, in the fitted model. Attitudes, norms, and control each predicted intention to perform resuscitation significantly. Worry about infection changed how cultural barriers related to attitude between high- and low-concern groups. The authors suggest training should target the strongest barriers and build confidence, supportive norms, and positive attitudes together.
pmc-13237877:
Dominic Simon and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a cancer-style staging system, adapted for infections around man-made hips, gives consistent answers in different hands. Three raters classified 185 infected hip replacements on their own, 84 acute and 101 chronic, then repeated the exercise ninety days later. The PJI-TNM scheme borrows the tumor, node, metastasis logic of oncology staging.

Agreement was strong. The same rater reproduced earlier scores at very good levels for both acute and chronic infections, and raters agreed strongly with each other, slightly less so for chronic cases. The authors conclude the scheme is robust enough for routine use in grading these infections. Consistent staging, they argue, supports clearer treatment decisions and fairer matches between hospitals and studies.
pmc-13239177:
Aynias Seid and Semira Nureddin studied 182 tuberculosis patients in Ethiopia in 2026, asking whether type 2 diabetes feeds multidrug-resistant TB. Genetic probe assays listed the resistance mutations in each patient's bacteria, and blood tests sorted the patients by diabetes status. Forty-four patients carried both diseases.

Fifty resistance mutations were found across the resistant isolates, and drug resistance ran far more common in the diabetic group. Two mutations known for high-level resistance and easy spread led the catalog. In the models, past TB treatment and the diabetes pairing each raised the odds of multidrug resistance. pmc-13239377:

pmc-13239477:
Yao Wang and co-authors build a prediction tool for a painful side effect of rectal cancer treatment in a 2026 paper. pmc-13239577:
Carlos Alberto Velasco-Benítez and team survey child gut specialists about stubborn constipation in a 2026 paper. pmc-13239977:

pmc-13241377:
Geng and co-authors at Qilu argue hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries need start-to-finish thinking. Hard carbon's graphitic patches, nanopores, and defects jointly decide sodium storage. pmc-13241777:

pmc-13242177:

pmc-13242477:

pmc-13242777:

pmc-13242977:

pmc-13243177:

pmc-13243877:

pmc-13244977:

pmc-13246377:

pmc-13246777:

pmc-13247777:
Wei Gao and co-authors review how donor liver preservation has evolved in a 2026 survey. Cold storage on ice stays the standard way to hold a graft before transplant. Cooling slows cell activity and stretches safe storage to about half a day.

pmc-13248977:

pmc-13249777:
Dörr and colleagues compare two kinds of older epilepsy patients in Berlin clinics, in a 2026 Journal of Neurology study. pmc-13249977:

pmc-13250177:

pmc-13250877:

pmc-13251077:

pmc-13254077:

pmc-13256777:

pmc-13257277:

pmc-13257577:

pmc-13257677:

pmc-13257777:

pmc-13258977:

pmc-13259277:

pmc-13260377:

pmc-13261977:

pmc-13262277:

pmc-13263277:

pmc-13263477:

Exposure raised liver enzymes linked to injury and altered gut barrier proteins, suggesting a leakier intestine. Helpful bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus declined, while several potentially harmful groups increased. The authors warn that sustained high intake damaged both liver and gut in this animal model. Human relevance still needs direct study before firm conclusions.
pmc-13264377:
Hui Yu and colleagues study artificial intelligence pilot zones and city carbon intensity in China in a 2026 spatial analysis. Computing growth raises energy demand, yet smarter systems can also cut waste. The national pilot zone program was treated as a policy experiment. The team measured effects on emissions per unit of output in pilot cities and neighbors. Pathways through productivity, green innovation, energy efficiency and computing demand were traced at city level.

Pilot status lowered carbon intensity locally and in surrounding areas. Productivity gains and green technology innovation carried the benefit across borders, while efficiency gains stayed local. Rising computing demand pushed emissions the other way, but mitigation dominated overall. Gains were strongest in eastern, resource-based and digitally advanced cities. Coordinated regional planning is the policy lesson.
pmc-13264577:
Alefe Luiz Caliani Carrera led a 2026 pilot trial in dogs of a stem cell product injected into the knee joint after bone surgery. The dogs had a common knee operation that levels the shin bone top after ligament damage. The product holds the helpful fluids stem cells release, without the cells themselves.

Twenty pet dogs were split by chance into a treated group and a dummy injection group, with neither owners nor vets knowing which was which. Treated dogs were less lame and in less pain by day 15, while the other group caught up near day 60 to 90. Joint wear scores rose in the control group but fell in the treated group. Bone healing at day 30 was also better with treatment. The authors see promise as an add-on therapy.
pmc-13264877:
Eva Kagenaar and co-authors wrote a 2026 protocol for the SORT study, which compares two strong treatments for bladder cancer that is confined to the organ but has grown into muscle. Both follow chemotherapy first: one removes the bladder, the other uses high-dose radiation and keeps it. A randomized trial failed to recruit, so proof must come from records.

They will copy a trial's rules on real-world data, a method called target trial emulation, and adjust for baseline differences. The main outcome is death from any cause at three years. Costs and cost-effectiveness will also be compared, along with death rates at five years.
pmc-13264977:
Zhanna Sarbassova led a 2026 report on a pilot training program in autism care for health workers in Kazakhstan. Children with autism need joined-up care from many professions, yet local training was scarce. A mixed team of specialists and parents built a 60-hour course covering detection, management, rehabilitation, and family support.

The pilot ran in Astana with 49 health professionals in two cohorts. After training, correct use of the newer diagnosis code system rose from about 74 to about 88 percent, and all doubt about that system vanished. Knowledge of autism subtypes grew, and recognition of who leads team care rose from about 29 to about 46 percent. Staff also reported better grasp of referral routes and family support tools. The authors present the course as a scalable model for Kazakhstan and similar settings.
pmc-13265177:
Yanyan Yang and colleagues build a survival model for glioblastoma from long non-coding RNAs, in a 2026 study. Glioblastoma is the most malignant brain tumour type, with poor outlook. Long non-coding RNAs do not build proteins, yet they can steer cell behaviour. Their joint value for prognosis was the focus here.

High-risk tumours showed distinct immune cell mixes and checkpoint patterns. Five hub RNAs were highlighted, including SOX21-AS1. That RNA linked with a key immune signal and with better outlook, suggesting a protective role.
pmc-13265677:
Xiongxiong Jing, Shuanglong Hou, and Yajing Li link long-term sensory impairment to falls and hip fractures among older adults, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Vision and hearing loss are common with ageing. Combined loss may steadily erode balance and safety. Average impairment accumulated over time was the exposure studied.

Risk rose in step with impairment level. The highest quarter of combined impairment faced notably higher fall risk. Hip fracture risk more than doubled in that group. Most hip fractures follow falls, magnifying the concern. The authors advocate ongoing monitoring of both senses as part of fall and fracture prevention in older people.
pmc-13265877:
Xihuai Xiong and colleagues study why eggshell quality falls as ducks age, in a 2026 multi-part study. Sixty Shanma ducks compared a young group with an old group. Shell properties, blood calcium markers, gut microbes, and uterus gene activity were measured. Ageing effects proved broad.

Old ducks laid thinner, weaker shells with uneven calcium deposits. Blood vitamin D fell while bone turnover markers rose, signalling disturbed calcium handling. Gut diversity shrank and tissue wear appeared in gut, bone, and uterus. Hundreds of uterus genes changed, centred on calcium signalling. Shell strength tied closely to bone markers, microbes, and calcium genes.
pmc-13266177:
Chen Zhang, Xuhui Chen, and Yongan Sun compare dementia burden across Japan, China, and India, published in 2026. Global burden data from 1990 to 2023 were analysed for cases, deaths, and disability years. Countries sit at different demographic stages. Forecasting models projected burden to 2038.

China carried the highest absolute burden in 2023, with the highest standardised case rates. Japan had the highest standardised death rate. India showed the fastest yearly rises in deaths and disability. Drivers differed: ageing, population growth, and epidemiological change mixed differently per country. Air pollution led risk factors everywhere. Disability years are predicted to rise in all three.
pmc-13266577:
Li-Jia Liu and colleagues describe a new plant species in a 2026 paper from Sichuan, China. Field work in Yajiang County found a mint-family plant much like a known species but with clear differences. Its leaves, flower spikes, and small leaf-like bracts did not match the known plant.

The team checked 12 leaf and flower traits and read more than a thousand genes from 45 plant samples. Both lines of evidence marked the plant as a separate species, named Elsholtzia yajiangensis after its home county. It is known only from that one site so far. The authors list it as data deficient and warn that diversity in the Hengduan Mountains may be undercounted.
pmc-13266777:
Shaopeng Zheng and colleagues examine in 2026 whether changing blood urea patterns predict death in severe pneumonia patients on ventilators. They used a large intensive care database and followed 3,609 adults who started invasive ventilation within a day of admission. The ratio of urea nitrogen to creatinine served as a marker of stress and breakdown in the body.

Grouping patients by how that ratio moved over five days produced three patterns. Those whose ratio started highest and rose fastest died most often within both 14 and 28 days. The pattern held across sex, age, and blood sugar groups. Tracking this simple ratio over time may help teams spot patients who need closer watch.
pmc-13266877:
Xiaohui Xu and Yushang Cui report in 2026 on removing benign lung growths called hamartomas when they sit deep in the center of the lung. Peripheral growths are easy to snip out, but central ones once forced removal of a whole lobe. The authors reviewed 22 patients who instead had only the affected lung segment removed between 2016 and 2021.

Every growth was removed fully, with no deaths in hospital, no severe complications, and no regrowth during follow-up. Based on where growths sat, the authors propose three location types, each matched to a recommended operation. For the deep central type, segment removal preserved lung tissue safely, offering an alternative to the older lobe-removing approach.
pmc-13266977:
Sai Venkata Gayathri Ayyagari and a large microscopy team report in 2026 how tiny local structure changes alter magnetism in high-entropy oxide films. These oxides mix six metals in equal shares, and swapping one metal can reshape behavior. The team compared a manganese-bearing film with a chromium-bearing one using electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and computer calculations.

The manganese film showed stronger exchange bias and more magnetic frustration. Imaging revealed two crystal structures living side by side in that film, while the chromium film held a single structure. Spectroscopy found mixed chemical states for cobalt and manganese, matching the calculations on which sites atoms prefer. Local chemistry, the authors show, drives the magnetic personality of these mixed oxides.
pmc-13267277:
Vittoria Vardanega and colleagues model prenatal testing for sickle cell disease in England in a 2026 paper. Current screening tests the mother, then the father, then offers invasive testing when both carry the gene. When the father cannot be tested, women may wait or miss out. A blood test of the mother alone, called non-invasive prenatal testing, could fill the gap.

Using a decision tree, the team set the lowest test accuracy a future study should demand. One scenario allowed under 10 missed cases a year nationally; a stricter one allowed at most 2. The stricter bar needed about 99 percent sensitivity. Both scenarios implied study sizes too large for a single forward-looking study. The authors suggest design workarounds for rare conditions.
pmc-13267977:
Yuya Saruta and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare liver growth in a young adult. Mesenchymal hamartoma is a harmless liver lesion usually seen in infants. Their patient was a 31-year-old woman whose screening ultrasound found a small liver mass. A year later it had grown from 23 to 68 millimeters, raising concern.

Her long use of birth control pills pointed doctors toward a hormone-linked liver tumor called adenoma. Scans showed a well-edged mass almost 75 millimeters wide near a large liver vein. Judging the growth risky, surgeons removed the rear section of the liver with robot help, vein included. Tissue study showed the harmless hamartoma, with fibrous tissue, spindle cells, and stray bile ducts, and no cancer. The case shows how this rare lesion can fool imaging.
pmc-13269077:
Jingwei Duan and co-authors report in 2026 that a lung tumor can reshape gene activity across the whole brain of a mouse, hinting at a lung-brain metabolic axis. They used a genetically driven small cell lung cancer model and read gene activity in nearly forty-nine thousand brain cell nuclei. Tumor tissue and blood were profiled in parallel for comparison.

Brain changes were widespread and cell-specific. A gene tied to inhibitory signaling rose broadly in basal ganglia and inhibitory neurons, while young myelin-making cells stalled and myelin genes fell together. Two neurotransmitters, glutamate and GABA, ran high in both mouse tumors and patient blood samples. Blocking a GABA receptor with a drug slowed tumor growth in living mice, a lead for follow-up causal studies.
pmc-13269177:
Yuki Morita and co-authors published a case series in 2026 on stomach surgery for patients with many small hormone-linked stomach tumors. These tumors often grow alongside an immune attack on the stomach lining. Removing the lower stomach cuts a hormone that feeds the tumors, but its value was unclear.

Eight patients treated from 2005 to 2023 were reviewed, with a median age of 60 years. Before surgery, most had more than 20 tumors, and hormone levels were very high. After surgery, the median hormone level fell from 4,800 to 68. Tumors shrank in two patients and vanished in six, with no return of disease or deaths during follow-up.
pmc-13269277:
Caojinge Li and co-authors dissect in 2026 how four hornet species living side by side divide their food and, in parallel, host different gut microbe communities. The team combined family trees from a mitochondrial gene, DNA barcoding of gut contents for diet, and bacterial profiling of the gut itself. The four species split into two evolutionary branches, and their habits matched that split.

One branch leaned on beech-order plants with differing insect prey between its two species, while the other branch favored bee prey and certain flowering plants. Within branches, finer splits appeared: one species hunted honeybees while its cousin took solitary bees, easing competition. Predicted microbe functions also differed by branch. The authors caution that larger samples must confirm the host-diet-microbe alignment.
pmc-13269377:
Andres Marmol-Perez and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on muscle loss in young survivors of childhood cancer. This loss, called sarcopenia, combines weak grip strength with low muscle mass. The study asked whether survivors with muscle loss report worse quality of life.

The study included 116 survivors with an average age of 12.1 years. Grip strength and body scans sorted them into no, probable, and confirmed muscle loss groups. Most quality-of-life scores were alike across the groups. One clear gap stood out: girls without muscle loss scored better in total, physical, mental, and school life than girls with confirmed loss. No such pattern was reported for boys.
pmc-13269577:
Lukas Zierke and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a cargo protein called CLN8 in acute pancreatitis, a sudden painful inflammation of the pancreas. CLN8 normally ferries digestive enzymes from their making site toward storage compartments. Using mouse cells and mice lacking the protein, the team watched how the disease unfolded without it.

Loss of CLN8 softened the early phase of the illness but did not prevent it. The key enzyme still reached its compartments and was partly activated, pointing to backup delivery routes. Later, injury grew worse, with more cell stress and more self-eating of damaged cell parts, shown by raised marker proteins. The authors say those later stress responses drive severity.
pmc-13269977:
Adam Wawrzeńczyk and co-authors published a review in 2026 on biomarkers for monitoring eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic immune disease of the food pipe. Symptoms match tissue activity poorly, so patients need repeated camera scopes. The review sorts candidate markers by body compartment: tissue, fluids near the tissue, and blood.

Signals tied to type 2 inflammation define the disease but measure weakly in blood. Tissue gene signatures and markers sampled close to the food pipe tracked inflammation and treatment response far better. Structural markers showed that tissue healing does not always mean the lining is restored. The authors propose combining molecular and low-burden tools to cut scope use, after prospective testing.
pmc-13270177:
Margherita Neri and co-editors introduce in 2026 a seventeen-article collection on drug harms, medication adherence, and forensic markers in children and pregnant patients. These groups face higher drug reaction risk because bodies are still developing, dosing is often off-label, and pregnancy changes how drugs move through the body. Reactions in them are also underreported and understudied.

Studies in the collection range from a nasal sedative's effect on shivering during cesarean birth to a comparison of injection routes for a bleeding-prevention drug after delivery. Others examine epilepsy drug safety data in pregnancy and pin down dose windows for anesthesia drugs that prevent shivering and itching. The editors call for better surveillance, age-fit dosing, adherence support, and forensic methods that can untangle medication errors after harm occurs.
pmc-13270477:
Jaouad Nguadi and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 65-year-old man with advanced heart failure who received a CRT-D device, a pacemaker-defibrillator that resynchronizes the heart. The procedure used 50 milliliters of iodinated contrast dye and succeeded. Four hours later he developed spinal myoclonus, sudden generalized muscle jerks sensitive to touch.

His consciousness stayed clear and brain-wave tests were normal. Brain and spine MRI on day three showed no stroke, bleeding, or inflammation. Kidney function stayed stable. Fluids and clonazepam, a calming drug, brought complete resolution within 72 hours. At three months he had no nerve after-effects. The authors call it the first such case after this device procedure.
pmc-13270877:
Yulena Osorio-Navarro is lead author of a 2026 journal article reporting the whole genome of a new fungus species, Xylaria chamelensis. Specimens were collected from a legume family pod in tropical dry forest in Jalisco, Mexico. Xylaria fungi mostly live on dead matter, though some live inside plants or cause plant disease.

The team grew the fungus in pure culture, sequenced its genome, and compared it with relatives. The assembly spans 51.93 million DNA letters and predicts 11,238 protein-coding genes. Shape evidence plus genome evidence support naming it a new species, forming its own line in the Xylaria family tree. The data serve future work on fungal naming and plant links.
pmc-13271477:
Clare T. M. Doherty is lead author of a 2026 process study inside the STRENGTH trial. That trial tested a behaviour change programme inside cardiac rehab for people with heart disease. The study explored how participants experienced activity. It also asked what helped or hindered staying active, and how context shaped engagement.

Interviews and focus groups covered both trial groups. Attendance records and diaries checked how faithfully the programme was delivered. Both groups valued social support, staff oversight, and set sessions. The programme group added tailored support, outside accountability, and self-monitoring. Those raised awareness and confidence. Low exercise confidence, though, may have held back activity done alone.
pmc-13272177:
Xiaoshan Wei and coauthors report in 2026 two older patients whose optic-spinal inflammatory disease, NMOSD, appeared alongside cancers of the stomach outlet and pancreas. This autoimmune disease attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord, and certain tumors can trigger it. Atypical cases in older patients deserve a cancer search.

One man developed stroke-like symptoms after stomach cancer surgery, then optic neuritis with the disease's signature antibody present. A woman's diagnosis rested on symptoms, steroid response, and relapse imaging after her antibody test came back negative. The report widens the tumor list linked to the disease and describes a tumor-like spinal lesion pattern.
pmc-13272577:
S. Ghosal and A. Ghosal pooled trials on waist size in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. A large waist signals belly fat and higher risk for heart and metabolic disease. The review compared lifestyle steps and newer weight loss drugs based on GLP-1, a gut hormone.

The team gathered 21 randomized trials with 3,196 adults, covering diet, exercise, combined programs, and GLP-1 based drugs. On average, treatment cut waist size by more than four centimeters compared with control groups. The drug based therapies and diet alone showed the clearest cuts. Exercise results varied more. Waist change also tracked change in deep belly fat. The authors note possible bias from small studies, so results need care.
pmc-13272977:
Liyang Jiang leads a 2026 real-world study of adebrelimab-based treatment as a first therapy for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in China. Median time before the cancer grew was 6.47 months, and median survival was 13.77 months overall. Results were close to trial results for brain spread and fluid cases, but benefit looked limited for liver spread, where median survival was 10.51 months. Severe side effects occurred in 42.3 percent of patients, with no new safety signals found.
pmc-13273377: The notice is a correction only, issued in 2026 for an article by Bryan Marr and co-authors on immune effects in mice exposed to sustained low dose ionizing radiation. It reports an error in Figure 4: in panel B, the volcano plots for the 10 mGy and 100 mGy doses were accidentally the same image, duplicated during revision. The corrected figure appears with the notice, and the right image had been among the files seen in peer review. The original article has been updated. No data or conclusions are changed.
pmc-13273477:
Oumaima EL MIAYAR and Abdelaziz Berrado reviewed why health recommender systems rarely reach clinical practice in a 2026 systematic review. These systems suggest tailored health actions from patient data, and many prototypes exist. Few survive the move into real clinics.

Following standard review methods, they examined 136 journal articles from 2014 to 2025 across six dimensions, from clinical intent to ethics and workflow fit. Weak adoption was not mainly an algorithm problem. Instead, intended use, evaluation design, and integration paths often failed to line up, so systems proved themselves in ways clinics could not use. The authors reframe the stall as a lifecycle coherence problem and urge design that plans for deployment from the start.
pmc-13273877:
Chen and colleagues argue that a very high ejection fraction in heart failure is a warning sign, not a strength. Their 2026 journal article studies 200 patients with supranormal ejection fraction. That means the heart pumps out 65 percent or more per beat.

Patients split into two phenotypes by cause. Group A, with 88 patients, had valve or blood pressure overload. Group B, with 112 patients, had intrinsic heart muscle disease. That group included hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and cardiac amyloidosis. Both groups had a median ejection fraction of 69 percent. Group B patients were younger, at 56.0 years on average versus 68.8 years in group A. Their hearts were stiffer, with worse event-free survival. The adjusted hazard ratio for that outcome was 3.91 in the fully adjusted model. The authors urge a red-flag workup for such patients.
pmc-13274077:
Christine Chin-jung Hsieh and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on a possible treatment for tuberous sclerosis complex in mice. The inherited disease switches a growth signal called mTOR too high, harming brain wiring and the myelin coating on nerve fibers. Many patients develop learning and behavior problems.

The team gave a drug named J4, which raises levels of the brain chemical adenosine, to mice carrying one faulty copy of the Tsc2 gene. Treated mice showed better thinking, less anxiety-like behavior, and healthier white matter on brain scans. Myelin looked stronger under the microscope, and key myelin proteins rose. Two overactive brain markers also fell toward normal.
pmc-13275677:
Uju Maryanne Onuorah and co-authors write a 2026 perspective on implementation science for maternal and child health in Nigeria. Proven care exists, yet high death rates persist because programmes often fail in delivery. Weak systems, scarce resources, and social barriers all widen that gap.

Case examples show how the frameworks fit Nigerian services. The authors see room in digital health, workforce training, and cross-sector teamwork, and they urge that implementation science enter national strategy.
pmc-13277677:
Desirée Estela Porcari and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to their workplace digital wellbeing questionnaire paper. Table 6 gains its omitted row, and the full appendix questionnaire appears for the first time.

The corrected table reports scores for about twelve hundred respondents across technostress, self-efficacy, positive attitude, and aversion scales. The appendix prints the Italian questionnaire on confidence with workplace technology, item by item. Early items ask how sure workers feel about understanding software terms and describing hardware functions. Response options run from not at all to very much. The correction restores material readers need to reuse the instrument.
pmc-13278477:
Dala N Daraghmeh leads a 2026 survey of pharmacists in Palestine on probiotics and prebiotics. These are products that add helpful gut microbes, or feed them. Pharmacists are easy-to-reach advisers on such goods, but their knowledge had not been measured locally. Four hundred of them filled in a survey on knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice.

Most showed moderate knowledge. About a third reached the high band, and about a tenth scored poorly. Views were positive: most believed the products give health benefits and were willing to recommend them. Advice habits varied, with weak access to proof and low confidence as barriers. Age, training on the topic, and prescription volume showed modest links to knowledge in adjusted analysis.
pmc-13278877:
Wentao Bo, Ying Yi, Biao Zhao, and Hang Dong review an RNA-modifying enzyme called NAT10 in cancer, in a 2026 article. NAT10 is the only known writer of a chemical tag, ac4C, placed on RNA molecules. Tumours lean on it to survive low oxygen, nutrient stress, and treatment attack.

Tagging stabilises key RNA messages and boosts their protein output, reinforcing growth signals. Downstream effects reach sugar metabolism, DNA repair, drug pumping, vessel growth, and immune suppression. Feedback loops with major cancer pathways lock those stress responses into permanent adaptations. Blocking NAT10 is proposed as a way to break resistance to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Open questions cover its partner proteins and context-specific behaviour.
pmc-13279177:

In rare cases it can shift to a harsher form inside neck lymph nodes, the glands that filter fluid. Both patients were women with neck swelling.

Each woman had full thyroid removal with neck node surgery. Tissue tests showed cancer that had changed form in the nodes, in one case to a squamous type and in the other to a high grade type. The team also reviewed seven past cases, with ages from fifty six to seventy nine years. Signs were most often neck lumps. The report warns that changed cancer in nodes needs prompt, full treatment.
pmc-13279277:

The maps show how local cell groups run ovary work.
pmc-13279477:
Anna Sofie Buhl Rasmussen and a large team report a 2026 study of a cancer drug in spinal fluid of young patients. Adult data show imatinib enters spinal fluid poorly, yet child data are sparse.

The study ran at many centres and drew paired blood and spinal fluid samples over time. A precise lab method weighed the drug and its main active break down product in both fluids. Math models tracked levels across fluids and across visits. Young patients held the gene join type or a like type that may also respond. Sound child data can guide dose and choice of drugs that reach the brain better.
pmc-13279877: Soojung Jo and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their study of political ideology and HPV vaccine awareness, based on a national health trends survey. The error sat in the author affiliations, where three units at Purdue University were merged in one line by mistake. The notice splits them back out: the School of Nursing, the Department of Public Health, and the Regenstrief Center for Healthcare Engineering, each in West Lafayette, Indiana. Author order and the study content stand as first published.
pmc-13280577:
Ade Herdian Putra and team write a 2026 letter on mental health care in palliative oncology nursing. The letter asks what training nurses need to deliver such parts responsibly, safely and with fidelity. Clear competency frames guard patients and nurses.
pmc-13280877:
Langson Chilufya and colleagues published a 2026 catalysis study anchoring a copper-bearing polyoxometalate cluster onto graphene oxide to break starch down into glucose. The simulations attribute the performance to cooperation: the cluster and the graphene oxide shuttle protons and keep the starch chains accessible to the active sites. The authors offer the design as a template for hybrid catalysts for sustainable biomass conversion.
pmc-13281077:
Rina Nishiyama and Tetsushi Nonaka studied how singers lock in time with a partner in a 2026 set of tests. Thirteen women sang a carol chorus in unison through earphones. At times the other voice was a real singer. At times it was a fake voice made by singing software. Video of the partner was shown in half the trials and hidden in the rest. With a human partner, singers matched more closely and sang a touch ahead of the beat. That forward lean grew stronger when video was on. With the fake voice, the lean and match were weaker. The authors say small wobbles in a real voice, plus sight of the body, help singers guess what comes next. Fake partners, they add, give fewer of those clues.
pmc-13281777:
Xinhui Li and colleagues presented a new math method for brain scans in a 2026 paper. Brains are read in unlike ways, by shape scans and by activity scans. Tying the two together is hard, since the data are vast and tangled. Older tools often force simple rules and blend all people into one map. The new method hunts for hidden bundles of signals in each scan type. Bundles can be any size and can link across types or stand alone.

The method also lets each person's map vary at fine scale. Tests on fake data with known answers showed it found the true bundles. It was then run on two large real datasets of shape and activity scans. Its bundles tracked with age, sex, and illness traits in later checks. The authors say the tool can expose joint and solo patterns that older tools flatten away.
pmc-13281877:
David G Armstrong and colleagues tested a soaking wound dressing in people with diabetes in a 2026 study. Foot ulcers are a heavy burden in diabetes and drag down daily life. The dressing pairs soft silicone with a super-absorbent core that drinks wound fluid. Twenty-eight adults with shallow, clean ulcers joined at eight Polish centers. Care ran up to six weeks with pressure-relief footwear. The team tracked wound size, life quality, benefit felt, and movement.

More than three in four wounds shrank by at least a fifth. About one in five closed fully with new skin. Life quality scores improved a great deal, most in mood and daily life. Patients' felt benefit rose as well. Movement levels held steady, and footwear use topped ninety-five in one hundred hours. No harm was tied to the dressing in the report. The authors call the early results hopeful.
pmc-13282277:
