The team hunted for the transcription factors among oxygen-response genes that carry prognostic weight, drawing on bulk and single-cell data and mapping how tumor cells talk to their neighbors. From those regulators they built a predictive model that sorts patients into risk groups by expected survival. The authors argue the key factors illuminate how this cancer works under low oxygen. They could serve two uses at once: forecasting which patients face the worst course, and pointing at targets for new treatments. Such treatments would attack the tumor's hypoxia machinery directly.
pmc-13313177:
Junting Yang and co-workers report a large safety study from China, published in 2026, on a vaccine that guards against human papillomavirus. Their work tracks the HPV-16/18 vaccine with the AS04 adjuvant, sold as Cervarix, and looks for links to pregnancy outcomes and diseases of the immune system.

The team used health records from the Yinzhou platform for the years 2010 to 2020, covering people aged 9 to 45 years. Of 1,002,399 people in the records, 891,463 met the study rules, and vaccine uptake was 11.95 per 1000 persons in the target age group. Rates of a few spine and lung diseases were higher in vaccinated women. Yet the authors could not show the vaccine caused them, since other factors and wrong codes may explain the gap.
pmc-13314577:
Natividad Cuende, Ander Izeta, and Beatriz Domínguez-Gil warn in a 2026 commentary that new European rules may recast human organs as trade goods. They welcome a European Commission plan to update the Organ Directive under a Biotech Act, to match fresh science on organ handling.

Their worry is the new wording on organ processing. Its carve-outs might let organs changed by gene or enzyme work be classed as medicinal products or as goods under business law. Treating organs as medicines could shake the gift basis of donation and public trust, they argue. It could also put access to this life-saving care at risk and strain the money base of health systems. The piece urges lawmakers to keep organs as non-commercial goods while rules catch up with science.
pmc-13314777:
Obhuli Chandran M. and colleagues test deep learning rebuilding of head CT scans in a study issued in 2026. Non-contrast head CT is the standard scan for brain ills, but repeat scans stack up radiation and cancer risk over a life.

The team set three arms side by side. One used low-dose scans rebuilt by a deep learning tool called Precise Image. One used low-dose scans rebuilt by the older iterative method. One used standard-dose scans with that same method. Each main group held 96 patients, as counted in the report, all scanned on the same 128-slice Philips machine. Expert eyes and hard numbers graded image quality in each arm. The deep learning route aims to keep scans crisp at a far lower dose, a gain that matters most for patients scanned again and again.
pmc-13315177:
Yanhua Feng and colleagues describe a retrospective study from 2026 of a keyhole operation for twisted neck in young children. The condition comes from a tight neck muscle on one side, and surgery is used when exercises and other care fail. The team used a small camera under the skin layer to cut the tight muscle.

Forty-four children under age 10 were treated between 2019 and 2023 and followed for at least 30 months. Operations took about 35 minutes with very little blood loss. Neck rotation and side bending improved sharply by final follow-up, and scoring covered head tilt and face balance. The method avoids a visible neck scar.
pmc-13315677:
Takashi Hiruma and a large team combined gene testing with heart ultrasound strain measures in 2026 to sharpen risk sorting in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients whose heart pumping later weakens face dangerous rhythms and end-stage failure, yet current tools spot them too late.

The study defined sarcomere-positive status by harmful changes in sarcomere genes and measured left ventricular and left atrial strain by speckle tracking. The main outcome was pumping strength falling below an ejection fraction of 50 percent, in 101 patients at the start of the reported follow-up. Adding atrial strain and gene data aims to flag decline earlier.
pmc-13316277:
Sriram Gubbi and colleagues explore in 2026 whether faults in the MRN DNA repair complex drive some thyroid cancers, a role rarely considered beside the usual MAP kinase drivers. They describe a patient with metastatic oncocytic thyroid cancer that resisted radioactive iodine and kept growing on lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab.

That patient carried a harmful change in NBN, one of three MRN genes. A query across three thyroid cancer data collections found MRN harmful variants in 35 of 762 patients, a share of 4.6 percent in the reported count, and all such patients had anaplastic cancer. Repair defects may matter in that aggressive subtype.
pmc-13317777:
Zhiquan Li and co-authors chart, in a 2026 bibliometric study, research where eczema and inflammatory bowel disease meet, two barrier illnesses that share immune and microbe faults. No map of this joint field existed, so they counted and clustered its literature.

English papers and reviews from 2000 to 2025 across two databases yielded 1,542 publications, with output climbing steeply after 2020. The United States led in volume, citations, and teamwork reach, and Harvard anchored the institution network. Four themes emerged: gut microbes and immunity, shared inflammation paths, modern drugs such as biologics and JAK blockers, and genetics. The field's center of gravity is shifting from describing links to testing treatments and safety.
pmc-13318477:
Hassami Sawadogo and co-authors report a 2026 case series on children's urological emergencies treated at the regional hospital in Dédougou, Burkina Faso, where published data from regional centres are scarce. Records covered one year, from April 2025 to March 2026.

Only 28 children aged up to 15 years were included, almost all boys, with an average age of 8.22 years across the series. Injuries made up the largest share, including scrotal trauma and three cases of goring by cattle, followed by testicular torsion and blockages. Torsion cases arrived after long delays, and two-thirds needed removal of the testicle, yet every child survived. The authors call for community awareness and staff training.
pmc-13318577:
Xin Xue and co-workers report a 2026 rat study of Shao-Ma-Zhi-Jing granules, a preparation used clinically for Tourette syndrome, in animals made to show tic-like behaviour with the chemical IDPN. They probed immune balance, brain inflammation, and gut microbes together.

Measurements used flow cytometry, blotting, and gene tests for immune markers, plus sequencing of gut bacteria. Treatment calmed the repetitive behaviours, rebalanced helper and regulatory T cell signals, and lowered inflammatory proteins TNF-α and IL-6 in blood and brain tissue in the treated animals. Gut microbe mix also changed, and its links to immune measures shifted. The authors connect the benefit to calmer microglia and a named signalling pathway in the striatum.
pmc-13318777:
Sulaiman A. Alsalamah offers a 2026 review of how changes in bacterial genes drive virulence and drug resistance. Such changes arise by chance or from physical, chemical, and bodily triggers. They create the variety that natural selection acts on. Knowing their patterns matters for fighting drug resistance.

The review covers how these changes arise, the biases in them, and repair systems. It traces how genetic changes strengthen disease traits and defeat antibiotics. Where changes land across genomes is not fully random. Repair pathways and existing biases shape where changes land. New tools expand what scientists can see. CRISPR editing and single-cell sequencing now reveal these processes in fine detail. The author calls for continued watch and lab study to predict how bacteria adapt.
pmc-13319077:
Yanhu Ji and colleagues present a 2026 time-series study of air pollution and hospital admissions for ischemic stroke in Zhangzhou, China. Daily admissions, weather, and six pollutants were tracked from 2020 to 2023. A Poisson model estimated short-term effects by sex, age, and season. Burden was calculated against WHO and Chinese air standards.

Four pollutants raised admission risk: fine particles, coarse particles, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. Sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide showed no significant link. Each 10-unit rise in fine particles carried a relative risk of 1.0356 in their model. Effects ran stronger in men, in people under 65, and in the cold season. Overall, 7.0 percent of admissions, some 854 cases, traced to pollution above WHO guideline levels.
pmc-13319377:
Walter Mdekera Iorjiim and co-authors test a plant compound in fruit flies in a 2026 study of aging harm from an HIV drug. The drug can speed up wear on body function and shorten fly life. The compound, drawn from moringa leaves, is known for guarding nerve cells and fighting cell damage.

Flies fed the compound lived longer, climbed better, and bred more than plain fed flies, and their defense enzymes rose while a damage marker fell. When flies got both the drug and the compound, deaths dropped and movement, breeding, and a key nerve enzyme held up better. The dose that killed half the flies in tests is also reported for safety context.
pmc-13319477:
Yujie Xia, Sheng Han and Lanting Lyu investigate, in 2026, how Chinese hospitals judge which new medical tools to adopt. Hospital-based health technology checks should weigh safety, benefit and cost before purchase. Top-tier hospitals in China face over a hundred adoption requests a year, straining budgets and planning.

Seventeen leaders from six major hospitals, including vice presidents, department heads and pharmacy heads, were put questions. Most hospitals lacked a dedicated review team, and decisions rested mainly with medical affairs and pharmacy offices. Safety and how well things work outranked cost as criteria, and few sites used formal tools. Managers and clinicians often put different things first. Most of those asked still wanted such systems urgently. The authors advise project-based teams backed by government data platforms.
pmc-13319677:
Waleed Sultan and co-authors set normal size values for neck discs in a 2026 study drawn from ten years of disc tests. Scans alone cannot reliably tell which neck disc causes pain, and normal disc fill amounts were poorly known. Disc tests that inject fluid and note pain spots offer a direct check, but safe fill amounts need a firm base line.

A total of 135 discs with contained fill were kept for study, while discs with leaks were set aside. Mean fill was near a quarter of a unit and stayed alike across neck levels. Discs that hurt on testing took more fill at four mid neck levels than discs that did not hurt. The values can guide safer dosing.
pmc-13320277:
Siyu Liu and co-authors build shot given micro gels for severe muscle loss in a 2026 study that restores a missing sugar chain to tissue scaffolds. Big muscle wounds scar over and lose strength because the body cannot rebuild bulk on its own. Scaffolds made from cleaned animal tissue carry helpful cues, yet cleaning strips out sugar chains that hold growth signals in place.

Tiny gels made in fine channels were coated with the missing sugar chain and tested on muscle starter cells. Coated gels helped cells cling, grow, drift, and mature, and gene reads showed a growth path switched on as the driver. In rats with a shin muscle wound, high coat gels sped true regrowth, blood flow, and strength at eight weeks.
pmc-13320477:
Camila Baldin and a large team report a 2026 field study of soybean farmers in southern Brazil who work with the weed killer 2,4-D. The group measured signs of liver strain, cell stress, and DNA-linked harm in exposed farmers and compared them with organic farmers who did not use the chemical.

Urine tests found the weed killer in most exposed farmers and in a quarter of the comparison group. Blood tests showed more signs of cell stress and shorter telomeres, the caps at the ends of chromosomes, in exposed farmers. Common liver enzymes did not differ, yet the stress pattern and poor use of protective gear point to a need for close health checks.
pmc-13320677:
Sydney A. Weinandt and a large team report a 2026 outbreak of a contagious cancer in soft-shell clams in Puget Sound, Washington. Most cancers stay inside one animal, but a few spread as living cells from host to host. The team found high levels of this bivalve cancer at two West Coast sites, unlike the low levels long seen on the East Coast.

Gene and water tests showed the outbreak came from infected cells carried from the East Coast, and the clam group affected mixes two clam types. New sensitive ways to measure cancer cells in seawater were built for tracking spread. Watching a hybrid host group respond offers a rare chance to see host change in real time.
pmc-13321377:
Oluwatosin Babasola and co-authors model bird flu spread across species in a 2026 study. Highly pathogenic H5N1 moves among wild birds and poultry, with rare jumps to people. Many past models treated each host group apart, missing cross-species links. The new model joins wild birds, farm birds, and humans in one system, guided by family tree data.

Threshold values for spread were derived for each group, and sensitivity checks flagged the strongest drivers. Simulations showed strong, wide vaccination cut spread and human cases, while less bird to human contact also helped. Combined sanitation and targeted poultry culling gave the largest drop in spread under optimal control tests.
pmc-13321677:
Soohyun Cho and colleagues study, in 2026, newer migraine antibodies in older Korean patients, a group with little real-world data. The drugs block a migraine-related peptide signal and work well in general populations. Nine university hospitals contributed records for 107 patients aged sixty-five and over treated between 2022 and 2025.

Response meant a sizeable drop in monthly headache days at three, six and twelve months. On a strict intention-to-treat basis, where missed visits counted as failure, about two fifths reached the halfway response mark at three and six months. Counting only patients actually seen, rates were higher and rose over time. Headache days fell significantly overall. Side effects were mild, mainly constipation and injection site reactions, with one unrelated death. Female sex predicted better early response.
pmc-13322177:
Martyna Syposz and co-authors show, in 2026, that snowmelt timing governs breeding in an Arctic seabird across its whole range. Little auks are small plankton-eating birds that nest in rock crevices at high latitude colonies. Climate change is shifting seasonal cues, raising fears that chicks will hatch out of step with food peaks.

Multi-year data from four colonies with different climates linked hatching dates closely to local snowmelt, because melting snow opens access to nest crevices. No steady trend in snowmelt timing appeared between 2000 and 2024, so the link reflects year-to-year variation. Later hatching within a year meant slower chick growth and lower survival everywhere, though year-level effects on survival showed in only one colony. Future earlier snowmelt may advance breeding, the authors note.
pmc-13322277:
Margot Evelin Bernedo-Itusaca leads a 2026 study of thinking skills at high altitude in Peru. Life under chronic low oxygen raises red cell counts and blood thickness, which may starve the brain of oxygen. The team studied 200 healthy young adults, 50 each in Lima, Arequipa, Puno, and La Rinconada, cities from near sea level to 5100 metres.

Blood oxygen fell and haemoglobin rose with altitude, peaking at 19.47 grams per decilitre in La Rinconada, where oxygen saturation dropped to 81.64 percent in the study. Moderate to severe thinking impairment appeared only in that extreme altitude group, where just 10 percent tested unaffected. Sleep quality was also weighed beside altitude effects.
pmc-13322677:
David A. Connor and co-authors validate automated home cage monitoring for early drug safety checks in a 2026 rat study. Brain related side effects sink many drug candidates, and the standard observation battery relies on brief, subjective human scoring. An automated Home Cage Analyzer watches rats in their own cages around the clock.

In a crossover design where each rat served as its own control, three known drugs were tested: amphetamine, diazepam, and chlorpromazine. The system caught expected stimulant and sedative effects across light and dark phases. At the top amphetamine dose, floor movement fell while rearing rose sharply, a nuance brief checks could miss. The team backs the tool as a first line screen.
pmc-13322877:
Shuping Liu and colleagues test whether acupuncture links to faster recovery in Guillain-Barre syndrome, in a 2026 prospective study. They enrolled 128 patients admitted between April 2025 and March 2026, all receiving standard care, with 58 also receiving acupuncture and 70 not.

After two weeks, more patients in the acupuncture group met the set gains on the Hughes disability scale and on summed muscle strength scores. Starting features were well balanced between groups, and several statistical checks supported the link. Acupuncture stood as an independent predictor of short-term improvement in their models. The authors frame the result as added benefit on top of immunoglobulin therapy, not a replacement for it.
pmc-13323777:
Qian Guo and colleagues review the lesser-known second step by which iron enters the brain. Their 2026 paper explains that iron crossing the blood-brain barrier must pass two membranes: first the luminal side facing the blood, then the abluminal side facing brain tissue. Step one is well mapped, but step two has stayed murky, even though the brain depends on a steady iron supply and suffers when the balance tips either way.

Work since the discovery of the exporter ferroportin 1 in 2000 has sharpened the picture, the authors argue, pointing to ferroportin 1 as the key player in step two. They weigh two export routes borrowed from gut biology, ferroportin paired with hephaestin and ferroportin paired with ceruloplasmin, as the likely machinery at the brain side of the barrier. The review gathers the current evidence for each route and marks where proof is still thin.
pmc-13325377:
Doretta Cuffaro and colleagues devise a color test for dopamine in banana peel waste in a 2026 study. Banana peel is rich in dopamine, and measuring it cheaply could turn food waste into a valued resource.

In a magnesium and ammonium buffer at pH 9.4, dopamine forms a purple-blue pigment that absorbs strongly at 595 nm. Plate readings gave 5000 micrograms of dopamine equivalent per gram of dry peel, close to the 5700 from a chromatography check. The test stayed linear with a detection limit of 1.8 micrograms per mL. It runs at tiny scale with almost no sample prep. Farms and processors could screen waste streams quickly with it.
pmc-13326077:
Denzil Johnson, Nkiruka Umaru, and Cathal T. Gallagher set out a research agenda for reforming pharmacy discipline in the United States in a 2026 article. Weak or slow discipline of unfit pharmacists puts patients at clear risk.

Boards weigh cases through panels that seat practicing pharmacists with heavy workloads and little regulatory training. That setup leans toward coaching and rehabilitation over firm sanctions, which may underplay public protection. The authors map the United States framework of practice law, entry standards, and board powers. They argue the transatlantic comparison can show where decision design fails and which reforms deserve testing first.
pmc-13327877:
Chiara Catelli and co-authors check lungs from multi-trauma donors for transplant in a 2026 review of 125 recipients. Donor lungs are scarce and donors are growing older, while trauma donors are often young yet may carry bruised lungs. The study compared 36 recipients of trauma-donor lungs with 89 recipients of other donor lungs, treated from 2013 to mid-2024.

Early results, including graft dysfunction and intensive care stays, looked alike, and six-month survival ran higher in the trauma group before adjustment, at 91.7 percent against 75.3 percent in the raw figures. After matching for age and other gaps, survival, lung function, and long-term airway decline matched closely. Trauma lungs, chosen with care, should not be turned away on origin alone.
pmc-13328377:
Navazh Jalaludeen and a large team test outcome predictors in stiff-heart heart failure in a 2026 exploratory study. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction resists simple forecasts. The team measured left atrial stiffness by speckle tracking, walking distance, and blood markers in 43 patients, whose mean age was 77.2 years.

Over a mean follow-up of 24.5 months, five patients died and 21 were hospitalized. Atrial stiffness predicted death independently, with a hazard ratio of 1.81 in their model, alongside the standard natriuretic peptide marker. Six-minute walk distance and growth differentiation factor 15 predicted hospital stays. Combining chamber mechanics, fitness, and blood signals may sort risk better than any single test.
pmc-13329877:
Nequesha Mohamed and team compared osteoarthritis outcomes in sedentary and non-sedentary diabetic patients. Their 2026 study found diabetic patients from 2010 to 2018 in a database. It matched sedentary patients one-to-one with non-sedentary patients for 2,238 pairs, then compared five-year rates of osteoarthritis, joint pain, and joint replacement. Osteoarthritis, a disease of aging, often occurs with diabetes, which can speed joint damage, while inactivity may add to the risk.

Sedentary diabetic patients had more osteoarthritis, 38.9% against 29.6%, and much higher five-year joint pain, 36.0% against 27.3% in the comparison group. Among diabetic patients with osteoarthritis, knee and hip replacement rates at five years did not differ much between groups. The team concludes that lack of activity may worsen osteoarthritis and joint pain within five years without raising replacements. It marks sedentary diabetic patients as a group for early help and exercises to improve joint function and slow progression.
pmc-13330577:
Zian Liu and colleagues link body weight, blood thickness, and brain rhythms at high altitude in a 2026 study. Long-term residents of Lhasa, Tibet, had resting brain waves recorded with a 64-channel system. Body mass index came from measured height and weight, and blood viscosity was estimated from blood indicators with a validated altitude model.

In total, 123 residents entered the study, with main analyses run on 118 people after the small obese group was set aside. Four standard brain microstates were mapped. Higher body mass tied to thicker blood, and thicker blood tied to rarer appearance of one microstate. A mediation model supported that indirect path. Altitude brain adaptation may run partly through blood flow traits.
pmc-13331277:
Ryohei Ono and colleagues report kidney recovery after months without urine in a heart attack case in a 2026 article. A 57-year-old woman had heart attack with both cardiogenic and anaphylactic shock, then lasting no-urine kidney failure needing dialysis. Pump support through the skin kept circulation going for over 4 months.

Urine flow returned after 2 months of no output, letting dialysis stop in the reported course. A durable heart pump was implanted on day 138, and she stayed dialysis-free afterward. Kidney failure often bars durable pump use in the authors' country. Lasting flow support can still rescue kidneys in select cases, they argue.
pmc-13331777:
Maryam Masjedi Esfahani and colleagues present a 2026 case report of POEMS syndrome, a rare disorder driven by an abnormal plasma cell clone that is often mistaken for other nerve diseases. Their patient was a 37-year-old man with growing limb weakness and swollen groin lymph nodes.

Scans showed enlarged liver and spleen, widespread lymph node swelling, and thickened spinal nerve roots. Bone lesions mixed worn and hardened areas, a pattern that pointed away from a simple inflamed nerve condition. Electrical nerve tests confirmed a damaging polyneuropathy, and a node biopsy revealed Castleman disease of mixed plasma cell and hyaline vascular type, sealing the diagnosis. The authors argue that spotting this scan pattern early can speed clone-directed treatment and spare patients long delays.
pmc-13331977:
Leticia Rodríguez-Alcolado and colleagues study 2026 links between gene variants, clinical features, and allergic conditions in eosinophilic esophagitis. That disorder inflames the food pipe, driven mainly by food triggers that spark a local immune response rich in eosinophils, a type of white cell. Some patients progress to scarring that worsens symptoms and weakens treatment.

The sample frames the work around disease forms classed as inflammatory, mixed, or stricturing, and around allergic conditions often seen alongside it, such as asthma, eye and skin inflammation, and rhinitis. The study asks which gene variants track with which clinical patterns and allergy profiles. Readers gain a clearer map of how inherited variation may shape the course of this food pipe disease, a step toward better sorting of patients and more tailored care.
pmc-13332477:
Ranakishor Pelluri and a large team pooled real-world studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026 asking whether gabapentinoid drugs worsen flare-ups in people with COPD or asthma. These sedating pain and seizure drugs could plausibly harm patients whose breathing reserve is already thin, but the evidence was scattered.

Four cohort studies, reported across seven papers, met the review's rules after a search running to January 2026. Taken together, gabapentinoid use showed no significant link to flare-ups, with a hazard ratio of 1.12 and wide uncertainty. Split by drug, though, gabapentin at 1.27 and pregabalin at 1.37 each carried significantly higher risk, while mirogabalin did not, and event rates ran higher in users with an incidence ratio of 1.41. The authors call for long-term studies that can explain the drug-level differences.
pmc-13332777:
Matteo Gelardi wrote a 2026 letter to the editor responding to the BRISA study of severe asthma typing, which combined nasal cell sampling, induced sputum, blood, and circulating markers. Gelardi congratulates the authors and agrees that nasal sampling alone cannot replace sputum, but argues that verdict should sharpen, not shrink, the nose test's role.

Nasal cytology, he notes, directly shows the upper airway lining, revealing not just counts of eosinophils, mast cells, and neutrophils but also cell activation, lining damage, mucus output, and mixed patterns. In the BRISA group, 72 percent had allergic rhinitis and 50 percent had sinus disease with polyps, conditions that give the nose its own inflammatory character. The poor match between nose and sputum results, with a kappa of −0.0862, may reflect real differences between airway compartments rather than a weak test. He places nasal cytology as a complementary window inside precision care.
pmc-13333177:
Lu Huang and Jean-Pierre Djukic review spin crossover in metal complex catalysts in a 2026 survey. Some transition-metal complexes can flip reversibly between low-spin and high-spin states when pushed by heat, light, pressure, or fields. The trick was long studied for materials but only lately for speeding chemical reactions.

Flipping spin reshapes the metal's electron layout and stretches or tightens its bonds, which can redirect or accelerate a reaction. The review first covers the basics of the phenomenon and the main triggers, then walks through recent homogeneous catalysis studies with different transition-metal complexes, tracing how spin switching changes reaction pathways. Because a spin flip can quietly alter behavior, the authors recommend that anyone testing new catalysts built on common 3d metals should routinely check whether spin crossover is at play.
pmc-13333277:
Chuanhao Zhang and colleagues compared radiation alone against radiation plus chemotherapy for early head and neck cancers with small lymph node spread, in a 2026 multicenter cohort study. Adding chemotherapy is standard for advanced disease but brings heavy toxicity, and whether small-volume cases need it was unsettled.

The study gathered 240 patients with stage T1–2, N1–2a squamous cancers from centers in China and Canada, with a median age of 57.8 years and 21 percent HPV-negative, and balanced the groups by treatment weighting. Combined treatment did not significantly improve overall survival, with a hazard ratio of 0.50 and wide uncertainty, but it did improve freedom from progression, with a hazard ratio of 0.42. The pattern matches the NRG-HN002 trial's drop in local failure. The authors advise weighing the control gain against toxicity case by case and call for larger prospective trials.
pmc-13333377:
Tomáš Hanousek and co-authors assemble a three-part 3D forest dataset for Central European trees in a 2026 data paper, built to train and test the algorithms that read forest scans. Ground truth of this depth is what machine learning for tree measurement has lacked.

The core is a library of 3,618 individually cut-out tree point clouds from laser scanning campaigns at 47 Czech sites between 2009 and 2025. It covers 12 species with and without leaves, each tree paired with field traits and model-derived structure numbers. Second come 15,718 virtual airborne scanning scenes of 50 by 50 m, simulated with the HELIOS++ tool from procedurally grown forests at two point densities, with exact metadata for every tree. Third, 273 trees were fully rebuilt in 3D, woody skeletons from structure models plus realistic foliage. The authors host the collection in the Czech National Repository for segmentation, species naming, and virtual forest experiments.
pmc-13333477:
Chunyan Hu evaluates an ultrasound-guided swallowing program in a 2026 study of elderly patients recovering from radioactive therapy for medullary thyroid cancer. Eighty patients aged 65 and over with swallowing difficulty after therapy were compared over eight weeks. Forty received conventional nurse-led rehabilitation. Forty received a phase-based program using ultrasound imaging to watch the throat muscles and hyoid bone move, guiding exercise as recovery progressed. The guided group gained on oral intake, swallowing difficulty scores, and quality-of-life ratings, with suprahyoid muscle thickness up by a quarter and hyoid movement up by a fifth. Aspiration events fell from 15 to 9 percent and pneumonia readmissions from 15 to 5 percent, with no harms. Hu presents the approach as safe and scalable for cancer rehabilitation.
pmc-13335177:
Won Ju Hwang, Jungyeon Lee, and Zhengxiao Sun studied what nursing students learned from a COVID-19 disaster simulation in a 2026 qualitative study. Their aim was to shape a standard disaster nursing module.

Seventy-eight senior nursing students sent in reflective journals through an online platform after the simulation. Two researchers coded the journals on their own and merged their coding, drawing 235 core statements into four themes. The themes were experiencing disaster situations and learning, gaps in disaster nursing competency, understanding community resources and nursing roles, and professional growth with future educational needs. Students plainly showed gaps in crisis leadership and clear communication. The authors call for hands-on training formats that keep students safe and distanced, including lifelike virtual reality.
pmc-13336577:
Xiaolin Jiang and co-authors describe a 2026 chemistry advance for releasing hydrogen from formic acid, a liquid that stores hydrogen well. The hard step is removing a key hydrogen atom without making carbon monoxide. Their catalyst pairs one palladium atom with two silver atoms, held by a phosphorus-based frame and formate bridges.

Working in open air at 60°C, the pair beat single-metal versions and gave clean hydrogen with no carbon monoxide. Computer models and live spectra confirmed the two metals stay close and share the work through the reaction. The catalyst could be reused with good results. Clean, fast hydrogen release matters for portable fuel and green energy systems.
pmc-13336877:
Lina Zhu and co-authors reveal a guardian ring that keeps the cell's ribosome factory intact in a 2026 study. The nucleolus, a membrane-free zone inside the nucleus, builds ribosome parts. A gene-silencing complex called PRC2.1, tied to marked silent chromatin, gathers around it in a ring.

One part, PCL2, forms droplets whose fluidity it controls through a floppy region. PCL2 helps the nucleolar protein NPM1 assemble into five-part units and links nucleolar parts together, keeping ribosome RNA and protein output running. Cells need this support to keep growing. The work shows surrounding silent chromatin actively maintains the nucleolus rather than sitting idle nearby.
pmc-13337777:
Adilai Abula leads a 2026 rabbit study of a mixed scaffold for fixing gum and jaw bone defects. Five material options were compared, led by a blend with antler powder, chitosan, and platelet-rich fibrin. A commercial bone powder served as the positive control, and one group received nothing.

Fifty-four rabbits were split into six groups of nine, each with a one-sided defect. Animals were checked at 4, 8, and 12 weeks by eye, imaging, and tissue study. New bone area, ligament width, and mineral strength were measured. Implanted groups kept healthy gum form with shallow probing depths, setting up comparison of which blend rebuilt bone best.
pmc-13338477:
Graham H. Isaac and colleagues built a semi automated method in 2026 to read faint lines beside cementless hip stems on X rays. Such radiolucent lines can signal stem loosening after total hip replacement, but manual reading varies between observers. The team sought a steadier way to track the lines over time and link them to patient outcomes.

Their algorithm scored front and side X rays from 237 patients at surgery, one year, and ten years, with extra mid term films for 131 patients. Lines were classed as absent, benign, or significant. The method gives surgeons a more consistent tool for spotting loosening early and judging long term hip implant health.
pmc-13338677:
Myungsung Kim and colleagues evaluate Fruto, a campus mental health app, in a 2026 mixed methods study. College students face high distress but seek professional help at low rates. Fruto joins screening, information, counseling access, and campus directions in one place tied to the counseling center.

First, 16 students tried scenario prototypes and gave interviews that shaped revisions. Then students used Fruto for eight weeks while attitude and belief measures were taken before and after. The study checks both whether students accept the tool and whether help-seeking attitudes shift. Linking an app to real campus services is the core test.
pmc-13339777:
Carmen Carazo-Díaz and Luis Prieto-Valiente reflected in 2026 on sample size and confounder control in database research. Large medical databases invite hidden insights through statistics, yet researchers often ask whether a fixed sample size suffices to detect effects of interest. The authors argue no single cutoff separates valid from invalid sizes, since power rises gradually with many parameters.

Even inconclusive results carry lessons about precision and bias, and multivariate analysis must hunt confounders rather than assume them away. The reflection gives database researchers a sober guide: report power honestly, test confounding carefully, and resist turning sample size alone into a verdict on a study.
pmc-13340677:
A large ovarian cyst in a young girl traced back to thyroid failure, in a 2026 case report by Maysam Jehad Yousef Hamarsheh and coauthors. The 7-year-old arrived with sudden lower belly pain, and imaging showed a large, mildly complex cyst on the left ovary plus a smaller one on the right, with blood flow intact.

Blood tests revealed severe primary hypothyroidism with raised prolactin and estradiol and delayed bone age, fitting Van Wyk–Grumbach syndrome. The big cyst was removed keyhole-style and proved benign. Thyroid replacement normalized her hormones, and the remaining cyst shrank away, a reminder to check thyroid function before planning surgery.
pmc-13341077:
Two fusion strategies for two-level lumbar stenosis are compared in a 2026 study by Xiaoyang Sun and Dichao Huang. Records covered 124 patients treated between January 2023 and October 2025, split between bilateral laminectomy with fusion and total laminectomy with fusion.

The bilateral group left hospital sooner, lost less blood, and walked earlier. Their pain, disability, and function scores also improved more at every follow-up, with excellent or good results in 95% versus 91% under the MacNab criteria. Complications included three cases of nerve root irritation and two mild epidural issues. The findings favor the bilateral approach for this two-level disease pattern.
pmc-13341177:

pmc-13347077:

pmc-13349877:

pmc-13349977:

pmc-13350677:

pmc-13351877:

pmc-13351977:

pmc-13352477:

pmc-13354477:

pmc-13356077:

pmc-13357077:
