Their compound, shortened to DIBDO, answers the tumour's abundant glutathione by shedding iodine, which catalytically generates aggressive oxygen and iodine species.

The oxidative burst shuts down upstream caspases, yet directly activates gasdermin D, the pore-forming protein of pyroptosis, so cells burst and spill inflammatory signals. In mouse tumours the treatment drew in killer T cells, teamed with checkpoint blockade to suppress treated and distant tumours alike, and worked as a vaccine that left durable protection. The authors frame caspase-free pyroptosis as a wider doorway into immunogenic cell death therapy.
pmc-13393777:
Walji and co-authors present a 2026 scoping review of how patients and health care workers experience expanded carrier screening, genetic testing that checks would-be parents for many inherited conditions at once. Searching four databases yielded 1,433 records plus 19 further studies, and 45 studies met the entry rules. The team sorted the findings into six groups and mapped them onto a behavior model to guide real-world rollout.

Attitudes toward screening were broadly positive, yet choices raised barriers around cost, timing, too much information, and uncertain results. People valued personal and public-health benefits, while ethical, psychological, and equity concerns, including anxiety and unequal access, recurred across studies. Practitioners' confidence and sense of professional role shaped whether screening was even offered to patients. Primary care voices were notably underrepresented in the literature. The authors recommend behaviorally informed strategies and more personalized, accessible support around testing.
pmc-13393877:
Han and colleagues tackle, in 2026, how China might pay hospitals fairly for inpatient mental health care under per-diem payment, where each hospital day earns a fixed rate. Flat rates ignore how much care different patients consume. The team analyzed 25,510 inpatients admitted to two Chongqing hospitals between 2020 and 2024, modeling cost drivers and building a case-mix classification with a decision tree.

Twelve factors, including sex, age, insurance type, hospital level, comorbidity count, and length of stay, were tied to per-diem costs. The decision tree, using length of stay, hospital level, insurance type, and comorbidity count as splitting variables, sorted patients into 10 case-mix groups with similar daily costs. Lifetime prevalence of mental disorders in China is 16.57 percent by survey data, so payment design affects a large system. The authors offer the grouping as a foundation for mental health payment standards.
pmc-13394277:
Karthik G Pujar and seven colleagues designed new drug candidates against PDE4B, an enzyme that drains the messenger molecule cAMP inside brain and immune cells, as a route into Alzheimer's disease. Raising cAMP could calm brain inflammation and support synaptic signalling, but older PDE4 drugs are dose-limited by side effects, so selectivity for the B form matters. Starting from two known modulators, the team extracted the shared pharmacophore features and built six ring-based derivatives tuned for brain entry and pocket fit without leaning on metal binding.

Two pyridine-based candidates stood out for brain compatibility and stable binding in simulations. The series was checked in nerve-like PC12 cells for protection and in fruit flies as a living Alzheimer's model. The authors present the pyridine heterocycles as credible starting points for PDE4B-targeted Alzheimer's therapy, with optimisation still ahead.
pmc-13396577:
Anu Saavalainen and co-authors surveyed Finnish nurses and pharmacists about the written safety plans their care units keep for medicines, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Finnish law requires every health and social care unit to maintain its own protocol for safe medication management, yet nobody had mapped how those plans are built or what they cover.

An online questionnaire reached registered nurses and pharmacists across care settings. Answers were summarized and compared between professional groups and unit types with standard statistical tests. Gaps or thin spots in local protocols matter because most medication errors trace back to everyday routines rather than rare events, and the survey shows where units need support.
pmc-13396677:
Zhou and co-authors reveal, in 2026, that CD31, a protein known as a blood vessel marker, sits on brain microglia and worsens Alzheimer's disease. Single-cell data and experiments show CD31 sits mainly in microglia rather than neurons or astrocytes, and runs high in the brains of Alzheimer's patients and mouse models. The team reduced CD31 only in microglia of 5xFAD mice, a standard Alzheimer's model.

Knockdown, cutting hippocampal CD31 by about 25 percent in heterozygous animals, quieted the hyperactivated, disease-linked microglia state. With less CD31, recruitment of the phosphatase SHP2 was disrupted, leaving the transcription factor STAT3 more active, which switched on the enzyme MME that degrades amyloid-beta. Amyloid deposition and brain inflammation fell, and the mice's cognitive performance improved in the reported tests. The authors identify the CD31-SHP2-STAT3-MME axis as a drug development target for clearing amyloid from the Alzheimer's brain.
pmc-13397577:
Khalifa Al-Ghanim and colleagues redraw the map of risky zones for filler injections around the nose. Their 2026 analysis pools anatomy studies to replace the old danger-triangle idea with measured detail. Fillers can travel backward into eye arteries, so knowing exactly where vessels run matters for safe practice.

Twenty-eight studies, 21 on cadavers and seven using scans, fed measures of vessel width, depth, path and nearby landmarks. The vessels in focus feed the nose bridge, the nose side and the upper lip. Pooling those numbers yields a graded risk map and safer corridors for the needle, plus a firmer base for teaching drawings and clinic guidance.
pmc-13399077:
Kiavash Semnani and Mostafa Qorbani wrote this 2026 letter replying to comments by Zhang and Han on their earlier study of body-measurement indices and how well each one predicts disease risk. The letter accepts that parts of the original methods section were unclear and sets out to explain the analysis properly. It carries no new data of its own.

The authors clarify three points. First, their comparisons of predictive accuracy used the DeLong method, with a Bonferroni adjustment applied only when judging whether an index beat body mass index. Second, each index was tested in its own adjusted model rather than all indices entering one model, so overlap between indices could not distort the results. Third, when they call an index independent, they mean independent of known risk factors, not of the other indices.
pmc-13399477:
Edward Kumakech and a large team surveyed young women living with HIV in northern Uganda, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The questions covered wanting children and using family planning services built into their HIV clinics. The researchers recruited 423 women attending antiretroviral therapy clinics between November 2022 and April 2023, with a median age of 22. They asked about fertility desires and contraception.

Desire for children ran high: 88.9 percent of the women wanted a child, as the interviews recorded. Married women expressed stronger desires than single women, who reported desires 24 percent lower in the adjusted analysis. The service gap was stark. Among women who wanted children, only 30.1 percent had used the integrated family planning services at their HIV clinic, compared with 48.9 percent among women without fertility desires. The authors argue that clinics must close that gap, addressing marital expectations and contraceptive access together so women can plan pregnancies safely.
pmc-13400477:
Laila M Sherief and a large team check, in 2026, the livers of children who survived acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Egypt. Survival has improved greatly, but treatment and past infections can scar the liver slowly. The team used two needle-free methods together: an ultrasound stiffness scan and a blood-based fibrosis score.

The study covered 159 survivors at least two years past therapy and 99 healthy peers. Stiffness scans found fibrosis in three quarters of survivors, mostly at a moderate level, while the combined approach put advanced scarring at about six percent. Blood scores ran much higher in survivors than controls. Past hepatitis C, largely cleared by antivirals, still left higher scores behind.
pmc-13401577:
Aastha Bharwad, Janet Le, and Nirav Thosani wrote a 2026 review of endoscopic radiofrequency ablation for pancreatic and bile duct diseases. It is a heat treatment delivered through an endoscope for patients who cannot have tumours surgically removed, and the review is sorted by clinical use rather than by device.

Radiofrequency energy creates a focused burn that kills tissue in a controlled zone. One route reaches duct lesions through ERCP guidance with bipolar catheters, treating malignant bile duct narrowings and ampullary tumours. Another route uses ultrasound guidance and a monopolar needle to ablate pancreatic tumours, neuroendocrine tumours, and cystic growths. Needles that combine sampling with ablation form an emerging third category. Across past series, technical success usually tops 90 percent for both main approaches, with mostly low side-effect rates.
pmc-13401877:
Jianting Wen and co-authors reviewed the role of SIRT1, an enzyme that silences genes and runs on NAD, in rheumatic diseases, in a 2026 article. It also maps how traditional Chinese medicine compounds act on it. Rheumatic diseases share chronic inflammation and immune misfiring, and SIRT1 sits at the crossing of several key pathways.

Through routes such as NF-kappaB and AMPK, SIRT1 shapes immune firing, joint lining disease, cartilage breakdown, and body-wide inflammation across rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, lupus, and gout. The authors searched major archives through 2025 for studies of SIRT1 action in these diseases and for Chinese medicine compounds or mixtures with evidence of tuning it. Their account weaves the findings with the traditional medicine angle, looking for points where the two bodies of work reinforce or challenge each other.
pmc-13402577:
Ali Sayghe and colleagues built a cyber-defense system that pairs a digital twin with deep learning to catch attacks on industrial control systems. Their 2026 paper addresses water treatment, distribution, and chemical plants, where attackers now use artificial intelligence to evade standard defenses. A physics-consistent virtual replica can check whether sensor data obey plant physics.

The twin, a state-space model with a Kalman filter, predicts each sensor reading and flags deviations, gating scores from a memory network, a transformer, and an isolation forest. Across 56 attack scenarios in three benchmark datasets, the system reached 97.6 percent precision, 96.2 percent recall, and sub-50-millisecond latency, beating the best single baseline by 3.2 F1 points. The paper offers a fast, interpretable defense, pending tests on live plants.
pmc-13402677:
Ling and co-authors engineer, in 2026, rhenium single atoms anchored by sulfur on two-dimensional chromium boride, to co-produce syngas and lactic acid from biomass-derived feedstocks under light. A sulfur-mediated reconstruction converted unstable rhenium species into uniform Re-S4 sites whose electronic environment optimizes the energy landscape and stabilizes glyceraldehyde, the key intermediate whose carbon-carbon bond cleavage sets the product slate.

The system delivered a total syngas rate of 34.08 millimoles per gram per hour, with the hydrogen-to-carbon-monoxide ratio tunable across an unusually wide span, from 0.1 to 14.4, to suit downstream chemistry like methanol synthesis or Fischer-Tropsch fuels. Lactic acid, a platform chemical, came out at a yield of 90.8 percent alongside the gas in their runs. Apparent quantum yield at 420 nanometers was 3.93 percent in the reported tests. Large-scale outdoor sunlight-tracking trials validated robustness, supporting the design as a scalable, sustainable biorefinery concept.
pmc-13403377:
Xi Li and a broad team mapped a rare belly tumor in 2026, cell by cell. The illness fills the abdomen with mucus and scar-like tissue, comes back often, and has few drug options. They paired single-cell gene reads with other gene tests and tissue checks on matched first and spread tumors.

Tumor cells fell into states tied to mucus output and to more harmful growth. Spread sites held scar-forming helper cells, quiet immune cells, and dense tissue that kept defenders out. Notes from three treated cases hinted that drugs blocking new blood vessels may help. The atlas gives drug makers fresh targets to test.
pmc-13403477:
Diego Armando Leite Carvalho and colleagues tested tiny beads in 2026 that slowly release a red tree sap used in folk healing. The sap comes from an Amazon tree and is prized for calming swelling. Beads were made at three sap strengths and placed under the skin of 50 mice.

Plain beads and a sham group served as checks at three and nine weeks. All bead types sat well with body tissue and caused little irritation. The strongest beads broke down more and irritated least. Body-wide defense against cell stress stayed intact. Bone repair tests in living tissue are the proposed next step.
pmc-13403577:
Katherine A Davies and a large team built a glowing tracker in 2026 to follow Nipah virus inside living mice. Nipah can kill through lung and brain illness, and some survivors relapse years later. Mice lacking a key virus alarm gene were infected by nose or by belly injection.

Nose infection mostly stayed in the breathing tract, while belly infection spread through the body. Glow signals in the brain flickered on and off for up to 42 days after infection. Later tests found virus traces in small brain patches even after mice looked well. The pattern helps explain late relapse.
pmc-13404277:
Ayland C Letsinger and colleagues laid out a method in 2026 for tying brain signals to moments when mice choose to run on a wheel. Freely chosen running resists neat timing, since no handler starts or stops the mouse. Their workflow films posture, sorts behavior by machine learning, and lines signals up with run starts.

As a test case, they tracked a brain chemical in a memory area of male mice. The chemical rose just before runs began and stayed up during running. Sorting behavior by machine cut hand-labeling time by about 90 percent with high exactness. The template can extend to other chemicals and brain spots.
pmc-13404877:
Yunhuan Li and team built aligned core-sheath fiber grafts to stop vessel narrowing in small-diameter vessel regrowth. Their 2026 work takes on graft failure from clotting, inner wall overgrowth, or excess inner wall growth, and poor remodeling. A tube graft of aligned PLCL fibers with drug-filled cores was built to steer cells and calm inflammation.

In lab tests, aligned fibers boosted smooth muscle cell growth toward a contractile type, while the drug tanshinone sulfonate moved macrophages from inflammatory to repair-like states. Co-culture showed mutual steering: repair macrophages matured smooth muscle cells, and contractile muscle cells propped up repair macrophages, together curbing excess growth. Rat implantation confirmed patency, endothelial cover, and organized matrix like native vessels. The graft offers a versatile small-vessel plan, pending larger animal and human testing.
pmc-13407077:
Aya Narita and colleagues, in 2026, screened approved medicines for one that coaxes brain support cells to make more of a waste-clearing protein. Pericytes, cells wrapped around tiny brain vessels, produce lipocalin-type prostaglandin D synthase, a protein that helps scavenge waste, and its failure is tied to dementia, poor sleep, and slow recovery after injury.

From a library of 158 compounds, the antidepressant mirtazapine stood out. It raised production of the protein in mouse and human pericytes in step with dose, and protein tests confirmed more of it was released into the surrounding fluid. Because mirtazapine is already approved for depression, the team suggests repositioning it for brain conditions where waste clearance falters, pending further testing.
pmc-13407477:
Mehmet Sıddık Çadırcı and Martin Singull propose, in 2026, a new way to estimate how far a dataset's distribution sits from a bell curve, and to test multivariate normality. Their starting point is a classic fact: among distributions sharing the same averages and spread structure, the Gaussian bell curve carries maximum entropy, the information-theory measure of unpredictability.

That fact lets the gap to normality be written as an entropy difference, estimated here with nearest-neighbour methods whose consistency the authors review. Their test statistic shrinks to zero for genuinely normal data and stays positive otherwise. Computer simulations across dimensions and sample sizes showed accurate false-alarm control among the alternatives tried and promising power to spot non-normal data. The approach extends earlier entropy-based tests built for other distribution families.
pmc-13407577:
Rayanne Kethleen do Nascimento Silva and co-authors ran, in 2026, a sham-controlled trial of low-level laser therapy for painful neck-shoulder muscle knots. Fifty-two adults with chronic trapezius pain and trigger points received eight sessions over four weeks of either real 808-nanometre laser at 16 joules per point or an identical sham without emission.

Pain, trigger point counts, skin temperatures, and overall perceived effect improved or shifted similarly in both groups, with no significant advantage for real laser treatment on any of those measures. Neck function, however, improved significantly in the laser group. Both groups reported meaningful pain relief, suggesting strong placebo or care effects, while side effects stayed mild, mainly warmth. The authors read the result as a functional benefit without pain superiority at this dose.
pmc-13408277:
Ying-Ju Chao and colleagues tested in 2026 whether flushing the colon with water during colonoscopy finds more precancerous growths in everyday practice. Trials had already favoured the water exchange technique over the usual air inflation, yet busy real-world clinics might see different results. The team studied outpatient procedures at a high-volume Taiwanese centre.

After matching, each group held well over two thousand procedures. Water exchange lifted the adenoma detection rate by fourteen percentage points, with the biggest gain in the right side of the colon, and it also found more large adenomas and serrated lesions. Bowel cleanliness improved as well. The trade-off was time, with procedures lasting several minutes longer, mostly during insertion. Endoscopy units gain practical evidence for weighing detection gains against slower throughput.
pmc-13408577:
Mohamed Ayman and Amr ElNemr combine laboratory work with machine learning in 2026 to design ultra-high-performance concrete without quartz powder. Quartz brings strength yet raises dust-health and sustainability concerns for workers. The experimental half tested mixing order, sand type, admixture chemistry, and curing, arriving at a quartz-free mix that reached very high strength after heat curing.

The computational half assembled 550 strength records with full mix proportions, then tuned sixty-three candidate models with seven optimisation algorithms. A swarm-tuned gradient-boosting model predicted strength most accurately, and an explanation method ranked curing age as the strongest influence on the result. Engineers gain both a validated recipe direction and an interpretable prediction tool that can cut the number of trial batches needed for new mixes.
pmc-13409277:
Priyanka Chandratre and colleagues chart in 2026 the footprint of Behçet's syndrome in England, a multisystem inflammatory disease considered rare in the West. Linked general practice and hospital data covering two decades yielded over fifteen hundred new cases. Incidence settled below one per hundred thousand people per year by 2021, while prevalence roughly doubled across the period as patients accumulated.

A matched comparison with over eleven thousand controls confirmed the classic ulcer triad at dramatic odds. Genital ulcers were strongest, then eye inflammation, then mouth ulcers. Crohn's disease also appeared more often among cases. Genital ulceration was the manifestation whose first recording came closest to the eventual diagnosis, a median of about eight months ahead. The authors suggest rising prevalence reflects recognition and survival as much as new disease, and they offer the timelines to help doctors shorten the diagnostic odyssey.
pmc-13410577:
Rix and colleagues report on a meeting charting Africa's growing role in precision oncology, cancer care tailored to each tumor, held in Windhoek, Namibia, in 2026. The meeting, titled around using functional genomics in care, ran from 23 to 26 September 2025. More than 160 people from 21 countries shared talks, panels, and planned discussions, and the authors distill the meeting into priorities for cancer genomics across the continent.

Delegates weighed renewed investment in genomic innovation, fairer data practices, and stronger cancer registries as foundations for precision care in Africa. Sessions mapped where sequencing capacity, trained staff, and sample networks already exist, and where they lag behind need. The report argues African populations must be represented in the genomic datasets guiding drug development, or precision oncology will underserve them. Rix presents the shared consensus as a practical agenda for funders, registries, and research centers.
pmc-13411977:
Suli Dai and colleagues traced in 2026 how a circular RNA, circSPARC, drives esophageal squamous cell cancer through a growth signal. The Wnt pathway stays switched on in this cancer, yet how circular RNAs keep it running was unclear, so the team combined lab and animal tests with RNA binding studies.

CircSPARC grips a processing protein, HNRNPC, to block a protective long form of EPN2. That form normally helps clear a Wnt receptor from the cell surface, leaving the growth signal stuck on. Restoring that long form slowed the cancer, pointing drug hunters toward breaking the circSPARC grip as a new treatment angle.
pmc-13413077:
Elizabeth García-León and colleagues characterize in 2026 the fungus behind the charcoal rot that strikes sesame crops in Mexico's northern Sinaloa state. The disease is sesame's most damaging worldwide, yet Mexican work on the pairing was sparse. Six isolates from diseased roots were identified by shape, a species-specific DNA test, and family trees built from two gene regions, then checked for their ability to cause disease.

All six isolates proved to be Macrophomina phaseolina, and every one was pathogenic in their tests. Friendly Trichoderma fungi slowed the pathogen's growth by up to 63 percent in dish contests. Three farm fungicides also restrained it, each with its own potency range across isolates. The authors say both the biocontrol fungi and the chemicals merit field-level research for sesame growers.
pmc-13413577:
Aobo Wang and co-authors combine thermal physics with a neural network in 2026 to spot hidden faults inside the tiny coils of safety relays. Ageing enamel, peeling insulation, and shorted turns all heat differently, yet the coils are sealed and too small to inspect directly. Their method couples a quick thermal circuit model with a two-dimensional heat simulation for calibration, generates temperature traces for each fault type, and feeds line profiles into a one-dimensional convolutional network.

The hybrid thermal model matched full finite-element results within about 1.7 percent error in the reported simulations. The trained network classified 160 test cases with 98.13 percent accuracy across normal, aged, delaminated, and short-circuited states. Physical rebuilds and feature visualizations backed the separation, pointing toward non-destructive relay screening.
pmc-13413677:
Long Gao and colleagues follow in 2026 a set of phosphorus-cycling bacteria through the yearly green tides that choke the southern Yellow Sea. The bacteria carry phoD, a gene for an enzyme that frees usable phosphorus from organic matter, and they react quickly when conditions shift. Sequencing tracked their communities before, during, and after blooms of the seaweed Ulva prolifera.

Community structure changed distinctly by stage, with bloom and post-bloom assemblages resembling each other more than the pre-bloom one. Common types proved the more sensitive, widening or narrowing their niches as the tide rose and fell, while rare types held diversity steadier. Chance processes dominated how communities assembled overall, though the tide pushed rare members toward stronger selection. Links among microbes tightened during the bloom, suggesting a more stable network.
pmc-13413777:
Ruimin Chi and co-authors test in 2026 whether exercise protects joints in obese rats partly by reshaping gut microbes and a fatty acid they make. Obesity-linked osteoarthritis grinds cartilage down, and the gut-joint axis is a suspected pathway. Rats ate a high-fat, high-sugar diet with or without exercise while the team imaged cartilage and bone, sequenced gut bacteria from droppings, and measured short-chain fatty acids in blood.

Exercised rats kept healthier cartilage and lost less bone beneath it than sedentary diet-matched controls. Exercise trimmed several bacterial families and boosted Akkermansia, a genus tied to gut lining health in their sequencing. It also prevented the fall in acetic acid seen in sedentary rats, and higher acetic acid tracked milder joint damage. The authors propose the microbe and acid shifts as part of exercise's protection.
pmc-13413877:
Cunyu Lan and co-authors pool in 2026 the randomized evidence on high-intensity interval training for people who barely move. Short, hard intervals promise time-efficient gains, yet results in truly inactive adults have been inconsistent. Their meta-analysis searched six sources through July 2026 and combined 24 trials with 877 participants, comparing intervals against doing nothing and against steady moderate training, with bias and certainty formally graded.

Against no exercise, intervals trimmed weight by 1.60 kilograms and lowered both blood pressure numbers and cholesterol measures in the pooled trials. Fitness, measured as maximal oxygen uptake, rose by 7.72 units against controls and beat steady training by 3.72 units on that measure alone. Most other outcomes matched steady training. Certainty stayed low or very low, and several results hinged on single studies.
pmc-13414177:
Xinxin Zhang and co-authors compare in 2026 two strains of a virus sprayed on tea pests, asking why one kills so much better. The baculovirus EcobNPV infects Ectropis caterpillars; strain QF4 killed 97.9 percent of larvae by day sixteen against 33.8 percent for the original QV strain in leaf-dipping tests. Gene activity in infected E. grisescens was tracked at seven time points across the first two days.

QF4 ran its whole program about six hours ahead of schedule compared with QV in the sequencing data. Modules for escaping the gut, copying DNA, and assembling new viruses switched on earlier and in tighter coordination. The authors argue virulence comes from this system-wide acceleration rather than any single gene, compressing the infection cycle and spreading the virus faster through the host.
pmc-13415177:
Jieun Jeon and colleagues test a kinase blocking compound, KMU-11342, against colorectal cancer in 2026 laboratory and tissue models. The compound had earlier shown anti-inflammatory effects. Tests covered flat cell cultures, three-dimensional spheroids, and organoids grown from patient tumors.

Cell density fell by about 59 percent at a half micromolar dose and about 83 percent at one micromolar. Treated cells stalled before division and died by apoptosis, the controlled cell death route. Organoids lost about 39 percent viability at one micromolar and about 77 percent at two. Computer docking pointed to two kinases, GSK3 beta and CDK1, as likely targets.
pmc-13415277:
Yeneneh Bekele-Reba leads a 2026 field study asking whether a rye chromosome arm can steady German winter wheat under climate stress. The arm, called 1RS, has long been bred into wheat from rye. Trials ran across fourteen contrasting environments, combining molecular diversity checks, field scoring, and genomic modeling.

Rain in 2021 matched the long term average, and yields varied widely by variety. Severe drought in 2022 cut average yield by about 14 percent. Lines carrying 1RS from the Insave rye source held yield well under drought, especially when two different 1RS segments were stacked. Benefits depended strongly on the wheat background receiving the segment.
pmc-13416877:
Umberto Cornelli and Claudio Casella offer a 2026 perspective on microplastics and nanoplastics as possible disruptors of metabolism. Tiny plastic particles have been found in human blood, placenta, lung tissue, and stool, showing wide spread through the body. The authors link these particles, on early evidence, to pathways tied to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

Animal work suggests particles may loosen the gut barrier, shift gut microbes, and alter bile acids. Particles reaching the liver could add low grade inflammation there. A concept the authors call drainage, lowering particle uptake from the gut, is proposed only as a theory. Safety and benefit remain unproven, they stress.
pmc-13417477:
Altaqi and Mashyakhy reported in 2026 two dental surgery cases that saved natural bone while treating root-tip infection. Two women, aged 38 and 27, had painful infected lower first molars that had already had root treatment. The team planned surgery with 3D scans and printed a guide that fixed cut size and root-tip removal level in advance. Cutting used a piezoelectric device, which vibrates to cut hard tissue while sparing soft tissue.

The surgeons lifted out a window of bone in one piece, treated the root tip, then put the same bone back as a graft. The bone window was held with plugs of platelet-rich fibrin, a material made from the patient's own blood. Both patients healed routinely and stayed free of symptoms at checks twelve to eighteen months later.
pmc-13418077:
Emma De Ravin and co-authors profile NRAS gene variants in thyroid nodules sent for molecular testing, in a 2026 database study. NRAS changes are the commonest mutations in nodules with uncertain needle biopsy results. Records covered 87,817 suspicious or malignant graded nodules tested with the Afirma system, of which about 13 percent carried NRAS variants.

Two hotspot variants made up 99 percent of NRAS cases. Extra mutations appeared in about 4 percent, most often in a gene called EIF1AX, and a promoter variant tied to aggressive disease paired with NRAS at over twice the solo rate. Pathway activity split NRAS nodules into two clusters needing outcome follow up.
pmc-13418377:
Wang and colleagues test whether stem cells from umbilical cord can protect the brain from the confusion and memory loss that follow surgery. Such perioperative brain disorders strike patients hardest and lack treatments. Their 2026 study models the problem in aged mice with a shin bone fracture. The cells are given by vein. Behavior tests, tissue checks, and protein profiling then trace how the benefit works.

Treated mice learned and remembered better, lost fewer hippocampal neurons to cell death, carried less brain inflammation, and kept more of the spines where neurons connect. The cells released a growth factor, beta nerve growth factor, which switched on proteins and quieted an inflammatory pathway tied to nerve decay. Blocking that factor in the cells, or forcing the decay protein up in the brain, erased the benefit. The pathway, the authors argue, points to cell free drugs that mimic the stem cells' signal.
pmc-13418477:
Qingjing Shao and colleagues survey sexually inexperienced college students in Guangdong about genital warts and HPV vaccination, in a 2026 report of a 2017 survey. Two HPV types cause most cases of the wart condition. Over two thousand students with no sexual experience answered an online questionnaire on knowledge and vaccine acceptance.

Knowledge was low: about a quarter knew the wart condition and under a fifth knew HPV. Only about 3 percent were vaccinated, yet over half accepted vaccination in principle. Believing the vaccine safe and effective, and knowing the condition, each raised acceptance. Education before sexual debut is the authors' main message.
pmc-13418677:
Valerie Cotter and colleagues describe a nurse-led phone-care program in 2026 for people with dementia and their care partners after emergency department visits. Most such visits end with discharge home, yet many could be prevented if families had timely help, and emergency rooms can distress patients with dementia without fixing the root problem.

The program, built into the ED-LEAD trial across 79 emergency departments, blends two earlier tested phone-support models into regular nurse calls after discharge. Health systems gain a blueprint for easing emergency crowding while giving families steady, person-centered backup at home.
pmc-13418777:
Haoyang Yuan and colleagues traced a mitochondrial control chain in lung adenocarcinoma in 2026, centering on an enzyme, TAMM41, that builds a key membrane fat. TAMM41 ran high in tumors and tracked with poor outlook, yet its role in cancer growth was undefined.

Experiments showed TAMM41 sustains energy production and curbs cell death, while a desuccinylase, SIRT5, marks it for destruction by the ligase UBR5, and removing TAMM41 shrank mouse tumors. The paper nominates TAMM41 as a drug target where mitochondrial metabolism drives lung cancer for teams seeking metabolic targets in current practice.
pmc-13420277:
Shixin Nie and colleagues describe a surgical technique for the awkward case where a donor meniscus graft turns out too large for the knee receiving it. An oversized graft can fold, push out of the joint, and raise contact stress, all of which hurt results. Sizing by scans still carries error, with width measures off by up to 2.9 millimeters in the reports cited and length by up to 3.8 in the same accounts.

The authors favor fixing the graft with bone plugs and add a pull-in tunnel at the front horn to seat an oversized graft snugly. Step-by-step description lets other surgeons copy the fix mid-operation when sizing surprises them. Transplant work lives or dies on fit, so a rescue method for the common oversize case has practical worth beyond one center.
pmc-13420377:
Haoyuan Wu and colleagues test a proposed reason why species crowd near the equator and thin toward the poles, one of ecology's oldest patterns. Their idea is that evolution itself is biased by scale: types adapt toward places where fitness gains run higher, slowly piling diversity where conditions reward most. They tested the bias in the lab with Escherichia coli as the model system.

Experimental lines of the bacterium showed the predicted drift toward higher-fitness ground. A matching fitness slope across latitudes could then feed the diversity gradient seen in nature. The authors present the findings as a first experimental foothold for the idea, not a settled answer. Lab proof in a microbe gives field ecologists a mechanism they can hunt for in larger creatures.
pmc-13420677:
Anjali Wagle and colleagues ask in 2026 whether inherited heart-muscle disease and sarcoidosis can coexist and confuse diagnosis. The two conditions share imaging features, and three patients with gene-linked cardiomyopathies were later found to have sarcoidosis outside the heart.

Despite scans raising concern for heart sarcoidosis, only one patient showed active heart inflammation needing immune suppression, while the others were treated as primary genetic disease. The paper warns that heart imaging alone cannot settle the question, pushing clinicians toward careful, patient-by-patient judgment for cardiologists weighing immunosuppression in genetic heart disease.
pmc-13421277:
Pierpaolo Alongi and colleagues tested total-body PET/CT in 2026 for prostate cancer detection using a fluorine-18 piflufolastat tracer on a 194-centimeter scanner. The team reviewed 103 patients scanned for initial staging or suspected recurrence, judging detection rates and how results tracked prostate-specific antigen levels.

Scans were positive in 88.3 percent overall and in all staging cases, with primary lesions, lymph nodes, and bone the top sites, while higher PSA strongly predicted positive scans in recurrence. Urologists gain a high-yield staging tool whose value rises steeply with PSA in suspected recurrence.
pmc-13421477:
Hagiwara and colleagues present a 2026 paper on making computer-aided diagnosis tools safer when doctors work beside artificial intelligence. The authors use a systems method, STPA, which traces how control actions in a work process can turn unsafe, and add checks on whether system explanations hold up.

The analysis flagged hazards such as automation bias, where doctors accept a system answer too readily, and misread explanations that bend judgment without being noticed. From each unsafe action the team derived design guidelines that builders can trace back to a named hazard. The guidelines push for clear transparency, explanations that stay coherent, and trust that matches the tool's real skill. The result is a practical bridge between safety analysis and product design for diagnosis tools, where a wrong call can cause serious harm to patients.
pmc-13422077:
Huan Hu and four colleagues present, in a 2026 study, the first ten-year mortality picture for the workers who responded to the 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident. Roughly twenty thousand emergency workers took part, and their long-term health has been a public concern ever since.

The analysis followed 19,358 men from 2012 to 2021, linking records to national death statistics. Overall mortality ran below the general male population's, with 708 deaths recorded. Cancer measures sat below parity early, then crept above it in the final period, a trend the authors flag as marginal and in need of continued watching. Suicide showed no elevation. Standardised ratios adjusted for age and calendar year throughout.
pmc-13422877:
Wenbo Song leads a large team estimating, in a 2026 study, how many rural Indian adults live with two or more chronic conditions at once. The team also asks which habits travel with that burden. Earlier Indian work leaned on cities and the elderly, missing most of the people at risk.

Data came from the third follow-up of a long-running Andhra Pradesh family cohort, with 5,332 adults averaging about thirty-five years old. Fourteen percent had multimorbidity, and the share climbed steeply with age. Tobacco use was among the behaviours statistically tied to it, alongside daily drinking, inactivity and poor sleep in their adjusted models. Pattern analysis grouped the conditions into recurring clusters, each with its own behaviour profile. The authors stress prevention aimed at younger rural adults.
pmc-13423077:
Happy Asiimwe and seven colleagues lay out a protocol for a systematic review of what African medical students know, believe, and do about antimicrobial resistance, the fading power of drugs against infections. Student habits matter, the team argues, because today's trainees become tomorrow's prescribers, and country-level surveys have never been pulled together for the continent.

The reviewers will search PubMed and Scopus, CINAHL and Google Scholar, plus African Journals Online for studies from 2015 to 2025, taking both quantitative and qualitative work. Findings will be combined in narrative form, with a statistical pooling if the data allow. Bias will be checked with a standard appraisal checklist. No ethics approval is needed, since the review reuses published studies.
pmc-13423177:
Yuxi Wang and four colleagues propose a Social Prism Model to explain why people with social anxiety read the same social moment so differently from others. Working inside a Bayesian frame, where the brain weighs prior expectations against fresh evidence, they ran eight experiments. The experiments tested how people judge the emotional tone of social cues, and they involved 541 participants.

Anxious participants processed incoming evidence normally. What differed was expectation: they carried two strong prior biases at once. One was a negative lean tied to intolerance of uncertainty and fear of judgement. The other was an over-positive lean tied to negative social learning. Computer simulations showed how shifting those prior settings alone reproduces biased judgements, placing expectation, not perception, at the heart of anxious interpretation.
pmc-13423477:
Takashi Tamura and eight colleagues evaluate a gentle tablet treatment for rectovaginal fistula, an abnormal opening between rectum and vagina that can follow low rectal surgery. No standard, low-burden cure exists. Care often means a stoma plus repeated invasive procedures. The team therefore tried vaginal estriol tablets, a local hormone therapy, in five patients treated between 2008 and 2024.

Every patient already had a diverting stoma. All five fistulas closed, taking a median of 125 days. Camera review showed new blood vessel growth in the vaginal lining of three patients. All three healed from the vaginal side. One fistula recurred and closed again after further treatment. No side effects appeared.
pmc-13424777:
Hu and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a man with burning in the urethra, the urine tube, that lasted about six years with no infection ever found. The 35-year-old had first had a urinary infection, but repeated tests later showed no active infection and no major prostate inflammation. Guesswork treatments brought no lasting relief.

Scans showed only mild, nonspecific prostate changes. The team then used an integrative plan built around a modified traditional herbal formula, Gancao Xiexin decoction, aimed at symptoms rather than germs. His pain score fell from eight of ten to four within one week, and reached zero after two months, while anxiety, sleep, and bowel symptoms also eased. The report argues care should shift from repeated antibiotics toward symptom-focused management.
pmc-13425577:
Mariam Atobiloye and colleagues examined a brachytherapy boost for stage II endometrioid endometrial cancer in a 2026 database study. Standard adjuvant care after hysterectomy often uses whole pelvis radiation, while vaginal cuff brachytherapy has only conditional support as an added boost. The authors queried the 2023 National Cancer Database for fully staged T2N0M0 cases treated after hysterectomy.

They tested whether adding the cuff boost to pelvic radiation tracked with better overall survival and described national patterns of care. Gynecologic oncologists gain outcome evidence for a treatment choice that guidelines currently leave uncertain. Staff can use these facts when they talk with women about what added care may give and what it may cost in time and side effects.
pmc-13425777:
Priyanka Krishnamoorthy and coauthors surveyed media influence on adolescent food habits in Salem district, Tamil Nadu, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Social media food advertising now reaches teenagers more strongly than older media, while food labels affect choices unevenly depending on understanding. Questionnaires covered 385 adolescents aged 10 to 19 chosen by stratified random sampling.

Responses linked demographics, media exposure, eating habits, and label reading, with chi-square tests probing ties to junk food intake. Public health readers gain local evidence on how advertising exposure and label habits relate to what teenagers actually eat.
pmc-13425877:
Tahir Burak Sarıtaş and Çağla Keskin Sarıtaş survey how Turkish bone and joint surgeons guard against infection in first-time joint replacement. Infection around an artificial joint stays a major setback, and practice may drift from guidance.

In an anonymous web survey from December 2025 to January 2026, 278 specialists described their drug and prevention routines. Cefazolin was the first-choice preventive drug for all of them, while clindamycin led at 73.4 percent when a penicillin-type allergy was present. Hospitals get a benchmark for where routines agree and where they vary.
pmc-13427577:
Yuedian Ye and co-authors report, in 2026, two ways one protein helps kidney cancer grow and spread into veins. The protein, called suprabasin or SBSN, was higher in tumor tissue than in healthy kidney. High levels also marked tumors that had grown a clot-like extension into a vein, a pattern tied to worse outlook. Lab tests tied SBSN to faster cell growth and movement.

Inside cancer cells, SBSN switched on a signal chain ending in CD44, a surface protein linked to spread. It also raised a second protein in nearby vessel cells, which kept those cells alive and helped them form tubes. Blocking either route could starve tumors of blood while slowing the cells themselves. The authors propose SBSN as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13427777:
Charlotte Levé and colleagues compare two sedation drugs for awake brain surgery, where patients must stay rousable yet safe. Continuous sedation speeds waking but risks shallow breathing and low oxygen, so their centre swapped propofol for dexmedetomidine in April 2019.

Adults having awake craniotomy from April 2017 to July 2021 were studied before and after the switch, with 103 patients in total. The earlier group got propofol with remifentanil, while the later group got dexmedetomidine plus low-dose propofol. Low oxygen, high carbon dioxide, circulation stability, and adverse events were the measures that mattered.
pmc-13428077:
Zeng and colleagues compared in 2026 the phenolic compounds in seeds of five litchi cultivars and tested how well the seed extracts calm inflammation and pain. Litchi seeds are a leftover of fruit eating, rich in phenolics, and folk practice has long used them for sore, painful conditions. Whether the cultivar changes the chemistry and the effect was unknown.

Twenty compounds were identified in the purified extracts, with three standing out as the main actives. The Heiye cultivar carried the richest phenolic load. Extracts from all five curbed inflammatory signals from immune cells in dishes, and strength tracked the level of the three main compounds. In mice, the extracts also reduced ear swelling and pain responses. The authors propose litchi seed waste as a source of anti-inflammatory ingredients.
pmc-13429277:
Shomaru Ito and co-authors examine what physical traits relate to dynamic balance, meaning how well a person stays steady while moving, in healthy university students. Their 2026 study uses the modified star excursion balance test, in which students stand on one leg and reach in three directions.

Thirty-five students took part in this cross-sectional study, and the team measured ankle motion, knee and ankle strength, back strength, and muscle mass. Balance scores correlated with several traits, including ankle plantarflexion strength and lower-leg fat-free mass, across all reach directions. When the traits were tested together in regression models, no single factor stood out as an independent predictor. The authors conclude that balance reflects several physical functions combined rather than one dominant trait.
pmc-13429577:
Talal Almeelbi and Fawaz Alghamdi build a single score for beach water quality along the Red Sea coast at Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Coastal swimming water shapes public health, above all near cities, yet scattered measures make beaches hard to compare.

Samples from three sites were judged on acidity, dissolved oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, E. coli, and enterococci, weighted by importance for swimmer safety. Ratings followed World Health Organization and Saudi ambient standards, then merged into one index. Obhur Al-Shamaliya scored generally good, giving managers a plain tool for warning or clearing a beach.
pmc-13430277:
Samantha R Allen and colleagues report further development and validation of the Compassionate Healthcare In Action questionnaire, called CHIA, in this 2026 paper. The tool measures how patients experience compassionate care, focusing on behaviours that can be observed rather than general impressions.

The team checked face validity, meaning whether items look right to users, through cognitive interviews with 21 UK service users. Survey data from 311 people then guided the removal of seven items, leaving a 14-item scale with a single underlying factor. A second survey of 301 people confirmed that structure and showed strong internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and validity. The authors present CHIA as a brief measure that health services can use across different care settings.
pmc-13430477:
Hsiao-Chuan Liu and co-authors wrote a 2026 editorial arguing that the bond between patients and the treatment team forms part of care in daily radiotherapy. An earlier piece from the group treated family waiting time outside the room as care work rather than empty time. The new piece turns that same lens toward brief talks before and after each session.

Inside the room, days run on tight tasks such as setup, image checks, and machine time. The authors note that patients still bring fear, hope, family life, and news from home through the door with them. Small habits carry weight here: a greeting, eye contact, and time for a slow reply. One older patient spoke with great effort, yet staff waited for his words at his own pace each day.
pmc-13431677:
Kachikis and colleagues compare how long vaccine antibodies last in pregnant patients and older adults. Their 2026 prospective study follows people who received a first respiratory syncytial virus vaccine in 2023 or 2024, a shot recommended in pregnancy to protect newborns. Samples came from 36 vaccinated pregnant participants and 16 vaccinated older adults, collected for up to fifteen months.

Antibody levels twelve to fifteen months after vaccination were similar in the two groups, suggesting maternal vaccine antibodies hold up for at least a year. Binding antibody levels and neutralising antibody levels, the kind that block the virus, tracked each other closely. The durability question matters because United States guidance does not currently recommend revaccination in later pregnancies, relying instead on antibody treatment for infants. The authors present the one-year persistence as evidence informing that policy.
pmc-13432177:
Nicholas Brian Shannon and Bruce Ashford reviewed in 2026 how immune drugs now weave into surgery for head and neck cancer that can still be cut out. Standard care has hit a survival wall, with more than half of patients seeing the cancer return. Giving immune drugs before surgery uses the still-intact immune system as a built-in vaccine site.

Fresh large trial reads show that immune drugs around surgery stretch the time free of bad events. Surgeons must learn new traps, such as telling fake growth on scans from true growth in spots where a wrong call risks grave harm. Drug pairs raise full-clear rates at the cost of more side harm. Single immune drugs alone spare tissue planes and rarely stall surgery. Blood-based tumor traces join older markers as tools to pick patients and track response.
pmc-13434377:
Cho explains propensity score methods in a 2026 clinician-oriented review aimed at nose and sinus research, where randomized trials are often impractical. In real-world studies, sicker patients get different treatments, which biases comparisons. A propensity score estimates each patient's chance of receiving a treatment from their traits, letting researchers build fairer comparisons without randomization.

The review covers matching patients with similar scores, weighting methods that rebalance groups, and doubly robust approaches that combine scoring with outcome models. It explains diagnostics for checking balance, how the choice of method changes which patients the conclusion applies to, and design steps that should be fixed before outcomes are seen. Cho stresses that these tools fix only measured differences, not hidden ones, and gives practical guidance tailored to surgical and long-term rhinology questions.
pmc-13434477:
Buri Vinodhkumar and colleagues assess heat-wave characteristics and mechanisms over Qatar from 2003 to 2024, where rising temperatures and more frequent extremes threaten a hot, arid state. Heat waves were defined as daily maximum temperatures above the 95th percentile for at least three consecutive days.

Thirty-two events were detected at Al Udeid station, mostly from May to September, rising gradually by 0.1 events per year. Events formed under cloud-free skies with weak surface-pressure anomalies. Heat built into a deep dome linking the ground to air at 900 hectopascals, held up by sinking air above, a mid-air inversion layer, and weak surface updrafts. Forecasters get a mechanistic portrait linking large-scale subsidence and land feedback to Qatar's fiercest heat.
pmc-13434677:
Jung and Kim dissect how a plant virus travels through a plant without its usual travel gear in this 2026 study. Tobacco mosaic virus was thought to need its coat protein to spread systemically, from one leaf to distant ones through the phloem, the plant's food-conducting tissue. The team split systemic movement into three steps: loading, riding the vasculature, and exiting. They tested a coat-protein-free virus at each step.

The mutant virus still entered and rode the vessels. Long-distance transport itself survived. Instead, two bottlenecks appeared. It underused the internal phloem pathway that carries viruses upward efficiently. And it often failed to exit into new leaf tissue, lingering as vein-associated traces. Boosting the virus's defense against plant silencing raised its accumulation. It did not increase its escape. Adding cucumber mosaic virus as a helper did. That let it break out and infect the leaf blade.
pmc-13434777:
Yuan Wang and coauthors track how digital farming and new farm productivity grew together across China from 2012 to 2023 in 2026. Panel data cover all 31 provinces. Scores for both trends rose year by year, yet both stayed fairly low overall.

Joint balance moved from poor fit to bare fit over the span. The east leads, the center wrestles with hard gaps, and the west closes ground. Web access and leisure farming count among the top blocks. Wealth, farm strength, and state support lift the joint score. Factory growth drags it down. Province plans should differ by region.
pmc-13436377:
Marisa Haenni and coauthors track resistant E coli in French veal calves from birth farm to sorting center in 2026. Calves fed waste milk from treated cows carried far more resistant germs. Selective plates plus genome reads trace the strains and their genes.

Farms feeding waste milk showed 30.3 percent carrier calves versus 13.1 percent where milk was dumped. Overall 12.5 percent carried resistant germs at origin, and 6.2 percent more picked them up in transit. Of 176 strains read, most carried a CTX-M gene, while the rest bore chromosome changes. Two clones spread across farms. Chain wide hygiene is the fix.
pmc-13436677:
Hannah E Miller and coauthors ask whether manikin skin tone sways student thinking in a mock cardiac arrest in 2026. Fourth year students at one school ran the same arrest case on light or dark skinned manikins in rotation. After the first shock each student wrote a free text list of possible causes.

Of 196 usable forms, one hundred came from dark skinned manikin runs. Substance use as the lead cause appeared once in that group and never in the light group. Full list placement of substance use is the main outcome scored. Even tiny gaps in first thoughts can steer early care. Simulation equity checks may belong in course quality reviews.
pmc-13437177:
Maho Suyama and colleagues report a severe allergic reaction that struck during general anesthesia without any of the usual skin signs. Their 2026 case involves a 29-year-old man set for jaw fracture repair. About fifteen minutes after anesthesia began, his oxygen level eased downward while his blood pressure dropped and his heart raced, yet his skin showed nothing.

A shot of epinephrine turned his condition around quickly. Blood tests later found raised levels of tryptase and histamine, two markers that support the diagnosis of anaphylaxis. The authors stress how hard such a reaction is to spot under anesthesia, since low oxygen and falling pressure have many other causes. Ruling out those causes fast while giving epinephrine early is the core of good care, they argue. Follow-up allergy testing, patient teaching, and a ready response plan at each unit help guard against a repeat event.
pmc-13437377:
Kent Hecker and colleagues checked whether the many scores used to pick veterinary students really measure different things. Admissions teams at Calgary's veterinary faculty weigh grades and test scores, plus interviews, situational judgment tests, essays, and file reviews meant to capture personal strengths. Their 2026 study pulled records for 338 applicants from the 2022 to 2024 cycles and examined how the scores hang together.

Scores within each family clustered as expected, with small to moderate links across families. A factor analysis sorted the measures into three clean groups: academic ability, social-emotional skill, and context drawn from the applicant's file. The mini-interview fed both the social and the context groups, marking it as a two-sided tool. The authors read the results as support for treating entry scores as one combined system rather than rival measures. They propose follow-up work on whether the three strands predict success through training and into practice.
pmc-13437477:
Wongsakorn Chaochankit, Somkiat Sunpaweravong, and Chutida Sungworawongpana tested two common risk scores against death after surgery to remove the food pipe for cancer. Their 2026 study reviewed 123 patients treated with curative intent between 2012 and 2024. Twelve patients, just under ten percent, died within thirty days. The team compared a five-item frailty index with the anesthesiology physical status scale that grades overall sickness.

The physical status scale sorted risk better than the frailty index, though both performed modestly at best. In adjusted analysis, the status scale kept an independent link to thirty-day death while the frailty score did not. Patients who died also spent longer in intensive care and in hospital, and suffered more severe complications. The authors conclude that neither tool alone reads this operation's danger well. They call for a purpose-built model for esophagectomy that folding in body function, fitness, and the specifics of the procedure.
pmc-13438677:
Munn and colleagues draw lessons from linking the Canadian Neuromuscular Disease registry with health data across five provinces. The linked data come from billing and hospital records. The work was meant to exploit data for tracking rare muscle diseases over time. These records suit long-term tracking, but neuromuscular diseases are hard to spot from codes alone. Key clinical details are missing.

Registry linkage could fill those gaps. Registry number and quality have improved sharply over the last decade, the authors say. Their commentary walks through the hands-on hurdles of cross-province research. These range from each province's own rules to data access hurdles met along the way. The stakes are high. Care for these patients costs from 3,000 dollars to over 500,000 dollars per person each year. They argue the linked approach is worth the friction for disease tracking. It also helps judge response to costly new therapies.
pmc-13439477:
Tsan-Chi Chen's team silenced MUC4 in 2026 in human corneal cells to map what this surface mucin does for eye health. MUC4 coats the corneal surface and supports wetting and barrier function, yet its internal regulatory role was unclear. Lentiviral silencing was followed by viability, movement, mitochondrial, and signaling checks, including protein arrays for pathway activation.

MUC4 loss cut viability through death signals, boosted movement through focal adhesion signaling, lowered maximal respiration and spare capacity with key mitochondrial proteins down, and switched on MAPK-linked kinases. The paper positions steady MUC4 as a brake on migration and a guard of cell energy. Eye teams get a mechanistic map linking mucin loss to barrier failure and inflammation.
pmc-13440177:
Yan Feng and colleagues test whether a single intensive clinic day improves pregnancy diabetes care, reporting a 2026 retrospective study. Gestational diabetes raises risks for mothers and babies, and insulin resistance sits at its core. The centre compared 252 patients split between a one-day outpatient package of full diabetes management and a routine nutrition consultation alone. Follow-up ran to six weeks after birth, with blood sugar, stress hormones, iron markers, and tissue-damage markers tracked.

The one-day group left with lower fasting insulin, lower insulin resistance scores, and lower after-meal sugar than the routine group. Stress hormones and an iron-storage marker also ran lower. Insulin use, later sugar problems, early birth, and oversized babies all occurred less often. The authors tie the gains to calmer stress response, better iron handling, and less oxidative damage, while noting that one centre's records limit certainty.
pmc-13440777:
Abiha and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a child with a rare spine birth defect. Caudal regression means the lower spine and tailbone fail to form fully. Most cases appear once, with no family pattern behind them. Their patient also had tangled spine coverings and repeated skin infections.

The patient, a 12-year-old boy, had sore-like spots along his back since birth. Scans showed missing lower spine bones and a spinal cord pulled too low. Surgeons freed the cord and removed a cyst found wound around nerve roots. Scans of his mother showed a milder form of the same defect. The case supports checking close relatives when this pattern runs in families. His steady state after surgery was a welcome result for the family.
pmc-13440977:
Karasinski published a 2026 study on school results for children with communication disorders. Language skill underpins learning in class, since teaching flows through words. The study compared fourth graders with such disorders against classmates with typical language. Data came from a large national study that followed children from kindergarten.

Classmates with typical language scored higher in reading, math, and science alike. Family income tracked scores too, with each income band scoring above the one below. Math stood out as a relative strength for children in both groups. Girls led in reading, but no sex gap appeared in math or science. The author urges speech specialists to team up with classroom teachers. Extra support at school, she argues, should start as early as possible.
pmc-13441777:
Sizhe Wang and colleagues review how exercise protects against diabetes at the level of body mechanisms, writing a 2026 narrative review. Diabetes affected an estimated 589 million adults in 2024 and ranks among the world's leading killers. Drugs control sugar well but carry side effects and cost. Exercise is cheap, low-risk, and proven, yet its inner workings deserve a clear map. The review gathers mechanisms across type 1 and type 2 disease.

Pathways covered span muscle sugar uptake, insulin sensitivity, fat and liver handling, and the vessel and nerve damage behind complications. Damage patterns are sorted into large-vessel disease, small-vessel disease, and the diabetic foot where nerve, flow, and infection problems meet. Exercise styles are compared for strength of benefit, from aerobic training to resistance and interval work. The authors position regular movement as a mechanistic therapy in its own right, not merely lifestyle advice.
pmc-13442377:
Tomoya Nakai reviews how brain scans link mental ideas such as attention and memory to brain activity in a 2026 paper. Labs have long used tight tasks that change one thing at a time. Newer work uses films, stories, and music that feel much closer to real life.

Nakai argues that each style hides its own bets about what counts as proof. Tight tasks place those bets in the task plan, while rich tasks place them in the choice of traits and models. He urges teams to mix both styles and to lean on computer models built from scan data. That mix could stretch scan work past watching and listening toward thought, choice, and math problems.
pmc-13442477:
Heijligenberg and colleagues meta-analyzed 47 European studies with 159 effect sizes, covering 177,169 teens. They tested whether school track, vocational versus academic, predicts sexual health. Layered school systems sort teens early. Single studies clashed on how much the track itself matters for results.

The pooled link was clear, with an effect size of 0.279 in favor of academic-track teens across the pooled sexual health scores. Gaps were strongest in certain domains. Vocational students had less sexual knowledge. They more often said they had early sex, and more often had teenage pregnancy than academic peers in the pooled data. The link also ran stronger in samples where over 75 percent of students had no migration background, in the subgroup checks. Heterogeneity was high, with an I-squared of 80.23 percent. It stayed after subgroup checks, so the authors urge a cautious reading.
pmc-13442677:
Jia and colleagues charted two opposite blood pressure faults in 183 Parkinson's patients at one center: orthostatic hypotension, pressure plunging on standing, and supine hypertension, pressure too high lying down. Each patient underwent an active stand test with beat-to-beat monitoring, and a subset had brain blood flow tracking during the challenge.

Orthostatic hypotension occurred in 72.1 percent of patients, and 27.9 percent had the symptomatic form with felt dizziness or faintness. Supine hypertension was present in 21.9 percent, and it was tied to older age, existing hypertension, and more advanced Hoehn and Yahr stage in the regression model. Female sex and blood pressure medication use were associated with lower odds of the standing pressure drop in this cohort. Higher lying pressures predicted steeper drops on standing, while antihypertensive therapy blunted the decline, an interplay the authors say complicates treatment balancing.
pmc-13442877:
Zhigao Huang and colleagues propose a 2026 method for picking interpretable decision trees by the work a typical case actually triggers, rather than by worst-case size alone. Their Soft-D selector scans pruned candidate trees and keeps the one with the lowest average path length among those whose accuracy stays within a chosen tolerance of the best.

Across eleven benchmark data sets and repeated test folds, the selector cut average depth by 47.4 percent against unpruned trees and by 12.1 percent against an accuracy-first pruning rival at a tolerance of 0.02. The authors show the tolerance itself trades accuracy against simplicity, and that refitting can shift depth in some folds. The method suits deployment teams that must justify each decision without paying for needless complexity.
pmc-13444377:
Basil Masinza and colleagues pool gender gaps in anxiety and PTSD across sub-Saharan Africa in a 2026 review. Health research often skips sex splits, which blinds care design. Their search kept 175 studies with adult, sex-split rates: 75 on anxiety, 86 on PTSD, and 14 on both.

Eastern Africa gave 61 percent of the studies in the pool. Pooled anxiety sat at 39 percent for women against 30 percent for men in the counts. PTSD pooled at 39 percent for women against 26 percent for men. Odds for women ran about one and a half times male odds for each state. Most named risk factors centered on women, while trauma loads led for men. The authors urge sex-aware screens and care plans.
pmc-13444477:
Di Wu and colleagues review cryptic transcription, a source of rogue RNA that grows with age in a 2026 paper. Healthy cells lock gene bodies against false starts, so gene reads begin only at true promoters. Age wears those locks down.

Loss of the H3K36me3 mark trims DNA methylation, while promoter-like marks pile inside gene bodies. Gene readers then fire from hidden inner spots, which yields cut or junk messages and dud proteins. Stem cells lose self-renewal and fate skill under that noise. The review maps each lock, from histone marks to reader factors, and ties each to cell aging signs. The authors frame the noise as both a mark and a driver of aged tissue.
pmc-13445077:
Madison S. Smith and colleagues compare step counts from the same model of wrist and hip activity tracker worn at once by adults with Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 study. Tremor and stiffness could skew counts by body site, yet few home studies have checked the two sites side by side. The work tests whether the wrist, the more common site, can be trusted.

Twenty-one adults wore both devices during waking hours for seven days. Mean daily steps came out close, near fifty-two hundred at the wrist and fifty-four hundred at the hip, with a mean gap of about one hundred fifty steps. Agreement rated as good overall, which supports wrist wear for steps and for extra measures like heart rate and sleep that a hip device cannot give.
pmc-13445377:
María de la Hoz García and colleagues survey rural adults in Spain on their contact with nature, in a 2026 study written in Spanish. The survey asks how that contact tracks felt stress and quality of life. The adults, aged eighteen to seventy, receive care through primary care clinics in a rural county of Guadalajara province. Nature is framed as a health asset worth weighing in daily care.

Staff analyzed replies from 208 adults picked at random within age and sex bands. Stress ran lower in people with more exercise, more time in natural settings, or a view of nature from home or on trips. Use of open natural spaces linked on its own to better physical quality of life, and house plants linked to better mental scores.
pmc-13445677:
Joohyun Chung and colleagues compare older adults who got home-based palliative care with those referred but never enrolled, in a 2026 records study. Care at home lifts quality of life in serious illness, yet use stays low and uneven, and many mistake it for last-days care only. The team looked for who falls through the gap.

Records covered 567 patients at one facility in the eastern United States across 2022 and 2023. No clear gaps appeared by sex or race between the two groups. Age, insurance type, and referral source did split the groups: enrolled patients skewed older, more often held Medicare Part B cover, and more often came from larger hospitals. The authors call for targeted steps to even out access.
pmc-13446477:
Zulfiya Khalmuratova and colleagues report the crystal structure of a menthol-based ester, worked out with X-ray data, surface analysis, and computer modeling, in a 2026 study. Menthol, the cooling heart of peppermint oils, is a handy scaffold for new molecules with tuned traits. The title ester joins a benzoate group to menthol through a short linker.

Inside the crystal, weak carbon-to-oxygen contacts link the molecules into chains running along one axis, and soft van der Waals forces fill the gaps between chains. Surface maps show where those contacts sit, and density calculations add charge and energy detail. The work extends the record on menthyl esters, a family prized in scent, flavor, and skin goods for their cool feel.
pmc-13446877:
Lars Sävendahl and colleagues pool three trials to compare a weekly growth hormone, somapacitan, with daily shots in children short of the hormone, in a 2026 analysis. Daily shots burden families for years, so a weekly form must prove it grows children as well and as safely. Data came from the REAL 3, 4, and 6 trials.

At one year, height speed matched between the weekly and daily groups. At three years the speeds still ran close across children who stayed weekly, stayed daily, or switched from daily to weekly partway. Most side effects were mild and unlikely tied to treatment. Growth held steady through puberty in both arms and across puberty stages, which supports the weekly dose as a lasting swap.
pmc-13447177:
Qiang Hu and Yuanshui Sun review in 2026 how poor nutrition before and after surgery raises the risk of wound infection. Malnourished patients heal more slowly and fight infection less well. Clinics have several scoring tools, yet each captures a different slice of risk, which can leave teams unsure which one to use.

Two detailed tools best define clear malnutrition based on weight, intake and muscle loss plus patient report. Three blood and body based scores give fast, objective risk numbers for busy settings. Rather than picking one winner, the authors propose a step-by-step path that screens early, confirms the pattern, grades risk, acts, then checks again after surgery. They stress that the path is a model needing prospective testing before routine adoption.
pmc-13447277:
Wanrong Chen and colleagues improve prediction of how tree trunks narrow with height for Chinese fir in a 2026 forestry study. Trunk shape shifts as trees grow, guided by the need to stay stable against wind and weight. Fixed formula models miss that change, while black-box algorithms hide the biology, leaving room for a middle path.

Data from five hundred sixteen felled trees fed flexible additive models, which allow curved effects without fixed formulas. A model using only separate effects failed to beat the standard benchmark formula. Adding an interaction between trunk thickness and relative height cut prediction error sharply and beat both the benchmark and tuned machine learning rivals. Larger trees showed stronger base flare, a pattern the interaction captured and forest managers can use for sharper timber estimates.
pmc-13447377:
Aizhan Kassymova and colleagues propose a secure serverless design for digital civic participation platforms in 2026 work set in Kazakhstan. City governments want wider citizen input with transparency, yet older e-participation systems struggle with scale, secure identity checks and rules on where personal data may live. Treating each citizen action as an event in an ongoing decision flow anchors the new design.

A prototype handled up to ten thousand simultaneous users with steady response times across load levels. Costs ran below a comparable container-based setup, and the smart modules added little delay while catching suspicious activity in controlled tests.
pmc-13447477:
Rana Almaghrabi leads a large team reporting a team-based stewardship programme that cut blood culture overuse in emergency departments in 2026 work. Blood cultures guide treatment of bloodstream infection, yet over-ordering outside intensive care breeds false positives, extra antibiotics and cost. The programme joined cleaner sample collection, ordering guidance and antibiotic oversight across adult and child emergency care.

Four months of the programme in 2025 were compared with a four-month baseline earlier that year. Culture event rates fell sharply in both adult and child groups, while contamination dropped by most of its earlier level. Use of several broad antibiotics fell markedly, including complete stoppage of one reserve drug's measured use. Guideline compliance rose close to full, with no culture-related return visits within thirty days reported.
pmc-13447577:
Jangho Lee and colleagues engineer tiny packets from fetal stem cells to attack cancer metabolism in 2026 work. Solid tumours thrive by fermenting sugar into lactate even with oxygen present, creating an acidic shield that blunts immunity. Treated cancer cells made less lactate, shifted toward oxygen-based energy production and dialled down a key fermentation gene. The rewiring raised harmful oxygen by-products, upset reducing balance and triggered programmed cell death. In mice, treatment lowered tumour levels of fermentation and fat-making proteins and slowed graft growth, offering a metabolism-first route against solid tumours.
pmc-13448077:
Nafiseh Nasirzadeh and colleagues develop a 2026 UV-protective workwear textile using zinc oxide nanoparticles with cold plasma treatment. pmc-13448177:
Pinelopi Anagnostopoulou and colleagues run a 2026 pilot study of how personal heat exposure in preceding days affects vital signs, labs, and hydration in people with cystic fibrosis versus family controls. pmc-13449377:
H. S. Rugo and a large team detail in 2026 the safety and patient-reported outcomes of datopotamab deruxtecan in the phase III TROPION-Breast01 trial. Nausea led the drug's effects at 51.9 percent, though severe cases were rare at 1.4 percent. Mouth sores affected 57.2 percent and eye surface problems 43.9 percent, mostly mild, with preventive mouthwash, anti-nausea drugs, and artificial tears widely used. Lung inflammation attributed to the drug occurred in 3.9 percent, including one fatal case. Chemotherapy's signature burden was blood toxicity instead. Patients on the conjugate kept their quality of life, pain control, and function longer before deterioration.
pmc-13450577:
Filippo Lixi and co-authors describe a 2026 case where insulin eye drops plus a gel plug healed a severe, numb eye surface. The patient, a man aged 52, had late-stage nerve-linked eye damage after herpes, with a wide open sore and melting of the clear front of the eye. His sight in that eye had fallen to seeing hand motion only.

The sore shrank week by week and closed fully by eight weeks, with no side effects noted. Sight rose to counting fingers at one meter, and the team calls for controlled trials of the pairing.
pmc-13451777:
Shirani, Miller, and Freeman modeled how species' range edges evolve when animals choose habitats matching their own traits, rather than dispersing randomly as classic theory assumes.
