Their mathematical model lets individuals follow the environmental gradient toward conditions suiting their phenotype, producing adaptive gene flow toward the margins instead. Counterintuitively, this sharpened range limits and reduced character displacement where the two species overlap, instead of dissolving the borders entirely. The effects grew strongest under weak selection, specialized resource use, or high sensitivity to environmental conditions in the simulations. Matching habitat choice drove backward, edge-to-core movements that interact with competition to set the limits, and the authors identify its competitive advantage in steep gradients.
pmc-13451877:
Daryl Kai Ann Chia and co-authors report in 2026 a phase two trial of chemo plus a vessel-blocking drug before big surgery for bowel cancer spread to the belly lining. Such spread fares worse than spread to other single sites. Patients went on to tumor-cutting surgery with heated chemo washed through the belly.

The team found the pre-surgery course safe to give. Median survival after the full course reached a little over forty months. Two tissue marks split outcomes: high levels of a low-oxygen switch in tumor cores tracked better survival, while high levels of a growth factor in belly fluid tracked worse. The marks may help pick who gains most from the heavy course.
pmc-13452177:
Geraldo Balieiro Neto and co-authors test in 2026 how feed fiber level sets the power of two rumen additives in cattle. Four cattle with rumen ports rotated through diets in a Latin square plan, crossing low and high fiber with either a standard drug pair or a plant-based additive. Intake, chewing time, rumen acidity, and methane were logged.

High fiber diets drove more intake, chewing, and methane, roughly triple the gas of low fiber diets by day. Within high fiber diets, the plant additive cut methane by about a quarter against the drug pair. Within low fiber diets, it lifted useful acid output instead. The authors say fiber level, more than additive choice, steers the rumen.
pmc-13452277:
Robson Conceicao Silva and a very large team lay out in 2026 the plan for a trial of gentler strength training in heart failure. Standard rehab loads can strain weak hearts, so the trial sets heavy training against light training with blood flow partly pinched by cuffs. Fifty-two patients with mid-grade symptoms will be split by lot between the two arms.

Training runs four months under watch, with eight more months of follow-up. The main score is change in a blood strain mark, with life quality, heart scans, fitness, and events as side scores. Learning models will hunt for who gains most from each arm. No results are reported; the paper is the trial's blueprint.
pmc-13452377:
Marvin Bubeck and a very large team show in 2026 that two immune signals team up to kill the gut's activated helper glia in bowel diseases. Those glia keep the gut wall and its immune balance in trim, yet their fate in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis was murky. The team read 390 gut samples, checked the pattern in public sets of over a thousand patients, and cut the path apart in mice.

Fresh activation marks for the glia emerged, sorted by disease kind and gut zone. The paired signals, interferon gamma and tumor necrosis factor, drove the activated glia to die while sparing quiet ones. Blocking a death gene in glia tested the chain. The work reframes glia loss as a driver, not a side note.
pmc-13452777:
Wendelspiess and co-authors compared two ways of rebuilding the perineum after cancer surgery or severe infection at one center, from 2013 to 2023. One way uses perforator flaps, which spare muscle by threading tissue on tiny vessels. The other uses traditional muscle-carrying flaps. They tracked complications and surveyed patients about long-term quality of life after reconstruction.

Perforator reconstructions made up 58 percent of cases and non-perforator 40 percent, with one combined approach. Cancer defect coverage drove 68.9 percent of the operations performed. Complication rates were identical at 50 percent in both groups. That is a sobering figure reflecting this difficult surgical territory. Donor-site harm was clearly worse with muscle flaps, where every complication reached the serious grade III level requiring intervention. Patient satisfaction paradoxically ran higher in the muscle-flap group, 100 versus 66 percent, though its follow-up was far longer. Quality-of-life scores numerically favored perforator patients.
pmc-13452877:
Sally Campbell and six co-authors review liver transplants given for bile duct cancers that surgeons could not cut out. Their 2026 study covers 98 patients at one center from 2007 to 2025, the largest such set from a single center. The cancers fall into three subtypes based on where in the bile system they grow.

The perihilar subtype, near the liver's duct junction, made up 54 of the cases, and a mixed subtype added 28 more. The diagnosis before surgery proved wrong in about a quarter of cases once the removed liver was checked. Cancer came back in 40.8 percent of patients, at a median of 16 months, while five year survival for the whole group reached 58 percent. Spread to lymph nodes, subtype, and tumor size each predicted return on their own.
pmc-13452977:
Mansour and co-authors report an exceptionally rare brain tumor in a child in this 2026 case report. Primary intracranial myxoma is a benign jelly-like growth that arises inside the skull itself, unlike the more familiar heart myxomas that can send fragments to the brain. Their patient, a healthy 10-year-old boy, had a first seizure lasting about 90 seconds with signs pointing to a left-sided origin.

Scans showed a well-defined growth attached to the brain's outer covering in the left frontal lobe, without much pressure on surrounding tissue. Surgeons removed it completely through a pterional approach, finding a soft, lobulated, gelatinous mass, and microscopy confirmed myxoma. Heart imaging found no cardiac source, confirming the primary diagnosis, and the boy remained seizure-free 18 months later.
pmc-13453477:
Asal sadat Morakkabi, Shahin Hassanpour, and Razieh Hosseini test whether glycyrrhizin, a sweet compound from licorice root, can shield mice from a multiple sclerosis like illness. Their 2026 study fed 40 male mice one of four diets, including chow laced with cuprizone, a toxin that strips nerve insulation and mimics the disease. One group got cuprizone plus a daily mouth dose of glycyrrhizin at 400 milligrams per kilogram.

Cuprizone alone cut the mice's balance time, movement, and grip strength, while blood markers of cell damage and swelling rose. Mice on glycyrrhizin kept stronger movement and grip across every test. Their blood also showed less damage marker and lower swelling signals, with stronger natural antioxidant defenses. The authors conclude the licorice compound guarded the mice against the toxin's harm, a lead for further study.
pmc-13453577:
Takahashi and colleagues surveyed 479 women attending breast cancer screening in Minamisoma. The city was hit hard by the 2011 Fukushima disaster. Screening centers sat more than 20 kilometers north of the damaged nuclear plant.

Nearly half the women, 47.4 percent or 227 of 479, scored at or above the threshold for moderate mental distress on the Kessler scale used. Believing radiation likely caused breast cancer nearly tripled the odds of general breast cancer anxiety, with an odds ratio of 2.99 in the regression models. The same belief raised the odds of mental distress itself, at an odds ratio of 1.76, a statistically robust association. Breast cancer anxiety alone, however, was not significantly tied to distress, suggesting radiation perception is the connecting thread.
pmc-13453677:
Zhe Liu and thirteen co-authors build a three part score to flag which patients with cancers near the pancreas will fare worst after surgery. These periampullary cancers often waste muscle and weight, which saps tolerance for later drug treatment. Their 2026 study covers 533 patients at two centers who had the major operation that removes the pancreas head.

The score sorted patients well in training and in two check groups, beating all 12 rival nutrition scores. High risk patients faced 3.29 times the risk of major complications. Complications then made treatment delay far more likely, and delay cut the time free of disease. About a fifth of the harm flowed through that chain, the team estimates.
pmc-13453777:
Xiaoqian Wang and four co-authors review how shifts in cell fuel use drive cardiac fibrosis, the scarring that stiffens the heart. Each shift helps wake fibroblasts and feed collagen output, and the lines cross talk in ways that lock the scar program in place. Blocking or rerouting single steps eases scarring in lab work, which makes metabolism a tempting drug frontier. Yet the authors warn that the same fuels serve healthy heart cells, so blunt blocking could backfire. They call for a fuller map and finer tools before clinics test metabolic fixes for heart scarring.
pmc-13453877:
Jerome Soquet writes to the editor arguing that a self named aortic root widening technique in fact descends from a 1983 Mayo Clinic paper. He holds that a device swap does not rename a maneuver. A Nicks widening, he notes, keeps its name whatever patch material is used. He grants the newer team likely never saw the 1983 paper. Priority, he concludes, belongs to Piehler unless an earlier report surfaces.
pmc-13454277:

Their 2026 study uses a 2025 national survey of 1,939 adults from a probability based panel. pmc-13455477:
Patrick Zeniecki and colleagues review screen-based simulation as a test for emergency medicine trainees in a 2026 rapid review. Scores clustered by training level, showing the method can separate junior from senior learners. Trainees also reported strong interest in the software. Evidence remains thin and small-scale, so the review presents screen simulation as a promising supplement, not yet a proven replacement for live assessment.
pmc-13457277:
Malena Hughes and co-authors tested whether a slow laboratory step in a horse tapeworm test could be shortened without hurting accuracy. They were processed with the standard timing or with spins shortened to five minutes or one minute.

The one-minute version produced positive counts in 86.2 percent of subsamples, compared with 70.7 percent for the standard method, and its counts varied less between repeats. The five-minute version landed in between, at 82.9 percent positive counts. The authors conclude that one-minute spins improve both detection and counting of tapeworm eggs.
pmc-13457377:

Tested against five rival optimizers on four waste datasets and four classifier types, the method averaged 92.71 percent accuracy and a macro-F1 of 0.9209, with strong precision and recall. The authors aim it at automated recycling and monitoring systems that must work across varied settings.
pmc-13458577:

The authors weigh these durable results against a treatment landscape crowded with immunotherapy.
pmc-13458977:

Such bacteria could deliver immune signals or tumor antigens directly inside a tumor. Safety, dosing, and patient differences remain major hurdles before clinic use.
pmc-13459277:

Overall survival, however, did not differ between the approaches in the combined analysis. The authors conclude the choice trades recurrence risk against surgical burden, not life expectancy.
pmc-13459377:
Hamideh Khesali and colleagues follow aortic valve disease after fever-linked mitral valve replacement in a 2026 cohort study. Fever disease often hits both valves, yet the fate of mild or moderate aortic disease after isolated mitral replacement was poorly known. At start, 9.2 percent had tight aortic valve and 67 percent had aortic leak, mostly mild. Start lesion grade alone predicted decline, with a hazard ratio of 4.2, while 20 percent of mild tight-valve cases reached severe disease. pmc-13459677:
Ritika Behl and Vivek Nemane surveyed in 2026 people holding Indian law degrees about depression around pregnancy and childbirth. Roughly half in each survey were unsure whether perinatal mental health services even exist. Majorities agreed the policy gap risks rights violations for women and children, and the authors seek targeted training for legal professionals.
pmc-13459977:
Hiroki Okada, Lin Feng, Xi Chen, and Erfei Bi announce in 2026 the draft genome of Kockovaella fuzhouensis, a basidiomycete yeast first isolated from mango flowers in Fuzhou, China. The strain is held in the CBS culture collection in the Netherlands. It has attracted cell biologists for its odd way of dividing: the nucleus travels through a long, narrow neck into the daughter cell before division finishes at the daughter's base.

Sequencing produced a genome of about twenty-three million DNA letters arranged in eight scaffolds, carrying roughly eighty-six hundred predicted genes and scoring high on completeness checks. The authors offer the sequence as a resource for genetic work on how this yeast builds its shape and divides. Those questions are hard to study without a reference genome.
pmc-13461477:
Yao, Zhang, and Feng studied in 2026 why kind behaviour links to wellbeing among Chinese university students born after 2000. The team surveyed 1,084 students and modelled how prosocial behaviour, meaning kind acts for others, relates to subjective wellbeing through two parts of meaning in life: having meaning and searching for it.

When motivation ran high, the links between kindness, meaning, and wellbeing grew robustly stronger. When motivation was low, the path through searching for meaning vanished and the whole link weakened a lot. The authors argue motivation must sit inside studies of kindness and wellbeing, not beside them.
pmc-13461577:
Jeong Uk Lim and colleagues studied which starting health measures predict survival and side effects after cell therapy for solid tumours. The therapy infuses engineered or trained immune cells, a treatment proven in blood cancers but newer for solid tumours.

Records covered 122 patients treated at a Texas cancer centre between 2016 and 2025. Higher starting inflammation, measured by C-reactive protein, linked to shorter survival, while larger cell doses linked to longer time without growth. Lung diffusion capacity also tracked survival in patients who had lung function tests. Cytokine release syndrome, a feverish immune storm, hit 57.4 percent of patients, more often when starting white cell counts ran low, Lim reports.
pmc-13463377:
Michael Schnapper and colleagues trace, in a 2026 records study, how celiac disease and type 1 diabetes unfold together in children. Among 136 children with a positive celiac blood marker, 113 were confirmed with celiac disease, fifteen stayed positive without confirmation, and eight had a borderline result. Celiac disease was diagnosed after diabetes in about four fifths of cases, yet came first in nearly a fifth. Children diagnosed with celiac disease first had more gut symptoms, stronger markers, and poorer sugar control. Follow-up sugar levels ran higher in confirmed celiac disease than in the borderline group. The authors urge continued screening in both directions as children grow.
pmc-13463477:
Using tissue from 128 patients, Liu and colleagues reported in 2026 on a long non-coding RNA in non-small cell lung cancer. Such RNA regulates other genes without making a protein. This cancer type accounts for most lung cancer cases. The team measured the RNA, called LY86-AS1, in tumors and in two lung cancer cell lines. They tested what happened when its level was raised.

Tumors carried much less LY86-AS1 than healthy tissue. Patients with the lowest levels fared worst, making it an independent marker of poor outlook. Raising LY86-AS1 in the cell lines slowed growth, movement, and invasion through tissue barriers. The team traced the effect to a chain of regulators. LY86-AS1 soaks up a small RNA named miR-132-3p. That frees a second gene, RB1CC1, to do its growth-limiting work. Reversing any link in the chain reversed the benefit.
pmc-13463977:
Samarla and colleagues present a 2026 protocol called CALM-CXR for classifying chest X-rays into normal, bacterial infection, and viral infection classes. Calibration means the stated confidence matches reality, checked here with temperature scaling and thresholds chosen on a separate data slice. Evaluation used 4,840 images, split so no patient group leaks between training and testing. Each stage keeps its own probabilities, so a wrong final answer can be blamed on the right stage. Auditability is the point: regulators and hospitals can inspect where the system fails instead of trusting a single score.
pmc-13464077:
Yu and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the protein corona on nucleic acid nanodrugs. The corona is the coat of blood proteins that sticks to nanoparticle medicines once they enter the body. These nanodrugs carry nucleic acids such as gene-silencing RNA or messenger RNA. The coat, not the engineered surface, is what cells actually see. It can decide where a medicine goes and whether it works.

The review explains how the coat forms within moments. Flow, particle size, and surface chemistry steer which proteins settle. The resulting layer changes everything downstream. It affects crossing gut mucus, surviving in circulation, and reaching the right organ. Entering cells and escaping their recycling compartments also depend on it. Disturbed blood flow at vessel branches raised total protein adsorption by about three quarters in one study. Rather than only fighting the coat, the authors survey designs that recruit helpful proteins as targeting guides.
pmc-13464277:
Cai and Cao described in 2026 a protective maneuver used in a woman of 75 whose atrial fibrillation was long-standing and persistent. Destroying that small heart vein helps stop the rhythm problem. Ethanol escaping through the vein's far end can injure the heart's natural pacemaker, though.

Imaging showed contrast from the vein draining straight into the right atrium. That is exactly the route endangering the pacemaker and the heart's electrical relay. Before any ethanol flowed, the team threaded a wire into the far segment. Controlled heat of just 10 watts sealed it shut. Ethanol was then injected in two slow doses totaling six milliliters. No pacemaker arrest or relay block occurred. The lung veins were fully isolated, and the fibrillation stopped during the procedure.
pmc-13464577:
Yang and colleagues engineered in 2026 a whole-tumor cell vaccine for cancers that ignore modern immunotherapy. These so-called pMMR and MSS tumors form the majority of solid cancers. Their stable DNA gives the immune system few alarms. The vaccine uses tumor cells stripped by gene editing of TGF-beta1, an immune-dampening signal. A stimulant that mimics viral RNA is mixed in. The product is designed to sit ready off the shelf.

Vaccinated mice fought tumors growing elsewhere in the body. They developed fewer lung metastases and resisted spontaneous bowel tumors. The vaccine also teamed up with a standard checkpoint-blocking antibody, raising complete response rates. Removing the dampening signal changed the battlefield two ways. Suppressive immune cells stopped accumulating. The vaccine cells switched on an internal alarm pathway, making them more visible to the immune system. Mice gained long-term protection even against unlike tumor types.
pmc-13464677:
Kwang Kun Cho and five co-authors review artery embolization for gut bleeding caused by cancer. Such bleeding often resists scope treatment and drugs, so doctors thread a catheter into the artery and block the leak from inside. Whether a pre-scan leak sign changes results was the open question.

Forty patients treated from 2012 to 2023 split into twenty-five with contrast leaking on CT scans and fifteen without. Technical success hit every case, and bleeding control matched across both groups. Two patients died within a month, one in each group, and survival ran alike too. A shock index above one, a sign of unstable circulation, was the one factor tied to worse survival.
pmc-13464777:

pmc-13465177:

Validation runs from lab benches to literature cross-checks across several species. The editors frame the set as a bridge from raw expression data to system maps, disease markers, drug targets, and stress tolerance clues.
pmc-13465477:
Chen and co-authors mined the MIMIC-IV database in 2026 for how feeding timing relates to blood chemistry after heart surgery. The measure was the anion gap, a blood value reflecting acid buildup. Among 195 intensive care patients who received tube feeding, 83 were first fed before surgery and 112 after. The groups started with similar illness severity. Anion gap was compared at admission, 24 hours after surgery, and discharge.

Feeding timing showed no clear tie to delirium, deaths, or length of stay, though. Discharge anion gap itself tracked with in-hospital mortality. The authors call the signal hypothesis-generating, since sicker patients may simply have been fed later.
pmc-13465677:
Yi Guo, Yizhen Yan, Li Zhao, and Shanshan Mao review one side of aging in a 2026 narrative review. They examine how vitamin D interacts with the chemical tags that switch genes on and off. Aging brings drifting DNA methylation, altered histone marks, and disordered helper RNAs. Vitamin D, working through its own receptor protein, can nudge several of those systems.

The review moves from basic aging changes to vitamin D signaling, then to effects in immune, muscle and bone, and nervous tissues. Trial evidence gets a sober reading: large randomized studies show little gain from vitamin D alone, with clearer effects when paired with exercise and better nutrition. Responses also vary widely between people and doses.
pmc-13465877:
Evelyn-Gabriela Nastase-Rusu and co-authors compare three ways of growing heart fibroblasts taken from adult mice, a routine but tricky lab task, in a 2026 methods study. Fresh heart cells divide poorly and suffer under harsh tissue digestion, so small protocol changes can decide whether a culture succeeds. Each method uses a different enzyme strategy to free the cells.

One route digests tissue in steps with two enzymes, another perfuses the heart's own vessels with collagenase, and a third uses a commercial enzyme blend in one continuous run. The team measured cell survival after isolation, checked which cell types came through by flow analysis, and watched whether the fibroblasts settled and grew. Their comparison aims at a repeatable recipe other labs can trust.
pmc-13466077:
Tong and colleagues set out in 2026 a pilot trial plan for personal sleep apnea care in heart attack survivors. Sleep apnea, where breathing stalls in sleep, affects most such patients. Big trials of standard apnea care showed no heart benefit, possibly because patients quit and care is one-size-fits-all. This Australian pilot enrolls patients with apnea confirmed by oxygen dips. Half choose an airway pressure machine or a fitted mouthpiece, plus coaching and engagement tools. The rest get usual care for six months.

Feasibility comes first: how many accept the study, accept treatment, and use it nightly. Secondary measures cover treatment effect, heart health markers, and patient reports. Earlier trials saw only about four in ten patients manage four nightly hours of machine use, a practical worry this design answers. If personalization proves workable, the results will shape a much larger trial of heart outcomes.
pmc-13466377:
Anna Alyasova and a large team review treatments for cancer spread across the lining of the abdomen, a pattern common in advanced gut and gynecologic cancers, in a 2026 article. Drugs given by vein reach this lining poorly because a barrier blocks entry, even after major surgery removes visible tumor. The review draws on recent trials and pooled analyses.

Options walked through include heated chemotherapy washed inside the abdomen during surgery, pressurized aerosol delivery, and light-based therapies. Patient selection and a spread score strongly shape who benefits from the heated approach. Newer pairings add immune drugs, guided light dosing, and nano-carriers, each aiming to push more drug into stubborn deposits.
pmc-13466477:
Natália Piffer Pasquali and colleagues fire a dental laser at zirconia crowns to check whether the cleaning step weakens them, in a 2026 study. Sixty crowns took part, split between solid ultra-translucent zirconia and a layered version with porcelain over a zirconia core. Half of each group received laser treatment on the inner bonding surface.

Crowns were glued onto tooth-like supports and crushed until they failed. Laser treatment did not lower breaking strength or reliability in the statistical tests. Solid crowns carried higher loads than layered ones, which tended to chip and peel, while solid crowns shattered outright when they finally gave way.
pmc-13468277:
Nulibiya Maihemuti and co-authors test in 2026 the total polyphenols of quince fruit against obesity in mice. Quince from Xinjiang has a long history as both food and medicine, and it is rich in polyphenols. Earlier work by the team hinted at anti-obesity effects. Obese mice raised on a high-fat diet for 12 weeks then received the quince polyphenols for 6 weeks, with body weight tracked throughout and blood fats measured at the end.

The study reads out the classic obesity panel: triglycerides, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, alongside the sugar and fat metabolism pathways the polyphenols might act through. Diet-driven obesity drags in fatty liver, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress, so a food-derived compound that trims several markers at once earns attention. The authors frame quince polyphenols as a candidate functional ingredient whose mechanism now needs pinning down.
pmc-13468777:
Emmanouel T. Michailidis, Theodoros A. Tsiftsis, and Nikolaos I. Miridakis secure vehicle-to-vehicle communication in 2026 against an eavesdropping car whose channel cannot be measured directly. Their scheme drafts a friendly jammer vehicle that also acts as a radar. It senses and tracks the eavesdropper motion with an extended Kalman filter. It then broadcasts artificial noise aimed into the null space of the legitimate receiver, degrading only the spy reception.

The tracking uncertainty is carried into the design honestly, through covariance matrices that widen the jamming when the estimate is shaky. A finite-blocklength secrecy framework fits the ultra-reliable low-latency traffic these links carry, where messages are short and deadlines hard. Optimization runs at two time scales, slot-level for sensing resources and slower for transmit design. Cooperative jamming turns a nearby car into a bodyguard for platoons and convoys that cannot stop to negotiate security.
pmc-13469077:
Ovunc Akdemir and co-authors present a surgical case series, published in 2026. It describes a salvage operation for four patients. Their thumb replantation had failed during surgery. Blood flow to the thumb was lost. The staged approach parked the thumb in the groin. A pocket of tissue kept it alive. Tendons were rebuilt in later stages. The bone was stabilised as well.

At twelve months, all four patients kept thumb motion. It remained measurable. Pinch strength and protective feeling were retained too. Clinical stability was good. No pain occurred on maximal pinch effort. Four highly selected patients cannot prove the method beats alternatives. The authors stress this. They call for larger multicentre series with longer follow-up.
pmc-13469277:
Omari and co-authors present a 2026 case report of early-onset neonatal sepsis. The condition is a bloodstream infection in the first days of life. Here it was caused by the uncommon bacterium Morganella morganii. The patient was an extremely preterm infant, born well before term. Blood cultures grew the organism shortly after birth.

Lab testing showed the bacteria were susceptible to gentamicin. That antibiotic was part of the baby's starting treatment. Yet the infant failed to improve on it. Clinicians then changed the antibiotic regimen. They weighed the lab results against the baby's actual condition rather than trusting the report alone. The infant then recovered markedly. The authors warn that a reassuring sensitivity report does not guarantee a drug is working. In a fragile newborn, bedside response must guide therapy.
pmc-13469977:
Wei and co-authors review the skin colonisation that makes a drug-resistant fungus so hard to contain. Their 2026 paper covers Candida auris, an emerging pathogen with high mortality, strong transmissibility, and a record of hospital outbreaks. Unlike its relatives, it persists on patients' skin, and that persistence is treated here as the engine of its spread.

The review systematically assembles what is known. It covers the epidemiological patterns of skin colonisation and how the fungus reshapes the skin's resident microbiota. It also covers the host immune mechanisms it navigates. Finally it covers the molecular machinery of attachment and survival on skin. It then evaluates decolonisation strategies, from antiseptic bathing to experimental approaches, noting how underdeveloped they remain. The authors aim to give infection prevention a firmer theoretical base and to point research toward targeted interventions that clear the skin reservoir rather than chasing outbreaks afterwards.
pmc-13470877:
Rai and co-workers in Algeria and Italy showed in 2026 that the broth a lab uses can flatter a drug's strength against urine germs. Tests that guide drug picks are run in one set broth. Real urine shifts in sour grade and salt load by hour and by meal. The team grew two set germ strains and one from a patient's urine across sour and salt spans. They then dosed all with gentamicin, a stock urine drug.

Salt baths made both germs harder to kill, with clear zones shrunk by a wide mark. Sour shifts at the far ends made the drug bite harder. The split that counts most came in urine like broth. The patient germ's clear zone shrank by a third there. The dose to stop it rose eight times past its plain broth mark. The authors say set tests may hide true drug fail in the tract.
pmc-13471177:
Khanabadi and colleagues reported in 2026 the removal of a pancreatic head tumor in a 66-year-old man carrying two extra risks: type 2 diabetes and a slow blood cancer, chronic lymphocytic leukemia. He arrived with painless jaundice of three weeks. Scans and biopsy confirmed cancer of the ampulla, the junction where bile and pancreatic ducts meet the bowel. The operation itself is among the most demanding in surgery.

Preparation carried the case: a team tightened his blood sugar to a target range, drained the blocked bile duct, guarded against infection, and watched his leukemia. Surgery and recovery ran smoothly, with no pancreatic leak or fistula, the classic complications. Pathology showed stage I cancer with no spread to lymph nodes, though the nodes carried his leukemia cells. The authors credit structured team preparation and enhanced-recovery protocols for making curative surgery safe in a medically complex patient.
pmc-13471277:
Cai and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the case that NMDA receptors, the brain's learning switches, also help drive atherosclerosis, the artery disease behind heart attacks and strokes. Outside the brain these receptors sit on immune cells, vessel wall muscle, and lining cells. The review assembles genetic links, cell mechanisms, and drug evidence, plus modern tools targeting receptor subtypes selectively, sparing the brain's versions.

The mechanisms converge on plaque growth: in immune cells the receptors skew cells toward inflammation and disturb fat handling. In vessel muscle they promote the switching that thickens walls, and in the lining they worsen early dysfunction, the first step of disease. Human evidence adds intrigue: a receptor-blocking drug, amantadine, used for Parkinson's, was linked in one study with lower rates of death, heart attack, stroke, heart failure, and rhythm problems. The authors see a repurposing chance, provided such drugs can hit vessels without touching cognition.
pmc-13471577:
Kılıç tested whether the quick stain tests breeders use to judge chrysanthemum pollen actually predict whether that pollen can germinate. The 2026 study compared five staining methods and eight germination media across three cultivars, Chic, Swan, and Barolo, counting 1,000 pollen grains per cultivar under fresh and heat-killed conditions.

Most stains flattered the pollen: safranin, IKI, lactophenol blue, and acetocarmine reported apparent viability of 76 to 98% across samples, while the TTC stain said only 4 to 8% were alive. Real germination sided with TTC, reaching just 0.1 to 7.3% on the best media, far below the rosy stain estimates. A simple medium of polyethylene glycol plus boric acid, used in hanging drops, performed best among the germination recipes.
pmc-13471877:
Samina I Ansari and co-authors test a pathway question in 2026. Does executive function carry the effect of weak social skills into emotional and behavioral problems in young people? Inner and outer troubles are common in childhood, and more common still in neurodevelopmental conditions. Their two moderated mediation models compared autistic and typically developing children and adolescents side by side.

Poor metacognitive functioning, the planning and monitoring side of executive skills, carried social skill deficits into inner troubles only in the autistic group. Behavior dysregulation carried the same deficits into outer troubles in both groups. Formal tests of group difference on those pathways came out negative. So the diagnosis did not statistically moderate them. The authors still urge early screening of distinct executive domains to catch weak spots sooner.
pmc-13472277:
Reetendra Singh and colleagues show in 2026 that the surface shape of a substrate, not just its crystal mismatch, can flip the strain inside a Mott insulator film. Vanadium sesquioxide films on sapphire feel two competing strains. One is a compressive squeeze from lattice mismatch. The other is a tensile pull from differing heat expansion. Annealing the sapphire left it either atomically flat or stepped.

On stepped surfaces, defects formed near the steps and let the compressive strain relax. The tensile pull then won, and the films stayed insulating at every temperature. On flat surfaces the squeeze held, suppressing the metal insulator transition instead. Resistance differed by many orders of magnitude between the two nominally identical films. The authors promote surface morphology as a practical dial for strain engineering in correlated oxides.
pmc-13472777:
Luo and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of a spinal blood vessel fault that was nearly missed because early scans pointed at common spine wear. The patient was a 49-year-old man whose legs weakened and numbed over one week, then worsened sharply in two days. A fistula, an abnormal artery-to-vein link on the cord's covering, was slowly choking the cord.

Lower-back scans showed disc bulging that seemed to explain the symptoms, a trap the authors call diagnostic anchoring. Yet bladder and bowel trouble and the speed of decline did not fit that story. Chest-level scans showed a long swollen cord segment and winding vessels on its surface. Vessel imaging confirmed the fistula, and surgery to cut the link restored flow, with steady recovery after.
pmc-13473077:
Ann-Katrin Schwenzer and co-authors extend a separation method for proteins in 2026, pairing electric separation with mass spectrometry. The method keeps proteins close to their natural state while sorting fine variants that differ by charge. Past work used one fixed acid level, which limited which proteins could be studied well. Here the team tunes the acid level to each protein and can switch between gentle and harsh spray fluids.

The tuned setup sorted between 45 and 100 variants for well-known antibody drugs, counting forms not reported before. Blood hemoglobin could also be split into forms that differ by sugar damage, rust-like change, or bound sulfur groups. Keeping weak bonds intact let the team see whole protein groups, not just single chains. The method offers drug makers a sharper check on product quality.
pmc-13473277:
Aimaier and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction tool for pneumonia after severe stroke that adds frailty and nutrition risk to the usual clinical signs. Stroke-associated pneumonia is a common and serious setback in intensive care, and older scoring tools miss many cases in the sickest patients. Frailty and poor nutrition both shrink the body's reserves.

The team studied 293 patients in a Chongqing neurocritical care unit, of whom 126 developed pneumonia. Frailty and nutrition risk did not just add up; together they raised risk more than the sum of their parts. A chart-based model using age, feeding tube use, a blood inflammation ratio, frailty, and nutrition risk sorted patients far better than the standard score. The authors offer the tool for early, targeted prevention in stroke units.
pmc-13473377:
Karthikeyan and Sundar proposed in 2026 a deep learning system that recognises stress in crop plants from images. Early spotting of disease, insects, and nutrient shortage protects yields, but stresses can look alike and some classes are rare. A quantum-inspired interference gate, built from ordinary neural operations, sharpens the features without quantum hardware.

Extra modules include attention fusion, a loss function that focuses on hard examples, weighted sampling, and per-class threshold tuning. On the OLID-I dataset the model reached a macro-F1 score of about ninety-one percent, a balanced accuracy measure. It scored about ninety-six percent on PlantVillage and about ninety percent on PlantDoc, beating compared CNN, Transformer, and hybrid models. The authors offer the system as an efficient tool for precision farming, where early stress alerts guide treatment.
pmc-13473477:
Sonam Nagar and three colleagues built in 2026 a deep learning ensemble that sorts heartbeats into arrhythmia classes from ECG recordings. Heart disease leads global deaths, and catching abnormal rhythms early can prevent sudden cardiac death. The team used a standard heartbeat dataset of 109,446 samples across five classes: normal, supraventricular ectopic, ventricular ectopic, fusion, and unknown beats, with severe imbalance between classes.

Each signal was first turned into a 224 by 224 colour scalogram image using a wavelet transform. A hybrid network then read it, combining a residual convolutional network, a bidirectional LSTM for time patterns, and a transformer encoder for long-range links. Balanced sampling and class weighting handled the imbalance, and five-fold cross-validation checked robustness. Test accuracy reached 94.73 percent, though precision of 76.51 percent and an F1 score of 77.40 percent show rarer beats still challenge the model.
pmc-13473677:
Shima Shabani and Rahim Ghadari screened in 2026 a family of helicene-based molecules as hole-transport materials for perovskite solar cells. Cell efficiency depends heavily on these small molecules, which carry positive charges away from the light-absorbing layer, and computer screening offers a cheap way to test candidates before synthesis. Using density functional theory and its time-dependent variant, the team evaluated helicene diphenylamine compounds with varied groups in ortho and meta positions.

Nine members showed energy-level alignments suited to good hole extraction, while the rest looked unsuitable. Their absorption peaks fell between about 355 and 369 nanometres, fitting standard cell designs. The standout, bearing an amine group in the meta position, had the narrowest band gap at 2.70 electronvolts, the most red-shifted peak, and charge-separation metrics showing excellent separation, plus low reorganisation energy. The authors identify it as a highly hopeful hole-transport material for these cells.
pmc-13474677:
Shao and co-authors characterized a hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae strain cultured from the bone marrow of a 53-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, an almost unheard-of isolation site for this pathogen. Their 2026 study compared four matched isolates from his bone marrow, blood, liver abscess, and lung fluid, confirming all as the K1-ST700 lineage by typing and whole-genome sequencing.

His labs told the severity plainly: platelets had crashed to 7 billion per liter and procalcitonin, an infection marker, hit 17.83 against a normal ceiling under 0.5 in the reported units. Background mortality for such infections runs 28.4% at thirty days and 42% once invasive.
pmc-13474777:
Lingfei Zhang and colleagues review in 2026 how cell power plants reshape their fuel use in diabetic kidney disease. That disease is the top cause of long-term kidney failure worldwide. The review covers kidney and immune cell types one by one, since each handles fuel in its own way. A key thread is metabolic memory, where past high sugar keeps harming cells after sugar falls.

Chemical marks on genes and proteins help store that memory, and power plants sit at the center of the marks. Care ideas range from lab-stage compounds to drugs already in clinic use. Each is judged on how it resets fuel handling. Joining fuel science with gene-mark science opens fresh routes past current care limits.
pmc-13474977:
Sun and colleagues charted when acute aortic dissection strikes in east China in 2026, using records from 1,038 confirmed patients treated between 2009 and 2025. A dissection is a tear in the wall of the aorta, the body's main artery, and it kills quickly without care. The team looked for daily, weekly, and seasonal rhythms, and compared the two dissection types and men against women.

Men made up 73.9 percent of patients, and the average age was 55.7 years at the time of the tear. Onset peaked in the early evening, with 21.4 percent of cases starting between 5 and 8 pm, and dipped in the small hours after midnight. Winter carried the heaviest load at 32.6 percent of cases, while summer carried the lightest at 17.4 percent, a seasonal gap the analysis rated highly significant for hospital planning.
pmc-13475177:
Guckel and co-authors reviewed protected heart rhythm ablation in 2026, where machines support blood pressure while doctors burn away the faulty circuits causing dangerous ventricular rhythms. Support devices included a small heart pump called Impella, a lung-heart bypass called ECMO, and implanted assist pumps known as LVADs.

Support was used in 68 patients, or 36 percent of the group, and immediate procedure success and major complication rates matched unsupported cases. Deaths in hospital ran higher among supported patients, which the authors attribute to their worse starting condition rather than the procedure itself. Within advanced heart failure, patients on ECMO or an LVAD saw rhythms return more often, at a hazard ratio of 3.66, while Impella-supported patients showed no such penalty.
pmc-13475377:
Sanjeev Sockalingam and twenty colleagues published this 2026 report of a workshop rethinking the targets of obesity care. Fifteen themes emerged. Must-haves included genuinely multi-part care spanning drugs, behavioural support and surgery. They also required sensitivity training for healthcare providers, and valid outcome measures covering complications and patient-reported results. Should-haves added mental health tracking and personalised metrics. The won't-have list rejected stigmatising language, appearance-based success markers and short-term interventions. pmc-13477277:
Masayuki Nakamura and the REVEAL-HCM investigators present a 2026 Japanese registry study on sex differences in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a condition where heart muscle grows too thick. The analysis compares how women and men presented and which factors were linked to death from heart causes.

Once age, symptom severity, atrial fibrillation, and wall thickness were taken into account, much of the extra risk was explained. The findings point to later diagnosis and different heart shapes as part of the gap.
pmc-13478177:

Full-wave simulations confirmed effective focusing and improved matching in the 4 to 7 THz band. The design scales across frequencies, suiting THz imaging, new mobile links, satellite dishes, and radar where transmitter and receiver spots vary. The lens offers a low-profile option for flexible beam alignment.
pmc-13479377:
João Matos and eight colleagues reviewed in 2026 how fairness is measured in AI-based clinical prediction models. Predictive AI can improve care but also entrench bias, and what fairness itself means in this setting remains unsettled.

They screened 820 records from five databases covering 2014 to 2024, kept 42 studies, and pulled out 63 fairness metrics. The metrics formed a fragmented field, leaning on threshold-based measures with thin clinical validation; only 19 were built for health care, and just one for clinical use. Gaps in uncertainty reporting, intersectionality, and real-world fit lead the authors to urge clinically meaningful metrics first.
pmc-13479577:
Jianqiang Wang and coauthors published a 2026 survey study of adolescents in underdeveloped regions of China, linking childhood trauma, mental health, and the wish for emotional support from chatbots. The sample was very large at 14,380 middle school students. Standard questionnaires measured trauma history and mental health status, and students reported whether they wanted emotional support from generative artificial intelligence.

About 32 percent reported childhood trauma and about 17 percent had mental health problems. Machine learning with explanation tools identified which factors best predicted wanting chatbot support. Network and Bayesian analyses then mapped how trauma, symptoms, and support needs connect. The authors probe why current chatbot support shows limited benefit: the needs it must meet are tangled with trauma histories in ways a generic companion misses.
pmc-13479977:
Taoli Liu and coauthors published a 2026 study of light and hormones in rice tissue culture, focused on the Indica variety T98B. The authors present light as a hormone-tuning tool for faster transformation pipelines.
pmc-13480277:
Wadie David and colleagues report a 2026 pair of cases where heart closure devices broke loose and were fished out without surgery. Neither patient needed open surgery or suffered major harm. With plug use rising, the authors call for rehearsed rescue plans in every lab that fits them.
pmc-13480377:
Raquel Sánchez-Barquilla and co-authors present a 2026 surface science study on tuning a catalyst oxide with a rare-earth additive. Live microscopy and X-ray tools watched the islands shrink and rearrange under reducing gas, backed by computer models. Samarium seeded outside vacancies first, stretched the crystal lattice, and then coaxed more vacancies of the oxide's own kind, speeding the whole reduction and locking in reduced phases. pmc-13482277:
Llonch and colleagues ask which starting cells make the best stem cells for growing early human germ cells. Despite line-to-line variability, stem cells from both sources successfully formed the germ cell-like cells. Differences in X-chromosome state did not generally block the process. The findings guide future patient-specific studies of fertility disorders using whichever clinical sample is available.
pmc-13483677:
Wenxin Mu and colleagues review light-activated treatment for white patches inside the mouth that can precede cancer. Response was checked shortly after the first session and again after the final session, with follow-up for return of lesions.

The patches shrank by about three quarters on average after the full course, and nine in ten patients responded at least partly. Return of lesions was still common, affecting close to half the followed patients over roughly eleven months, and two patients progressed to malignancy. Thick surface tissue predicted return most strongly, while non-smoking status lowered the hazard. Measuring tissue thickness before treatment may help set expectations and follow-up intensity.
pmc-13484477:
Zhang and colleagues upgraded the cold-water pools used to test fertility in special rice lines whose pollen dies or survives depending on temperature and light. pmc-13486377:

Flipping the right switch could disable a master regulator.
pmc-13486477:
Pourmadadi and colleagues engineered a tiny starch-based carrier that releases a plant compound preferentially in acidic surroundings like those inside tumors. Their 2026 carrier wraps quercetin in a starch and polyacrylic acid gel stiffened with silica particles, built by a double emulsion method, which nests droplets inside droplets.

The carrier trapped about 80 percent of the quercetin offered and loaded it to nearly half its own weight in the best formulation. Particles averaged about 171 nanometers across, small enough to circulate and enter tissues. pmc-13487177:
Ying and colleagues built a survival-prediction chart for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer from a large United States registry, then checked it on Chinese hospital patients. The chart's discrimination held up across all three checks, scoring near 0.69 to 0.70 on the concordance measure used. Agreement between predicted and actual survival was good in the external group as well. Ying says the tool captures portable prognostic relationships, not just quirks of one database.
pmc-13487977:
Sophearen Ith and colleagues model how weather shapes herpangina risk in Japan in a 2026 analysis spanning 2001 to 2024. More than two and a half million cases were included. Risk peaked near moderate warmth and very high humidity, while rainfall raised risk at both very low and very high weekly totals. The authors say these patterns give health services lead time to warn families and prepare clinics before seasonal peaks arrive.
pmc-13488577:
Anat Dominsky Rozenfeld and co-authors study births during the COVID-19 pandemic at a large hospital in a 2026 review of past records. The team looked at women who gave birth to single babies over two years. Some women had the virus while pregnant, some were thought to have it, and most did not. Rates of early birth, surgery birth, and diabetes in pregnancy were set side by side. The records came from one big center that kept full charts.

Women with the virus had more early births than women without it in the reported figures. Surgery births also ran higher in that group. Diabetes in pregnancy was more common among women with the virus as well. The authors note that one hospital's records may not fit all places, and they ask for wider checks.
pmc-13489577:
Lini Sholihah and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis, published in 2026. It asks whether mothers' diets in pregnancy affect allergy in children. The team searched major databases. They covered studies from 2014 to 2024. Results were pooled across study types. These included randomised trials and cohort studies. A case-control study was also included.

Across 41 studies, one link stood out. Mothers' egg intake in pregnancy linked to lower odds of childhood eczema. It also linked to lower odds of food allergy. Vitamin D intake linked to less childhood rhinitis. Rhinitis is the nasal allergy condition. No clear links appeared elsewhere. Vitamin D showed no link with asthma. Fish oil showed no link with hay fever. The authors call for better-designed prospective studies.
pmc-13490377:
Duan and team asked whether steadier blood sugar protects muscle in older people with type 2 diabetes. Muscle wasting, called sarcopenia, stalks older diabetics, and a modern glucose marker, time in range, captures how long sugar stays in the target zone each day. Their 2026 study monitored 310 hospitalized patients aged sixty and older with wearable glucose sensors and assessed muscle mass, grip strength, and physical performance.

About 32 percent of patients met the sarcopenia criteria used in this hospital sample. Each ten-point rise in time in range came with about seventeen percent lower odds of sarcopenia after adjustment. Patients spending at least seventy percent of time in range faced about sixty-two percent lower risk than those under fifty percent. Time in range also rose in step with muscle mass and grip strength. Duan advises watching muscle closely in elders whose glucose runs out of range.
pmc-13490477:
Ge Yang and others determine the structure of the Nipah virus nucleocapsid, the protein shell that protects its genome. In 2026, the cryo-electron microscopy study resolves the building at near-atomic resolution without imposing helical symmetry, revealing irregular packing and bending that likely reflect the natural particle. Nipah virus is a lethal zoonotic germ with no approved vaccine or antiviral.

Detailed analysis maps contacts between nucleoprotein units and between protein and RNA, including a earlier unrecognized loop that bridges adjacent turns. Mutagenesis and minigenome tests confirm that these contacts support nucleocapsid hold. The structure refines understanding of viral building and exposes vulnerabilities that antiviral design could exploit.
pmc-13491677:
Susan Chinelo Ifeagwu and three co-authors analyze in 2026 who held health insurance in Uganda, where no national scheme was running, using the country's 2016 demographic and health survey. Knowing who manages to get coverage can guide the planned national program. The survey reached more than eighteen thousand women and five thousand men across the country.

Only a small share, about one person in seventy, had any insurance at all. Coverage climbed steeply with wealth and schooling, and insured people used health services more often. Being married, older, and wealthier each tracked with greater service use, as did simply knowing that insurance exists. The authors argue the national scheme will need public education campaigns and deliberate inclusion of informal workers and poorer households.
pmc-13491777:
Huanqi Tang and seven colleagues follow in 2026 a toddler with Sotos syndrome, an overgrowth and intellectual disability condition, who carried a gene variant never reported before. The seventeen-month-old boy showed the classic facial features of the syndrome along with severe speech and motor delay. Gene sequencing found a brand-new change in NSD1 that cuts the protein short and removes several working domains.

Despite continuous rehabilitation, the boy's developmental score slipped from the mid-forties to about forty by twenty-eight months, an unusually slow trajectory for this syndrome. Brain imaging showed an underdeveloped corpus callosum, the bridge between brain halves, and reduced white matter. The authors present the case as a warning that some variants bring heavier disability, strengthening the case for early genetic diagnosis and long multidisciplinary follow-up.
pmc-13492177:
Jag Lally and four colleagues tell in 2026 of a woman whose stubborn, fiercely itchy scalp psoriasis vanished only where doctors blocked a nerve. Her plaques had resisted creams and oral medicine, and insurance denial ended the one drug that helped temporarily. Reasoning that sensory nerves feed psoriatic inflammation, the team injected numbing medicine around both greater occipital nerves at the back of the head.

Nearly six months later her itch was gone and plaques had cleared exactly inside the territory those nerves supply, while psoriasis raged on in neighboring scalp she never treated otherwise. No creams or systemic drugs were used in the meantime. A single case cannot prove a therapy, yet the sharp anatomical border makes coincidence unlikely, and the authors propose nerve blocks as a cheap office-based option worth testing.
pmc-13492877:
Mahmood and colleagues surveyed in 2026 pregnant women in Mosul, Iraq, on their knowledge of pregnancy risk factors. Mosul's health system was badly damaged by conflict, making maternal knowledge vital. The cross-sectional study enrolled 420 women attending antenatal clinics between January and April 2024. A standard questionnaire measured knowledge, attitudes, and background factors.

The mean knowledge score was about sixteen out of thirty, a moderate level. Only about a quarter of women showed good knowledge of pregnancy risks. Scores were significantly higher in women with more education, urban residence, higher income, and private-sector antenatal care. The authors conclude knowledge gaps are wide and socially patterned in post-conflict Mosul. They argue interventions should target women with less schooling and those using public clinics.
pmc-13493977:
Johanna Liuhanen leads an eight-author team asking in 2026 whether inherited risk for schizophrenia also makes people crumble faster when kept awake. One hundred twenty healthy young adults endured thirty-eight hours without sleep in laboratory studies while a reaction-time test probed their vigilance every few hours. Each volunteer carried a polygenic risk score, a tally of thousands of small genetic contributions to schizophrenia.

Higher risk scores predicted steeper vigilance collapse, but only in women. The link peaked in the early morning window, between four and ten, when sleep deprivation bites hardest anyway. Men showed no such pattern at any hour. Whether this female-specific fragility reflects the disorder's underlying biology, and whether it extends to older adults, now needs direct testing.
pmc-13494077:
Donal J. Buggy and others examine whether people with type 2 blood sugar illness should stop or continue glucose-lowering drugs before elective surgery. In 2026, the secondary analysis covers a forward-looking study across twenty-one EU countries and eighty-nine centers, enrolling over five thousand people between 2021 and 2024. The main outcome is days alive and out of hospital within thirty days.

Continuing metformin on the day of surgery was linked to a small adjusted difference in that outcome, while no association emerged for SGLT2 blockers or GLP-1 dock agonists, where numbers were smaller. Guidelines conflict on this question, and the editors' key points lean toward continuing metformin, while noting that these data remain limited.
pmc-13494177:
Michael I McBurney and colleagues pool data from four omega-3 trials in a 2026 analysis of blood markers in healthy adults. The Omega-3 Index gauges how much of two fish-oil fats, EPA and DHA, sit in red blood cell walls. Earlier observational work tied a higher index to a lower neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, a simple inflammation marker drawn from a blood count, so the team tested whether supplements move both.

Pooling 436 people, they found the index rose on EPA plus DHA and fell slightly without them. The inflammation ratio dropped in the supplemented group and barely changed in controls, and bigger index gains went with bigger ratio falls. A second marker, red cell size spread, did not track with the index. The authors say trials in people with high inflammation markers are still needed to show whether these shifts change health outcomes.
pmc-13495277:
Seonmi Yun, Cheolhwan Kim, Koeun Jung, and Suk Won Han study, in a 2026 paper, how visual attention in healthy adults ties to social skill and problem behavior. Attention guides what the eyes take in first, and past work links it to social functioning in clinical groups. Fifty adults did a cueing task, where a hint shows where a target will appear, and filled two questionnaires on behavior and social life.

The classic cueing gain appeared: people answered faster when the cue was right. A bigger cueing gain went with fewer self-reported problem behaviors and with better social functioning scores. Problem behavior and social difficulty also tracked together. The authors read attention as one quiet support under everyday social life, even outside clinics, and suggest the link deserves study as a possible training target.
pmc-13495477:
Bekir Bogachan Akkaya and colleagues study, in a 2026 paper, how the heart's right side behaves just after aortic surgery. The right ventricle often looks weaker on scans after heart surgery, yet its measures may not fall in step. The team compared ultrasound measures before and soon after planned aortic operations in 102 patients.

All three right-side measures fell: lengthwise motion, area change, and a tissue speed. The lengthwise measure fell hardest, by about eighteen percent, against twelve for area change. A ratio joining the two, offered as an exploratory index, sat near one point one on average. The pattern did not differ between open and keyhole approaches, and the index showed no tie to recovery markers such as intensive care stay. The authors warn that a sagging lengthwise number alone may overstate true right heart trouble after surgery.
pmc-13495677:
Daniel K Arens and colleagues isolate, in a 2026 study, viruses that kill Enterococcus faecalis, the bacterium behind many failed root canals. The organism survives on little food and builds thick biofilms, shrugging off cleaning and antibiotics. The team fished fourteen such viruses, called phages, from wastewater and tested them against several bacterial strains, including two taken from mouths.

Several phages attacked a wide range of strains, up to sixteen, and held bacterial growth down even at low doses. They also tore into mature biofilms, cutting them by nearly all in the best tests. The authors present the set as fresh antibacterial agents for stubborn dental infections. The set also joins the growing library of phages aimed at this versatile pathogen, which drives urinary, heart, and wound infections too.
pmc-13498577:
Mekonnen Sisay and co-authors map in 2026 how multiple vitamin and mineral shortages cluster among women of childbearing age in Ethiopia, a problem often called hidden hunger. Shortages frequently overlap in one person, yet their geography was poorly known for non-pregnant women. The team drew on the 2015 national micronutrient survey, which recorded blood measures and home locations for women aged 15 to 49.

Among 1,450 women, about two in five carried several shortages at once across zinc, iron, iodine, folate, and vitamins A and B12 measures. Rates were highest in eastern areas, with hotspots around southern Afar, Dire Dawa, Harari, and eastern Oromia, plus parts of the Somali region. Spatial models linked the pattern to local factors, giving planners a map for directing supplements and food programmes where need concentrates.
pmc-13500477:
Shenghong Li and co-authors simulate in 2026 landslides of western Guizhou Province, China, in tabletop analogue models to learn how slope and layer stickiness steer collapse. Five experiments were built from field geological parameters of typical local slides, varying the topographic dip angle and the viscosity of a silicone layer standing in for a weak detachment surface. Deformation was watched as the models evolved under gravity.

Slides tended to start where dip angles ran high and discontinuity strength ran low in the experiments. Three deformation sequences emerged depending on conditions, with the back edge, middle, and front edge of the mass taking turns leading the movement. Matching patterns appear in real slides along a regional oil and gas pipeline corridor, which the authors cite to argue the models can guide disaster prevention, land-use caution, and early warning design.
pmc-13500677:
Bessala and colleagues swabbed surfaces in birth wards in Yaounde, Cameroon, hunting for the drug-resistant germs that threaten mothers and newborns in exactly the rooms meant to protect them. Hospital surfaces are a recognised reservoir for resistant germs, yet Central African wards had never been surveyed with both culture testing and full genome reading. Their 2026 study covered four wards, testing recovered bacteria against thirteen antibiotics and reading the full genomes of the resistant finds.

Nineteen isolates produced ESBL, the enzyme that defeats penicillins and newer cephalosporins, and most were multidrug-resistant. Two last-resort drugs still worked, but resistance to a third had already appeared, which the authors call alarming. Genome reading identified widespread lineages of E. coli and Klebsiella and plasmids, mobile DNA rings, carrying drug-defeating genes between strains. They urge far stricter cleaning in these wards.
pmc-13501577:
Shahrzad Abolhassanzadeh-Mahani leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 optimization study on packaging a probiotic bacterium together with its food source. The team co-encapsulated Lactobacillus brevis strain LSe and the prebiotic fibre fructo-oligosaccharide inside calcium alginate beads. A response surface method with a central composite design searched for the best recipe. The winning formulation used 3.0 percent sodium alginate, 1.2 percent prebiotic, and 2.0 percent calcium chloride by weight per volume.

That recipe trapped 84.7 percent of the bacteria initially and 99.2 percent after 24 hours, with small measurement spreads. Encapsulated cells also grew far better in culture than free cells, reaching an optical density of 0.70 against 0.15 in the comparison. In simulated stomach and intestinal juices, however, survival did not differ significantly between wrapped and free cells. The authors conclude the system's real strengths are loading and growth support for functional foods, not gut protection.
pmc-13501677:
Hanna Chidwick leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 study of care access for adolescent girls and young women in Uganda's artisanal and small-scale mining communities. These workers face mercury exposure and high HIV risk while living far from facilities. The work formed part of a larger mixed-methods project in Busia, Mubende, and Namayingo, drawing on surveys, interviews, focus groups, and talks with leaders and policymakers. Findings were analysed through the Tanahashi model of access to care.

The young women wanted facility care, including family planning, yet reported obstacle after obstacle: staff shortages, few youth-friendly services, scarce resources, long distances, and costs. Judgemental provider attitudes hit hardest, especially toward unmarried girls seeking reproductive care. Pockets of availability and acceptability existed, but contact coverage broke down. The authors argue for stronger health systems in mining areas, plus formalizing the sector and rights-based accountability from national policy.
pmc-13502377:
Brown and colleagues describe a teaching experiment in which nurse practitioner students practised talking with vaccine-hesitant patients in artificial intelligence simulations. Students in a paediatric primary care master's programme at a private university in the US Southeast completed two commercial simulation assignments, BodySwaps and Re:course AI. Each staged difficult conversations with virtual patients and caregivers and gave immediate feedback. The 2026 article reports how the students judged the experience.

Nineteen students completed the feedback survey, rating the Re:course AI scenarios more positively than BodySwaps on realism, ease of use, and usefulness for learning. Four fifths said they would choose AI simulation again in future courses, and about two thirds judged it as effective for learning as standardised patients or task trainers. The authors present AI roleplay as a safe rehearsal space for one of primary care's hardest conversations.
pmc-13502477:
Sunil K Jyani leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 toxicology case solved by asking about traditional medicines. A 55-year-old woman developed three months of worsening watery diarrhoea that turned to frequent black stools, then a painful stocking-pattern nerve injury. Her slippers slipped off unnoticed, and leg weakness advanced until she could no longer walk. She had taken unsupervised herbal preparations and Ayurvedic Bhasma, mineral-based remedies, for seven years. Testing stayed inconclusive because the classic skin signs of chronic arsenic poisoning were absent.

A careful medication history finally prompted heavy metal screening, and urinary arsenic confirmed chronic toxicity. The suspected preparations were stopped, and supportive care alone, with no chelation drugs, did the rest. Her gut symptoms and anaemia resolved, strength returned gradually, and she walked independently again. The authors stress considering arsenic in unexplained chronic diarrhoea with painful neuropathy, even when the skin looks normal.
pmc-13502977:
B. V Sumanth and others study subclinical hypothyroidism and lipid profiles among rural residents of Chamarajanagara District, India. In 2026, the hospital-based one-time study enrolls 496 adults aged eighteen to seventy-five, testing thyroid function and lipids, with 490 analyzed after exclusions. Subclinical disease means raised thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal thyroid hormone and no overt symptoms.

About sixteen percent met subclinical rules, and bad blood fats were more common in that group. The gap was driven by higher total blood fat and other blood fats, with triglyceride elevation in nearly sixty-nine percent versus thirty percent in euthyroid people. High- and low-density fat carrier did not differ. The authors recommend routine thyroid-stimulating hormone screening in medical practice.
pmc-13503277:
Daniel Maxwell and others examine data problems that undermine famine prediction and response. In 2026, the analysis covers availability, quality, timeliness, and sharing of data in famines and near-famine emergencies, where deep hunger more than doubled from 2023 to 2024, hitting Gaza and Sudan hardest. High-quality data are prerequisites for any credible model.

Biased, incomplete, inconsistent, or outdated inputs distort machine minds and machine learning tools, while misuse, weaponization, and politicization threaten analysis itself. The authors call for ethical data democratization, proactive sharing governed by ethical reasoning, to strengthen early warning, real-time analysis, and collective response.
pmc-13503777:
Wenbo Zhao and others report printed in 3D multi-coat stretchable circuits with slanted link gaps. In 2026, the work swaps standard punched upright holes, which focus stress and deform under stretching, with printed slanted between-coat links that spread stress and reduce Poisson-effect warp. Stretchable circuits promise worn tech, soft robots, and human-machine links.

The printed devices stretch to 646 percent strain and survive over 11,000 cycles at 100 percent strain, beating earlier multi-coat devices. Demos include a cord-free-powered display stable under large stretching and a four-layer body-hugging tracking system. The printing plan also widens design freedom and speeds making.
pmc-13503877:
Dongqi Cui leads a team linking faulty sleep spindles to poor social memory in autism, in a 2026 study. Social memory lets an animal tell a known peer from a stranger. Spindles are brief waves in light sleep that help lock in memories.

The team found weak spindles tied to weak social memory in mice. A small brain hub that gates sensory flow makes the spindles, and a class of fast neurons there drives them. Boosting that hub's path to a relay zone fixed spindles and social memory in mice with a gene fault tied to autism. The team also trained models that flag autism in children from spindle traits in sleep records. The work hints spindles could serve as a sign of the condition.
pmc-13504777:
Dania Hany M Elazzouni and others compare denture base materials after man-made aging. In 2026, the study tests standard heat-polymerized polymethyl methacrylate, CAD/CAM-milled polymethyl methacrylate, and 3D-printed photopolymerizable resin. Ten samples per group were tested at baseline and after five thousand thermocycles between five and fifty-five degrees Celsius. Denture longevity depends on surface integrity, mechanical durability, and heat hold.

Aging clearly roughened all materials, most for printed resin and least for milled polymethyl methacrylate, which also started hardest and lost least hardness. Printed resin softened most. The standard and printed resins gained mass, while the milled resin lost mass. Milled polymethyl methacrylate emerges as the recommended denture base for aging resistance.
pmc-13507277:
Xue Zhao, Shunmei Qiu, Changhong Ye, Xiaowen Sun, Yingying Luo, and Yuan Liu survey, in 2026 work, how mood relates to care dependence in older cataract patients in Guizhou, China. Cataracts cloud vision and daily independence, yet feelings may shape dependence beyond eyesight itself. The clinic study enrolled 452 patients in early 2025 and scored positive mood, negative mood, and self-regulatory fatigue, meaning depleted self-control stamina.

Brighter mood tied to greater independence and less fatigue, while darker mood tied to more dependence and more fatigue. Fatigue itself predicted dependence and carried part of both mood effects in the path model. Support programs might protect independence by easing emotional strain and restoring self-control energy.
pmc-13508277:
Hallie C Wright and others launch KhufuEnv, a helper toolkit for building computer workflows in plant and animal breeding. In 2026, the open-source system gathers genomic data handling and analysis tools into one buildable system, built for simple runs, single-threaded runs, and quick finishes. The NCBI Sequence Read Archive now holds over thirty-six petabytes, yet many tools handle only narrow formats.

Proof-of-concept tests found again known counted trait loci for cold hardiness in peanut and bare skin in dogs. They also found a possible sex-choice region in Amborella trichopoda, and worked out runs of same-gene shares in canines from shared data sets. Breeders and teams with minimal computer practice gain fast, flexible workflows for diverse species.
pmc-13508377:
Mehmet Emre Sezgin and three co-authors explore whether knowing how AI works relates to phone-related anxieties, in a small 2026 pilot study. Two digital states were tracked: fear of missing out, and nomophobia, the unease of being without a phone. Fear and phone anxiety scores came from 2019 and 2025, while AI literacy was measured in 2025. The team looked for patterns across those time points. Only thirty people took part, so the study brands itself exploratory from the start.

Trends hinted that higher AI literacy went with lower phone anxiety yet slightly higher fear of missing out. None of those interaction patterns reached statistical meaning. AI literacy was measured once, at the later date, which blocks any claim that it caused earlier states. They call for larger studies with repeated measures before anyone builds policy on AI literacy as a mental health lever.
pmc-13509177:
Jeongmi Lee and Seung Hyeun Lee introduce a special journal issue on closing the gap between lab discovery and bedside care in lung cancer, in a 2026 editorial. Treatment for both major lung cancer families has entered an era of precision care, the editors argue, powered by translation between bench and clinic. The issue gathers nine papers: eight original studies and one wide review. Topics span protein fingerprints of tumors, metabolic weak points, and radiation planning. Real-world results for immune drugs and messenger RNA vaccines as a fresh immune platform also feature.

These drugs first give striking response rates in patients with the right mutation. Resistance, though, almost always emerges and caps long-term survival, through side mutations or bypass routes. The editors say the collection breaks down walls between molecular biology and practice. Its shared goal is smarter treatment order and longer survivorship for lung cancer patients.
pmc-13509277:
Zhang and co-authors report in 2026 that a chemical cousin of sanguinarine, a plant alkaloid with known anti-tumor effects, fights osteosarcoma, the most common malignant bone tumor of adolescents. Sanguinarine itself is limited by poor water solubility and possible organ toxicity, so the team screened thirty related compounds for a better candidate. One, called analogue 25, stood out in tests on two osteosarcoma cell lines.

Analogue 25 suppressed growth of U2OS and MG63 cells, halting them at the G0/G1 checkpoint, with half-maximal effects around 1.48 and 1.95 micromoles per liter in the two lines. It pushed cells into apoptosis, programmed death, by raising cleaved caspase-9 and BAX. It also triggered ferroptosis, an iron-driven death route, through the NRF2 and GPX4 pathway after raising reactive oxygen species. In tumor-bearing mice it outperformed sanguinarine without liver or kidney toxicity.
pmc-13511177:
Stephanie Bowe and six co-authors review whether biologic immune drugs can be given safely to people who have had cancer, in 2026 work. These drugs transformed care for psoriasis, arthritis, and asthma, yet they dampen immunity, which raises fears of feeding a past or current cancer. Patients with cancer were shut out of the key trials, leaving doctors with thin direct proof.

Large health databases and real-world reports suggest the drugs can be used with care in some patients with a past cancer after joint discussion across specialties. Evidence for people with active cancer stays very limited, and most studies still exclude those with any cancer history. The authors call for longer follow-up and for registries that include such patients from the start, using new data tools to watch outcomes across wider groups.
pmc-13511377:
Arne Bokemeyer and seven co-authors pool German registry data to compare three biologic drug families for Crohn disease under routine care, in 2026 work. The analysis covered 1567 adults who started an anti-TNF drug, ustekinumab, or vedolizumab, drawn from three prospective registries joined in one data warehouse. Outcomes ran over 24 months and included remission on a standard bowel activity score, quality of life, and how long patients stayed on their drug.

After early treatment, remission was slightly more common with anti-TNF drugs than with the other two. By 24 months the picture flipped, with ustekinumab ahead of anti-TNF on remission while vedolizumab sat between. Staying on therapy differed too, highest for one anti-TNF drug and lowest for the other. Symptom scores fell and stayed low in all groups. The authors say overall performance was strong, with gaps that were real yet modest.
pmc-13511677:
Dominykas Varnas and Vaidotas Urbonas review the short-term safety of fecal microbiota transplantation in children at one Lithuanian hospital, in 2026 work. The treatment moves gut microbes from a healthy donor into a patient's bowel and is proven for repeated C. difficile infection, with use growing for other gut and mind-related conditions. Records covered 73 children who received 108 transplants by colon scope between 2017 and 2025, using material from three screened child donors.

About one procedure in ten brought a side effect within three days, all of them mild or moderate, with none rated serious. Loose stools were the most common effect, followed by vomiting. Rates differed by reason for treatment, with the lowest seen in procedures done for autism. The authors say scope-delivered transplantation looks safe in the short term for children, while noting that the underlying illness itself may shape risk and must guide future study design.
pmc-13512477:
