Jian Zhang and colleagues survey in 2026 hydrogel fibers, thread-like strands of water-rich gel, as building material for soft robots. Thin fibers respond faster than bulky gels because fluids reach their centers quickly, and shaping the fiber turns swelling into bending or twisting.

The review compares fiber designs: two-faced, layered, core-and-sheath, hollow, spiral, gradient, and woven forms, each converting swelling into a different motion. It also weighs production methods and triggers such as heat, light, and acidity against speed, force, durability, and ease of manufacture. Weak points include drying out, freezing, and drift when surroundings change. The authors close with design principles for moving these fibers from lab demos toward practical, autonomous soft machines.
pmc-13512877:
Andrés Mauricio Garcia-Sierra and six co-authors compare national health strategies and policy documents across selected Latin American and African countries, in 2026 work. Both regions juggle social inequality, environmental risk, and a double load of infectious and chronic disease. The study pairs strategy texts with epidemiological trends to find shared drivers and region-specific ones.

Systemic gaps recurred in access to care, environmental protection, and prevention, with primary care systems stretched thin in both regions. Health financing leaned heavily on outside support in many settings, and structural drivers sat beneath the headline disease figures. The authors press for stronger primary care, firmer domestic funding, and direct action on environmental determinants. Cross-regional exchange, they argue, can spread workable ideas faster than either region inventing alone, as long as local context shapes each adoption.
pmc-13513277:
Vieira and colleagues planted flowers in lawn turf in 2026 and watched which ones bees visited most. Mown lawns cover vast ground in the United States but give bees no nectar or pollen, and native bee numbers are falling. The team tested three clover types and common selfheal, all plants that stand up to close mowing.

Over two years at two sites, bees used every flower species planted, and they often picked certain blooms even when other flowers were more plentiful. For starting the plants in old turf, covering the ground with weed fabric or using herbicide worked best among five methods tried, which ranged from hard mowing to full soil turning. The authors say flower-rich turf strips can link green spaces and feed bees across towns.
pmc-13513377:
Zhongjun Gong and colleagues present a data resource paper, published in 2026. It profiles gene activity in the heads of three related scarab beetle pests. The species have different daily rhythms. Two emerge from the soil every twenty-four hours. The third follows a rare forty-eight-hour cycle. It is a major Asian crop pest. All three were sampled at one moment. The daily species were active then. The other was not.

Core clock genes showed similar activity across species. Vision and protein breakdown pathways differed. Behaviour, timing, and host plants all varied together. The authors present the data set strictly as a descriptive resource. It is for later rhythm research. It is not proof of any single cause.
pmc-13514677:
Noman Ahmed leads a ten-author team testing a feed additive for broiler chickens in a 2026 feeding trial. The additive, guanidinoacetic acid, is the raw material birds use to make creatine, a molecule central to muscle energy. The researchers combined three additive doses with two energy levels in the feed, including a diet cut by 100 kilocalories per kilogram. They raised 360 male Ross-308 chicks in thirty-six pens for thirty-five days.

The highest dose, 1.2 grams per kilogram, improved final weight, weight gain, feed efficiency, and carcass yields for breast and thigh, while meat lost less water in storage and cooking and showed better colour readings. The additive largely made up for the energy cut, keeping birds on the leaner diet growing well. Ahmed's team backs the top dose as a practical tool, especially for producers in hot climates.
pmc-13515477:
Kukolj and colleagues tested in 2026 how an epigenetic drug affects myeloma cells and the bone marrow support cells around them. The drug N-azacytidine can work against myeloma, but its effects on marrow stromal cells, which support blood formation and bone remodelling, were little known. The team treated a myeloma cell line and stromal cells from patients under low-oxygen conditions.

The drug strongly curbed the myeloma cells: metabolic activity, cell cycle progress, and marker expression all fell after seventy-two hours. Stromal cells, from both myeloma patients and healthy controls, kept their viability at the same doses. However, the drug did block mineralisation, the late step of bone building, at higher doses when stromal cells were exposed directly. The authors conclude the drug hits myeloma while largely sparing its support niche.
pmc-13516177:
Oliveira and colleagues studied a stem extract of Doyerea emetocathartica in 2026. The plant grows in Brazil's dry Caatinga region and is used in folk care for pain, so the team asked whether it truly relieves pain and how it acts. They measured its main component, cayaponoside D2, then tested the water-based extract in rats using two standard pain models.

The extract reduced pain behavior in both the acetic acid writhing test and the formalin test, with the clearest effects at the two higher doses. It worked mainly in the later, inflammatory phase of the formalin test. Blocking drugs showed the pain relief runs largely through mu opioid receptors, the same family morphine uses, with a smaller role for delta receptors. The extract held a notable amount of cayaponoside D2 per gram.
pmc-13517477:
Md Hashibur Rahman, Hyuncheol Jeon, Haham Kim, and Seunghyung Lee present a systematic evidence map, published in 2026. It covers functional fish feeds. These feeds help farmed finfish withstand stressful water temperatures. The authors followed PRISMA guidance. They organised feeding-trial evidence on special ingredients. The ingredients aim to support heat and cold tolerance. Immunity and stable metabolism are also aims.

The mapped trials point to several helpful ingredients. They include sodium butyrate, selenium, and astaxanthin. Probiotics, plant extracts, and algae products also help. They help most when several responses improve together. These include antioxidant defence and gut condition. Survival also improves. Evidence stays uneven across species and study designs. The authors call for more standardised trials, especially in marine fish.
pmc-13517677:
Wentao Fei and seven colleagues build a blood test for a costly cattle germ in a 2026 study. Mycoplasma bovis drives pneumonia, mastitis, and joint disease, shrugs off whole antibiotic families, and has no good vaccine, so herds need early, accurate detection. Their competitive ELISA uses a lab-made protein from the germ as bait and a tagged antibody that fights the animal's own antibodies for the binding spots.

Validation ran strong: ninety percent sensitivity, about ninety-six percent specificity, and no confusion with related germs. Repeat runs varied by less than ten percent. Among over a thousand field samples, about fifty-six percent tested positive, and agreement with a shop-bought test topped ninety percent. Extra checks on disputed samples favoured the new test's accuracy. Fei's team offers it as a dependable herd-screening tool for a pathogen that hides well and spreads fast.
pmc-13519077:
Dahlgaard and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of a drug target called claudin 18.2 in stomach and junction cancers.  The team pooled studies that tested paired samples: the primary tumor and a metastasis from the same patient.

Eleven studies with 896 paired samples were pooled. About one in five pairs disagreed: a tumor positive for the target could have a negative spread site, or the reverse. That discordance is large enough to matter, because a patient can be offered or denied a targeted drug based on which lump was sampled. The authors argue that testing only the primary tumor misclassifies a real share of patients. Re-testing spread sites, or testing both, would sharpen who gets these new drugs.
pmc-13520177:
Karissa Hough, Matthew Sclafani, and Russell Burke track diamond-backed terrapins in 2026 with satellite tags at two Long Island, New York sites. These small salt-marsh turtles are imperiled, and older radio methods suggested tiny home ranges under a square kilometer. Twenty-one adult females carried Argos satellite tags, and the location data were cleaned three different ways for comparison.

Home range estimates barely changed across processing methods and covered the same areas. Distance measures agreed between the two model-based cleanups, while using only top-quality fixes doubled them. Ranges and movement looked similar at both sites despite differing urbanization. Satellite results also showed larger ranges than older methods found, reshaping conservation thinking for the species.
pmc-13520277:
Limei Cui leads a five-author systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026 grading how accurately large language models sort emergency department patients by urgency, compared with triage nurses. Eight databases yielded 11 studies covering 3,088 real or simulated cases through March 2025.

Pooled accuracy comparisons against nurses were inconclusive, with an odds ratio of 0.65 amid very high inconsistency between studies. For spotting the sickest patients, models caught only 61 percent while correctly clearing 97 percent of others, giving moderate overall discrimination. Cui and colleagues conclude the tools might assist triage as adjuncts, yet their weak sensitivity for critical cases bars unsupervised use until prospective safety trials are done.
pmc-13522077:
Del Arco and colleagues ask in 2026 whether exercise-based prehabilitation, training begun before surgery to build physical readiness, reduces pain after breast cancer surgery. The approach helps in other operations, but its effect on pain here was unsettled.

The systematic review gathered six randomized trials with 519 women. Their programs ran from one to nine weeks and mixed aerobic work, resistance training, mobility, and stretching. Only three trials, with 157 women, could be pooled for the main outcome of pain one month after surgery. The pooled result pointed slightly toward less pain with prehabilitation, but the difference was small and statistically non-significant, and the estimate rested on few studies. The authors describe the programs as safe and feasible, and call for larger, higher-quality trials.
pmc-13522477:
Santoro and colleagues published a 2026 study of higher-order brain models, which track how groups of brain regions act together rather than in pairs. Many such tools exist, drawn from information theory and topology, but nobody had mapped how they differ. Pairwise maps alone miss group dynamics that shape thought and behaviour.

Using resting and task brain scans from one hundred Human Connectome Project subjects, Santoro grouped the metrics into redundant, synergistic, and topological families. All families followed the brain's gradient from sensing areas up to higher areas, yet each one told a slightly different story. Higher-order tools beat pairwise maps at telling people apart from their scans. Pairwise models stayed strong at saying which task a person was doing.
pmc-13522577:
Sigurpalsdottir and colleagues used nanopore sequencing in 2026 to read DNA methylation, chemical marks that help control gene activity, across an unusually large set of blood samples. Most methylation studies cover far fewer people or far fewer sites. By sequencing long DNA strands directly, the team could map marks across the whole genome and even tell which parent a stretch of DNA came from.

They analyzed 7,284 whole blood samples and covered about 17.96 million CpG units, the sites where methylation usually occurs, reporting that over twenty percent of sites changed with age, mostly through hypomethylation, a gradual loss of marks. A clock built from 1,373 CpG sites estimated age with a median error of 2.43 years across donors. They also found 702 parent-of-origin-specific age-related sites, mostly at imprinted genes, including paternal-allele hypermethylation at DIRAS3 that grew with age.
pmc-13522777:
Tanvi Varadkar leads a team combining two targeted treatments for triple-negative breast cancer in a 2026 study. This aggressive subtype lacks the usual hormone targets, spreads readily, and often returns after treatment. One treatment links an antibody aimed at a surface protein called CD276 to a cell-killing drug. The other is a gene therapy platform directed at mitochondria, the energy centers of the cell.

Together the treatments killed cancer cells more strongly than either alone across three cell lines, harmed mitochondrial function, and raised immune activity in tumors. Spread was suppressed in mice, and tumors in patient-derived grafts shrank almost completely. Body weight and tissue checks suggested low overall toxicity. The authors argue the pairing deserves further development for hard-to-treat disease.
pmc-13523277:
Hyung Gyu Jeon and co-authors compare knee loading during running in people with chronic ankle instability in a 2026 biomechanics study. Twelve patients with the condition and twelve controls ran in a laboratory while a musculoskeletal simulation estimated forces inside the knee joint and the contribution of each leg muscle. Ankle instability is known to alter leg mechanics, raising concern about early joint degeneration at the knee.

Patients showed greater backward and sideways knee shear forces than controls, plus a larger total compressive load over time, although peak compression did not differ. Stronger quadriceps contribution drove the extra loading. The authors suggest rehabilitation that addresses coordination of muscles above the ankle may help protect the knee in people whose ankles remain unstable after sprains.
pmc-13523477:
Michelle Hill and Jenni Godsell report a 2026 qualitative study of Australians living with severe difficult-to-treat hypertension, meaning blood pressure that stays above target despite proper medicine use. Over one third of Australian adults have hypertension. The interviews also probed awareness of renal denervation, a procedure on kidney nerves offered as a treatment option.

Twelve participants, average age 65 and diagnosed on average 22 years earlier, took part in hour-long interviews online or by phone. Analysis produced four themes covering diagnosis and monitoring, effects on quality of life, day-to-day management, and views of renal denervation. Participants described a heavy burden and stigma linked with the condition. The authors urge services to add psychosocial support and patient education to standard clinical care for this group.
pmc-13525577:
Correale and co-authors examine a measurement problem at the heart of trials for developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, the severe childhood conditions where seizures arrive with profound learning and behaviour difficulties. For many families the non-seizure burdens matter more than seizure counts, and gene-targeted treatments are coming, yet the standard tests of cognition and adaptive behaviour were built for other populations. Their 2026 review surveys the issues and the available instruments.

Common tools suffer floor effects here: children cluster at the lowest possible scores, so real but small improvements, the kind families notice at home, vanish from the data. The authors recommend developmentally appropriate measures, alternative scoring that credits small steps, careful session planning to reduce missing data, and blending numbers with qualitative reports. They close by asking for proper validation work in these rare populations before pivotal trials lock in endpoints.
pmc-13526777:
Lim and colleagues survey how the world feels its air in this 2026 study spanning the ten most populous countries, from India and China to Nigeria and the United States. A quota sample of 10,618 respondents across 1,372 localities answered questions on knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, practices, and concern about air quality, and answers were matched against each area's fine particulate pollution levels.

A paradox emerged: people breathing dirtier air knew less about air quality yet worried more. Higher particulate exposure tracked with lower knowledge scores but higher concern, more protective practices, and stronger attitudes about pollution. The patterns bent with demographics, including age, sex, education, urban or rural residence, political ideology, and smoking status. The authors argue that information campaigns should target the most exposed communities, whose concern is high but whose knowledge lags, and tailor messages to the demographic groups each exposure level actually contains.
pmc-13526877:
Li and colleagues built an artificial tactile interneuron in 2026 that copies how the spinal cord fuses touch signals before they reach the brain. Human touch merges strain, pressure, and temperature into compact spike patterns that carry object properties. Their device joins three sensor types with a memristor neuron, an electronic element that fires like a nerve cell, on one hybrid platform.

The system emits unified burst spike trains whose timing encodes an object's size, hardness, and temperature in a single stream, ready to feed a spiking neural network. On a twenty-class object recognition task, the hardware-based encoding paired with a software network reached accuracy above ninety percent. The authors present the design as a compact, low-power route to multimodal touch for intelligent edge devices, machines that must sense and decide locally without a data center.
pmc-13527277:
Hong-Hsi Lee and colleagues derive, in a 2026 theory and simulation study, how water diffusion outside brain cells depends on the mix of cell bodies and neurites in gray matter. Diffusion MRI infers tissue microstructure from water movement, and the long-time limit of outside-cell diffusion anchors such models. White matter relations were known, while gray matter's mixed geometry blocked a formula.

Borrowing effective medium theory from nineteenth-century conductivity problems, the team coarse-grained tissue as spheres for cell bodies and cylinders for neurites embedded in a matrix. Closed-form expressions gave power-law scaling of outside-cell diffusivity with the volumes of the spaces around each element. Monte Carlo simulations and realistic tissue geometries corroborated the formulas, and in vivo MRI data were fitted as a demonstration. A protocol for measuring cell body size follows.
pmc-13527477:
Yasmine Gillespie, Alexander M Hammond and Kiran Motaparthi published this 2026 case. She was a 60-year-old woman with kidney disease and hypertension, treated for three years with hydralazine, a blood pressure drug. She presented with one day of purple spots on her feet and fingers, plus worsening breathlessness. Urine tests showed blood and protein, creatinine had crept up, and a chest scan found a cavitary lung nodule.

Skin biopsy showed small-vessel vasculitis, and blood tests revealed high levels of both major ANCA antibody types, alongside anti-histone and anti-DNA antibodies and low complement. Kidney biopsy showed pauci-immune glomerulonephritis, the kidney pattern of ANCA vasculitis. Weighing the drug history, the authors settle on hydralazine-induced ANCA vasculitis as the diagnosis. Her kidney and lung problems improved after stopping hydralazine. They stress that recognition matters, since steroids are the mainstay once the drug is withdrawn.
pmc-13527977:
Wen Xu and ten colleagues report a 2026 study using body composition scans to predict outcomes in advanced lung cancer. The patients had non-small cell lung cancer treated with combined immuno-chemotherapy and radiotherapy. The team studied 87 patients. From scans at the third lumbar vertebra they extracted texture features, called radiomics, from muscle and fat tissue.

Six machine learning models were built from the best features. A combined model adding a total fat index performed best. Its area under the curve reached about 0.86 in training data and 0.83 in test data. Patients labeled high risk had clearly shorter progression-free survival. The authors propose the model could flag who benefits most from adding radiotherapy. Larger confirming studies would still be needed.
pmc-13528077:
Katsuya Ueno and eight colleagues report gene findings in Dandy-Walker malformation in a 2026 study. The condition is a birth defect of the back of the brain. The cerebellum's middle part is partly or fully missing, and a cyst fills the space. Three patients had whole-genome sequencing. Two carried variants in tubulin genes, named TUBB2B and TUBB3.

Tubulin faults are known to shrink the cerebellum in other disorders. Finding them here suggests some Dandy-Walker cases belong to that family of diseases. The classic genetic culprits for this malformation sit in other genes entirely. A genome-first approach caught what targeted thinking might miss. The authors urge adding tubulin genes to the workup of similar cases. More patients are needed to show how often this overlap occurs.
pmc-13529077:
Kaushal and colleagues tested whether a structured educational video shown before elective cesarean section lowers mothers' anxiety, in a 2026 randomized trial that paired questionnaires with brain-wave measurements. Ninety first-time pregnant women having planned cesareans under spinal anesthesia took part. They were assigned to routine counseling alone or routine counseling plus the video, with anxiety measured at baseline and again shortly before surgery.

Kaushal found the video group reported clearly lower anxiety scores before surgery than controls. They also showed lower theta-beta ratios, a brain-wave pattern linked to anxious arousal, both before and an hour after surgery. Questionnaire scores and the brain measure correlated positively, supporting the brain signal as an objective anxiety marker. The video group also needed sedative medication during surgery far less often, at about one in nine women versus one in three. That makes the cheap video an easy addition to routine care.
pmc-13529777:
Deming Wang and colleagues built the first large, finely labeled video dataset for minimally invasive glaucoma surgery. Published in 2026, the multicenter dataset holds millions of frames marked for surgical tools and anatomy. Glaucoma surgery is intricate and technique-sensitive, so computer navigation aids need precise training data to guide surgeons safely.

Labels support two tasks: recognizing surgical phases and segmenting tools and anatomy pixel by pixel. The resource aims to train vision models that assist in real time, improving precision and safety during operations that lower eye pressure. By pooling cases across centers, the dataset also broadens the range of anatomy and technique models must handle. Readers get a foundation for computer-assisted glaucoma surgery, with model building still to follow.
pmc-13530177:
Hakan Isık and co-authors introduce a 2026 forecasting network for chlorophyll levels that warn of algal blooms in the Black Sea. Satellite records from 15 estuary stations supplied the time series. Their design joins a memory-based neural network with exponential smoothing feedback, trained by a new arithmetic-mean search method.

Head-to-head tests against shallow and deep rival models covered many separate series. The new design won on standard error measures in most cases and took the best overall ranking. Formal statistical tests confirmed the gains were unlikely to be chance. Managers could use such forecasts for earlier bloom warnings.
pmc-13531877:
Saffet Ulutas and colleagues test in 2026 a black seed compound, thymoquinone, on infected diabetic wounds in rats. Diabetes was induced, wounds were cut and seeded with staph bacteria, then groups received the compound in peanut oil, plain oil, a standard antibiotic cream, or nothing for 14 days.

Wounds on the compound closed far faster than untreated or oil-only wounds, matching the antibiotic cream without beating it. Bacterial counts dropped sharply by days three and seven. Microscopy showed better surface regrowth, more repair tissue and collagen, and fewer inflammatory cells, supporting a dual healing and germ-fighting action.
pmc-13532777:
Heidi Taipale and colleagues use Swedish national records from 2009 to 2024 to study diabetes drugs in people with bipolar disorder. Diabetes, excess weight, and bipolar disorder often occur together, yet effects of GLP-1 drugs on bipolar care were unknown. The cohort held 14,694 people who used any diabetes drug.

Comparisons within each person showed semaglutide linked to a lower risk of hospital care for mental health reasons. Two other drugs in the same class showed no such link, and sick leave showed no clear link. Readers see an early signal that needs a randomised trial to confirm.
pmc-13534377:
Yuma Shiomi and colleagues present in 2026 a non-radioactive lab method to measure activity of ornithine decarboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in polyamine production. Polyamines support cell growth and must stay tightly controlled, yet older assays need radioactive materials and special facilities. Their method feeds cells a labelled form of ornithine instead.

Labelled product was measured by liquid chromatography with mass checks, with clear peaks in test samples and near-zero signal in controls. Tweaks to time and dose kept results linear and precise, and a known blocker lowered activity as expected. Labs gain a safer tool for polyamine research.
pmc-13534677:
Donna Li and a large team report an immunology study in mice, published in 2026. It covers two tiny chemical change sites on a signalling protein called NEMO. DNA damage triggers changes at these sites. The changes activate the NF-kappaB pathway, a master immune switch. The team engineered mice whose NEMO cannot be changed at the matching positions.

The engineered mice had B cells that formed germinal centres poorly. Their antibody responses to viruses were weaker. The team traced the fault to a CD40-specific signalling defect. Without sustained modification of NEMO, a downstream switch called RelA stayed weak. This blocked the gene programmes B cells need. They need them to multiply and produce antibodies.
pmc-13536577:
Alyssa Sales and colleagues explore in 2026 how people view tongue swab testing for tuberculosis in Viet Nam and Zambia. Millions of TB cases go undiagnosed each year, and sputum collection is hard for many patients. Interviews between late 2023 and early 2024 covered 76 patients, caregivers, and health workers.

Most people preferred tongue swabs, calling them comfortable and easy compared with coughing up sputum. Trust in staff, hygiene, spread risk, result speed, and above all test accuracy shaped acceptance. Swab testing looks workable for wider use if accuracy holds up in daily practice.
pmc-13536677:
Bijing Wu and colleagues offer a 2026 review of CAR-T cell therapy, a treatment that retools patient blood cells to attack cancer. The therapy has produced strong remission rates in blood cancers that returned or resisted other care, yet many patients relapse and solid tumors respond poorly. The review organizes failure, improvement, and rescue options into a single guiding framework.

Failure is traced to tumor changes such as loss of the target, tired or short-lived T cells, and a surrounding tissue environment that suppresses attack. Proposed fixes include drug combinations, dual-target designs, and newer cell types such as engineered natural killer cells. Rescue options after failure range from switching targets to stem cell transplant. The authors argue that matching treatment to measured markers offers the clearest path forward.
pmc-13536877:
Mohadeseh Jafari and co-authors track drug resistance markers in malaria parasites from southeastern Iran in a 2026 study of one hundred isolates collected in 2022 and 2023. Three genes tied to drug response were typed for known changes, and results were compared with samples from the same region about a decade earlier. Shifts in single changes and in combined gene patterns were examined for treatment implications.

A classic chloroquine resistance change remained nearly universal despite the drug withdrawal, possibly sustained by related malaria in the area. Other changes shifted notably, including a rise in a pattern linked to weaker response to a current partner drug. Changes in the third gene were common yet showed no immediate threat to the main combination therapy. The authors urge continued marker watching.
pmc-13538377:
L. T. Sun and colleagues uncover how colon cancer cells survive sugar shortage in a 2026 cell study. Fast growth and poor blood supply leave tumor centers starved of glucose, yet cells keep dividing. Focus falls on fumarate hydratase, an energy cycle enzyme that runs low in this cancer and normally restrains growth. Starvation tests, gene activity checks, and protein tracking traced a chemical tagging process on the enzyme.

Starved cells tagged the enzyme for destruction through a cleanup route, letting its raw materials pile up. Piled fumarate stabilized a protective protein that raised two guards against iron-driven cell death, letting cancer cells keep growing. The authors frame the enzyme and its tagging as fresh drug targets for blocking starvation adaptation in colon cancer.
pmc-13538677:
Tushar Mehta and Mukesh Meena combine tissue, chemical, and imaging analyses to explain a maize fungus's attack in a 2026 study. The fungus causes leaf spot disease, yet how infection and toxins interact stayed unresolved. The strain was confirmed by multi-gene sequencing, and its metabolite mix was profiled. Young maize plants faced live fungus, crude extract, or purified lead toxin in parallel.

The lead toxin dominated the mix alongside three other compounds. Treated plants developed spreading dead and yellowing lesions, with severe pigment loss, membrane leakage, and fat oxidation, plus reactive oxygen buildup and cell collapse under imaging. Defense enzymes surged but failed to contain damage. Live fungus hurt most, then crude extract, then pure toxin. The authors credit combined metabolite action plus oxidative stress as the core drivers.
pmc-13539677:
Hyeseon Yun and Eun Kyoung Choi develop and pilot a web-based program that builds resilience in mothers who faced childhood adversity in a 2026 feasibility study. Harmful childhood experiences can pass between generations through parenting stress, so boosting maternal resilience is a prevention target. Built under a complex intervention framework and a nursing adaptation model, the eight-session group program ran online. Five South Korean mothers with multiple adverse experiences and preschool children piloted it.

Retention and attendance ran high, and satisfaction scores were near the top of the scale. Resilience and parenting behavior scores improved significantly in the small pilot, with health, self-esteem, competence, and mother-child interaction trending favorably. Participant feedback refined the program. The authors present the theory-driven design as a template for breaking intergenerational cycles.
pmc-13539877:
Luana Marques leads a 2026 case-control study following preterm children who were born with infections grouped under the name STORCH, which covers syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes. Such infections often pass unnoticed in pregnancy yet can harm brain development.

The study tracked 248 preterm children over their first two years, comparing those with congenital infection against those without. Infected children scored lower on thinking and language measures, and their thinking scores slipped between six and eighteen months, though movement scores improved. Intensive care seizures, sepsis, family income, and birth factors shaped outcomes in both groups. The authors stress preventing these infections early in pregnancy.
pmc-13540877:
Pratyasha Sharma, Srikala Bhandary, Sayan Das, and Syed Taha review, in a 2026 systematic review, mouth symptoms tied to food allergy in children. Such signs can be the first visible clue of allergy and may affect eating, dental health, and quality of life.

Four databases were searched through December 2025, leaving twelve paediatric studies. Itching and tingling of the lips, tongue, and palate right after eating specific foods, especially fruits and nuts, were the commonest reports, with mild swelling of lips and mouth lining close behind. The pattern fits oral allergy syndrome, mostly in school-aged children also sensitive to pollen. The authors urge dentists to recognise and refer these children early.
pmc-13542177:
Jie Ma and colleagues propose an image method in 2026. The method merges visible and infrared pictures. It also clears smoke in a single pass. Older pipelines de-smoke first and fuse later. That order stacks errors and heavy computation. The new design is lightweight by intent.

Convolutional layers read local detail in each picture. Transformer blocks read global context across the scene. Both sit inside an encoder-decoder frame. Training ran in two stages. A small internal network suppresses smoke within the features. Tests spanned several smoke densities. The method beat mainstream fusion rivals on sharpness and error scores. The authors pitch it for surveillance use.
pmc-13542277:
Agnieszka Budnik and colleagues published a 2026 population study testing whether blood proteins known from heart research also track with age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. The analysis used the Białystok PLUS cohort in Poland, covering 699 people aged 50 and over who had eye photographs graded for the disease. Ninety-three participants had macular degeneration, and 92 cardiovascular proteins were measured in their blood serum.

After accounting for age, three proteins stood out. People with the eye disease had lower galectin-4 and lower TNFRSF10C, a receptor involved in cell-death signalling, alongside higher von Willebrand factor, a protein tied to blood vessels and clotting. Each marker alone separated cases from non-cases only modestly. Still, the pattern supports shared vessel and inflammation pathways between heart and eye disease, and the authors suggest such markers might eventually sharpen early risk screening.
pmc-13543377:
Florian Jaklin and colleagues published a 2026 ultrasound study challenging the idea that Morton's neuroma, a painful thickening of a nerve between the toes, is usually a one-foot problem. Every patient referred with suspected neuroma between January 2023 and December 2024 received a standardised scan of both forefeet, whatever side hurt. Enlargements of at least three millimetres counted as lesions, and the team recorded their spaces, sizes, and symmetry.

The 226 patients carried 568 lesions between them, concentrated between the third and fourth toes. Fully eighty-one percent had lesions in both feet. Among patients with symptoms on one side only, three quarters still had a lesion on the painless side, and bilateral cases were usually mirror images. Size related to position and shape, not to whether a lesion hurt. Routine two-foot scanning, the authors suggest, better captures the true burden of this condition.
pmc-13544877:
Swati Gupta and colleagues published a 2026 letter describing bilateral Rasmussen encephalitis combined with cortical venous thrombosis, a pairing not previously reported. Rasmussen encephalitis is a rare inflammatory brain disorder causing drug-resistant focal seizures and shrinkage of one hemisphere, usually in children. A 25-year-old man had lived with poorly controlled focal seizures since age eight. Over the previous year he grew dependent and began seizing on the other side too, pointing to the second hemisphere.

He arrived in continuous seizure activity, deeply drowsy, with facial and limb jerking on the left and a weak eye movement. Scans showed marked shrinkage of the left hemisphere and a fresh stroke-like lesion on the right. Bilateral disease rules out the hemisphere-removal surgery used in one-sided cases, leaving immune treatments such as steroids and immunoglobulin. Only about sixteen bilateral cases were documented worldwide, making each report valuable.
pmc-13547177:
S Deidda and a multicenter team ran a 2026 randomized trial comparing two gels for wounds after open hemorrhoid surgery, a procedure known for painful recovery. One hundred nineteen patients received either a gel made from a bacterial extract or a standard ointment combining hyaluronic acid and silver sulfadiazine. Healing was graded by how much new skin covered the wound, and patients scored pain, burning, and itching over 40 days.

Both products eased pain similarly. Yet the bacterial extract gel healed wounds faster, with complete healing in about 85 percent of its patients by day 40, against about 52 percent for the ointment. Burning and itching also eased more, and satisfaction was far higher, with no reported side effects.
pmc-13548177:
Xu and colleagues ran a discrete choice experiment in 2026 on what Chinese residents want from supplementary voluntary health insurance, extra private cover bought on top of public schemes. Knowing preferences helps design plans people will join. More than 1,300 people in three provinces weighed paired plans that varied in premium, benefit package, deductible, payout rate, and cover for preexisting conditions, with an opt-out.

The payout rate mattered most, at about a third of total importance, ahead of premium cost at about a quarter. Respondents would pay the most, near fifty US dollars, to lift the payout rate from half to nine tenths of a bill, and least to cut the deductible. People with sharper risk awareness, stronger insurance knowledge, better number skills, higher education, income, and urban homes showed stronger interest and higher willingness to pay. The authors urge targeted education and varied plan designs.
pmc-13548577:
Conrad Oakes and Lior Pachter reanalyze a large rat exercise dataset in a 2026 transcriptomics study. A national consortium had mapped molecular changes across nineteen tissues as rats trained in endurance exercise over time. Working from the public RNA sequencing data, the pair asked whether gene activity could reveal how much training an animal had done, and whether finer gene-isoform detail hid extra signals.

Gene expression patterns predicted training amount with striking accuracy. Looking at isoforms, the alternative versions of genes produced by splicing, exposed biologically meaningful differences that whole-gene counts had masked. Screening for viral traces turned up a possible new virus that may have dragged down some physical measurements. The authors offer their approach as a template for squeezing more from big molecular datasets in other species and conditions.
pmc-13550377:
Jing Zhang and colleagues link a splicing factor's disappearance to doxorubicin resistance in breast cancer cells, in a 2026 bioinformatic study. Alternative splicing, the remixing of gene messages, goes wrong in cancer and can help tumors resist drugs. The team compared resistant MCF7 cells with their drug-sensitive parents and catalogued the splicing changes. They hunted for splicing factors whose loss tracks with those changes. A large patient cohort helped them build the correlation network.

Resistant cells showed widespread splicing shifts and sharply reduced ESRP1, a splicing factor of epithelial cells. Sixty-one splicing events tied confidently to its levels. Four affected genes help organize the cell's skeleton, fitting a picture where splicing rewires cell shape for survival under drug pressure. With only two samples per group, the authors flag the work as hypothesis-grade and call for bigger validation.
pmc-13551677:
Nefert Candace Dossou, leading ten colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study of respiratory syncytial virus in older adults across four university hospitals in north-western France. RSV is known mainly as a children's virus, and adult burden is undercounted because hospital coding serves billing purposes. The cohort covered everyone aged 60 or older who tested positive during the 2022-2023 season, from September to January.

The study included 647 patients with mean age near 78 years, most carrying a chronic respiratory or cardiac condition. About four fifths were hospitalized, oxygen was needed in over two thirds of cases, and in-hospital mortality reached 11 percent in the reported figures. Many survivors were readmitted within 90 days or lost autonomy, underlining a heavier burden than coding suggests.
pmc-13551777:
Adria Lopez-Gramaje, with nine colleagues, published a 2026 study of how liver disease dulls thought. In cirrhosis, a mild brain disorder follows a shift toward inflammation in the body. A drug called rifaximin can reverse that shift. The team took tiny packets shed into blood, called vesicles, from patients. They injected the packets into rats and tested the rats' thinking and brains.

Packets from sick patients carried more of a key inflammatory protein. They caused strong thinking harm in rats. Brain inflammation rose, and glutamate receptors shifted in the memory center. Packets from drug-treated patients lost the extra cargo. They also lost the harmful effect. The team argues the packets carry the signal from body to brain.
pmc-13554077:
Vakkalakula Bharath Sreenivasulu and Narasimhulu Thoti compare three tiny transistor designs for future computer chips in a 2026 study. Transistors keep shrinking, and the gate-all-around style now leads the race below three nanometres. Their two new designs add upright bridge channels to widen the path for current. A standard sheet design served as the yardstick in careful three-dimensional simulations.

Both new designs drove stronger current than the standard sheet. The bridge design with the fullest channels scored highest and held up best as parts shrank. Tests of signal gain and speed also favoured the new shapes. Circuit trials showed faster switching and quicker ring circuits at every voltage tried. The authors back both designs for fast logic and radio chips.
pmc-13554177:
Joshuan J Barboza leads a six-author team pooling trials of a steroid given around children's heart surgery in a 2026 analysis. The drug, methylprednisolone, is meant to calm the body-wide inflammation that heart-lung machines stir up. Eight trials with 1,735 children were gathered from five databases. Death in hospital or within thirty days served as the main outcome.

The drug did not cut deaths in any clear way across the pooled trials. Children on the drug did leave breathing machines a little sooner, by about a quarter of a day. High blood sugar struck more than twice as often under the drug, though. Infection rates and intensive care stays matched the control groups. The authors weigh a small breathing gain against that sugar risk.
pmc-13554777:
Daisuke Miyahara and colleagues study heart-lung links after mitral edge-to-edge repair. Its value in functional mitral regurgitation was unclear. Their 2026 study covers 1,059 patients with functional mitral regurgitation who had repair. It was scored after repair as TAPSE over systolic lung artery pressure.

Impaired links, defined as TAPSE over SPAP below 0.36, hit 30.7 percent of patients after repair. The impaired group showed lower event-free survival, and the impairment predicted the composite outcome on its own. The link ran stronger when lung pressure was high. Diabetes, lower ejection fraction, smaller left ventricle, and larger left atrium before repair also predicted impairment.
pmc-13555977:
Myriam Mrad and ten colleagues published a 2026 proposal for a national registry that would track diseases linked to climate change in Lebanon. The country faces sharp swings in weather, heavy air pollution, and a weak health system, yet it has no single system that joins environmental data with health data. Their work asks how far existing surveillance can capture climate-sensitive illness and what a shared registry would need.

The team reviewed surveillance models from around the world and the region. They also consulted officials, academics, clinicians, and aid groups. Their review found that some outcomes sit inside disease-specific systems, while long-term conditions, mental health, and extreme weather effects fall outside joined-up monitoring. The paper lays out short, medium, and long term steps toward a registry that Lebanon and similar countries could build on.
pmc-13557877:
Mateusz Gap and six colleagues reviewed in 2026 how the nervous system feeds the growth of small cell lung cancer, one of the most aggressive cancers known. Attention has shifted from seeing nerves as bystanders to treating them as active partners in this disease. Their narrative review searched the literature from 2020 to late 2025 for work tying nerves to how the cancer starts, spreads, and responds to treatment.

Cancer cells were found to form working synapse-like contacts with neurons, and cutting the vagus nerve early altered tumour development in experimental work. Chemical messengers, their receptors, and nerve growth factors all shaped the tumour's surroundings, while partner cells in the brain sheltered metastases. The authors survey possible countermeasures, from blocking adrenaline receptors to interrupting synaptic signals, and frame nerve-cancer crosstalk as a future treatment frontier.
pmc-13558277:
Daisuke Douchi and fifteen colleagues tested in 2026 whether a Japanese grading system for chemotherapy response under the microscope predicts survival in pancreatic cancer. Patients received chemotherapy before surgery, and pathologists graded how much tumour the drugs had killed in the removed tissue. The retrospective study covered 117 consecutive patients treated at Tohoku University Hospital between 2010 and 2022.

Most tumours showed weak responses, graded at the lowest levels, while only a handful responded strongly. Patients whose grade reached the substantial response threshold lived far longer, with median survival more than double that of weak responders, and every one of them achieved a complete margin-free removal. The link held in adjusted models alongside scan-based progression status. The authors validate the grading system as a meaningful way to sort prognosis after preoperative treatment.
pmc-13558677:
Qi Li and three colleagues profiled in 2026 the tiny vesicles that multiple myeloma cells shed into bone marrow, and showed how those parcels reprogram nearby immune cells. Protein cataloguing of the vesicles, called exosomes, found their cargo concentrated in immune regulation pathways. Exposed macrophages in culture shifted into the M2 state, the wound-healing mode that tumours exploit to suppress attack, through a signalling route centred on the ERK pathway.

One familiar drug changed the picture: simvastatin, a cholesterol lowering statin, cut the cancer cells' vesicle secretion and thereby reduced the macrophage shift. The authors read the vesicle traffic as a deliberate immune evasion channel that helps myeloma furnish its protective niche. Blocking that communication, whether at release or at reception, is proposed as a therapeutic lever to reopen the marrow to immune attack.
pmc-13558777:
Zheng Xin and four colleagues forecast in 2026 solar power output minutes to hours ahead by first grouping similar days, then predicting within each group. Ultra-short forecasts keep grids stable as rooftop and farm solar floods in, yet sunlight's flicker defeats simple models. Their clustering step warps time series onto each other with feature weights that adapt, favouring the measurements that vary most, and a pruning step keeps the computation lean.

Each cluster feeds a hybrid predictor: a sharpened temporal convolutional network reads the multivariate patterns and geographic links, while a memory network decodes the longer trend. Tests on real data from a solar plant in Australia beat the benchmark models at every horizon from five minutes to four hours. The authors argue that sorting the weather regimes first is what lets the predictor stay reliable when conditions swing.
pmc-13559977:
Michael E. Shepherd reviews how federal and state policy shaped the rural health crisis in the United States and what might repair it. His 2026 qualitative review reads four decades of policy alongside scholarship on recent reforms and on the politics blocking them. Rural areas now show thinner access to care and worse outcomes than urban ones.

Large federal investments such as the Hill-Burton Act first brought modern care to rural communities. Patchy, non-universal policies since the 1970s, plus growing corporatization of health care, then let access wither. Telehealth expansion, mobile health services, subsidized transport, and reimbursement changes offer some hope in his account. Shepherd warns that a recent federal law will likely deepen the damage. He concludes that incremental fixes may not suffice, and doubts the political climate will permit the larger agenda he favors.
pmc-13560177:
Rui Shi and colleagues follow doxorubicin heart damage in miniature pigs with repeated cardiac MRI scans and tissue checks over thirty-two weeks. Their 2026 study gives the chemotherapy drug intravenously in repeated doses, then tracks heart function, strain, and T2 relaxation time from baseline onward. Early detection of this cardiotoxicity remains difficult in patients.

The heart's pumping fraction stayed fairly preserved, drifting down without a proven gap. Strain measures told a sharper story: circumferential and radial strain worsened clearly, with radial strain bottoming out around week twenty and staying impaired. T2 values rose during treatment, signaling water changes in the muscle, then partly recovered by the final scan. Tissue checks showed swollen, hollowed mitochondria during dosing that mostly healed, while fiber architecture stayed abnormal. The authors argue that combining T2 mapping with strain separates reversible injury from lasting structural change.
pmc-13560577:
Timo Schurr and colleagues propose a study testing whether modern psychometrics can sharpen the symptom scales used to judge antipsychotic drugs in schizophrenia trials. Their 2026 protocol targets the PANSS and BPRS, clinician-rated scales whose redundant or weak items may add noise that blurs true drug effects. Secondary analysis of pooled trial data supplies the material.

Item-level data from phase two through four trials will be drawn from the YODA and Vivli sharing platforms and harmonized. Factor analysis, item response theory, and network analysis will each build refined scoring models, checked for stability across age and sex. Drug effects will then be estimated twice, by conventional totals and by the refined scores, with the gap between effect sizes as the primary outcome. The authors hope the comparison guides how future trials should measure symptoms.
pmc-13562477:
Xiaolong Liu and thirteen colleagues report that switching off one rice gene helps the crop withstand salty, alkaline soil and yield more grain. The gene, OsRbohD, makes an enzyme that produces reactive oxygen species, harsh chemicals that build up under stress and damage cells. Using gene editing, the 2026 team created rice lines with the gene knocked out, plus lines with extra copies for contrast. They tested seedlings and field plants against wild-type rice in poor soils.

Knockout plants held less of the damaging chemicals in seeds, leaves, and roots. Germination, root growth, leaf survival, and salt balance all improved. In badly affected soil, grain yield rose by amounts ranging from about 13 percent to well over double, helped by fuller grain heads. Extra gene copies made plants more sensitive instead. The authors offer gene suppression as a breeding route for farming on degraded land.
pmc-13571577:
Luan and co-authors build a three-dimensional genome map that keeps a hybrid rice plant's two parents separate. Their 2026 paper uses phased Bridge-Linker Hi-C on Shanyou 63, an elite hybrid line. The method resolves chromatin architecture per haplotype. The team adds allele-resolved maps of RNA polymerase II contacts and phased gene activity data.

The maternal and paternal genome copies shared broadly similar folding, but allele-specific differences were widespread. One haplotype often bound the transcription machinery more strongly and formed more long-range loops to distant genes. Those stronger contacts were significantly tied to biased expression of the corresponding gene copy, even where binding near the gene's start looked equal between copies. The authors conclude that subtle differences in how each parental genome engages the transcription machinery and wires its loops reshape which copy gets heard in hybrids.
pmc-13572377:
Sabrina Sghirripa, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 brain-wave study of how age changes the way people shut out distractions. The task tested visual working memory, the short store for what the eyes just saw. Brain waves in the alpha band, 8 to 12 hertz, may help block input that is not needed.

The team recorded brain waves from 24 younger adults and 24 older adults during a match task. Distractions of varied strength popped up while people held items in mind. Strong distractions hurt both groups, but weak ones hurt only the older group. Younger adults raised alpha power while they held items; older adults showed little change. Higher alpha before a distraction also went with better scores in the younger group alone.
pmc-13572477:
Wei Lin and Sanjeet S. Grewal tested whether smarter methods can predict how thinking will change in one Parkinson's patient at a time. Thinking loss varies wildly in Parkinson's, from steady decades to fast decline, and a guess for one person would transform care. Their 2026 study ran ten machine-learning method groups across 26 setups in two patient groups totalling 1,541 people.

Sorting patients by motor type worked well as a control, but scores from the standard MoCA screening test stayed near chance, even with 42 gene data points. Only fuller thinking tests lifted scores. The authors say the block is tests, not models: clinics need better thinking tests before one-person guesses become possible.
pmc-13574777:
Elisa Lodolo, with eleven colleagues, reports a 2026 scan study of how pushing the lower jaw forward opens the throat airway. Sleep apnoea, where the airway shuts in sleep, affects over a billion people. Mouth devices that hold the jaw ahead help mild cases, yet the exact shape changes were murky.

Eight donated bodies were scanned with a jaw device set at rest, then stepped ahead two millimetres at a time to twelve. A fixed measure plan covered the airway gap, the tongue, and the mouth floor. The upper airway gap widened from the four-millimetre step, and a lower gap from six. Lower tongue and floor parts shifted first, from the earliest step. Two readers agreed closely on the numbers. The authors offer the plan as a shared yardstick for tuning such devices.
pmc-13576177:
Aisha C Bründl leads a 2026 tracking study of Eurasian curlews breeding across Great Britain. This large wading bird is in decline, and its migration habits vary from staying put to long flights along the East Atlantic route. GPS tags followed 80 birds across a 703 kilometre north-south spread of breeding sites.

Northern birds left wintering grounds earlier and breeding grounds later than southern birds, yet both arrived to breed at similar times. Warmer weather pulled spring departures and arrivals earlier, while warm, wet, calm spells delayed autumn moves. Birds that raised young successfully left latest, likely due to chick care, and that pattern was driven by southern birds with lower breeding success. Repeat tracking showed each bird kept its own timetable across years. The authors tie failed breeding to earlier departure in the south.
pmc-13576277:
Junyou Li leads a 2026 study of a nanoparticle platform that attacks tumours with four modes at once. Standard light-based therapy needs oxygen, which deep tumours lack. Their system pairs two plant-derived agents so the light reaction works without oxygen, producing superoxide radicals, while a manganese step makes further radicals and eases oxygen shortage.

One ingredient raises peroxide levels inside the tumour, powering a glow reaction that triggers gold particles to clump together for heat therapy deep in tissue without outside light. Stress on the cells' power units drains energy, frees mitochondrial DNA, and switches on an immune alarm pathway. The tumour setting shifted toward inflammation, with more attacker macrophages and fewer suppressor cells. Animal tests showed strong tumour clearance and blocked lung spread.
pmc-13578577:
Jitka Starekova and Mark E Schweitzer argue for sharper language about sex and gender in medical research, in a 2026 essay. The two words were long used as if they meant one thing, which blurs what a study really measured. Sex, they write, should name biology such as chromosomes, hormones, and body parts, while gender names identity and social context.

Major style guides and reporting rules now push for that split. Brain imaging shows the stakes well, since the brain is shaped by biology and by lived experience at once. Some disease gaps by sex look firmly biological, like higher rates of one movement disease in men. Other brain findings need care, since size and social factors can fake a sex effect. Clear terms, the authors say, guard the truth of the data.
pmc-13579677:
Gowri Gowda, Matthew Vuoncino, Rafael Ricon, and Misty D Humphries review a plan to place stents before a hard cancer operation near the body's two great vessels, in a 2026 study. The operation clears leftover lymph nodes after chemo for testicular germ cell tumors, and masses often grip the aorta and the big vein beside it. Bleeding during surgery is a grave risk, met in the past by open rescue work.

Charts covered thirty nine patients, eight of whom got stents placed ahead of surgery for risky anatomy. The stented group lost far less blood on average than the rest, a gap the authors call meaningful despite the small count. Stents did not add noted harm in this set. The authors present pre placed stents as a useful shield for hand picked high risk cases.
pmc-13582677:
Sarah Araten, Shivani Gokhale, Archana Pradhan, Ralph A Gigliotti, and Betsy Mathew bring strengths based training to first year medical students, in a 2026 program report. New students face imposter feelings, exam strain, and steep learning curves. Each student takes a strengths finder test early in the first year. Each learns their top five talents in a large session. Small groups led by doctors then talk the results through.

Survey answers came from six hundred sixty three students, with written reflections from one hundred sixty nine. Students embraced the course warmly and often repeated its core growth principles: effort builds skill, setbacks teach, and talent can grow. The authors read the warm uptake as backing for a strengths first start to medical school.
pmc-13583577:
Dionysios Adamopoulos and colleagues asked if a wide main lung artery foretells death after valve swap through a tube. They looked back at 337 people with bad aortic valve narrowing who had heart pressure tests and CT scans before the swap. A wide artery meant at least 29 millimetres in men and 27 in women, a group that held 192 people.

Artery width tracked with lung pressure read straight from the heart, and wide-artery people died more in year one, with a risk ratio of 2.59. When artery width was set beside aorta width, the link grew stronger, and it held after other ills were weighed. A plain CT read may thus sharpen risk ranks before valve swap.
pmc-13584477:
Hesham M. Al-Sharani and colleagues ask whether brushing teeth twice a day in toddlerhood pays off in the teen years. Their 2026 study uses a long-running Australian child survey that began with more than five thousand babies. Children who already had tooth decay by age 2 or 3 were set aside, leaving a group whose later decay could be counted as new.

Among close to three thousand children, those who brushed twice daily at that young age developed decay by age 14 or 15 less often than children who brushed less. The gap held up under five different ways of doing the math. In better-off areas the protection looked strong, while in poorer areas it shrank and lost firm ground. The authors say brushing drives should pair with wider fixes for poor areas.
pmc-13586277:
Luca Bolognini and colleagues built AlmaSDG, the first pilot set tagging papers by their input to every UN Sustainable Development Goal. Schools and funders need scalable ways to track research input to Agenda 2030, but strict benchmarks were lacking. Their 2026 paper tells of teamwork with green experts who tagged papers across all goals with several taggers.

Checks used match between taggers and tests with pre-trained models and tools. The authors present AlmaSDG as a benchmark for methods that assess research impact on green development, letting tools that map papers to goals be judged fairly. As a pilot, it opens the way for larger, multi-tagger sets in research judging.
pmc-13587377:
Camila Simoes and a large team describe Uruguay's first medical genomics program for rare diseases. Rare diseases together touch about seven percent of people, and most are genetic, yet patients often wander for years without a name for their condition. Rich countries use full gene reading to end that search, while Latin America lags for cost and training reasons. Their 2026 report covers 203 public-system patients read by exome or genome sequencing.

The exome route named a cause in close to half its cases, and the genome route in about a third. Because Uruguayans carry mixed ancestry that global databases underrepresent, the team built population-aware filters to cut false alarms. Answers shortened the diagnostic road and changed care for many. The authors present the program, built with local training at its core, as a model other low-income settings can copy.
pmc-13588977:
Wellington Gianoti Lustre and seven colleagues test whether contrast ultrasound can take over leak watch after aneurysm repair. Patients with a stent-grafted aorta need lifelong scans for endoleaks, but the standard CT angiogram piles up radiation and kidney-straining dye. Their 2026 prospective study ran thirty patients, average age near seventy-nine, through plain duplex ultrasound, contrast ultrasound, and CT within one month, judging the first two against CT.

Contrast ultrasound caught nearly nine of ten leaks the CT found and stayed right on nine of ten clean cases, for an overall accuracy of ninety percent. Plain duplex found only a third of leaks despite never crying wolf. Scans agreed in five of six patients. The authors recommend contrast ultrasound as the front-line watch, saving CT for unclear cases and procedure planning.
pmc-13589677:
Shelly L Gray and six colleagues report a 2026 study of older adults in primary care who stopped a drug that acts on the brain or nerves. Such drugs include pain opioids, sedatives, and some drugs for mood or muscle spasm. The team asked a plain question: when one drug stops, does a new one take its place? They also checked whether the new drug was one that guides warn against for older people.

Among 2,182 people, 442 target drugs were stopped, and only 42 stops led to a swap. One in four swaps still used a drug flagged as risky for this age group. Gray and the team urge clearer advice for prescribers, so that stopping one unsafe drug does not simply start another.
pmc-13591077:
Mohamed El Idrissi and six colleagues test a light driven route to make ammonia from nitrate waste. Ammonia feeds farms and may serve as a fuel, yet the factory method burns much gas. Their device uses a copper iron oxide plate that catches light and drives the change, cleaning nitrate from water at the same time. Plain plates made no liquid product, so the team screened added metal helpers.

Platinum proved best, and tuning how it was fixed to the plate gave a yield of 92 percent toward ammonia at low voltage. Metal coating also formed a surface layer that slowed plate decay, though long term stability still fell short. El Idrissi and the team call the plates a viable path to solar ammonia.
pmc-13591677:
Wenxuan Qi, Wenhua Zhao, and Li Chen sort, in 2026, people with type 2 diabetes into metabolic types to find who risks poor blood sugar control. Working back over records of 320 patients, they grouped people by liver enzymes, blood fats, insulin resistance, and fatty liver signs. Two profiles emerged. One carried a heavy liver and metabolic load, with higher long term sugar markers and far more poor control.

Longer time with diabetes, higher liver enzyme and fat levels, and stronger insulin resistance each raised the risk on their own. A combined model sorted patients with high accuracy. Qi and the team say a quick profile from routine tests could flag patients who need closer care before control slips.
pmc-13592077:
Aleksandra Deptuch and six colleagues design a three part liquid crystal blend that freezes a rare layered phase into a glass. Liquid crystals flow like liquids yet line up like solids, and some stack into tilted layers with a spiral twist. The team measured the blend's structure with X-rays, its light behavior under microscopes, and its electrical response across temperatures. Pure parts were measured beside the blend for comparison.

The blend held a wide antiferroelectric layered phase, where tilt flips layer by layer, and its hexatic phase turned glassy on cooling rather than crystallizing. Layer spacing and tilt data hinted that molecule pairing shifts between phases. Heat tests caught the glass change clearly, while electrical spectra showed only smaller side relaxations, Deptuch and the team report.
pmc-13593177:
Yanjia Hu and three colleagues review, in 2026, how glioma tumors bend the brain's own cells into allies. Glioma is the most aggressive primary brain cancer, and nearly every case returns despite surgery, radiation, and drugs. Their synthesis covers the tumor's neighborhood: immune cells drafted and reprogrammed by the tumor, plus resident brain cells co opted into service. Fresh single cell and spatial mapping studies reveal the neighborhood's patchwork layout.

Drafted myeloid cells wall off real immune attack while feeding growth. Neurons wire straight into tumor cells and spur them with signal chemicals, and support cells pave invasion routes and blood supply. Hu and the team argue that striking the neighborhood, not the tumor alone, offers the best route past treatment resistance.
pmc-13593677:
Ege Arzuk, İbrahim Pinar, and Burak Kuzu designed and built a new family of fourteen candidate anticancer compounds based on an imidazopyridine scaffold with a benzyloxymethyl group attached. In their 2026 study the compounds were checked with detailed chemical analysis, then tested against five human cancer cell lines.

Lung cancer and triple-negative breast cancer cells proved most sensitive. One compound, IPO9, stood out, killing lung cancer cells at a low dose while sparing normal cells far better, a pattern the team calls a favorable selectivity profile. The active compounds pushed cancer cells into programmed death by lowering the protective BCL-2 protein, raising its opponent Bax, damaging the cell's energy centers, and switching on caspase-3, an executioner enzyme. Computer docking placed IPO9 neatly in the BCL-2 binding pocket, supporting the laboratory picture.
pmc-13594477:
Brynn Dechert and Martin LaPage report a nurse-practitioner-led service for heart-device care around MRI scans in congenital heart disease. MRI with implanted heart devices was long feared unsafe, yet recent evidence shows minimal risk, even with non-conditional devices or abandoned leads. Their look-back study covered 28 patients scanned between November 2022 and February 2025.

A certified nurse practitioner led compatibility checks, scan programming, and rhythm monitoring, spending a median 100 minutes per monitored scan. No patient showed a meaningful lead change, worrying rhythm, or symptoms during scanning, including the 65 percent with non-conditional devices. The authors present nurse-led device care as a safe service working alongside physicians.
pmc-13594677:
LaMont and Jain develop a new mathematical route for reading selection from evolutionary trees. Their 2026 paper tackles a known weakness. Standard methods treat lineages as if they multiply freely. That ignores resource limits, which make an allele's growth depend on its competitors. Correcting for that normally requires averaging over every possible frequency history, which is computationally out of reach.

The authors define a quantity called the fitness potential, formally the logarithm of reproductive value. Using a duality with stochastic optimal control, the branch of mathematics for steering systems under uncertainty, they show this potential lets the unknown population history be averaged out analytically. The resulting likelihood enforces competition while accounting for drift in finite populations. It enables lean, site-specific estimates of selection coefficients from phylogenetic trees.
pmc-13598577:
Sevil Ghafarzadeh-Rad, Soheila Valizadeh, and Hamidreza Ashayeri recount the unusual course of a small prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor through two pregnancies. The 32-year-old woman's microprolactinoma, just seven mm across, had shrunk neatly on cabergoline, bringing back her cycles and fertility, and her first pregnancy passed without tumor trouble in their 2026 case report.

The second pregnancy defied the pattern. Despite resuming cabergoline, the tumor ballooned to macro size, 25 mm, pressing on her vision. At twenty-eight weeks she had apoplexy, a bleed into the tumor, with sudden headache and complete sight loss, but she said no to surgery. After the birth her eyesight came back and the tumor shrank to micro size on the ongoing drug. The authors warn that pregnancy can drive big swings in even small prolactinomas. Such swings can later reverse. Drug response cannot be taken for granted from one pregnancy to the next.
pmc-13600377:
Steven M Albert leads an eleven-author team introducing a 2026 tool that screens older homes for hidden health hazards. Standard home care assessments often skip indoor air problems and moisture mold, though both can block safe aging at home. Their Healthy Home Assessment Tool pairs resident reports with coordinator observations during visits, working with a local agency on aging.

The pilot covered 41 low-income households whose residents had a median age of 76. Coordinators completed the tool on visits and shared written results with residents, suggesting fixes. Mold odor appeared in 23 percent of homes and water damage in nearly half. Fine particle levels topped the recommended limit in 61 percent of homes, and radon ran above the action level in about a fifth. Readings matched the tool's reports for smoking and visible mold. Albert's team judges it practical for routine visits and care planning.
pmc-13611177:
Weimin Lou leads a twelve-author team refining contact-free screw thread measurement. Contact gauges are slow and sample only a few points, while laser point clouds blur the thread edges that matter. Their system pairs a laser scanner capturing the three-dimensional cloud with a camera locating thread edges at sub-pixel sharpness. A joint registration step transfers the camera's edge precision onto matching cloud points, correcting crest positions.

The corrected cloud then passes through a coarse-to-fine pipeline: principal-axis alignment, a Fourier estimate of pitch, and multi-resolution refinement. On a real screw specimen, the method measured pitch with an error of 0.0423 millimeters, matching a pure vision approach. The authors present the hybrid as a dependable route to high-precision thread inspection. It keeps the full three-dimensional shape that cross-section methods throw away, borrowing the camera's edge accuracy.
pmc-13612277:
Lizhi Jiang leads a five-author team testing whether watching brain pressure changes outcomes after severe brain hemorrhage. At Taihe Hospital, 120 patients who had clot evacuation surgery were sorted by whether a drain also monitored intracranial pressure continuously, then matched into two groups of 57. The team compared recovery at three months, neurological scores, daily-living independence, complications, and blood markers of stress and tissue damage.

The monitored group fared better on nearly every measure. Favorable three-month outcomes reached 87.72 percent against 49.12 percent without monitoring. Stroke scale scores were lower, daily-living scores higher, and complications ran 7.02 percent against 22.81 percent. Blood levels of endothelin-1, MMP-9, oxidation products, cortisol, and norepinephrine all came out lower in the monitored group. Hospital stays were shorter, though operations took longer. The authors caution that the drain itself may have helped by draining fluid, not just measuring, and that a retrospective design cannot prove cause.
pmc-13614277:
Sanseong Lee and colleagues solved a heat problem in organic solar cells by coating a key layer with a nitrone compound. Organic cells are cheap, printed panels, but their molybdenum oxide layer decays under heat and drags performance down.

The coating grabs loose molybdenum sites through its strongly polar head, pinning the oxide in place. Depth scans showed wandering oxide, not a fading work function, was the main decay path in heated cells. Coated cells kept nearly all of their starting efficiency, about 18 percent, after 2,000 hours at 85 degrees. The trick also worked across three other common cell blends, Lee reports, widening its use.
pmc-13614977:
Tamotsu Sudo leads a large team surveying in 2026 how hospitals across Japan use comprehensive genomic profiling, broad DNA testing that hunts for treatment clues in cancer, for women with gynaecologic cancers. The tests are now common in cancer medicine, yet daily use in this field was unmapped. The survey went to 98 hospitals in training or cancer genome networks, and 68 gave full testing counts.

Those hospitals had run 6,964 profiling tests in all, 922 of them for gynaecologic cancers, with a median of ten per hospital. Hospitals with more board-certified gynaecologists used the tests more. The team also tracked how often results led to trial treatments and how inherited findings were handled. Staffing, it turns out, shapes whether advanced testing reaches patients at all.
pmc-13615277:
Park and colleagues published a 2026 review of neuroprosthetic technology, meaning devices that replace or support damaged senses. Losing hearing, sight, or touch cuts independence and quality of life, so engineers have long tried to restore those signals artificially. The review organises the field by sense and by where each device acts.

Park covers hearing devices that target the cochlea, brainstem, or auditory cortex, and sight devices aimed at the retina, optic nerve, or visual cortex. Touch restoration through the skin nerves and the touch cortex is also surveyed, with gains and limits for each route. Restored sensation still falls far short of natural feeling, the authors note. They point to denser electrodes, better decoding, and stimulation tuned to each patient.
pmc-13615977:
Chong Yao and colleagues present in 2026 a chromosome-level genome for the white-striped long-horned beetle, a forestry pest whose larvae tunnel through wood and often kill trees. Until now the lack of a good genome has blocked study of how the beetle does its damage. Combining three sequencing methods, the team assembled 327.96 million DNA letters into 18 scaffolds, with 94.5 percent anchored to ten chromosomes.

Quality checks found 98.8 percent of expected genes present, and 12,030 genes were labelled in total. Repeats made up 28.04 percent of the genome. One chromosome was identified as the X sex chromosome and shown to match its counterpart across beetles. Forest scientists now have a base map for finding the beetle's weak points and designing control methods that target this pest alone.
pmc-13616577:
Hannah Fovaeus leads a team compiling Sweden's national record of cardiac arrests in hospitalised children, using the national resuscitation registry from January 2005 to September 2025. Countrywide figures are scarce, and reports from elite children's centres may flatter the picture. The registry held 525 events, with 344 at ordinary hospitals and 181 at the two national centres for highly specialised child heart care.

Outside the big centres, 31.7 percent of arrests happened on general wards, 26.2 percent in emergency departments, and 22.7 percent in intensive care. Survival at thirty days was the main measure, with return of circulation and one-year survival also tracked. A full national view stops planners from mistaking the results of two flagship hospitals for the experience of every child in the country.
pmc-13620077:
Michaela Adamcova and Lukáš Petráň review troponin, a protein famous as the switch for muscle contraction and as the blood marker doctors use to spot heart attacks. New work shows its subunits also appear in many non-muscle cells, doing jobs far from contraction. The review gathers experimental evidence and fresh computer analyses on those hidden roles.

Reported activities include steering gene transcription, reshaping the chemical tags that control DNA access, supporting mitochondrial energy work, and handling calcium signals. Troponin also appears in tiny vesicles cells release and can slow new blood vessel growth. In cancer, its effects flip by type and setting, sometimes aiding tumors and sometimes restraining them. The authors argue the mechanisms behind these roles are still murky, which makes troponin a rich target for the next round of basic research.
pmc-13621477:
Chloe Clifford Astbury led a large international team that treated antibiotic resistance in food systems as a problem of system dynamics, not just bad habits. Thirty-nine stakeholders from industry, policy, research, and civil society in Canada, Senegal, and the Netherlands built shared diagrams of how resistance grows in their food systems during group workshops. The team then read those diagrams for recurring trap patterns.

Three traps appeared across all three countries: milking a shared resource for short-term gain, leaning on antibiotics instead of investing in alternatives, and letting antibiotic-heavy production dominate the market. Stakeholders' priority fixes matched the traps. Rules and surveillance answered the first; balanced investment in prevention and animal management answered the second; consumer pressure plus regulation, to level the field, answered the third. The authors argue that lasting progress needs interventions designed with the whole system in view.
pmc-13624577:
Mary Knowles and colleagues describe a 53-year-old woman whose rare vessel disease took two years to declare itself. She came to hospital again and again, with blood tests showing a weak positive result for the antibody linked to her condition.
